en: The Tenth Chapter:
Vijñapriyā: (vi, ka) Now, at this opportune moment...
The meaning is that this is because the order of the topics has been transgressed, and not because it follows the sequence of those [topics]. — *Locanā*

(La, a) Now, desiring to define the poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), he introduces them with the word "atha" (now). The meaning is that he states the ornaments according to their essential nature (*svarūpa*) and their specific varieties (*viśeṣa*).
Thus, he states the ornaments that have reached their proper occasion:—

Those unstable properties of word and meaning which produce an excellence of beauty and assist the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth are called *alaṅkāra* (ornaments), like armlets and other such jewelry. (VisSd 10.1)
Just as armlets and other ornaments, by surpassing the beauty of the body, benefit the embodied person,
so too alliteration, simile, and the like, by surpassing the beauty of word and meaning, are benefactors of rasa and the rest.
— *Locanā*

(Lo, ā) "As for the word *yathā* (thus): the status of being an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) consists merely in the excellence of the beauty of the word and its meaning. For instance, since [figures] such as *yamaka* (chiming), which are set aside by a separate effort through the determination of *rasa* and so forth, and *anuprāsa* (alliteration), which possess a uniform connection, and even *rūpaka* (metaphor) when employed without due consideration, do not assist *rasa*, they are considered ornaments."
As stated by the author of the Dhvanyāloka: "In compositions such as those employing *yamaka* (rhyme/pun), a separate effort is required;
therefore, even for one who is capable, these [figures] do not possess the status of being subordinate to rasa."
Even for this capable poet,
regarding such difficult feats as *yamaka* (rhyme), for example:
"Because of the effortful persistence in a single form of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), which is the principal element..."
"In all compositions, alliteration is not the illuminating factor."
Thus, having observed the application of metaphor (*rūpaka*) and the like, he himself stated:
"By virtue of being intent upon what is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣātatparatva*), and never by way of being the primary element (*aṅgitva*);
at the [proper] time, there is the grasping and abandoning [of elements], and no desire for an over-extension (*nirvahaṇa*) of the figure."

Even when they have been established as subordinate elements (*aṅga*), the diligent examination [of them] serves to prove the subordinate status of the group of ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) such as metaphor (*rūpaka*).
Thus it is said.

“On your cheek, a row of leaf-designs has been crushed by the pressing of your palm; this nectar-sweet essence of your lower lip has been drunk away by your sighs; repeatedly catching in your throat, your tears cause your breast to heave. O you who are indifferent to our entreaties, it is resentment for your beloved that has arisen within you, and not we.”
On the cheek— that is, on the surface of the temple—
is a leaf-pattern, produced by the pressing of the palm— that is, by the compression of the hand.
The lower lip's nectar— delicious as nectar and sweet like ambrosia— was pressed, rubbed, kissed by sighs,
drunk, and struck.
The tears,
having become stuck— that is, clinging— to the throat, [reached] the slope of the breasts.
He repeatedly, again and again, causes the edge of her breast to tremble;
in this manner, the hero reproaches the heroine.
Passion— that is, anger—
has become dear to you, O you who are devoid of consideration,
O you who refuse to comply!

The connection is: "We do not become dear or beneficial [to you]. Here, by means of the action of crushing the leaf-stalks, it is understood that there is a reproach: "Your anger, which robs you of good fortune, has become dear to you," and "we, who act in accordance with your wishes, are not beneficial to you."
The heroine is one's own (svīyā) and of middle temperament (madhyā), while the hero is deceitful (śaṭha);
this is the erotic sentiment of separation (vipralambha-śṛṅgāra) caused by jealous anger (māna).
In this context, the statement containing the apprehension (*sopalambha*) is a jest;

it is the figure of speech known as *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), as in the following passage from my father’s *Prabhāvatīpariṇaya*, in the description of Prabhāvatī: “She is the ancestral home of the arts, a cage for the bird-like minds of lovers, and the medicinal elixir for subjugation.”
It is the supreme skill of the Creator;
it is the magical spell in the world-conquering enterprise of the King Smara; it is the fetter for the eyes of the three worlds, yet the ultimate ornament of them all.

In such cases, since the poet’s mind is occupied with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) that sustains the figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), these [figures] are accomplished without a separate effort; therefore, there is no fault.
For this reason, they are "extremely nourishers of *rasa*.
As stated by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*: "That whose composition becomes possible through being impelled by *rasa*..."
That ornament is considered a form of *dhvani* (suggested sense) which cannot be accomplished without a distinct effort;

likewise, even those other ornaments that appear difficult to compose when analyzed are, for a poet whose mind is absorbed in *rasa* and who possesses creative intuition (*pratibhā*), realized through a competitive impulse of "I first, I first.
For example: [Example omitted per instructions]
“Victorious is this Rasa-Gandhaka-Parpaṭī, an immortal pill for mortals that pacifies acidity, subdues the three humors, and acts as a fish-hook for those desiring to eat.”
In such cases,
even when rasa is present, the alliterations (anuprāsa) and other figures do not enhance it.
For example, the alliteration in the verse beginning with “auvaṭṭai ullaṭṭai.”
When his friend had gone elsewhere, the lotus grove remained silent; as the bees moaned in distress, the *cakravāka* bird before him looked upon his beloved and grew despondent.
The lover, separated from her, neither tasted the lotus stalk nor cast it away; he merely pressed it against his throat like a bolt against his life-breath as it sought to escape.

In this instance, because the lotus stalk—which serves as the excitant (uddīpana)—is an auxiliary factor that culminates in the taking of life through effort, the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding it as a bolt for obstructing life is not an ornament that assists the rasa; for it is incompatible with both the erotic sentiment of separation (vipralambha-śṛṅgāra) and its semblance (tadābhāsa). It will be stated in the discussion on poetic fancy that "there is no simile here."

Thus it has been well said that figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) are auxiliaries to rasa and the like by means of enhancing the beauty of word and meaning. Figures of speech are "unstable," meaning they do not have the necessary presence that characterizes the qualities (*guṇa*). Vijñapriyā: [This is the commentary on the above.]
(vi, kha) "These are not possessed of qualities"—because sweetness (*mādhurya*) and the other [qualities] pervade the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and other sentiments, they necessarily reside therein.
*Locanā*:
(lo, i) Having restated the verse [as] "they are unstable," he explains it.

Regarding the phrase "not of these": it means that qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth do not abide as properties of *rasa*—which conforms to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) within sentences—nor does the loss of the status of poetry (*kāvyatva*) occur even in the absence of figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) in certain cases.
Just as the qualities are stable properties of *rasa*, these [figures] are not [stable properties] of word and meaning (*śabda-artha*).

Thus, it has been shown that figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) are distinct from the poetic qualities (*guṇa*), because they constitute the non-metaphorical attributes of word and meaning, are unstable, and serve to enhance the beauty of word and meaning by way of contributing to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

Since word and meaning [are to be discussed], and since the word must be addressed first because it is the object of the initial cognition, and because the figure of speech "Appearance as a Tautology" (*punaruktavadābhāsa*)— though it pertains to both word and meaning— was classified among the verbal figures (*śabdālaṅkāra*) by the ancients,
he states that very one first:
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ga) Regarding that, first, demonstrating the seed for describing *punaruktavadābhāsa* as a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*) despite its being an ornament of both word and meaning, he says: "Even of a verbal ornament... [Locanā].
(Lo, ī) Having introduced [the topic] with equal reference, he states its divisions: "of word and meaning.
The meaning is that it "indicates" (lakṣayati). This refers to that which appears at first glance as a repetition of the meaning.
That which appears as a tautology is [the figure] Punaruktavadābhāsa; it consists of words that possess different forms.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
gha) "That which [occurs] at first sight" means that there is no repetition of meaning even in the formal vow (*praṇidhāna*), but only at the initial stage.
There is no possibility of redundancy at all because of the difference in form and word; as for Locanā: (lo, u) there is only the appearance of redundancy upon a superficial reading.
The cognition is like a tautology (punarukta),
yet in its final conclusion it is not so;
therefore, this is the figure of speech named "Appearance of Tautology" (punaruktavad-ābhāsa), which possesses meaningful significance.
By the phrase "occurring in words of different forms," the exclusion of *yamaka* (rhyme) is intended.
Here, even in such instances as "navapalāśapalāśavanaṃ puraḥ" ("the forest of fresh palāśa leaves before one's eyes"), there is an appearance of tautology at first sight;
however, that [tautology] resides in words of identical form.
Example:
May Śiva— the wearer of serpents as earrings, whose cool rays are manifest like the white beams of the moon,
and who captivates the heart— ever protect the worlds from calamity.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ṅa) "Bhujaṅgakuṇḍalī" means that Śiva, who has serpents as his earrings, may protect the worlds from misfortune forever.
Of what nature is he? He possesses earrings in the form of serpents; likewise, he is one whose bull (vṛṣa) is cool and refreshing due to the manifest, white rays of the moon;
and he is captivating, enchanting the heart.
Locanā:
(lo, ū) the serpent Kuṇḍalin;
and one who possesses a coil.

The three words *śaśi*, *subhrāṃśu*, and *śītagu* have, at first sight (*āpātataḥ*), the meaning of "moon. However, in their final sense (*paryavasāne*), they mean: "he whose rays (*aṃśavaḥ*) are bright (*śubhrāḥ*), radiant (*ujjvalāḥ*), and like those of the moon, whose rays are cool (*śītāḥ*)," and whose beams (*gāvaḥ*) are [thus] lovely (*kāntayaḥ*).
From *apāyāt*, [the form] *apāyataḥ* [is derived]; [may he] protect (*avyāt*).

Hara is Sadāśiva and Manohara. Here, although both *pāyāt*— derived from the root *pā*— and *avyāt*— derived from the root *av*, meaning "to protect"— appear in the optative mood (*liṅ*), there is an appearance of tautology.

In the final meaning, however, by taking the elided *a* caused by the euphonic combination (*sandhi*), the word *apāya* possesses the status of being a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).
Here, words such as *bhujaṅgakuṇḍali* appear to be tautological because they seem to mean "one whose earrings are snakes" at first glance;
yet, in their final sense, they have a different meaning, such as "one who possesses earrings in the form of a serpent."
In the phrase "pāyādavyāt," this is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) pertaining to the action (*kriyā*),
because the word "pāyāt" culminates in the sense of "apāyāt.
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding the phrase "apāyāt" (from the removal), it concludes with the word "paryavasānāt" (because of the conclusion).
This conclusion occurs there due to the reconnection with the elided vowel *ā*.
Between the two words "bhujaṅga" and "kuṇḍalī," only the first one is capable of being replaced [by a synonym].
"Haraḥ Śivaḥ" applies to the second [name] alone;
"Śaśisubhrāṃśu" applies to both.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) "Of the first alone," because even when it is said "the coiled serpent" (*sarpakuṇḍalī*), there is the appearance of redundancy;
[and] "of the second alone."
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the mantra] possesses the capacity to withstand reversal;
for even when "O Mṛḍa, be gracious" is uttered, it remains the same.
This applies to both as well.
The syntactical connection is with "the capacity to endure transformation.
This is because even when the words "moon" and "cool-rayed one" are employed, the same state [of the object] persists.
— Locanā.
And he states the reason for this being both a verbal and a semantic ornament: "bhujaṅga," etc.
This refers to the capacity to withstand substitution (*parivṛttisaha-tva*);
[the word] *ahi* means "one who wears earrings" (*kuṇḍalī*).
Even when it is stated as "sarpakuṇḍalī" (the serpent-earringed one) and so forth, there appears to be a redundancy;
therefore, in this context, the word *kuṇḍalī* does not admit of substitution.
Likewise, [in the case of] "Haraḥ Śivaḥ" (Hara is Śiva).
This should also be understood in cases such as the following:
"The one who never abandons [his nature] shines" (*bhāti sadānatyāgaḥ*). This is not [an instance of] both [types of *śleṣa*].
Thus, by virtue of its capacity or incapacity to withstand the substitution of words, this possesses the character of being an ornament of both types.
Vijñapriyā:
"It shines" (*bhāti*)—this is an illustration of a portion of the statement from the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: "The constant renunciation of wealth shines in [the quality of] steadfastness."
In this context, "Your Honor" (*bhavān*) always shines as one who does not bend, meaning he is devoid of subservience to others;
thus, the sense is that he is a mountain (*parvata*) because he is immovable (*sthiratāyām agaḥ*).
Here, there is the appearance of a tautology between the words *dāna* (giving) and *tyāga* (renunciation).
In this case, neither of the two [words] can withstand transposition.
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) Furthermore, because it occurs together with "giving" (*dāna*) and "renunciation" (*tyāga*) in the third syllable and so forth, there is the appearance of tautology (*paunaruktya*).
Always, at all times, by not bowing;
through the act of not bowing,
the word *aga* results in the sense of "mountain."
It is not a matter of two types of gift or renunciation. Rather,

depending on whether they can or cannot withstand a shift [of meaning], in some cases there is the status of a semantic ornament (*arthālaṅkāra*) due to their ability to withstand such a shift, and in other cases there is the status of a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*) due to their inability to do so.
The meaning is that defects, merits, and ornaments are established as residing in either the word or the sense, because they are restricted by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is a similarity of sounds even when there is a difference in vowel;
however, mere similarity of vowels alone is not counted [as a figure], because it lacks aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*).
Anuprāsa is the placement [of sounds] with excellence due to their following after [the same] rasa and other elements.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, jha) states the figure of speech called Anuprāsa: "Anuprāsa" and so forth.
By the word *mātra* (only) in the phrase "similarity of vowels only" (*svaramātrasādṛśya*), the similarity of consonants is excluded.
Consequently, in the verse "Who indeed have obtained fame by serving in the region and in the home? (*ke vā te sevayā deśe gehe ca lebhire yaśaḥ*), there is no alliteration (*anuprāsa*).
However, when there is similarity of mere consonants, as in "the cheek of an angry monkey" (*kupitakapikapolatā*) and so forth, there is indeed alliteration.
In some cases, even when there is equality in both [the literal and the intended], as in "the shaken mango blossom" (*dhūtacūtaprasūna*),
or as in "an ocean of virtues, a kinsman to the virtuous, a friend to living beings— you are another person [altogether]";
it should be understood that in such instances, a mere similarity of sound is excluded.
He states the derivation of the term *anuprāsa* [alliteration] as "by means of rasa and so forth.
And *anugama* (following) refers to suggestion (*vyañjanā*),
because rasa and the like are suggested by words and sentences characterized by *anuprāsa*.
From the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the speaker's ingenuity is understood.
*Locanā*:

Regarding "alliteration" (*anuprāsa*)—in the sense that there is a similarity of sounds even when there is a difference in vowels—the term "sounds" (*śabda*) refers exclusively to consonants (*vyañjana*).
Because vowels do not serve as a substratum for other vowels,

this [repetition] is not an ornament (alaṅkāra), since it is experienced by connoisseurs that even when a mere vowel is repeated many times— as in "bālā yāti" and so forth— there is an absence of charm if there is a dissimilarity of consonants.
This very point has been stated in the Vṛtti with the words "in the case of a mere vowel," and so on.

Furthermore, by the phrase "even when there is a disparity of vowel" (*svarasya vaiṣamye 'pi*), cases such as "the water of the Kāverī" (*kāverīvārī*) are excluded from this [category of alliteration].

By the word "even" (*api*), it is shown that in examples such as "in the evening, O you of frog-like wicked resolve" (*darduraduradhyavasāya sāyam*), although there is a disparity in the vowel due to the word *duḥ*, there is still alliteration because of the similarity of the consonant *d*.

In examples such as "before the forest of fresh *palāśa* leaves" (*navapālaśapalāśavanaṃ pura*), alliteration takes precedence over and sublates the *yamaka* (rhyme), as the latter is an exception to the former.
In examples such as *darduradura*, there is no *yamaka* because the letter *da* of the first word *dura* possesses the *mūrdhan* (retroflex) quality due to the influence of the following *ra*.
In cases such as *duradhyavasāya sāyam*, there is only *anuprāsa* and not *yamaka* because of the presence of the *anusvāra*.

Furthermore, in examples such as *ākarṇya karṇamadhurāṇi*, although the first word *karṇa* is inherently devoid of a vowel, there is a disparity in vowels due to the intrinsic nature residing in the second word *karṇa*.

In such instances as "The eastern quarter is adorned by the moon Naitrānanda," one should not conceive that there is an absence of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) due to the distant separation of the letter *da* joined with *na*, *ra*, and *pha*;
for there is no interruption of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), as it has been said: "It is 'not distant' because it awakens the latent impression produced by prior experience.
Chequered alliteration (*cheka*) is the multiple repetition of a group of consonants at once. (VisSd 10.3)
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ña) Regarding that, he states the definition of *chekānuprāsa* [alliteration]: "In the term *cheka*, what is intended here by 'conjunction of consonants' (*vyañjanasaṅgati*) is merely the difference between single consonants."
Therefore, there is suchness for the two [eyes] and for the *tṣa* letters and so forth.
Locanā (*lo*, *e*) states their distinctions:
By the word "saṅgha" (group) here, it is meant that a single consonant is not repeated many times, nor even once, in various ways, both in terms of its essential form and its sequence.
This very point is stated in the commentary by the phrase "in various ways" (*anekadhā*) and so forth. *Cheka* refers to *che kānuprāsa* (alliteration).
"In various ways" (*anekadhā*) means both by way of intrinsic nature (*svarūpataḥ*) and by way of sequence (*kramataḥ*).
Similarity based on a difference in sequence, as in the case of "rasaḥ" and "saraḥ," is not the province of this poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṭa) "In many ways" (*anekadhā*): the state of having many elements (*anekadhātva*) consists in the similarity of both phonemes and their sequence.
He states that such a single-element state (*ekadhātva*) is the domain of *sāmyānuprāsa* (alliteration by similarity), as in the example *sarorasa*.

Nor should it be argued that, given such equality of phonemes and sequence, there would be no distinction between *anuprāsa* (alliteration) and *yamaka* (chiasmus); for in the case of *yamaka*, there is also equality of vowels, which constitutes this distinction. — *Locanā*.
In the case of *rasa-rasa*, there is similarity between the two sounds by their very nature (*svarūpataḥ*), but not by position (*kamataḥ*);
whereas in cases such as *kauvarau* or *vārī*, there is similarity by position as well, just as in the case of the two *va*s.
An example from my venerable father is as follows:
"Taking up the fragrance of the bakula flowers and making the bees blind with joy at every step,
this wind, purifying the waters of the Kāverī, approaches very slowly."
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṭha) "Having taken"—the blinding of the bees is their following [the scent] solely out of greed for fragrance, without perceiving any other object. Here, there is a combination of the words *gandha* (fragrance) and *andhī* (blinded).

In the examples "kāverīvāri" and "ityasaṃyuktayoḥ," as well as "pāvanaḥ pavanaḥ," there is a single repetition of many consonants. Because it is employed by the clever (*cheka*), this is known as *chekānuprāsa*.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ḍa) Since both types of phonemes are intended here as constituting the category of the *saṃgha*, it shows that multiple phonemes possess "simultaneity" (*sakṛttva*) in this context—by the word "here.
It is precisely because they are employed by that [single effort].
And thus, the term *cheka* (clever) is a conventional (*nirūḍha*) metaphorical expression applied to that which is employed by such a person.
Consequently, although alliteration (*vṛttyanuprāsa*) may also be employed by the clever, the term *cheka* is not used for it, because the convention (*rūḍhi*) does not apply there.
— *Locanā*.
(Lo, o) Regarding the conjunct *n* and *dh*:

the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of a previously established name is provided in some way by means of [the rule] beginning with "cheka. Furthermore, there is a single similarity among many things, or multiple similarities occurring repeatedly.
When there is a single occurrence of a consonant even once, it is called *vṛttyanuprāsa*.
Locanā:
Regarding "of many" (*anekasya*):
the oneness (*eka*) is the singlefold similarity of many meanings or phonemes (*vyañjana*).
The second [type] is the similarity of a syllable occurring multiple times; by the term "multiple times" (*asakṛt*), the exclusion of *chekānuprāsa* is intended.
Thus, since there is similarity of a single consonant either once or multiple times, *vṛttyanuprāsa* is fourfold.
In one way, by its very nature alone,
and not even by way of succession;
in many ways, both by its very nature and by way of succession.
Regarding the phrase "even once," the word "even" (*api*) implies "even more than once.
*Vijñapriyā* (commentary on verse vi,
ḍha) states that this refers to the alliteration (*vṛttyanuprāsa*) expressed by the term "of many at once" (*anekasyaikadhā*).
Therein, he explains the meaning of the term *ekadhā* (in one way) as "by its very own nature" (*svarūpata eva*); the meaning is "by the very nature of the phoneme and the letter.
He explains the state of being "manifold" (*anekadhātva*) in the phrase "or even manifoldly" (*asakṛd vāpyanekadhā*) by the word "manifoldly" (*anekadhā*).
In this context, the word "of many" (anekasya) is to be construed [with both];
thus, when many [sounds] occur in many ways simultaneously, it is *cheka* alliteration; but when they do not occur simultaneously, it is *vṛttyanuprāsa*.
Regarding the phrase "even once for a single [word]," he shows what is implied by the particle *api*—namely, that it is because of the word *api* in the expression "even once" (*sakṛd api*).

However, alliteration (*anuprāsa*) occurring even once in a single instance is not accepted as poetry (*kāvyaprakāśa-sammata*), because no aesthetic variety (*vaicitrya*) is experienced therein. This is the case in the example beginning with *jātacyuta*.
However, when there is a similarity of natural resonance (*svarasa*), that [type of *śleṣa*] is also accepted, as in the example "the shaken mango blossoms.
An illustration is as follows:
"Those [days] which aroused a fever in the ears with the tumultuous, sweet warbling of cuckoos playing among the mango sprouts shaken by bees greedy for the fragrance of blooming honey, and..."

"How, indeed, are these days passed by travelers—days made bearable only by the joyous thrill of union with their beloveds, who are as dear as life itself, attained for a moment through the focused concentration of meditation?"
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṇa) "Unmīlat... and so forth.
According to Amarasimha: "The term *kākalī* refers to a subtle sound in the Kali age, but when clear, it refers to a sweet sound."
By those clamorous sounds of that nature;
here, in the phrase "these [are] by the surges of rasa," there is a simultaneous identity between the two rasas,
and not even by that same sequence.
In the second quarter, by that same sequence, there is [the repetition] of two *kalās* not once;
and in the first [quarter], there is [the repetition] of one *makāra* once.
And regarding the letter *dh*:
when the arrangement of phonemes functions with an activity directed toward the object of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*),
it is called *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration of style) because of its being placed with excellence through its conformity to that [flavor].
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta) Here, he demonstrates that many things can occur simultaneously—“these [are] with the surges of rasa.
Regarding the phrase “of the two rasas”: because the sequence of the letters *ra* and *sa* is absent in the word *rasa*, they occur as one.

Regarding "kalyoḥ": this means in the phrase "kokilakākalīkalavalaiḥ. He demonstrates that what is single can be both repeated and non-repeated by saying "in the first [instance]," referring to the letter *ta* in the word "dhūtacūta."

In the phrase "madhugandhalubdhamadhupetyatra," the meaning is "of the letter *dh*. However, in the phrase "samāsametyatra," because there is a single occurrence of multiple [sounds] in various ways, it is merely *śleṣa* (paronomasia); therefore, that is not shown here.
Regarding the term *vṛttyanuprāsa*, he explains the meaning of the word *vṛtti* as follows: "having rasa as its object."
The scope of rasa is vyañjanā (suggestion),
which is the function designated as *vṛtti* in the composition of things— that is, in the arrangement of the matter of the object through words.
He connects the meaning of the word *anuprasaṅga* (consequential discussion) therein with the phrase "by way of being followed by that."
The meaning is: "by way of such a connection of arrangement.
And "excellence" refers to the similarity of phonemes.
— *Locanā*:
Furthermore, in the verse beginning "prāṇasamāsamāgama," the nature of *yamaka* (rhyme) will be discussed.

Also, in the verse beginning "llāsairamī vāsarāḥ," a *saṅkara* (commingling) consisting of the "mutual entry into a single expressive word" (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) will be discussed, wherein the variety of *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration based on phonetic similarity) and the variety of *chekānuprāsa* (alliteration based on semantic similarity)— which has multiple grounds for similarity in the case of the *sarayaḥ*— coexist.
Nevertheless, disregarding the word *vāsara*, there is the mention of a variety of alliteration (*vṛttyanuprāsa*).
The same applies elsewhere.
[The phrase] "concerning the domain of rasa" means:
The *vṛtti* (mode) is the function whose object is flavor (*rasa*) and which is sustained by aesthetic relish (*svāda*).
This is according to the etymological derivation: "that by which the word is made to function (*vṛttyate*) for the purpose of manifesting flavor.

Therefore, the meaning is that even the composition (*racanā*)—consisting of soft, harsh, or intermediate phonemes suitable for flavors such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth—is metaphorically called *vṛtti*, because it possesses [the aforementioned function] in the manner described.
Because it follows that [consonant] and is characterized by that function,
the similarity of a consonant itself when it is articulated in the same place— such as the palate or the teeth— is called *śrutyanuprāsa*. (VisSd 10.5)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) He states another kind of alliteration called *śrutyanuprāsa*—namely, "because they are pronounced [in the same place]" (*uccāryyatvāt*).
The meaning is that even in the absence of identity of phonemes (*varṇa*), there is similarity due to being pronounced in the same articulatory location (*sthāna*).
Locanā:

"Because of being pronounced [as such]" means that the similarity of two or more consonants—whether by their being palatals (*tālavya*), dentals (*dantya*), or, by the force of the word "etcetera," gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*) and so forth—is what constitutes *śrutyanuprāsa* (alliteration based on sound).
And this *śrutyanuprāsa* "the Goddess of Speech bestows upon some person of creative genius."
Thus do the Easterners praise [this figure].
An example:
"Those women who, with their very glance, revive the Mind-born (Cupid) whom he had burnt with his glance."
We praise those victorious, beautiful-eyed women of Virūpākṣa.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) "Burning with her glance"—I praise those beautiful-eyed women who are victorious over Virūpākṣa.

Having stated the victory and defeat [of the eye] through its "crookedness" (*vāmatva*), which consists of both ugliness and beauty, she also speaks of the result of that action: "burning with her glance."

By Hara, the mind-born god (Kāma) was consumed by fire with his [third] eye; yet by those [women], he was restored to life by their glances in the form of side-long looks. Thus, there is victory [over Śiva].
Here, the words "they restore to life" and "those who... [are used].

Regarding the word "jayinīḥ": here, there is similarity between the letter *ja* and the letter *ya* because they are articulated in the same place, namely the palate (*tālu*). In this same manner, examples for dentals and gutturals are also to be cited.

And this is called *śrutyanuprāsa* (alliteration of sounds) because it brings extreme pleasure to the hearing of sensitive readers (*sahṛdayas*). Furthermore, when consonants, as they occur, are repeated together with their initial vowel— because they are to be joined at the end— that is indeed *antyānuprāsa* (end-alliteration).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, dha) He states another type of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) called *antyānuprāsa*—namely, "if the consonant...
and "as it stands."

The meaning is that if a consonant— whether distinguished by an *anusvāra* or a *visarga*, or undistinguished, or even a vowel alone— is uttered at the end of a preceding word (*pūrvapāda* or *pūrvapada*), and such a consonant in its specific state is repeated together with the initial vowel (or the vowel preceding itself), then it is called "final alliteration" (*antyānuprāsa*).
He states the derivation of that designation as "because it is to be joined at the end":
just as one says *dhīraḥ* at the end of one quarter and *vīraḥ* at the end of another quarter,
or as one says *sāram* at the end of one quarter and *hāram* at the end of another.
One who acts thus [is called] *hārīti* in the mere sense of the vowel.

"According to the state" (*yathāvastham*) means distinguished by syllables endowed with anusvāra, visarga, or vowels as they occur. And this [mark] is generally to be employed at the end of a quarter-verse (*pāda*) or a word (*pada*).
An example of [a compound] ending at the end of a word is from my own work,
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, na) he explains "yathāvastham" as "yathāsambhavam" (according to what is possible).
The occurrence of any one of the *anusvāra*, *visarga*, or vowels is the meaning of the term "according to possibility" (*yathāsambhava*).

Regarding the phrase "distinguished by syllables" (*akṣaraviśiṣṭa*), it should be understood as they stand in their respective positions. He explains the state of being joined at the end with the words "And this... (*eṣa ca*).
By the word "mostly" (prāyeṇa), it is shown that the occurrence of this [verse] is only in meters such as *pajjhaṭikā* and the like, and not in *anuṣṭubh* or others.
The hair is like a cluster of blooming *kāśa* grass; the body displays the grace of a young elephant's trunk;
the eye is like a burnt cowrie shell; yet the mind does not abandon its abundant desire.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, pa) "Keśaḥ kāśeti"—this is a saying of the elderly. It refers to one whose body possesses the grace of a young elephant (*karabha*)—that is, a small elephant—who is white like a cluster of *kāśa* flowers and whose face is bent and wrinkled.
Nevertheless, the meaning is that the mind does not abandon its "analpam" (not small), i.e., its great desire or longing;
the word "tathāpi" (nevertheless) is to be understood through the force of expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*).
In this context, the words *kāśalāsa* have their final consonants distinguished by the vowel of their own visarga.
The words *kalpa* and *alpa*, distinguished by their final vowel together with its anusvāra, [end in] a final consonant;
and that final consonant occurs together with the vowel preceding it.
— *Locanā*.

Regarding the term "consonant" (*vyañjana*): because of the statement "as far as possible" in the case of *keśa*, [the rule applies]. In *vikāśa*, the letter *śa* is devoid of conjunct consonants and is joined with a vowel and a *visarga*, together with the vowel *a* situated with the letter *ka*. In *vilāsa*, it exists together with the vowel *a* situated with the letter *la*.

In the word *kalpam*, the meaning is that the consonant *l*— which takes the form of the letter *la* and is joined with the vowel *u* (anusvāra) and the letter *pa*— is together with the vowel *a* residing in the letter *ka*;
and in the word *analpa*, it is together with the vowel *a* residing in the letter *na*.
Because of the expression "generally speaking" (prāyeṇa), it is as stated by my father in his *Lakṣmīstava*:

"May she be victorious— she who is heard and studied, whose entire virtues are not contradicted by the Vedas, who transcends all qualities (*guṇātītā*), who grants fearlessness to the frightened, who bestows the destruction of the undisciplined, who is delighted by prostrations, who is well-married to the one clad in yellow garments (*pītāmbara*), who is drunk in by the eyes of the celestial damsels, who is abundant, and who is surrounded by a stainless luster."

In such instances, this alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is observed even when there is no joining of dental sounds. Furthermore, because its specific aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) is established through experience as distinct from the figures of speech mentioned by the ancients, it constitutes a separate figure of speech—as in the example: "Smiling gently, bearing the burden... and so forth.
The repetition of both word and meaning, despite a difference in their intended purport (*tātparya*),
is called *lāṭānuprāsa*— so says the *Vijñapriyā*.
(Vi, Pha) He describes the *anuprāsa* known as *lāṭānuprāsa*: "of word and meaning.
This means: of two words and their two meanings.
*Paunaruktya* is the repeated stating [of something].
Then, anticipating the fault of tautology, he says: "In the case of difference" (*bhede*).
The intended meaning (*tātparya*) concerns the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*).
By the word "only" (*mātra*), the distinction of meaning (*arthabheda*) is excluded.
Locanā:
Regarding the phrase "of word and meaning" (*śabdārthayoḥ*): *tātparya* is the state of being directed toward something else.

And that [distinction], whose own nature has been transferred to another object, is [referred to] by the word "that" (tat) because one intends to express its utility for the subject at hand as something to be predicated; it is [designated] merely by that [transferred status], but not by its own nature.
"Distinction" (bheda) means a particularity (viśeṣa).
An example:
O you with eyes like smiling lotuses, why are your eyes closed?
Behold your beloved, who has conquered Kandarpa yet remains subject to the power of Kandarpa.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ba) "O you with a smile like a row of *rājīva* lotuses"—this is a statement by a female friend to a proud woman who has closed her eyes in anger upon seeing her lover.
The meaning is that although he is a conqueror of Kandarpa by his very form, he is nonetheless under your sway due to his devotion to you; therefore, pride is inappropriate in this case.

In this regard, the distinction lies in the fact that in the first instance, the word *nayanakandarpa* has its intended meaning as the subject (*uddeśya*), whereas in the latter instance, that same word has its intended meaning as the predicate (*vidheya*). However, the referents of the words (*padārtha*) are non-different; for by the word "only" (*mātra*), there is an exclusion of difference only with respect to the meaning of the stem (*prakṛti*), and not with respect to the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*).

Here, although there is tautology regarding the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), because the primary element—the form of the substratum (*dharmī*) manifested by the nominal stem portion—possesses distinct meanings, it is indeed *lāṭānuprāsa*.
Vijñapriyā:

By the words "from this" (*ityataḥ*) and "vibhaktyartha-bhedaṃ," he demonstrates the distinction between the meanings of the case endings; [this is shown] by the phrases "of the meaning of the case ending here" (*atra vibhaktyarthasya*) and "of the primary one" (*mukhyatarasya*).
In the words *nayanakandarpa* (the Cupid of the eyes), there are two nominal stem portions (*prātipadika-aṃśa*).

Because that which is illuminated by them—that is, the meaning consisting of the substratum (*dharmin*) in the form of the "Cupid of the eyes"—is understood as being conjoined with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), it possesses greater primacy than the independent suffix due to its autonomy; for it is non-different from [the base].
This is the meaning:
"the eyes of that very one, and [his] eyes.
Here, the second occurrence of the word *nayana* has a different referent solely by virtue of its intended sense (*tātparya*) as being qualified by attributes such as auspiciousness and so forth.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ma) But where there is a difference even in the meaning of the base word (*prakṛti*), there is no *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration); thus he says "nayane" [in the verse].

Here, because the second occurrence of the word *nayana* intends the sense of "possessing good fortune" (*bhāgyavattādi*), he demonstrates that even the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) differs, since it is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) itself that differs—this is shown by the words "for here" (*atra hi*).
And thus it has been stated that this [repetition] is the province of *arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya* indication alone, and not *lāṭānuprāsa*.
For this very reason, when explaining the fault of "repeated words" (*kathitapada*) and so forth, those two—*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya* and *lāṭānuprāsa*—were mentioned separately.
(Locanā)
Regarding this:
"here" refers to the two case endings (*sup*);
"of the nature of the substratum" refers to the nature of the eye and so forth.
The mention of "case-endings" (vibhakti) is an elliptical indication; by this, gender and number are also included.
Having thus shown an unambiguous example for easy understanding, he now shows an ambiguous one: "nayane" (the two eyes).
This occurs merely by way of intended meaning (tātparya) and not by way of its own essential form (svarūpa).
And here, there is only the figure of speech known as *punaruktavadābhāsa* (the appearance of repetition),
and not a suggested (pratīyamāna) excellence (*viśeṣa*), because such a [suggested] quality lacks the cause for becoming subordinate through being hidden (*gūḍhatva*) and so forth.
Or for example:
"For him who has no beloved near him, the moon is a forest fire;
for him who has his beloved near him, the forest fire is the moon."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ya) He demonstrates that this [figure] occurs not only in a single word but also in multiple words—as in "yathā vā" (or for example).
In the phrase "yasya te," within the first half-verse, the state of being the moon (*tuhinadīdhititva*) is the predicate (*vidheya*), because it functions to remove heat (*atāpakaratvāt*).
Locanā:
(lo, ū) This [type of *śleṣa*] can also occur when it is based on many words; therefore, he provides examples for that, saying "or as follows" (*yathā vā*).

In the first half-verse beginning with "He who has no beloved in his presence," the connection is such that the moon (*tuhinadīdhiti*) is a forest fire (*davadahana*), while in the second half-verse, the forest fire is the moon.
Here, there is the repetition of multiple words;
and because this is generally favored by the people of the Lāṭa country, it is called *lāṭānuprāsa*.
Thus, alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is of five kinds.
Vijñapriyā: (vi, ra) "Of five kinds"— namely, *chekānuprāsa* (alliteration of meaningful syllables), *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration of meaningless syllables), and so forth.
Alliteration is fivefold: *śrutyanuprāsa*, *antyānuprāsa*, and *lāṭānuprāsa*.
However, in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, it is stated that *lāṭānuprāsa* alone is fivefold.
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) He concludes with the word "alliteration" (*anuprāsa*).
This is clear.
When there is a single meaning for a collection of vowels and consonants that otherwise has distinct meanings,
its repetition in that very same sequence is called *yamaka*.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, la) He speaks of a collection of *yamaka*s [punning repetitions]—starting with "when the meaning exists" (*satyarthe*).
The meaning is that when there is a sense, there is a repetition in that very same order of a sequence of words whose meanings are distinct.
In this context, the phrase "having distinct meanings" (*pṛthagarthāyāḥ*) must necessarily be included in order to exclude *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration).

For instance, in the case of *śamarate 'maratejasī*, where there are two instances of the *yamaka* [repetition] of *samaratā*, and in the case of *samarasamaraso 'yam*, where one of the two is meaningless, the mention of "having distinct meanings" would be inappropriate.
Therefore, he says that it was stated [only] when the meaning exists.
In this regard, both words may sometimes be meaningful and sometimes meaningless; or,
in some cases, one may be meaningful while the other is meaningless.
Therefore it was said: “when the object exists.
Vijñapriyā:
Here, [the phrase] “of both” refers to these two.

The intention is that when the meaning of either one of the two [words] is absent, there is a repetition of the combination of vowels and consonants in that very same order; such is another definition.
However, the "conformity with both" should be understood as being of the nature of having a single, non-different meaning. — *Locanā*
(Lo, ṝ) This very point is clarified in the *Vṛtti* with the words "atra" and so forth.
Here, "atra" refers to the *yamaka*; the meaning is "of the two words which constitute parts of the *yamaka*, namely the vowels and consonants."

The meaning is that [the suffix] is independent, as in the case of *priyatamāyatamāna* and so forth, where there is pointlessness (*anarthakatva*)—for if either of two [elements] or one of them were pointless, it would lack the status of being a word (*padatva*). Thus, in certain instances, its meaningfulness (*sārthakatva*) occurs through independence; for its pointlessness exists only by virtue of the assistance of the phonemes (*akṣara*) that constitute the parts of the word.
And here, because it is for the most part [the case], the meaningfulness and so forth have been stated with reference to two groups of phonemes;
however, in cases involving three or four repetitions, one should infer accordingly in accordance with the definition.
By the phrase "in that very same order," it is indicated that [the sequence] such as *dama*, *moda*, and so on, has distinct objects.

And this [type of *anuprāsa*] possesses a vast number of subdivisions because it occurs through the repetition of a quarter-verse, a half-verse, or a full verse, and because the repetition of the opening of a quarter-verse (*pādādyāvṛtti*) is of many kinds.
*Vijñapriyā*:
He states that its subdivisions are numerous with the words "And this" (*etacca*).

By the word "pādādi" (beginning with a quarter-verse), there is the inclusion of a single quarter, the third or fourth part of a quarter, and even an indeterminate portion thereof. A mere illustration is given:
“navapalāśa-palāśavanaṃ puraḥ sphuṭaparāga-parāgata-paṅkajam /” [Kumārasambhava 3.29]
He beheld that fragrant tree, its tender tips of creepers adorned with an abundance of flowers.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ṣa) "With fresh palāśa leaves," he,
Kṛṣṇa, beheld before him the fragrant spring.
It was such that it possessed palāśa groves—forests of *kiṃśuka* trees—with leaves as fresh as those of the young palāśa;
it was such that its lotuses were filled with pollen scattered by the wind;
and it was such that the tips of its creepers, even more tender than soft, were withered at their ends by the rays of the sun.

Alternatively, "mṛdulatāntam" means that which has a soft (*mṛdu*) end—that is, a tender tip—of a creeper, as desired by the youths; the verbal root *kāṅkṣ* (to desire) is used here with the sense of longing.
Of what nature is the divine fragrance?
Fragrant with heaps of *sumanas* flowers;
*locanā*:
(*lo*, *ḷ*) fresh *palāśa*, meaning a new leaf.
A forest of *palāśa* trees and a forest of *kiṃśuka* trees,
covered with the falling pollen of blossoming flowers.
Well-knit, soft and tender,
extended and wide.
“Latāntam” means *latām*.
When both [words] are meaningless, there is the example beginning with “*priyatamāyatamām*” and so forth;
here, there is the repetition of a word (*padāvṛtti*).
In the cases of "palāśapalāśa" and "surabhiṃ surabhiṃ," both [repeated] words are meaningful;
in "latāntalatānta," the first is meaningless;
and in "parāgaparāga," the second is.
The same may be cited in other cases as well.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, sa):
Regarding this, he states "here" (*atra*) to show that there is a repetition of the two meaningful words "palāśam" and "surabhim."
He demonstrates the pointlessness of either one [of the two] with the words "latānta," etc.
Locanā:
(lo, e) refers to cases other than the repetition of the feet and so forth.
Here is an example of the repetition of a quarter-verse (*pādāvṛtti*), as found in the description of the hermitage of the sages in *Kuvalayāśvacarita* by my venerable father:
*jīa ua jaṇa māṇaaṃ, jīa ua jaṇa māṇaaṃ* [Preserve the life of the people, O proud one; preserve the life of the people, O proud one.]
Some, however, desire *yamaka* even when there is a repetition of a single vowel and a single consonant,
as in the verse of the poet Govinda Ānanda, whose hand bears the seal [of this style]:
“Playing with one eye in the well and the other in my face, addressing me while speaking something to her own reflection— ”
Lifting up her pitcher-like breasts with her uplifted arms, her pure face brightened by a smile pregnant with instruction, she entered my heart.
“In the case of *yamaka* and so forth, there may be identity between *ḍa* and *la*, as well as between *ba* and *va*, and *ra* and *la*.
Regarding this, Locanā states: “In the phrase ‘in *yamaka* and so forth,’ the word ‘and so forth’ (*ādi*) includes *śleṣa* and other such figures.”
According to the principle stated thus, there is no loss of the *yamaka* (rhyme) in the verse "bhujalatāṃ jaḍatāmabalājanaḥ.
In the phrase "in *yamaka* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

In all instances such as "ḍaloḥ" and so forth, the letter *a* in the first syllable is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Regarding the term "vaveḥ," it has been stated that there is an identity between the *pa*-group and the *ya*-group belonging to another [word].
And in this case, it is merely a convention of the Alamkārikas.

There is also an instruction that the sound *la* may take the place of the sound *ḍa* when there is a unity between two liquids (*jala*). If one person should interpret a sentence intended for one purpose in another way—
either through punning (*śleṣa*) or through intonation (*kāku*)— that is *vakrokti* (circuitous speech), which is thus twofold.
"Of two kinds" refers to *śleṣavakrokti* (paronomastic circumlocution) and *kākuvakrokti* (intonational circumlocution).
*Vijñapriyā*:
[The author] states the figure of speech *vakrokti*: when a speaker utters a sentence with one meaning, another listener, through the paronomasia (*śleṣa*) of that sentence...

The meaning is that if one should apply one's own words through intonation (*kāku*) as having another intended sense, thereby making known a meaning distinct from the literal construction, then that is *vakrokti* (crooked speech) of two kinds.
He demonstrates its twofold nature with the word "śleṣa" (punning).
Locanā: (lo, o) *anyasyati* means it is stated by someone else with a different meaning.

When that [meaning] is employed through another meaning— either by means of a pun (*śleṣa*) with or without a break in the word, or by a change in intonation (*kāku*), or by a specific modulation of tone— it is *vakrokti* (indirect speech).
Therefore, the meaning is that it is of two kinds due to the combination of the two conditions of *śleṣa* (punning) and *kāku* (intonation).
The examples in order are as follows:
"Who are you? "We are here on dry land. "Now, your question concerns a specific detail. "What does that bird say? "Or rather, where is the Lord of Serpents, where Hari sleeps?"
"O ladies, you are truly marvelous! How strange is this god of love who, by his power, causes men—whose minds are devoid of discernment—to mistake us for women."
Vijñapriyā:
"(vi, kha) 'Who are you?'—
this is a question posed by a speaker toward someone whose name and lineage are unknown."

And that man, the disperser, being questioned, conveys through his own reply the intended meaning of the other's words—namely, "Who are you in the water?"—by means of a pun on those words, such as "We are indeed on land," and so forth.
The former speaker, however, says: "A question";
the meaning is that it concerns a specific object in the form of a genus or an individual belonging to your class.

The word *śrotṛ* means a bird (*viḥ*, *pakṣin*), while the remainder [of the compound] refers to the serpent Ananta (*anantanāga*); since these two are its support (*āśraya*), the question concerns them both—this is what he makes clear by his own answer: "What does he say?"—wherein Hari resides upon the bird Garuḍa.
The meaning is that Hari lies upon Śeṣa, who is infinite.
Having heard this, the questioner says out of anger: "You are *vāmāḥ*—that is, you are contrary and hostile because you hold a perverted view.
But the listener, making clear that the intended meaning is "you are *vāmāḥ* women," censures him, saying: "Oh, what a mockery!"
The ellipsis is "mockery and ridicule prevail in you"; the ellipsis is "of you whose mind is devoid of discrimination"; and the grammatical connection is "in us, who are men."
Here, he demonstrates the *śleṣa* (paronomasia), both with and without word-splitting (*sabhaṅga-abhaṅga-pada*), by saying "here.
Locanā: Who are they called? And [who are] in the water?
*Viśeṣa* means difference or dissimilarity;
*viḥ* means a bird; *śeṣa* means a serpent.
The word *vāmāḥ* refers to women who are perverse;
*viḍambarasikaḥ* means one who takes pleasure in mockery, being full of curiosity.
Here, because the specific term [“vi-ḍamba”] is capable of two meanings—“*viḥ* meaning ‘bird’” and “*śeṣaḥ* meaning ‘the serpent Nāga’”—there is a *sabhangaśleṣa* (a pun with a break).
But in other cases, there is no breach [of the rule]:
"At a time when the cuckoos are vocal and the mango trees are enchanting,
her heart does not grieve because of the abandonment of that wrongdoer."

In this case, the negative particle (*nañ*), which was employed by a certain female friend for the purpose of prohibition, is instead construed as having the sense of an injunction because it is uttered with a different intonation (*kākū*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ga) states that it is joined with an intonation: "at the time."
This is a statement by a female friend to another friend who provides consolation to a hero abandoned by his heroine out of anger.
The analysis of the compound is: "where the cuckoos are vocal.
*Sahakāra* refers to that flower (the mango blossom).
Regarding the phrase "by one [particle]" (*ekayā*): although there is no sentence employed therein that contains a negative particle (*nañ*) signifying prohibition, nevertheless,
by interpreting the sentence beginning with "at this time" (*atra kāle*) through the use of intonation (*kāku*), the very impossibility of a sentence possessing such a meaning [is established].

Nevertheless, since this sentence is understood from the context to be a statement produced by the hero’s sighing, its logical consistency is established solely through the interrogative intonation (*kāku*) and the particle *na*; thus, it should be understood that the *na* situated within the sentence implied by that [intonation] effects the construction of the injunctive sense for the *na* situated within its own sentence.
And this [explanation] is consistent only when such a context exists.
However, this is not an example when there is no such contextual factor (prakaraṇa) as a grasper [of the meaning].
Likewise, the negative particle (*nañ*) situated within an implied sentence possesses the sense of negation;
similarly, it is only a sentence qualified by a change of voice (*kāku*) and the negative particle that possesses the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*).
And so it is said: "Alas, O friend, because he is dependent upon his teacher, he is prepared to go to a very distant land;
he will not return while the spring is made lovely by swarms of bees and cuckoos."
At the time of the fragrance, he [is present].
Thus, the example stated by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* itself should be understood.
For in that case, there is the application by the second speaker of the preceding sentence—which intends grief—to the sense of being agitated by desire (*kāma*).
[This occurs] even when the words are of one and the same kind, despite the various languages.
Where there is a sentence, this is intended as "equal in expression" (bhāṣāsama).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, gha) He states the ornament of linguistic similarity (*bhāṣāsamālaṅkāra*)—namely, "by words" (*śabdaiḥ*).
"By words" means by phrases (*padaiḥ*).
A sentence is a collection of those [words], and its meaning is that it is composed of the same types of words across all languages, including Sanskrit and Prākṛta. — *Locanā*
"By sounds" means by those of a single kind, being of one type due to the absence of distinction; that is,
among the languages such as Sanskrit, Prakrit, and so forth.

"Bhāṣāsama" (Equal in Speech) is a distinct figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) that possesses a name corresponding to its meaning, derived from the etymological analysis: "that in which there exist words of identical form across various speeches.
Furthermore, what was stated by the scholar Caṇḍīdāsa—that this is merely a specific variety of the figure of speech *śleṣa* (Pun)—is incorrect.
Because there is no second meaning.
As it is said by me:
"Upon the shore of the lake of the monastery, where the anklets of beautiful jewels jingle with sweet and deep resonance..."
O playful parrot, you are devoid of passion; and even in the steady breeze carrying the scent of the *sārasa* lotus, you are indifferent.
Vijñapriyā: (vi, ṅa) "O Mañjulā! means: O friend! O you whose anklets are beautiful and set with jewels—O you who possess such anklets!
Alternatively, it refers to the bank of a monastery lake where the anklets produce a deep sound;
what kind of place is it? It is one where parrots are kept for the purpose of play.
The meaning is: "In such a place where the wind is preeminent with fragrance (*gandhasāra*), even though there are so many such excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), why are you tasteless (*virasa*)?
This verse is identical in all six languages: Sanskrit, Prākṛta, Śaurasenī, Prācyā, Āvantī, Nāgarī, and Apabhraṃśa.

In examples such as "sarasaṃ kaiṇaṃ kavvam" ("The poetry of poets is full of rasa"), although there is a similarity between the Sanskrit *sarasam* and the Prakrit *sarasaṃ*, this is not considered an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) because, despite the phonetic correspondence, there is no strikingness (*vaicitrya*) due to the absence of its occurrence within a sentence. Vijñapriyā: [Commentary]The provided text consists entirely of a repeating sequence of the character "A" and does not contain any Japanese, Sanskrit, Chinese, or other meaningful linguistic content to translate. Therefore, there is no translation to provide.

(Vi, Ca) This ornament occurs only when sentences are composed of words that are identical across all languages; however, he states that this ornament does not apply in cases where such a single word is used to form a sentence—namely, "sarasaṃ kaiṇa" (the poetry of poets is flavorful).
The meaning is: "the poetry of poets is flavorful."
The meaning here is that because the sentence is composed of such singularly charming words, there is the figure of speech *nāyaka* (the "hero").
*Śleṣa* (paronomasia) is intended when multiple meanings are expressed by means of words that possess double meanings (*śliṣṭa*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, cha) He states the figure of speech *śleṣa* (punning): "By means of *śliṣṭa*" [means] by those that denote both [senses], i.e., those that have a single form.
— *Locanā*:
Regarding the phrase "by means of [words] joined" (*śliṣṭaiḥ*):

by the term "multiple" (*aneka*), it is meant that when two or many meanings are expressed, because there is an absence of restrictive factors such as context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, they are conveyed through denotation (*abhidhā*).
By this, the exclusion of *dhvani* is established.
Now, is the expression of multiple meanings achieved by distinct words or by each word individually?
In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) even in instances such as "cow, horse, man, elephant."
Because, according to the principle that "it is illogical for a definition to be impossible [in its own subject] and for it to have multiple meanings," he says:
"by means of *śliṣṭa* [words].
This is because of the view that "there is a difference in words due to a difference in meaning."

According to the principle that "in the path of poetry, accent (*svara*) is not taken into account," even words that are distinct due to differences in their expressed meanings become devoid of distinction through simultaneous utterance.
For it is observed that the manifestation of a word occurs in three ways: by form, by meaning, and by accent.

Thus, when two words of different forms but identical sound (*samānaśruti*) are uttered according to that same principle, they each convey their own respective meanings in succession; wherever this occurs, it is *śabdaśleṣa* (verbal paronomasia) by virtue of the identity of the phonetic form of the words.

This explanation follows the opinion of the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and others, who maintain the rule that when a word can withstand substitution by another, it is a "pun" (*śleṣa*) of meaning (*artha*).

Others, however, say: "Indeed, there can be no comparison between 'earth' (*vasudhā*), 'greatly honored' (*mahita*), 'conquered in the past' (*purājita*), 'absence of fault' (*nirāgamanābhāva*), 'rains' (*varṣāḥ*), 'fragrant' (*surabhitavara*), 'boar-form' (*vāraha-vapuṣaḥ*), and 'trees' (*taravaḥ*) on the one hand, and 'Hari' (*hareḥ*) on the other, any more than there could be between a jar and a cloth."

In such cases, two [types of] production of sounds by a single effort are possible. If one were to accept that both [sounds] have the same form, then the potter himself would produce a hundred *gha* and *ca* sounds of identical form through a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
If that were the case, the conventional usage of difference would be annihilated.
[For it is said: "This alone is difference and the cause of difference, namely, the superimposition of contradictory properties and the difference in causes.

Furthermore, if it were possible for a speaker to utter two words at once with the intention of conveying both meanings, then even a potter desiring to produce a thousand pots could accomplish them all at once.
As it was stated by the venerable teacher Udyotakara: "Because speech functions sequentially.

Therefore, it is appropriate to adopt the view of those who maintain that within a single word, various objects of meaning are brought to life sequentially, each by virtue of its own respective causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
However, in this view, the reactivation of a second denotation—which contradicts the first—is untenable; thus, as in the case of [the verse] beginning with "I wandered in Janasthāna," here too—
Only the function of *vyañjanā* (suggestion) is taught [in such cases].

Thus, in the *dhvani* system, in instances where there is a restriction by context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, from that very word—assisted by the totality of conditions such as pronunciation and the like—there arises through its other operation the cognition of a meaning obtainable from another word, whether with or without a break in the compound.

However, in cases such as "by whom [it] was destroyed" (*yena dhvasta...*), where there is no restriction by context and the like, there remains a doubt regarding the denotation (*abhidhāna*) of both [meanings].

Where even upon the substitution of words there is a loss of both meanings, there it is *śabdaśleṣa* (verbal pun), because the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*) is the root cause. Where, however, even upon the substitution of words there is no impairment of those meanings, there it is *arthaśleṣa* (semantic pun), because the word is employed solely for the sake of that meaning.

According to this view, however, the compound *śliṣṭapadaiḥ* in the Sūtra and similar expressions should be explained as ending in a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*), meaning "those [verses] in which two conjoined meanings exist" (*śliṣṭau arthau vidyete eṣu*).
Regarding the phrases "denoting multiple meanings" and "the doubt regarding the denotation of multiple meanings":
since this sūtra is recited in the section on verbal ornaments (śabdālaṅkāra), it is established that the words therein cannot tolerate substitution (parivṛtti).
As for those who say, "A word produces another word," that is incorrect,
because there is no experience of a produced word;
furthermore, if meaning were understood through a word that has not been experienced, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Alternatively, it is because there is no rule for the production of a distinct denoted meaning from a distinct expressive word.
And thus, the designation of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) as residing in phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth is a conventional usage following the authority of the ancients.

For if one were to accept such a mode of utterance, then in cases like "durgālaṅghita" and "janasthāna," where two words are involved, it would follow that even there *vyañjanā* (suggestion) could not be admitted.

In passages such as "And he will speak to those who know his heart" and "The distress of both [kinds] of mountain-dwellers," the logical connection is that the meaning which first ascends to the intellect is the object of comparison (*upameya*), while the other is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
This applies to phonemes, suffixes, genders, verbal roots, and even words. (Viśvavidyā-sāra 10.11)
And it is eightfold due to the combination of case endings, numbers, and languages.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ja): He states its eightfold nature with the words "varṇa" etc.
The connection [of the words] ending in the sixth case (genitive) with the word "śleṣāt" (due to punning) is to be understood here.
It should be understood that in each of the three—phoneme (*varṇa*), suffix (*pratyaya*), and gender (*liṅga*)—there is a pair of phonemes, a pair of suffixes, and a pair of genders.
Likewise, duality should also be understood in the case of case-endings (*vibhakti*), numbers (*vacana*), and languages (*bhāṣā*).
In the case of the two words *prakṛti*, their suchness is indicated by the dual number itself;
their reality (*tattva*) consists in the identity of the two distinct forms and colors. — Locanā.

Regarding this, the view of Caṇḍīdāsa, Paṇḍitarāghavānanda, and others—that the eightfold nature of *śleṣa* (punning) based on its occurrence in phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth is incorrect—is untenable.
For it is as follows: the eightfold nature of *śleṣa* exists entirely by virtue of its occurrence in phonemes and other such elements.
And thus:
"When the ritual procedure has become crooked at its head, there shall be smearing with ashes;
likewise, there shall be an abode in the cremation ground, a passion for it, and nakedness."
In this case, because there is no specific context, the doubt arises as to whether it is Mahādeva or some poor man who is to be addressed. Therefore,
here we have a phonetic pun (*varṇaśleṣa*), since the *u* and *i* vowels of the words *vidhu* and *vidhi* take the form of the diphthong *au*.

In passages such as "by him by whom the Mind-born [Kāma] was destroyed" and "there may be the state of being Nanditā through service to the lotus-feet of Virūpākṣa," when the context is unknown, there arises a doubt: is this the speech of some devotee thinking, "May I become Nanditānandaka"? Or is it the speech of some devotee [thinking], "May I attain the status of belonging to the specific group of names beginning with Nanditānandin"?
Therefore, in this case, there is a pun (*śleṣa*) on the verbal suffixes *syāt* and *syām*.
In the word *nanditā*, there is a pun on the two case-endings (*vibhakti*), namely *-tal* and *-tṛc*. [The verse continues: "He who is repeatedly capable of destroying the wings of rival lineages..."
Bearing a hundred crores of tusks, that lord of the gods shines resplendent.

In this passage, there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) between the masculine and neuter genders in the phrase *śatakoṭidatām*, as well as between the two verbal roots *dadāti* and *dyati*, and their respective bases (*prakṛti*).
In the verse beginning with *yena dhvasta*, there is a *śleṣa* based on the difference between the case endings (*vibhakti*) and the compound (*samāsa*).
In the phrase *sarvasvaṃ hara sarvasva*, there is also a *śleṣa* of case endings, because both meanings remain subjects of doubt, as will be illustrated in the subsequent examples.

And in such passages as, "Ah, those who possess sweetness bestow upon him supreme beauty," there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) between the plural and singular numbers: do "those who possess sweetness" (*madhuratābhṛtaḥ*) refer to many people who bear sweetness, or does it refer to a single person who is supported by sweetness?
Furthermore, in the term *madhuratābhṛtaḥ*, there is also a *śleṣa* between the *kvip* suffix and the *kta* suffix.
In this case as well, in the phrase *dadhate*, there is a pun (*śliṣṭa*) consisting of the plural form of the root *dhā* in one sense and the singular form of the root *dadhat* in another.

Thus, having considered the possibility of the eightfold *śleṣa* within the scope of the figure of speech *śleṣa* through the statement of a cognition perceived by two [meanings] via denotation (*abhidhā*), there is no need for much dispute with those predecessors who cast aspersions [on the theory], even though they are our very source of livelihood.

Now, one might object: "In cases such as *yena dhvasta* ('by whom [it] was destroyed'), let that meaning which first ascends to the intellect be the expressed (*vācya*), and let the other be the suggested (*vyaṅgya*). What is the use of postulating the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia) even there? We reply: it is not so.
For in this case, if—due to being the object of a state of doubt and thus being undetermined—in instances such as *bhadrātman* ('of auspicious nature'), [the word were to function as a pun],...
And because [the meaning] has been determined in such passages as "and he will speak to those who know his heart," there is consistency in the existence of the postulation of two functions (*vṛtti*).

As for what was stated by the scholar Caṇḍīdāsa regarding the verse "the pain of both kinds of mountain-lords" (*vyathāṃ dvayeṣāmapi medinībhṛtām*), namely that there is a denotation of both: "At the time of the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*), he thinks, 'I am liberated'..."
At the time for eating sugar-candies and sweetmeats, he runs about brandishing his staff."
Thus, he echoes a common proverb.
For if one accepts the term *abhidhā* (denotation) in some instances, then why would the two [other] denotations be at fault even in cases such as "of the auspicious-natured" (*bhadra-ātmanaḥ*)?
Surely, it was precisely in this context of examining defects that the defectiveness of both the meaning and the word was established when they were ambiguous.
How then can poetic figurehood (*alaṅkāratva*) be asserted even when there is doubt regarding the expression, as in the verse beginning with "yena dhvasta"?

In cases such as "abalā acalā vā syuḥ" and "āśīḥ paramparāṃ vandyām," where there is a fault, the intended single meaning cannot be determined due to the force of doubt; because of this excessive distraction, there is opposition toward aesthetic relish (*svāda*).
In this case, however, it is established by experience that even when two meanings are intended, the charm consisting in the state of non-determination is conducive [to the aesthetic effect].

For this very reason, in the former instance, there is a lapse on the part of the great poet, whereas in the other, the employment of a means capable of conveying multiple meanings is something universally recognized. Furthermore, in the former case, while one meaning provides aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), the second meaning becomes adverse.
Having forcibly drawn that [object] out from there, one externalizes it;
however, in this case, when one of two meanings has ascended into the intellect, the other meaning serves as its cause for being drawn away into poetry and the like.
This very secret—that the desire to compose poetry is witnessed by experience through the determination of two meanings—is the essential point.

Thus, in such instances as “vaurivaṃśadavānala” (the forest-fire for the bamboo-clan), there is *rūpaka* (metaphor) because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between the meaning of the word *vaṃśa*— which is suggested by *vyañjanā* as "bamboo"— and its primary meaning [the clan], due to their being construed as a single unified entity. This is like the case of “gaurvāhīka” (the Vāhīka is a cow), where the *go* and the *vāhīka* are identified, or like “mukhacandra” (face-moon), where the face and the moon are identified.

One might object: "In cases such as 'The Vāhīka is an ox' (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), there is a sublation of the connection (*anvaya-bādha*) with the superimposed meaning of 'ox,' and since that meaning of 'ox' is the primary one, there is secondary indication (*gauṇī lakṣaṇā*) there. But here, the meaning in the form of the flute is suggested (*vyaṅgya*); how then can indication, which is sustained by the sublation of the primary meaning, exist?"
In this regard, the connection is as follows:

according to the view of those who maintain that "birth" (*jāti*) is the sole meaning of a word, once the denotative function (*abhidhā*) has ceased— because it conveys only the universal (*jāti*)— in accordance with the method demonstrated by us and the ancients in this very second chapter during the investigation of the designated referent (*saṅketitārtha*), [the process continues as follows].

Just as in the case of the cognition of the expressed connection (*anvaya*) being manifested by the manifestation (*vyakti*) which must be accepted as itself suggested (*vyaṅgya*), so too here, with respect to the object in the form of the flute-stick—which is suggested as a manifestation—there is a simultaneous perception (*tadvat-pratīti*) due to its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the genus (*jāti*) that is suggested; as in:
"The sun has set."

In such cases, because it is necessary [to convey the meaning], the bamboo-form object arising from the totality of factors such as the forest fire (*davānala*) possesses a primacy equal to the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) in examples such as "she goes to meet her lover.

Alternatively, by adopting the view that "this is a function longer and longer than an arrow," the word *vaṃśa* in the sense of the bamboo-form object is [connected] with the word *vaṃśa* in the sense of a lineage through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*anvaya*).

Because the suggested object—the form of the flute—is a single entity, it is metaphorically treated as non-different; and because it is that which is to be predicated (*vidheya*), it possesses primary significance (*mukhyārthatva*).

The term "due to *śleṣa*" (*śleṣāt*) connects with each member of the series beginning with "varṇa" (phonemes). Thus, [the meaning is] "due to the *śleṣa* of the two phonemes," "due to the *śleṣa* of the two suffixes," and so forth.
The examples in order:
"When fate has turned adverse, even a multitude of means becomes fruitless;
for the sun about to set, even a thousand hands were not enough to support him."
Locanā: (lo, ī) refers to the moon in the act [of creation], or to the Creator.
*Karāḥ* means both rays and hands.
Here, in the word *vidhau*, there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) because the vowels *u* and *i* in the words *vidhu* and *vidhi* take the form of the diphthong *au*.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, jha) "Pratikūlatām" means "hostility.
The particle "hi" has the sense of "indeed.
The meaning is that when the Ordainer (vidhātṛ), the creator, becomes adverse, the state of having many means—that is, the possession of numerous methods—becomes fruitless.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "for the support":
for the support—that is, for the protection—of the Lord of the Day (the Sun) as he was about to fall, there was no "thousand hands," meaning no thousand rays, nor even a thousand actual hands;
this is because the Moon (Vidhu) is adverse to him, and not because of the Creator (Vidhātṛ).
Regarding the phrase "in this injunction," he states that there is a unity of form through the modification of the two phonemes *u* and *i*: "In this context" (*atrety*).
"The rays of the moon, and the southern breeze—surely all of these pour forth nectar for those who rest upon the lap of their beloved."
Here, in the word "sudhākiraḥ," there is the coalescence (*śleṣa*) of the *kvip* and *ka* suffixes;
furthermore, because the plural and singular forms are identical in shape, there is also a coalescence of number (*vacana-śleṣa*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ña) He states the *śleṣa* of suffixes (*pratyaya*): "the rays" (*kiraṇāḥ*).

Since the *śleṣa* of case-endings (*vibhakti*) has been treated separately, it should be understood that here "suffix" refers to something distinct from a case-ending. The essence (*tattva*) [of this type of *śleṣa*] is the identity between two suffixes of different forms.
The meaning is "of women who rest upon the laps of their beloveds.
He says "moreover" (kiñca) because there is also a pun on the singular number here;
the essential point is that the same form applies to both expressions.
In this context, "kiraṇāḥ" ends in the plural,
while "samīraṇaḥ" ends in the singular;
in both cases, the words "sarva" and "kiri" apply.
In this context, in the phrase "sarva" (all), there is only a play on number (*vacanaśleṣa*) without a play on suffix (*pratyayaśleṣa*).
However, in the phrase "a word joined with a fault [conveys] a meaning," there is only a play on suffix without a play on number; therefore, these constitute two distinct types of *śleṣa*.
For here, when "doṣayukta" is construed with "padāt," the suffix *tas* is used for the ablative case (*pañcamī*);
but when construed with "arthe," the suffix *kta* is used, and in both instances the singular number (*ekavacana*) applies. — Locanā.
In the phrase *sarva eva*, the word *sarva* is both plural-terminating and singular-terminating.
Therefore, when it functions as an adjective for the plural-terminating *sudhākiraḥ*, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *kṛ* in the sense of "scattering" (*vikṣepa*).
But when [the word] ends in the singular number, the suffix *kap* is applied:
"The pair of breasts of that slender woman— blazing blue lotuses with blossoming eyes, ever-granting fragrance, and shimmering with radiant, tremulous beauty— is yours."
Here, there is a pun (*śleṣa*) between the neuter and feminine genders, as well as a pun on the number (*vacana*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi,
ṭa) states the pun on gender (*liṅgaśleṣa*) with the verse beginning "vikasat," etc.
Reality consists in the uniformity found even in the two genders.
May the blooming blue-lotus eyes and the pair of breasts of the slender maiden grant you constant joy.
He states the qualification for both with the word "shining" (*lasat*).
Regarding the eyes—there is a compound: "your two [eyes] are shimmering and tremulous.
And such are your two breasts, meaning they are captivating and heart-stealing; that is, your pair of breasts possesses a necklace with a shimmering, trembling gem set in its center.
Regarding this, he speaks of the commingling of word-play (*vacanaśleṣa*) with the phrase "and here" (*atra ca*).
The meaning is "here too.
Here, apart from the play on gender (*liṅgaśleṣa*), there is a play on number (*vacanaśleṣa*) in the word *dattām*.
As for the pun on gender (*liṅgaśleṣa*) without a pun on number (*vacanaśleṣa*), it is as in the example: "Hari and his name are destroyers of sin" (*haristannāma cāghanut*).
Here, although there is a difference in gender between "Hari" and "his name," they share the same form in the phrase "destroyer of sin" (*aghanut*);
the number, however, is not distinct.
Locanā:
Regarding "dattāmiti"— it is the second person dual ending of the root *dā* in the *parasmaipada*,
and the third person singular ending in the *ātmanepada*.
The word *lasat-tarala-hāriṇī* is in the dual number when qualifying the two blue lotuses of her eyes, but it is in the singular number and feminine gender when qualifying her pair of breasts.
By the inclusion of the word *api* ("also"), it is meant that there is not merely a play on gender (*liṅga-śleṣa*), but also a play on number (*vacana-śleṣa*).
[As in: "He will carry all the scriptures in his heart and speak them to those who know."
The prince brought about the destruction of his enemies and the prosperity of his friends.
