In this context, the term "will speak" (*vakṣyati*) refers to the verbal roots *vah* and *vac*;
the term "produced by capacity" (*sāmarthyakṛt*) refers to the verbal roots *kṛntati* and *karoti*. — *Vijñapriyā* —
(vi, ṭha) He states the *prakṛtiśleṣa* (punning on the base form): "This... and so forth.
This is a statement by the astrologers upon the birth of a prince.
The syntactical connection is: "He will bear [it] in his heart."
He will speak— that is, he will discourse upon— the treatises for those who are wise and learned;
he is the destroyer of the power of enemies and the creator and producer of the strength of friends.
Locanā:
Regarding the phrase "in *lo* and *ṛ*, [the roots] *vah* and *vac*": when the heart (*hṛd*) functions as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the root *vah* expresses the sense of knowing;
and when it is connected with the enemy (*amitra*) by virtue of its capacity, the root *kṛt* (as in *kṛntati*) expresses the sense of cutting.
In the case of *mitrasambandhitva* (the state of being related to a friend), the sense is that of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

Even though there is no difference in the case-ending (*vibhakti*), because there is a difference in the base-forms (*prakṛti*) alone, this is indeed a *prakṛtiśleṣa* (paronomasia of the base-form). Therefore, he says: "of two base-forms," as in the example beginning with *pṛthukārtasvarapātram*.
In this instance, due to the difference in both inflectional endings and compounds within the word-splitting (*padabhaṅga*), it is a *padaśleṣa* (word-pun),
and not a *prakṛtiśleṣa* (root-stem pun).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ḍa) He explains *padaśleṣa* (the punning combination of words): "pṛthukā" and so forth.
The essence (*tattva*) consists in the identity of form in two meanings resulting from the joining of two words that have either fewer or more syllables.
The passage beginning with "pṛthukārtta" has already been explained.
Here, he refutes the status of this as a *prakṛtiśleṣa* (lexical pun) by stating, "here, upon the breaking of the words.
In this case, the difference in case endings should be understood as being elided within the compound (*samāsa*).

Although the distinction from *prakṛtiśleṣa* is established by the very definition [of *padaśleṣa*] beginning with "deficiency or excess," nevertheless, its establishment is also shown by another method.
Thus, this is *padaśleṣa* (word-pun) when it is characterized by a difference in all [elements];
however, when there is a difference in the verbal roots (*prakṛti*) alone, it is *prakṛtiśleṣa* (root-pun). — *Locanā*.
The passage beginning with "pṛthuka" has already been explained in the context of stating that ambiguity is not always a defect.
Regarding the word "atra," the meaning is as follows:
For if the case-endings and so forth were identical, then a difference in the verbal roots alone would appropriately be termed *prakṛtiśleṣa* (punning on the root).
However, in this case, because the case-endings differ in words such as *pṛthvī* and *pṛthuka*, it is indeed a fault of the word (*pada-doṣa*).
He states that even when the case-endings and so forth are not different, because there is a difference in the words themselves, it is simply *prakṛtiśleṣa*.
And thus:
"The eyes of those reared in the forest were like lotuses brought to a state of agitation by greedy bees with many shafts."

In this instance, although words such as *lubdha* (hunter/cupid) and *śilīmukha* (arrow/beetle) possess double meanings (*śliṣṭatva*), it is a "śleṣa of the base" (*prakṛtiśleṣa*) because they are divided into distinct parts;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of every word being considered a *padaśleṣa*.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍha) Regarding the distinction from the mere *tanmātra* [elements], he also mentions the *prakṛtiśleṣa* (phonetic punning on roots) here with the words "thus led" (*evaṃ nītanām*).
This is a description of the two eyes of the heroine, which have been agitated by bees greedy for honey due to the delusion that they are blue lotuses.
Here, the meaning of the word "of the lotuses" (*kamalānām*) is to be understood as implied.
And thus, her two eyes were like those of old lotuses grown in the forest.
Regarding the specific qualities of the pair of eyes belonging to the old lotuses and the lady grown in the forest, he says: "nītānam" (led to distress).

By means of *bhūriśilīmukhaiḥ*—that is, by many arrows (*aneka-bāṇaiḥ*) acting as instruments—the hunters (*lubdhakaiḥ*, *vyādhaiḥ*) acting as agents, the old deer grown in the forest were led to a state of agitation.
In the forest and in the water, the full-grown lotuses have been brought to a state of agitation by greedy bees—many honey-seeking *śilīmukha* bees;
however, the distinction is that [the eyes] are thought to be two blue lotuses due to a delusion.
(The lexicon states: "The words *ali* and *bāṇa* both mean *śilīmukha* [arrow/bees]").
In this context, "the hunter and the bee" are the two primary subjects (*prakṛti*).
"Otherwise" should be understood as referring to the alternative case where the defining characteristics— such as being deficient or excessive— are absent.
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) "And thus":
when the word *kamala* has the meaning of "lotus," [it refers to] many *śilīndhra* bees, who are greedy and possessed of desire.
Regarding the sense of "a particular kind of deer," [the forest] is filled with many hunters and fowlers, and with *śilīmukha* arrows—that is, *bāṇa* arrows;
[the term] *vana*, *jala*, and *kānana* [are used here].
He will explain the form of the suffix (*pratyaya*) for all the case-endings (*vibhakti*) starting from the nominative (*vakṣyati*).
“Seize all the possessions of everyone; you are intent on cutting through worldly existence.
You approach with the face of helpful policy, yet your conduct is subtle.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṇa) He speaks of the pun based on case endings (*vibhaktiśleṣa*)—namely, "sarvasvam.

Even though there is a difference between the two words due to their being [respectively] a nominal stem (*suptiṅanta*) and a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), their identity (*tattva*) consists in their identical form.
"Everything" (*sarvasvam*):
this is a statement made by a devotee of Śiva both to a robber and to his own son and others.
"O Hara! You are the everything of everyone."

And because you bestow liberation, you are intent upon the severing of existence and its arising. Since from you there arises the presence—the manifestation—of the *naya* (method), that is, of another form of guidance or assistance, such is your "thin persistence," meaning your bodily state; you come, you arrive, you have reached [this state]. In the case of the bandit (*dasyu*), [the meaning is]: "You take away the entire wealth of everyone."
Be intent on cutting [this down];
bring about the presence and conformity of benefit; remove it;
expand that conduct which causes exhaustion for oneself and others.
Locanā: (lo,
e) "The all-in-all," O Hara, O Śambhu!
You are the all-in-all of the entire world; what have you not become? You are intent upon severing existence, which is to say, saṃsāra.
Bring the maintenance—that is, the functioning—of the body, which is joined with exertion, to a state of being directed toward service; the sense is:
"make the functioning of the body free from exertion. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), however: "take away—that is, destroy—the entire essence of everyone."

Be intent on cutting and breaking; bring about the face-to-face encounter with harm—meaning, do not perform any service. Extend your conduct—that is, your livelihood—which is fraught with exhaustion; expand it.

In this context, in the case of "hara," it is a vocative (*sup*) case ending when it is an address to Śiva; in another case, it is a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) from the root *hṛ*. The same applies to "bhava" and so forth.

And although the meaning of this particular variety [of *śleṣa*] is already understood through the blending of suffixes (*pratyayaśleṣa*), it is mentioned separately because it relies on a specific aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) arising from its occurrence within *subanta* and *tiṅanta* forms that cannot be accomplished by other suffixes.

In the *Vijñapriyā* commentary (*vi*, *ta*), the author demonstrates the uniformity of the two words here—even though the case-endings and verbal terminations are elided everywhere except for the word *āyāsi*, which contains both an elided and an unelided ending—by stating: "here... [referring to the verse].
He states the distinction of this [śleṣa] based on its connection with suffixes (pratyaya) in the words "asya ca" and so forth.

"Not to be accomplished by another suffix" means that those two, namely the nominal suffix (sup) and the verbal suffix (tiṅ), are such that they cannot be accomplished—that is, cannot be made understood—by any other suffix due to their own specific nature; the meaning is that this śleṣa exists within those [suffixes].
*Vicchitti* is variety (*vaicitrya*).
*Locanā*:
(Lo, Ai) A particular kind of *vicchitti* is established through the experience of those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*).
"O Great Goddess, O Umā, suddenly seize that mind of mine which has become deeply attached to the pursuit of worldly gain; quickly take away that mind which seeks many refuges."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) He speaks of a pun on words (*bhāṣāśleṣa*)—namely, "O Mahade!
On the side of the Sanskrit language: "O Mahade! O giver of festivals! (*utsavadātri*).

O Pārvatī, protect that well-known application of mine in the acquisition—that is, the mastery—of the Āgama, which is the Veda; the meaning is: "Grant me the practice of the Vedas, which is renowned among the company of sages."
What kind of attachment is it that binds the gods—that is, the cause of connection for the gods, meaning that which brings about my state of being a god?

Likewise, at this opportune moment—namely, death—suddenly seize and destroy that well-known delusion of the mind; what kind of mental delusion is it? It is one that has many resorts, having various kinds of objects as its domain.
The root *sṛ* means "to go.
According to the Prakrit interpretation: "O Consort of Hara, grant me the essence of Dharma; take away from us that hope which is subject to darkness and the cycle of coming and going.
O Consort of Hara, you are our refuge; may the delusion of my mind depart suddenly."
Thus is the Sanskrit;
and its meaning is: "O Consort of Hara, grant me delight in dharma."
From this cycle of birth and death, from this saṃsāra under the sway of darkness, take away our longing.
You are my refuge;
may the delusion of my mind depart instantly.
Locanā:
(lo, o) “mahade” means “O Great One.
From the perspective of Sanskrit—“mahade” means “O Giver of Festivals.”
O Umā, O Pārvatī!
The sense is: "In my bringing together of the Āgamas—that is, in the compilation of the Āgamas—please establish that attachment, that devotion."
The compound *samāsaṅga* is a descriptive term meaning "that by which an agreement (*sandhi*) or union with the *surāḥ*, the gods, is established.

Because the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) based on scripture is the cause for attaining heaven, it has a vast (*bahu*) and extensive (*bahula*) range (*saraṇa*, *prasāra*). Such is the delusion of the mind (*cittamoha*), the ignorance residing in the intellect (*manoniṣṭha*), [which arises] at the opportune moment.
"Sahasā" means "with speed," [instructing one] to take away or remove.
In the Mahārāṣṭrī Prākṛt tradition,
the word "mahaḍa" is used in the genitive case to express the sense of the dative.
Therefore he said:
"O Consort of Hara, grant me the nectar of the Dharma, which is better than the coming and going of those under the power of darkness; you are my refuge—may the delusion of my mind depart instantly."
Where there is coming and going, from that "my coming"— meaning from saṃsāra.
Here, between Saṃskṛta and Mahārāṣṭrī,
and between Saṃskṛta and Paiśācī, for example:

(kha) “He who endures even a single instance of desire— which is as hollow as a man’s wealth in gold, silver, or jewels— conquers that man who dwells in the company of women and is beyond comparison.”
He cannot endure the incomparable allure of courtesans who take delight in sensual pleasures and possess maidservants shimmering with gold and silver; yet he does not find pleasure in them.
Thus ends the shadow of the Paiśācī dialect.
As for the examples in Saṃskṛta and Saurasenī—(Ga):
“He always possesses that strength which is free from strife and which knows this world.”
"Having reached this opportune moment, I have brought the burden of the Māras under my control."
Then this sky was seen, its interior veiled by hundreds of swans,
having reached the eternal state where the enemy has ceased and all essence has departed.
Thus ends the *śūrasenī* dialect.
As for the examples of *saṃskṛta* and *apabhraṃśa*:
(gha) “O wise one, come; O you who dwell in the water, uproot the pride that has been seized by the waves.”

Regarding splendor (*tejas*), which consists of the removal of the expansion of pride and the rays of the sun, it is again threefold: that with a break (*sabhaṅga*), that without a break (*abhaṅga*), and that which possesses the nature of both.
Locanā:

(Lo, Au) Having thus explained the eightfold *śleṣa* according to its occurrence in phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth, [the author] again states it as threefold by way of another method—[indicated by] the word "again" (*punaḥ*).
And these three divisions are to be understood as occurring, as far as possible, within the eight previously mentioned types.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) "Again, it is threefold" means that this eightfold figure of speech (śleṣālaṅkāra) becomes threefold.
To the question "How so?", he says: "It is *sabhaṅga*.
This means that it consists of both [types], namely, it has the nature of being both *sabhaṅga* and *abhaṅga*. [The phrase] "the aforementioned eightfold division" refers to this.
In that regard, in the phrase *pṛthukārtta*, there is a pun (*sabhaṅga*);
in the phrase *kiraṇā*, [it is included] within *sarva eva sudhākira*, where there is no pun (*abhaṅga*);
and in the phrase *kahade*, [it is included] within *cittamoha*, where there is no pun (*abhaṅga*).
In examples such as "mahade," there is a pun (*sabhaṅga*);
thus, it is of both natures. Or, for example:
“May that Mādhava—who, as the Destroyer of the Mind-born (Śiva), formerly turned the body of Bali into a woman; who wears a serpent as his necklace and bracelets and bore the Gaṅgā;
whose praiseworthy name the immortals call ‘The Seizer of the Moon-adorned Head’;
and who himself brought about the destruction of Andhaka—protect you at all times.”

In this context, in the passage beginning with "yena," there is *sabhangaśleṣa* (pun with word-break), while in the passage beginning with "andhaka," there is *abhaṅgaśleṣa* (pun without word-break). Since both occur in a single instance, it constitutes a combination of *sabhanga* and *abhaṅga*; however, for fear of increasing the bulk of the work, it has not been cited separately.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, dha) Even in the following verse, he demonstrates the threefold nature—with the words "by whom [it] was destroyed" (*yena dhvastam*).
May that Umādhava, who is ever-giving (*sarvadā*) and Mādhava, the giver of all (*sarvada*), protect you.

In that regard, according to the Mādhava school, by "non-existence" (abhāva) is meant non-origination; that by which the cart (anaḥ) was destroyed is merely the manifestation of that [entity] possessing an eternal body in another form,
but not its origination.
Likewise, he who conquered Bali is the conqueror of Bali;
by whom the body was formerly made into a woman in the form of Mohinī—
this is merely a display of different forms within a single, eternal body.
The sense is that there is no difference in his body.
Furthermore, he is the slayer of Aghāsura, the serpent-like one who was arrogant and of evil conduct;
he is such that in him is the dissolution (*laya*), the state of absorption, of Rava, the Brahman consisting of manifold forms.
He who supported Mount Govardhana and the earth with his forms as the Tortoise and the Boar;
he whose praiseworthy name the immortals call "Moon-destroyer" and "Severer of Rāhu’s head."
Of what nature is he? He is himself the destroyer of the Andhaka lineage and its abode;
this is from the verbal root *kṣi*, meaning "to dwell" or "to go.
In the case of Umādhava (Śiva)—he is one from whom the Manobhava (the god of love) has been destroyed or shattered.
By whom the body of Viṣṇu, the conqueror of Bala, was made into a weapon for the destruction of the city of the Asura Tripura—
since at the slaying of Tripura, Viṣṇu’s body was turned into an arrow—
and who possesses a necklace in the form of a coiled serpent and bracelets as armlets.
He who bore the Gaṅgā upon his crest,
whose head is joined with the moon,
and whom the immortals praise by the name "Hara"—
Of what nature is he? He is the destroyer of the Asura Andhaka.
Here, he demonstrates the presence of the triad [of qualities] with the word "here" (*atra*).
He states the reason for presenting each [quality] in a single verse with the words "of the text" (*grantha*).
Locanā:
(lo, a) On the side of Hari—*manobhava* is Kāma;
*balijit* is Viṣṇu.
In former times, his body was made into a weapon for the sake of the Daityas;
he whose necklaces and bracelets were indeed serpents, upraised and of extremely circular form;
[he who drank] the Gaṅgā, which flows through three paths.
That which possesses the moon is "śaśimat. The destruction or ruin of the Daitya Andhaka is "andhakakṣaya";
he who effects that [destruction] is always Umādhava, the Lord of Gaurī.
In the case of Hari (Viṣṇu): by whom the cart (*anaḥ*) was destroyed;
by means of non-existence (*abhavena*), that is, by his nature as consciousness (*cidrūpeṇa*);
formerly, at the time of the fetching of the nectar (*amṛtāharaṇakāle*), his own body (*ātmana eva kāyaḥ*) was made into the form of a woman for the purpose of deluding the Asuras.
He who slays the arrogant and haughty serpent Kāliya; he whose dissolution occurs in the Sun, which is Brahman in the form of sound;
[he who lifted] the mountain named Govardhana and the earth.

He who churns the moon is Śaśimad-Rāhu; he who severs his head is [Śaśimadrāhu-śirohara]. He whose abode is the city of Dvārakā—the place of destruction for the Andhakas, those of the Andhaka lineage—is Tatkara.
He who gives everything is Sarvada.
Mādhava is the Lord of Śrī.
[The term] "sabhaṅga" refers to the perception of meaning through the breaking of word-divisions.
In this single verse, there are these two types of *śleṣa*: that which possesses word-breaking (*sabhaṅga*) and that which does not (*abhaṅga*).
On this point, some say: "Only *sabhaṅgaśleṣa* (split pun) is the domain of *śabdaśleṣa* (verbal pun).

Where, due to a difference in accents such as the acute (*udātta*) and so forth, two words—which are to be pronounced with distinct efforts—are joined together according to the analogy of lac and wood. — *Locanā*.

(Locative, vocative) Now, having restated the position of those who maintain that the domain of *śabdaśleṣa* (verbal paronomasia) consists exclusively of cases with a break (*sabhaṅga*), whereas *arthaśleṣa* (semantic paronomasia) consists of cases without a break (*abhaṅga*), he refutes it with the words beginning "here" (*iha*) and so forth.
The word "iti" connects with the distant word "upapattiḥ" (justification) following the phrase "they say" (*āhuḥ*).
"Sabhaṅga" (with pun) means that which is endowed with a pun (*bhaṅga*) within the arrangements of phonemes (*varṇavyūha*), or accompanied by a distinct word (*bhinnapada*) consisting of that [pun].
Its scope is that of verbal paronomasia (*śabdaśleṣa*); the meaning is that it arises from the manifestation of two types of meanings through the division of words.
Regarding the phrase "acute and so forth" (*udāttādīti*): the acute (*udātta*) is high-pitched;
the grave (*anudātta*) is not high-pitched.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of the nasalized sounds (*anunāsika*) and other such qualities contained therein, as well as the various modulations of tone (*kāku-bheda*).

Because they are pronounced with distinct efforts, there is no distinction such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth without a difference in effort; by this, it is intended that there is an extreme difference due to their respective effects—as in: "The cranes have lost their grace, the herons do not sport, and the *kaṅka* bird does not move about."
When Vikramāditya had passed away on earth, leaving behind only his fame, like a lake that has dried up.
Thus, in this case, with respect to the side of the king, there is "it" (sā) and "whom" (kam);
however, on the side of the lake, in the phrase "not so" (neti), that [connection] does not exist,
according to the analogy of the lac and the wood.

Just as two separate pieces of wood, when rendered inert by a particular means, attain oneness, so too do two distinct words—two *pada*s—attain a state of union within a single arrangement of phonemes (*varṇavyūha*). However, the "unbroken" (*abhaṅga*) variety is indeed *arthaśleṣa* (semantic paronomasia).

This occurs where, due to the non-difference of vowels and the resulting non-difference of words because they are pronounced with the same effort, there is a semantic paronomasia according to the maxim of two fruits on a single stalk.
Locanā:

(lo, i) The meaning is that it is indeed a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) based on meaning (*arthaśleṣa*), because even in the absence of a reversal of the verbal form itself, the meaning possesses a twofold nature.
"Wherein" [means...]
"Just as two fruits are on a single stalk, so too is there a connection between two meanings in a single word;
for that which is dependent upon something else is indeed its ornament.
The relationship between the adorned and the ornament is established through the relationship of the substratum and the superstratum, as is seen in the world."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, na) Regarding the state of being *sabhaṅga* (with word-break), he states the seed-reason for it being a *śabdaśleṣa* (verbal pun) in the phrase "wherein.
His view is that even in poetry where there is a *sabhaṅgaśleṣa*, the distinction of accents (*svarabheda*) must be taken into account.
Consequently, because they are pronounced by distinct efforts, there is a difference between the words as separate entities.
The meaning is that even though they are perceived as distinct, their conjunction (*śleṣa*) consists in extreme proximity, like that of lacquer and wood.
He states that this "unbroken" (*abhaṅga*) conjunction is a "conjunction of meaning" (*arthaśleṣa*) with the words: "But the unbroken... and so forth.
He states the reason for its being a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) of meaning in the phrase "where...

/ The meaning is that because there is no difference in the words due to their being uttered with the same effort, there is a *śleṣa* (coalescence) only between the two meanings attached to a single word, like two fruits hanging from a single stalk.
To the question, "How can it be an ornament of meaning (*arthālaṃkāra*) by that much alone?", he replies: "For that which has whatever as its substratum... /

The meaning is that when there is a pun (*sabhaṅga*), because the two words themselves are joined, the *śleṣa* (pun) therein is based on sound; and when there is a pun between two meanings residing in a single part [of a word], because those two meanings themselves are joined, the *śleṣa* therein is based on meaning. *Locanā*.
"Yo hi" means: just as in the world an ornament resting on the arm belongs to the arm and one resting on the neck belongs to the neck, so too does this [sound] rest upon the word; such is the sense.
"Like in the world" [is used] for this reason.
In the world, designation occurs precisely through the relationship of the basis and that which is based upon it, as in the case of "the king's man";
or rather, it is by way of arising, grasping, or— what amounts to the same— conventional usage.
Others do not accept this;

for instance, they maintain that here—in this context—there is a fixed rule because the sounds, subordinate suggestives, defects, merits, and ornaments are established as residing in the word and the meaning, following the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
"Others than those" means the authors of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and others who follow them, as well as ourselves;
for it is so stated here.

In this treatise on poetics (*alaṅkāraśāstra*), when the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is rooted in the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūla*), the designation "residing in the word" (*śabdagatatva*) applies to both *dhvani* and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*. However, when it is rooted in the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*), it resides in the meaning. Furthermore, it is quite clear that defects (*doṣa*) and so forth follow neither the presence nor the absence of the word nor the meaning.

Thus, even in the case of *śleṣa* (punning) involving a word with multiple meanings that does not break its grammatical construction, because it follows the presence and absence of the word, the sense is that it is indeed a "verbal *śleṣa*" (*śabdaśleṣa*).
Locanā:
(lo, u) He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Others"—that is, other learned authorities (*abhiyukta*)—do not accept or acknowledge that aforementioned view of the predecessors.
To provide the reason why they do not consider [these as faults], he says: "For instance" (*tathāhi*).

In this context of poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), those words whose meanings are compound-terms (*dvandva*) suffer no impairment even when expressed by synonyms; these are therefore considered to reside in the meaning (*artha-gata*).
However, there is a restriction that those which are not so [expressed] reside only in the word (*śabda-gata*); this is the implication according to the ancient authors of poetic figures.
Furthermore, there is no identity of words in expressions such as "the destruction of darkness" (*andhakakṣaya*),
because of the principle that "a difference in meaning entails a difference in words.
(Vijñapriyā)

(vi, pha) However, according to that particular view, even in cases where there are multiple meanings, if there is a difference in words, then in such instances as well, the verbal figure of speech (*śabdālaṅkāra*) produced by multiple *śliṣṭa* (punning) words remains entirely unobjectionable;
thus, he demonstrates that view with the words "And not... Andhaka.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "and yet there is no non-difference of words."
Regarding this, he states the reason: "by means of a difference in objects.
This means that because there is a difference between the words "jar" and "cloth" due to the difference in their respective objects—the forms of the jar and the cloth.
Thus, the point is that the pervasion of the difference in words by the difference in objects is established precisely through this example.
Nor should it be argued that various words with different meanings are not heard [in such cases], because their distinction is not perceived due to the defect of being uttered by a single effort.
*Locanā*:
Nor does the mere restriction of that [single effort] constitute the status of *śabdaśleṣa* (phonetic punning) for the unbroken [word].
He says "also because of the difference in words" with the words "and not," and states the reason with "by the difference in meaning.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "because it is seen by you yourselves from the established doctrine (siddhānta) which has been accepted as authoritative."

Furthermore, in this case, because it is the word itself that is primarily brought forth by the poet’s imagination as the means for awakening aesthetic variety (*vaicitrya*), it is indeed a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*).
For such variety does not exist in the composition of two dissimilar words; rather, it is variety itself that constitutes an ornament.

Moreover, if it were considered a semantic ornament (*arthālaṅkāra*) simply by looking toward the meaning, then alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the like would also result in being semantic ornaments, since they too look toward the meaning by being subordinate to rasa and so forth.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ba) But surely, since there is a difference in meaning at a place of *sabhaṅgaśleṣa* (split pun), by the example of the difference in accent you favor, there would likewise have to be a difference in accent due to the difference in meaning among multiple words that lack a split (*abhaṅga*). And thus, if the distinction [of accent] is grasped, how could the grasp of [word-]difference occur? Therefore, the pervasion of word-difference by difference of meaning is simply not a necessary condition; for this reason, multiple words are uttered with a single effort. Thus...
He says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
The meaning is that it is because the word itself, as the primary means of variety, is carved out—that is, taken as the object—by the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*).
Now, one might ask: what is the proof for the primacy of an indivisible word such as *andhaka*? To this, he says: "of two dissimilar words."

The meaning is that in a case such as *hariṇa* (where the word has two meanings), if a synonym for one of those meanings—such as *indu* (moon)—is employed, then just as in the phrase *hariṃ naumi* (I bow to Hari), there is no experience of the poetic charm (*vaicitrya*) consisting of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) even in the phrase *viṣṇvindrau naumi* (I bow to Viṣṇu and Indra).

Now, it might be argued that because it is dependent on the meaning (*arthamukhaprekṣitvāt*), *abhaṅgaśleṣa* (unbroken paronomasia) is called a figure of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*). To this, he says: "dependent on the meaning" (*arthamukha*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "of *anuprāsa* etc.," the inclusion of *sabhagaśleṣa* (broken paronomasia), *vakrokti*, and so forth is intended.
Regarding the phrase "by virtue of being subordinate to rasa, etc.":
"subordination to rasa" should be understood as having the sense of qualities residing in rasa.
By the word "etc.," it is understood that in the case of *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration), there is merely the state of looking toward the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*).
Locanā:

(lo, ṛ) As for those who say that whatever depends upon something is its ornament (*alaṅkāra*), even according to their view, because the strikingness (*vaicitrya*) here resides in the words, it is a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*); thus he says "moreover" (*kiñca*).
Strikingness (*vaicitrya*) is a supermundane elegance (*vicchitti*) consisting of the form of an ornament.
*Pratibhā* is wisdom characterized by ever-new manifestations. It is so called because of its "excavating" or "scratching out" [of meaning];
here he states the reason: "because it is dissimilar," and so forth.

"Dissimilar" means having a different phonetic form (*śruti*), as for example, in the phrase "the destroyer of the Andhakas," where instead of the word *kṣaya*, there are two other words, *vināśa* and *nivāsa*.
Anticipating the objection that this variety constitutes a figure of sense (*arthālaṃkāra*) because it is not perceived without a reflection upon the meaning, he says: "of the sense," etc.
[The objection is: "There would be a lack of focus on the meaning, and there would be a connection with variety in the pursuit of the meaning;

if that were so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to other figures of speech. To this he says: "Of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the rest. The meaning is this: for even in the case of alliteration and the rest, if they lack subordination to rasa and so forth, there is a contradiction with the [accepted] function [of poetry].

Since there is indeed a continuous contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of the object in the form of rasa and so forth, or of the object in the form of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth which manifest that [rasa], why are these also counted by you among the verbal figures (*śabdālaṅkāra*)?

Furthermore, if they were considered verbal figures simply because they are uttered with the same effort as the words, then even in cases such as "When fate has turned adverse" (*pratikūlatām upagate hi vidhau*), where there is a difference in the words, the status of being a verbal figure would undesirably follow; thus, this applies to both cases.
It is indeed a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, bha):

Since it is beyond dispute that what was stated by him as a semantic ornament (*arthālaṅkāra*)—on the grounds of being uttered with an identical effort—is actually a verbal ornament, he points out the over-extension (*atiprasakti*) of this principle even to the case of phonetic punning (*varṇaśleṣa*) and phonetic alliteration (*varṇānuprāsa*), stating: "pratikūlatam iti."
"In both cases" means: in the cases of both the presence and absence of a pun (*sabhaṅga* and *bhaṅga*). — Locanā:

Furthermore, regarding the claim that because a word is uttered with a single effort (*ekaprayatnoccāryatva*), it constitutes a figure of sound (*śabdālaṅkāra*), [the author] states "of the word" (*śabdasya*) to show that even so, there is the fault of being too narrow (*avyāpti*).

In examples such as *pratikūlatām* and *vidhau*, the vowels *i*, *u*, and *o* take the form of *au*, and thus they are uttered with a non-different effort; this is according to one who accepts *śabdaśleṣa* based on the difference of words in both cases, namely in "yena dhvasta... and "andhakakṣaya...".
But where the quality of *śleṣa* (punning) is not destroyed even when words are substituted, there [we have an example]: "With a slight [weight] it rises; with a slight [weight] it goes down.
Oh, how similar is the behavior of the scale-beam and of the wicked man!"
In such cases as these, there is *arthaśleṣa* (semantic punning).
[The author of] *Vijñapriyā* asks: "But if this were so, would it not follow that the poetic figure of *arthaśleṣa* would be abolished? To this, he says: "But where... (*yatra tu*).
He states that very same subject: "In that regard, by a small amount," and so forth.
Oh, the behavior of the end—the tip—of a scale, of a measuring-standard, and of a wicked person is indeed very similar; for it is said, "by a small amount," and so on.
By a small amount—that is, by a tiny object such as a *guñjā* seed.
In this instance, even with a slight degree of praise or slight censure,
and even when other words signifying "rising" or "falling" are supplied, there is no impairment of the status of *arthaśleṣa* (semantic punning). —
*Locanā*.

(Lo, Ḷ) Where, then, does semantic *śleṣa* (paronomasia) occur? To this he says: "Where indeed... When there is a substitution of words—that is, when a word is expressed by another synonym—the "tip of the scale" (*tulākoṭi*) indicates the excellence or deficiency in the weight of the gold and so forth.
In this context, even if words such as *svalpa* (very little) are substituted for terms like *stoka* (little), there is no loss of meaning;

however, since it is impossible for this [figure] to have a scope distinct from other figures of speech, some maintain that when other figures are present, it acts as an exception (*apavāda*), subverting them, and thereby serves as the cause for the emergence of their poetic suggestion (*pratibhā*).
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ya) Now, some say that since there is no scope for *śleṣa* that is not mixed with other figures of speech, whereas there exists a scope for other figures of speech that is not mixed with *śleṣa*, the general figure of speech [the latter] is set aside as an exception (*apavāda*), and thus *śleṣa* alone is the figure of speech; the other figure, being mixed with it, is merely a means of apprehending that *śleṣa*.
He shows that opinion with the words "of this" (*asya*).

Regarding "the state of being the cause for the arising of its intuition" (*tatpratibhotpattihetutvam*): "its intuition" (*tatpratibhā*) refers to the intuition directed toward another poetic figure; the meaning is that this *śleṣa* (paronomasia) possesses the state of being the cause for the arising of that very [intuition], which consists in its capacity to convey that object.
The meaning is that through the pun on words (*śabdaśleṣa*), only the intuition of the subject matter of the figure of speech *śleṣa* itself is produced;
it does not mean that the intuition of the subject matter of another figure of speech is produced.
And thus, in the case of a commingling with other figures of speech, *śleṣa* alone is the figure of speech.

Locanā: Regarding this, those who maintain that since this [figure] necessarily occurs by taking up the distinctness (*vicchitti*) of other ornaments, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the ornaments existing within its own scope— having set forth their position, he refutes it with the words "asya ca" ("and of this").
This is because these [other] objects are present;
because they are sublaters of that;
because those ornaments are sublaters [of it], and since there is no other scope [for them], they are fit to be designated by their primary name, having sublated that designation.
And its cause is by way of exclusion (*apavāda*).
Since its cause for the arising of the flash of intuition (*pratibhā*)—the awakening of the intellect—is those ornaments, it is called "the cause for the arising of that intuition.

Herein, this is investigated: in cases such as *samāsokti* (brief expression) and *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), because the second meaning is not directly denoted, there is not even a scent of this [ornament].

Vijñapriyā: Even in that view, the conclusion is stated— namely, "Thus here"— to demonstrate that *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is not an obstacle even when there is a confluence of all poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), but rather only when there is a confluence of a few.

Regarding this, he says "samāsokti... [etc. to show that there is no possibility whatsoever of the two [figures] being sublated by *śleṣa* when *śleṣa* is mixed with *samāsokti* and *aprastutapraśaṃsā*.
*Samāsokti* is the suggestion of the unmentioned (*aprastuta*) through the description of the mentioned (*prastuta*).
In some cases, it is mixed with *śleṣa*.
For example: "The twilight is full of passion, and the day is its forerunner;
oh, how strange is the course of fate that even so, there is no union!"

In this instance, because the description of the evening preceded by the contextually relevant day suggests the heroine preceded by the hero, there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) of the word-play (*śleṣa*) on the term *anurāga*, which signifies both "redness" and "passion.

Furthermore, the suggestion of the contextual subject through the description of the non-contextual is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Praise of the Non-contextual); and that sometimes occurs as commingled with word-play (*śleṣa*).
For example: "The pillar that stands firm always says, 'I am established';
yet the lotus pond, though full, you lead downward—this is not at all fitting."

In this context, by describing the non-contextual lotus pond through the people’s bathing with their staffs, there arises the cognition of the submergence of the wealthy populace who insult the singers present at the installation ceremony; thus, there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) of the word-plays (*śleṣa*) in words such as *madhyastha* and so forth.
Since the possibility of the figure of speech *śleṣa* does not apply to either of these two cases, he says: "not even its scent.
He states the reason for this here: "of the second meaning."
This is precisely because the second meaning of these two [verses] is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
The figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia) occurs only when both meanings are expressed (*vācya*).
In the case of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) and so forth—the phrase "and so forth" including the suggestion of simile (*upamādhvani*)—[the second meaning is not expressed].
As in the verse beginning "yathā durgālaṅghitā" and so forth.
Locanā:
(lo, ai) The word "thus" (*ittham*) is a reference by means of the pronoun *idam* to that which is about to be stated and is present in the mind.
In this regard, the following has been stated immediately prior:

according to the view of certain proponents of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣin*), there is what is called "synthetic expression" (*samāsokti*), as for example: “With passion aroused, her pupils trembling...”
The moon thus seized the face of night,
such that the entire garment of darkness, even though it had slipped away before her eyes, was not noticed by her due to passion.
An example of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) is as follows:
"O deer, enough with this agitation; O gayal, abandon your fear; O buffalo..."
"Rest at your ease; do not fear the hyena. Wander at will through the mountain caves, O invincible bear!
This lord of lions, who has seen the farthest reaches of all forest lands, rejoices solely in the thick showers of large pearls falling from the frontal globes of rutting elephant-kings."
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [figures such as] *paryāyokta* and others are included.
The second meaning may be either relevant (*prakṛta*) or irrelevant (*aprakṛta*), such as the conduct of the hero and so forth.
Because it is not directly expressed, and because the function of direct denotation (*abhidhā*) ceases once the relevant meaning has been understood, this is *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

In such instances as "The swan of the mind of the learned" (*vidvanmānasahaṃsa*), even though the figure of speech is a *rūpaka* (metaphor) containing a *śleṣa* (pun), the *śleṣa* is subordinated by the *rūpaka*.
This is because the meaning in the form of a lake is the primary one, serving as the locus of final rest (*viśrāntidhāma*),
whereas in a *śleṣa*, both meanings hold equal status.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, la) He states that even in the previously mentioned *śliṣṭaparamparitarūpaka* there is no occurrence of the figure of speech *śleṣa*: "O learned one, [you are] the swan in the lake that is the mind... Here, *mānasa* refers to the lake that is the mind (*mana*) of the wise; "therein, O swan" is the address to the king.
Here, he states the reason why *rūpaka* (metaphor) sublates *śleṣa* (paronomasia): "of the form of the lake," etc.
"The state of being the locus of rest" means being the object of the final comprehension;
for it is by virtue of being the support of the swans that the *rūpaka* itself possesses such a status.
The application of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) occurs only when there is repose (*viśrānti*) in both meanings.
For example, in the phrase "pṛthukārttasvarapātram," there is repose in the two sets of qualifying attributes which possess paronomastic meanings; thus he says: "For in *śleṣa*... — *Locanā*.
(Lo, o) The *śleṣa* (punning/metaphorical identification) is sublated—having first referred to it by the designation of *śleṣa*, it is then designated as something else.
This is because, by restating the object in the form of the mind (*citta*), it fails to attain the status of being the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), which is the locus of repose.
For here, the mind and so forth, their true nature concealed, assume the form of a lake and so on.
Therefore, in this context, in the verse "Lakṣmī embraces King Nārāyaṇa intensely," the embrace by Lakṣmī—which is appropriate for one who is truly Nārāyaṇa—is described as belonging to the king.
Likewise, in the phrase "The moon-face shines," there is a description of the face having assumed the nature of the moon, wherein the attributes of the moon are superimposed upon it.
Indeed, equality [of status] here is not like that in *rūpaka*, where one element is subordinate and the other is primary.
Because each [word] is introduced by conveying its own respective meaning individually through the power of its own specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*),
as in the case of the words *vahati* and *vacana* in "he will speak to those whose hearts know," or the words *pṛthu*, *kārtasvara*, and so on in "broad gold...

Furthermore, even in cases of apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*) such as "possessing nearby darkness yet having a radiant form," there is no *śleṣa* (pun), because the contradictory meaning, being merely manifested, lacks any further development.
Vijñapriyā:

[The author] states—beginning with "sannihita" [in the verse]—that even when there is an apparent contradiction based on a double entendre (*śliṣṭavirodhābhāsa*), there is no necessity for the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
The heroine has a radiant form, meaning her form is shining; yet she is also possessed of the darkness of childhood (*bālarūpa*) in her proximity, because she produces delusion.
The description of the child as having the nature of darkness:

here, the proximity of the solar disc—the embodiment of light—to a small amount of darkness appears as a contradiction due to the double meaning (śleṣa) of the words *bāla* (child/barely) and *bhāsvat* (shining). The author states the reason why the figure of speech *śleṣa* is not applicable here: "because of the contradictory meaning."
The meaning is "merely manifested" or "merely present.
This is because there is no growth [of the object] and thus no comprehension of its continuity;
for indeed, neither is the form of the sun present in the darkness, nor is the proximity of the darkness present in the solar orb.

Thus, even for contradiction (*bādha*), the status of the figure *virodhābhāsa* (semblance of contradiction) arises merely by its presence; however, for *śleṣa* (paronomasia), the status of being an ornament occurs only when there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the paronomastic meanings.
This is because, unlike *virodhābhāsa*, an ornament called *śleṣābhāsa* (semblance of paronomasia) is not admitted.
*Locanā*:

(Lo, au) "Bāla" means small and hair. Of the radiant one—of the Sun; or as if of the radiant one who possesses luster. Since there is an absence of darkness in the solar form, there is an apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*).
Just as there is no growth of rest in accordance with the appearance,
so it is also in the case of what appears to be a repetition.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(Vi, Śa) Furthermore, regarding the phrase "thus again attached": for the understanding of the identity of meaning between the words *bhujaṅga* and *kuṇḍalin* is not ultimate; rather, such an understanding occurs through *śleṣa* (paronomasia) merely at first sight.
Therefore, in verses such as "By whom [the mountain] was destroyed," [the identity is understood] between two contextual subjects.

In passages such as "nītānām-", where there is *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing) due to the connection of a single attribute between two subjects that do not belong to the same context, [the author] says—after stating that in the aforementioned instances Śleṣa (paronomasia) sets aside those various figures of speech and that Śleṣa is thus the sublater of other figures—to express his intended view: "by which... (yena).

Regarding the word *dhvastam*: the connection with what follows is that, although *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) exists in cases such as *yena dhvastam* and *nītānām*, and *upamā* (simile) exists in cases such as *svecchopajātā*, *dīpike*, and *sakalakalam*, it is proper that they be designated by *śleṣa* (paronomasia) alone.

In the verse beginning with "By whom [the world] was destroyed," there occurs the figure of speech *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing), consisting of the connection of a single attribute—namely, the phrase "by whom [it was] destroyed"—to both Mādhava and Umādhava, who are the two subjects under discussion. As it is said: "When there is a connection through a single attribute among subjects that are either the ones under discussion or others, that is *tulyayogitā*."
“Thus, according to the definition:
for here [in the verse], the meaning is that some are exclusively contextual (*prākaraṇika*) while others are exclusively non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*).

However, in the passage beginning with ‘nītānām’ (‘of those led away’), the object in the first half-verse—namely ‘nītāni’ and so forth—is construed with two things that are both non-contextual: the forest and the lotuses.”
In the verse beginning with *svecchopajātā* and so forth, *dīpaka* (the illuminator) will be shown along with its defining characteristics.
As for *punaruktavadābhāsa* (the appearance of repetition), it is as in the previously cited example beginning with *bhujaṅgakuṇḍalī*.
For that reason, the phrase beginning with "in *tulyayogitā*" is connected with the subsequent word "vidyamānāyām" [meaning "when it exists"]. [Example:
"Though its object has arisen by its own will, it does not yield when asked even with hundreds of entreaties; it gives pain through its pursuit;

out of delusion, it suddenly snatches away even life—alas, the flower-arrowed Lord is of little intelligence!"* *This verse illustrates how the power of Love (the flower-arrowed Lord) is both present and active, yet its nature is such that it causes suffering despite being sought after.*

And in such instances as this, because the contextual and non-contextual subjects are connected by a single attribute, there is *dīpaka*. As for the meaning of that verse: in the phrase "the lord is of little intellect," the sense of the word "and" (*ca*) is to be understood.
The phrase "vaktum" here means "to speak. Thus, *kaṣṭam* signifies distress.

Even the Flower-Arrowed One (the God of Love), though he is the Lord whose domain arises by his own will and who has attained authority over all the world by his own will, being of little intellect, does not reach—that is, does not obtain—the word "dehi" (give).
Because he lacks a body, the flower-arrowed god (Kāma) is not within the range of the word "dehī" (O embodied one);
nevertheless, with hundreds of arrows—countless shafts—he inflicts suffering.
A lord of the aforementioned nature does not, nor can he, come within the reach of the words "dehī" or "dadasva" (give) used among worldly people.
The meaning is that he does not become a speaker of such words.
Through hundreds of "quests"—that is, hundreds of quests consisting of the pursuit of others' wealth—meaning, through hundreds of such foot-soldiers (padāti), he inflicts suffering.
The meaning is that even without saying "give," he inflicts suffering by seizing everything through the agency of his foot-soldiers.
The meaning is that although he has the authority (*adhikāra*) and, having said "give me," possesses the capacity to seize everything, he does not do so because of his limited intellect.
In the same way, the flower-arrowed god (Kāma), due to the delusion he himself has bestowed, suddenly and unexpectedly seizes—that is, takes away—even life itself.
Here, the subject under discussion (*prākaraṇika*) is the Lord in the form described above, while the non-contextual subject (*aprākaraṇika*) is the flower-arrowed god.
The phrase "it does not go to those two," and so forth, is an *dīpaka* (illuminator) consisting of the connection with a single attribute.
As it has been said: "That is called *dīpaka* which [occurs] between the contextual (*prastuta*) and the non-contextual (*aprastuta*).
The phrase "connection with a single attribute" is the remainder [of the definition] in that context.
Locanā:
(*lo, ā*) "By one's own will" means that for whom the object of enjoyment has arisen and is based upon one's own will.
The meaning is that since he does not go to speak, it is impossible for him to communicate his own purpose there. "Give," "bestow"—
thus, through hundreds of such entreaties, hundreds of requests, which were made again and again because of the absence of any gift.
Due to delusion, a lack of skill in discerning the gravity or lightness of an offense, and unexpectedly— that is, suddenly—
even when the transgression is very slight.
In the alternative view, however, the object of desire is the woman and so forth who serve as its locus;
"he does not go to speak" means that he does not go to say, "Such is my desire at present."

"By merely [saying] 'the body' or 'the living being,' without regard for the distinction [between them], due to delusion there is no discernment of the self through hundreds of searches. "Kaṣṭam" is an indeclinable used in the sense of despondency.
The meaning is that [the figure] exists when the *dīpaka* (illuminator) is present.

Furthermore, in such instances as "This entire city has now become like the orb of the moon, filled with every sound (*sakalakalam*)," although a simile (*upamā*) is present, the pun (*śleṣa*) cannot occur because it must avoid this very domain [of the simile]. And these [other figures], even while avoiding the domain of the pun...
Since, in this context, the charm is perceived primarily through the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) due to its persistence, it is proper that the designation should be given to the *śleṣa* alone;
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that such a designation would never occur at all.
Thus says the *Vijñapriyā*.

In examples such as *sakalakalam*, the simile based on the double entendre (*śliṣṭopamā*)—which possesses two meanings, namely "possessing all arts" (*sakalakalāvat*) and "possessing the word *kalakala* (uproar)" (*kalakalaśabdavat*)—is indeed evident. In that case, since there is a mutual absence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), he confirms the status of both as figures of speech and states that among objects where both [figures] exist, *śleṣa* alone is more appropriate: "This belongs to *śleṣa*" and so forth. For in instances such as *pratikūlatām upagate hi vidhau*, *śleṣa* exists while excluding this specific scope [of simile], whereas *tulyayogitā*, *dīpaka*, and *upamā* exist while excluding *śleṣa* in many examples.
[The figure] is to be seen [in these cases].
He states the reason why the ornament of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) alone is appropriate in these instances: "because it produces aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) through its predominance.
"Otherwise" means...

The meaning is that even in these cases, only the three beginning with *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) possess the status of figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*). Regarding the phrase "of that designation," it means "of the designation as *śleṣa* (punning)."
Nor should it be argued: "How can there be the consequence of its absence?
For that [hetu] exists precisely in cases such as 'hostility' (pratikūlatām) and so forth.
For even there, since approaching with hostility is the cause for the futility of many means, the figure of speech *hetu* (poetic cause) is present.
Locanā: (Lo,
I) "Sakalakalam" means accompanied by the sound of clamor, and endowed with all-pervading splendors and arts.

The strikingness of these three figures—tulyayogitā and the others—is due to the poet’s employment of a word with double meaning (*dvayartha-śabda*) as a means for awakening a sense of aesthetic variety (*vaicitrya*).

Regarding this, it is said: first of all, *śleṣa* (paronomasia) does not, in an ultimate sense, have a scope that is indistinguishable from other figures, because its scope is distinguished [from them] by examples such as "yenadhvasta...
Nor is there *tulyayogitā* here.
And because there is no rule that both of these two meanings must necessarily be the expressed (vācya),
in this case, if one of the two— Mādhava or Umādhava— were restricted to being the expressed meaning, the other would necessarily be the suggested (vyaṅgya). —
Locanā:
(lo, ī) Here he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "In this case," because there is no restrictive rule regarding the status of being expressed (*vācyatva*).
This is because, in cases such as "by whom [it] was destroyed" and so forth, there is an absence of restriction by context (*prakaraṇa*) and the like, according to the manner previously described.
In the case of *mādhava* and *mādhava-artha*, there is a restriction that both must be expressed;
however, in the figure of speech *tulyayogitā*, there is no such restriction that both must be expressed.

By accepting the principle of *tantratā* (simultaneous application) regarding the two words, there is a restriction that both are expressed. Furthermore, according to the view of the *dhvanitantra* school, the point is that one is expressed while the other is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
He specifies this very point with the words "for here" (*atra hi*).
"Here" refers to the passage beginning with "by whom [ignorance] was destroyed" (*yena dhvasta* etc.).
Immediately after "for here," the phrase "in the acceptance of *tulyayogitā*" (*tulyayogitāṅgīkāre*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
Furthermore— while in *tulyayogitā* there is the cognition of a single attribute as being related to multiple subjects,
here, however, there is the cognition of multiple subjects each being related to their own respective attributes.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ka) Thus, having demonstrated the view of certain scholars that figures of speech such as *tulyayogitā* (parallelism), which have been shown by means of the exception (*apavāda*) to be subordinate to *śleṣa* (paronomasia), are sublated— because there is no domain for other figures of speech distinct from *śleṣa*, and because *śleṣa* itself is a general figure since there exists a domain for other figures distinct from it— [the following is stated].
To refute that, he says: "In this regard, it is replied.
Only if there were no distinct domain for *śleṣa* (paronomasia) separate from other figures of speech would it be a sublater [of them];
but that is not the case.
He says that for this [poem] as well, the object is distinct from those [other figures], beginning with "Not, first of all, in the ultimate sense.
He shows the object as being distinct from other ornaments with the words "by which it was destroyed," etc.;
here, the reading "yena dhvastam" and so forth is the correct one.

In some places, however, the reading is "yena dhvasta" and so forth. In that case, the meaning of the verse beginning with "iti" is that [the two are distinct] because their objects are separate, by virtue of that reason.

Here, one might suspect the presence of the poetic figure *tulyayogitā* (parallelism), since the two subjects under discussion, Mādhava and Umādhava, share a common attribute in the phrase beginning with "yena. To this, he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
He explains [the phrase] "in that" (*tasyām*):

the meaning is "in the case of *tulyayogitā* (parallelism). [An objection is raised: "But even here, there is the expressibility (*vācyatva*) of two contextual subjects. To this he replies: "For here... (*atra hi*).
In this case, there is no determining factor when both meanings are equally contextual (*prākaraṇika*).

Thus, if the speaker had commenced with only one meaning and uttered this verse, then—since the other meaning would be suggested (*vyaṅgya*) and Tulyayogitā would consequently have no scope here—this alone would be the domain of Śleṣa, distinct from the figure of Tulyayogitā. This is the sense.

Nor should it be argued that, even so, this *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is merely mixed with the figure of speech *vyaṅgyopamā* (implied simile); for when an ornament whose status as such is possible is merely suggested (*vyaṅgya*), it lacks the nature of an ornament.

Rather, it is designated as an "ornament" there solely because it is an *alaṅkāra-dhvani* (suggested ornament), and its status as an ornament in the state of being expressed (*vācyatā-daśā*) is merely figurative, according to the maxim of the "Brahmin who is a monk."

However, since the figures of speech *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) and *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (praise of the irrelevant) can exist as expressed meanings (*vācyatva*), they possess the status of figures of speech even when they are suggested (*vyaṅgyatva*).

Now, one might object: "Since both Mādhava and Umādhava share the same case-ending, they are equally the primary subjects (*prakaraṇikatva*); therefore, because both are expressed meanings here, this is merely *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing). To this, he says: "Furthermore... [and] "of a single attribute alone... etc.
But it does not mean [the denotation] of two properties that are not expressible by a single word;
"here, however" means in the passage beginning with "by which [it] was destroyed," and so forth.
In the phrase "of many," plurality is not intended;
the meaning is "of Umādhava and Mādhava.
By means of distinct attributes, the single word that is homophonous (śliṣṭa) possesses two distinct meanings, such as those in the forms of Anoma and Manobhava, and so forth.

In the phrase "sambandhitayā," the word "pratītiḥ" (cognition) is to be construed [with it]. Thus, it should be understood that the previous demonstration of *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) in the examples beginning with "yena dhvastā... and "nītānām... was merely a demonstration of the views of others.
In reality, however, it should be understood that it has been established that in those two cases, there is indeed *śleṣa* (punning compounding), which is devoid of *tulyayogitā*.
Locanā:
(lo, u) He states another logical inconsistency with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*).
This is the underlying intention:
"Having purified the quarters of the sky with her wanderings, at the end of the day,
the radiance of the sun— copper-red like the hue of a young leaf— and the cow of the sage both set out to go to their respective resting places."

In examples such as these, within the figure *tulyayogitā* (parallelism), there is a cognition of a single attribute—in the form of the commencement of going to their respective abodes—as being connected to two subjects, namely *saurabhī* and *prabhā*.

However, in the present case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is a cognition of many subjects—such as Mādhava and Uddhava—being connected to distinct attributes in the form of "by whom the mind-born [Kāma] was destroyed" and so forth; this is the logical connection (*anvaya*), because the words expressing the attributes are of different forms.
In *tulyayogitā*, however, although the commencement of going to the dwelling has different purposes, there is a unity through the determination of oneness (*ekatādhyavasāya*).
This is not the case in [the verse] beginning with "by whom [darkness] was destroyed," where there is no determination of oneness between the two attributes residing in Mādhava and Umādhava,
because since both are uncertain, they lack the status of being either the subject at hand (*prakṛta*) or not subject at hand (*aprakṛta*).

Although in *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing) as well, there is no status of being "contextual" (*prakṛta*) or "non-contextual" (*aprakṛta*) for the two [elements], nevertheless that distinction is intended there, because even the ancients accepted the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) in that case.
Furthermore, in examples such as "sakalakalam," the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is not the cause for the emergence of the semblance of a simile (*upamā-pratibhā-hetu*).
If it is argued that the full simile (*pūrṇopamā*) would otherwise be rendered devoid of scope—since there exists a domain for the full simile such as, "This face is as charming as a lotus"—we reply:
no. If there is no simile in cases like "sakala-" due to its being a verbal pun (*śabdaśleṣa*), then what offense has been committed by the semantic pun (*arthaśleṣa*) in "manojñam" and so forth?
[One might say: "Clearly, these two, simile and conjunction (*samuccaya*), are semantic ornaments (*arthālaṅkāra*); however—"
"Even here, it is possible by relying on a mere word as a universal."
Thus, according to the direction stated by Rudraṭa, since verbal similarity (*śabdasāmya*)—along with the similarity of qualities and actions—is also a cause for the employment of simile (*upamā*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, kha) Likewise, in examples such as "sakalakalam," even though a simile exists, it is [regarded] as an exception (*apavāda*), and thus only the pun (*śleṣa*) [is primary].

It has been stated that a designation ought to be made on the basis of predominance; in that context, he demonstrates that the ornament is *upamā* (simile) alone, not *śleṣa* (paronomasia)—as in the verse beginning with "sakalakalam" and so forth—by saying, "there is no emergence of the semblance of *upamā*.
Here, "the semblance of *upamā*" (*upamāpratibhā*) means the cognition of *upamā*.
That very [śleṣa] is the cause of its arising—that is, the cause for the arising of the cognition [of the simile];
such is not the case with the śleṣa itself;
the meaning is that the śleṣa is not what is made known by the cognition of the simile.
The simile (upamā) merely indicates the presence of paronomasia (śleṣa).
The meaning is that [the opponent's claim] is not correct because, in this case, paronomasia alone is the figure of speech (alaṅkāra).
Thus, he has stated that the figure of speech is indeed the simile, which consists in the similarity of qualities based on paronomasia.

Regarding that, he states the undesirable consequence of treating *śleṣa* (paronomasia) alone as the figure of speech while subverting the *upamā* (simile), beginning with the words "of the complete simile" (*pūrṇopamāyāḥ*).

For a *pūrṇopamā* occurs when there is the employment of all four—the object of comparison (*upamāna*), the object compared (*upameya*), the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and the particle such as *iva*.
Here too, the city is the object compared.
The object of comparison (*upamāna*) is the reflection in the mirror;

the common property (*sādharmya*) consists in the possession of both qualities by the complete and melodious form; and since the word "as if" (*iva*) is present, this is a complete simile (*pūrṇopamā*).

The meaning is that, because *śleṣa* (paronomasia) alone would be the figure of speech here due to its sublation [of other elements], the *pūrṇopamā* (complete simile) would result in being rendered objectless.

One might object: "But surely, the *pūrṇopamā* is simply a simile based on the similarity of qualities devoid of *śleṣa*; therefore, the very domain where that [similarity] exists should be the domain of the *pūrṇopamā*. To this, he raises the doubt with the example: "Like a lotus... (*kamalamiva*).

For here, *śleṣa* (punning) does not occur because of the similarity between the two actions alone—namely, the description of the quality of being "pleasing" (*manojñatva*) and the act of speaking—but rather because of the punning words themselves. To provide a counter-argument to that, he says: "If...
*Śleṣa* is of two kinds: verbal *śleṣa* (*śabdaśleṣa*) and semantic *śleṣa* (*arthaleṣa*).

If, in the case of "sakalakalam" (all-sounding), the figure of speech is considered to be *śleṣa* (paronomasia) alone by setting aside *upamā* (simile), then it would follow that even in cases such as "the face is like a lotus," *śleṣa* as a figure of sense (*artha-śleṣa*) would set aside *upamā*. The point is: what offense has been committed by the qualities such as "loveliness" (*manojñatva*), since they are equally connected through their shared application (*anvaya*) in both instances? However, if it is held that *upamā* alone is experienced there because of the presence of the word "iva" (like), then in "sakalakalam" and similar cases as well, it is precisely *upamā* that is experienced due to the similarity of words (*śabda-sādharmya*). With this intention, he cites Rudraṭa’s statement here as authority: "sphuṭamartha... (clearly the sense...).

Here too, even within the midst of verbal figures of speech (*śabdālaṅkāra*), in the verse "O lady with thighs like plantain stalks (*rambhoru*), passion arose for you in my heart and [in my body]," there is the figure of *samuccaya* (accumulation) due to the commonality of the words. —
*Locanā*:
(Lo, Ū) It is not only that the scope of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is distinct from other figures of speech;
he states [the following] because it is also impossible for it to exist in the domain of *pūrṇopamā* (full simile) and the like—namely, "entirely" (*sakala*).

In the section on *pūrṇopamā*, in cases such as "like a lotus," where there is *śleṣa* of the implied meaning (*lakṣyamāṇārtha*), what has been wronged by the acceptance of a distinction between the correlates (*pratisambandhin*)—the lotus and the face—with respect to the attribute of "charmingness"?
The sense is: since the fault is equal in the case of *śabdaśleṣa* (verbal punning), why do you not accept *pūrṇopamā* (complete simile) in this matter, yet claim to accept it there?
The implication is that both cases are identical. To explain how the two cases share the same logical principle, he says: "Clearly" (*sphuṭam*).
Accumulation (*samuccaya*) is, for example, "honored by the earth" (*vasudhā-mahita*), and so forth.
The commonality (*sāmānyam*) is a shared quality (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*).
Here, among the verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṅkāra*), it refers to the equality of qualities (*guṇasāmyam*).
"Like a lotus," and so forth;
and similarity of action, such as "the face shines like the moon.
Now, it might be argued that it is only the similarity of qualities and actions that ought to be the basis for the employment of simile (*upamā*).
In that case, because similarity is real,
whereas it is not so for the mere identity of words, because there the similarity is unreal.

If it is argued that, because a complete simile (*pūrṇopamā*) would otherwise be impossible, it is proper for the complete simile to apply when the equality of qualities and actions alone—being the domain of semantic punning (*arthaśleṣa*)—is set aside, and not when there is only an equality of words as in the example beginning with "sakala-," we reply:
No; for the general definition of simile, "simile is similarity" (*sādharmyam upamā*), does not exclude cases of equality of words.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ga) "Because the similarity there is unreal" means that the word lacks the property of being the lunar disc in the sky. This is the intended sense.
And therefore, since there is no possibility of a simile (*upamā*) in cases such as "sakalakalam" and so forth, let there be only the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia) there.

To avoid the contingency that the full simile (*pūrṇopamā*) would be rendered without scope, [the author] says "and therefore," suggesting that even in the case of similarity through qualities or actions, one should set aside *artha-śleṣa* and allow for the full simile itself.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "But in cases such as 'sakalakalam,' it is not the similarity of words (*śabda-sādharmya*) that serves as the cause for the application of a simile."

"Because of the commonality of the word (*śabdasādharmya*) and because of the absence of exclusion (*vyāvṛttyabhāva*)"—the meaning is that [the definition of simile] lacks exclusion due to its similarity of words, and also because it has the similarity of words as its object.
Furthermore, the commonality of the word is by way of the relationship of denotation (*vācakatā-sambandha*), the sense being that [the word] resides in that [similarity]. (Locanā)

In that regard, when there is equality of qualities and actions—whether on account of being real (*vāstavatva*), inherent (*svābhāvikatva*), unreal (*avāstavatva*), or non-ultimate (*atāttvikatva*)—it is logical that it falls within the scope of *pūrṇopamā* (complete simile), because there is no other alternative; this is the intended meaning. The phrase "of that which is undistinguished" (*aviśiṣṭasya*) means that which is not specifically designated. Regarding the equality of qualities and actions: [this applies] even when they are not specified as distinct.
And if similarity based on the identity of words were not a cause for comparison because it lacks reality,

then how could, in examples such as "vidvanmānasa-," the superimposition of a lake and so forth upon the mind and other bases— which serve as the substrata— be the cause for the superimposition of a king and so forth?
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, gha) For if, because the relation of denotative capacity lacks the function of determining the occurrence [of a linguistic operation], the similarity of form between words is unreal and thus cannot serve as the cause for an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), then how could the form consisting of the superimposition of non-difference between the two meanings through similarity—by virtue of being expressed by words—be the cause for the ornament of *rūpaka* in the case of *paramparita-rūpaka*? To this, he says: "In the case of similarity of words."
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) He states another objection with the words "or if" (*yadi vā*).

The meaning is this: if similarity of words in cases such as *sakalakalam* and so forth does not serve as the basis for a simile (*upamā*), then how is it that in "O swan of the mind of the wise" (*vidvanmānasahaṃsa*) and similar instances, the superimposition (*āropa*) of the king upon a swan has the unique function of [suggesting] the *mānasa* lake?

Furthermore, if a simile must be accepted only when there is actual identity [between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison], then how is it that you yourself accept a sublated simile (*bādhyabhūtopamā*) in such cases as "sakalakalam" and so forth?
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṅa) [Objection: Is it not the case that "similarity" (*sādharmya*) is simply a common property (*samāno dharma*), and if that [property] is unreal, such similarity is untenable?

However, in examples such as *vidvanmānasa*, since there is a superimposition of identity (*abhedāropa*)—which is produced by the mind (*āhārya*)—it is indeed possible even if the [property] is unreal, provided there is no defect in the form of the words being ambiguous (*śliṣṭa*). To this, he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
"An object of sublation that is like a simile" means that in the absence of being a simile, even its status as an object of sublation would be untenable. —
*Locanā*:
(lo, ḷ) Furthermore, he states another objection with the words "kiñca" (moreover).
The meaning is that *śleṣa* (paronomasia), being subject to sublation, has attained the status of an exception (*apavāda*) to all other figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*).
How can this be accepted?
The meaning is that only that which is established by a general rule (utsarga) can be sublated by an exception (apavāda).
Furthermore, in this case, it is the pun (śleṣa) itself that effects the accomplishment of the similarity (sāmya), and not the similarity that effects the accomplishment of the pun.

Because similarity cannot exist first through the bond of *śleṣa* (punning), it is more appropriate to designate the *upamā* (simile) alone as the primary element, according to the maxim: "Designations are made by means of the principal.

Now, if it is objected: "In the domain of verbal figures (*śabdālaṅkāra*), a commingling (*saṅkara*) of the relationship between primary and subordinate elements is not admitted; so how can there be a commingling of *śleṣa* and *upamā* here as a relationship of primary and subordinate? [The answer follows:]...
No, for even in cases such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*), such status [of being a *guṇa*] is not accepted when it is devoid of consideration for the meaning.
This should be understood to apply likewise to cases such as the *dīpaka* figure.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(Vi, ca) Now, one might object that in that very case, because of the similarity consisting in being cognizable by the word, the term "simile" (*upamā*) there is merely figurative; to this he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). "Of the *śleṣa* alone" means "of the word that is itself *śliṣṭa*" (possessing double meaning).
The phrase "establishing the similarity" means establishing the similarity that constitutes the basis for the simile (*upamā*).
The meaning is that this occurs only when the dual nature [of the object] is known, because it is through the cognition of such similarity— consisting of the meaning of a single word—
that the composition of *śleṣa* (punning) first takes place.
Because, in the absence of alliteration and verbal composition, the similarity between the city and the lunar orb would not be perceived—
since [the former] is the primary element (*aṅgin*) by virtue of being the object of ultimate comprehension—
and thus, when the perception of similarity arises through the recollection of the meanings of the punned words (*śliṣṭapada*), the simile (*upamā*) is subsequently perceived as that primary element.
The meaning is that *śleṣa* (paronomasia), however, is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) whose nature is to bring about the realization of that [primary figure].
The relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is the relationship between the realizer and the realized (*nirvāhaka-nirvāhyabhāva*).
This is likewise the case for *dīpaka* (illumination) and other such figures.
The meaning is that even in poetic figures such as *dīpaka* (illumination) and *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing), *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is their subordinate element (*aṅga*).
Locanā:
(Lo, e) Thus, in this case, the simile (*upamā*) possesses the status of the principal element (*aṅgin*) because it is the cause for the emergence of the suggestion of *śleṣa*.
He further confirms that *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) by means of another argument, stating: "Moreover, here... Similarity (*sāmya*) is the cause of *upamā* (simile);
[here, however, there is] a combination (*saṃkara*) based on the relationship of the subordinate and the principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).
The manner described as "but when there is a relationship of principal and subordinate among those [figures] that do not rest within themselves, it is *saṃkara* (commixture)" applies here.

The point is this: because there is no connection of meaning (*arthānanusandhāna*), the commixture of subordinate and principal status (*aṅgāṅgibhāva-saṃkara*) is not accepted for figures of sound such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*), since they are mutually independent;

however, since *śleṣa* (punning) and other such figures do involve a connection of meaning, they are dependent, and thus, given the possibility of mutual dependence, why is their commixture not admitted? This is the intended sense.
The principle of expressing a simile through a single common attribute should be understood to apply to *dīpaka* and other such figures as well.

This is the meaning: just as the presence of verbal similarity (*śabdasāmya*) constitutes the basis for a simile and thus makes it a constituent part of a *śleṣa*, so too does it constitute the basis for *dīpaka* and other figures, thereby making it a constituent part of those figures.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [examples of] *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) and so forth are included:
“Possessing fine wings, sweet voices, having adorned the quarters, and embarking upon their flight with pride,
the Dhārtarāṣṭra geese fall upon the surface of the earth under the power of Time.”
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, cha) Having thus established that in the verse beginning with "sakalakalam" there is only a simile (*upamā*) and not a pun (*śleṣa*), he states—starting with the words "satpakṣā"—that even in the case of a suggestion of a matter (*vastudhvani*) dependent on a pun, the figure of speech is not *śleṣa*.
This is a description of the autumn season, which is the contextual subject (*prākaraṇika*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here is as follows: at that time, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—referring to a specific kind of swan with black-colored beaks and feet—alight upon the surface of the earth due to the influence of the autumn season.
