*Pakṣam* means a wing or feather. *Āśāprasādhanam* means the accomplishment of their direction, that is, traveling in the various quarters.

Since the root *sādh*, as used by thieves and others, has the meaning of "going," the speaker's intention here lies in the inauspiciousness regarding the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the fact of their death is suggested through the power of the double-entendre (*śliṣṭaśabda*).
In this context, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—Duryodhana and the others—are "those who have adorned the quarters," meaning they have governed the entire circle of the directions;
for this very reason, their undertakings were arrogant with pride.

Being "of good wings" means they had excellent allies; yet, by the power of time—that is, by the power of Yama—they fall upon the beloved earth, despite being "sweet-voiced," meaning they possessed charming speech. This is the sense.
Locanā:
(lo, ai) "Having good wings" (satpakṣāḥ); here, "wing" (pakṣa) means both a feather and an ally.
"Adorned" means decorated and brought under their own control with excellence;
"the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra" refers to the swans, namely Duryodhana and the others.
[The author] here dispels any suspicion that this is intended as a mere simile (*upamā*).

Here, because the context of the description of autumn restricts words such as *dhārtarāṣṭra* to their meanings as "swans" and so forth, the meaning in the form of Duryodhana and others is a *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact) based on the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūla*).

Furthermore, since in this case the second meaning—the subject matter of the current composition—is intended solely for the purpose of being indicated (*sūcya*), the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) is not intended; thus, there is neither *upamādhvani* (suggestion of simile) nor *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Everything is clear.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ja) He states "here too" (*iha ca*) because neither the status of being a suggested simile (*upamādhvanitva*) nor the figure of speech of paronomasia (*śleṣālaṅkāra*) applies here.

"The present work" (*prakṛtaprabandha*) refers to the drama *Veṇīsaṃhāra*; "of its subject matter" (*tadabhidheyasya*) means of that which is to be conveyed by it; and "of the second meaning" (*dvitīyārthasya*)—namely, the death of the Kurus—is meant in the sense of being indicated (*sūcyatayā*), that is, as something suggested (*vyaṅgyatayā*).
But it is not by way of being compared to a swan; such is the meaning of the particle *eva*.
He explains that very point with the words "the object of comparison" (*upameya*) and "and there is no pun" (*na ca śleṣaḥ*).
The sense is that there is no denotability of both meanings simultaneously.
Thus, "everything is clear":
in verses such as "by whom [it] was destroyed," the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is indeed unmixed with any other figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
The meaning is that it has been clarified that in passages such as "sakalakalam," the poetic figure is indeed *upamā* (simile) constructed through *śleṣa* (punning).
Locanā:
(lo, o) The present work is the drama named *Veṇīsaṃhāra*.

Because it is intended precisely as a *sūcya* (to be indicated), it is stated right here in the context of the definition of drama: "One should indicate either the seed of the plot (*vastubīja*), or the principal character. The meaning is that there is a relationship of the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) between the swans and others on one hand, and Duryodhana and others on the other.
Furthermore, this is not *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Since the description of autumn itself is the subject at hand, the term "variegated" (*citram*) refers to the colors being the cause of the forms of lotuses and so forth. —
*Locanā*:

(lo, au) Now, he defines *citra* (puzzle-poetry), which, although it does not assist the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), was nonetheless classified among the ornaments by the ancients because poets have composed it for the sake of demonstrating their various powers. He begins with the verse starting "padma" (lotus).
Regarding its status as an ornament, the seed is simply the onset of wonder produced by the force of such skill and refinement.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), sword-figures, muraja-figures, wheel-figures, *gomūtrikā*, and so forth are included.

And because of the metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) of these phonemes—which produce aesthetic wonder by virtue of their specific arrangement in such a script—as being non-different from those phonemes that produce aesthetic wonder by virtue of their specific conjunction with the auditory space (*śrotrākāśa*), they constitute verbal figures of speech (*śabdālaṅkāra*). [The *Vijñapriyā*] states the figure of speech known as *citra*: "In the lotus... and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that since it is the arrangement of the letters themselves—reminders of the phonemes—that takes the form of a lotus and so forth, and since the letters are not sounds, it is untenable for this to be a verbal figure of speech (*śabdālaṅkāra*), he provides the following resolution:

"By such an auditory [perception]," which means that because of the specific inherence (*samavāya*) of the phoneme reminded by such a script within the ether in the form of the ear, there is a figurative identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the script with the phonemes that produce aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).

It should be understood that the conjunction with the auditory ether (*śrotrākāśa-samavāya*) produces the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) through this following sequence: such a conjunction generates the experience of the phonemes; from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [experience], there arises the recollection of the phonemes from the written script; and from that, the wonder [arises].
The pursuit of the series down to the "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is for the sake of obtaining the conjunction as defined by each respective phoneme.
Locanā:
(lo, a) Such a "deployment of letters" (*lipiniveśa*) is that which is experienced by the sense of sight;

it is a particular arrangement (*sanniveśaviśeṣa*), a specific mode of placement (*niveśaviśeṣa*) on a surface such as the ground, which, by its very nature, is conducive to the successful accomplishment of one's intended purpose.
The meaning is: "by virtue of that" means "having made that the cause.
[This refers to] the phonemes being experienced by such an auditory faculty, which—by implication—are the instigators of poetic figures (alaṃkāra) such as alliteration (anuprāsa).

The point here is that if one were to accept the status of a verbal figure merely on the basis of its following the presence and absence (anvaya-vyatireka) of the word *śabda*, then it would necessarily be included within the category of alliteration.
Among these, the *padmabandha* (lotus-arrangement) is as follows, from my own work:

“May she, who possesses a beauty like that of Māra, who is more lovely than the most excellent women of Māra, and who is the abode of the highest skill in subduing the wicked— may that charming woman, not being the goddess Ramā, be mine.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ña) She charms Māra;
she is Māramā, Suṣamā, Cāru, Rucā, Sārā, and Dhūttamā.
May that most excellent of women, who has conquered the greatest of rogues, be my Māramā.
Thus is the verse.

Its meaning is as follows: *sā* (she) is *vāmā* (beautiful), *mā* (me), *āra* (has come); she is distinguished by her lovely luster (*cārurucā*), and for that very reason, she is incomparable (*māsuṣamā*).

Possessing a supreme splendor equal to that of Lakṣmī, and thus like Rati, the most excellent consort of Māra—Kāma—why have they not come here out of deceit? To this he replies: "They are the most exceedingly clever."
"Most cunning" means "again.
To the question "How then has she not come?", he replies: "Naked"—that is, devoid of *vāsa*, which means a dwelling or residence.
Having heard this, the hero blesses himself: "She is beautiful (*vāmā*)."
Because it is connected with what precedes and, by way of repetition, is also connected later on, may that Vāmā—my Māra-mā, the goddess of desire—be mine.

By virtue of the repetition, the word "sā vāmā" is connected even later; and because that [word] belongs to another [syllabic] unit and refers to that [subsequent meaning], the substitution *me* occurs for *mama*.
This is an eight-petaled lotus composition (*aṣṭadala-padma-bandha*), with its syllables joined through both outward exit and inward entry at the cardinal petals.
However, in the intermediate petals it is otherwise;
the syllable of the pericarp, moreover, is joined [to the others].
In this manner, the *khaḍgabandha* and other such arrangements are also to be inferred.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) To demonstrate the method of its construction, he says: "This is the eight-petaled lotus arrangement.
And its eight-petaled nature is to be drawn with petals for the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Regarding the phrase "by means of entry and exit":
having written the first syllable upon the pericarp, two syllables each should be written upon the petals;
it should be understood that this is done precisely by means of exit and entry.
Locanā:
(Lo, Ā) She who brings about the destruction of Māra—Māra is Viṣṇu, so called because he sports with Lakṣmī; she is equal to his life-breath, that is, she is dear to him like his own life.
Bhāravadhū means Rati.
Even more than that, she is supreme and most excellent.
The meaning is that she has not become such as to be "attained" or "seized"—that is, to be the dwelling place of the most wicked.
Such is that renowned Ramā, Lakṣmī, who is my beloved (vāmā).
The connection is: "May they be desirous.
Regarding "this eight-petaled [lotus]":
having placed the syllable "Mā" in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should write the two syllables of "Ramā" there on the petals in the cardinal directions.

Having entered with the two syllables *su* and *ṣa* by means of the petal in the intermediate direction, one performs the exit and entry by means of the other two syllables, *cā* and *ru*, through the petal in the opposite direction.

Immediately after that, having placed the two syllables *ra* and *va* on the intermediate petal, and having entered again by means of the two syllables *dhū* and *rta* on the subsequent directional petal, one exits once more from the syllable at the pericarp (*karṇikā*) by means of the two syllables *ta* and *mā*.
Again, having entered the intermediate petal immediately following that, and then the cardinal petal, there is entry and exit by means of the two syllables "vā" and "sā."

Having emerged from the petal of the opposite direction with the two syllables "me 'stu," and having again emerged and entered the petal of the eastern direction with the two syllables "māra," one comes to rest at the syllable "mā" when it has reached the state of the pericarp;
this is the conjoined phoneme (*śliṣṭavarṇa*), which is the undivided phoneme (*abhinnavarṇa*).
The syllable at the pericarp is "Mā.
The sword-knot (*khaḍgabandha*) is as follows:
"She who is served by all beings—the foremost among gods, demons, brahmins, and serpents—bringing an end to suffering and heat, darkening the autumnal moon with her own radiance..."
May that daughter of the ocean protect you—she who is shared by her friends, whose necklace is joined with the Lord of the entire world, and by whom all sins have been destroyed.
However, it is not elaborated upon here because it functions as a mere excrescence within poetry.
*Locanā*:
"By functioning as a mere excrescence" means by being as insubstantial as a goitre that has entered into the middle of a poem.
Because it acts as an obstacle to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the *prahelikā* (enigma) is not a poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
That [type of riddle], consisting of the shifting or giving away of syllables and so forth, is merely a variety of expression.
Vijñapriyā (vi, ṭha) says "of rasa" in order to state the *prahelikā* (enigma).
It is not that the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) does not enhance the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), but rather that it is exclusively an ornament of expression; thus he says, "merely a variety of expression.
Consequently, since it possesses the general definition of an ornament—that "variety is an ornament"—the meaning is that it is indeed an ornament of expression.

He says that this action—consisting of the three types beginning with *cyutadattā*—as well as [the actions] beginning with *gupti*, exists; thus he states: "*cyutadattā*. *Cyutākṣarā* is one in which a syllable has been dropped.
*Dattākṣarā* is one in which an additional syllable has been added to what was stated.
*Cyutadattākṣarā* (the one with displaced and supplied syllables) is that in which one syllable has been displaced and another syllable is supplied in its place.
It consists of *cyutākṣarā*, *dattākṣarā*, and *cyutadattākṣarā*.
An example: [Example omitted per instructions]
“The cuckoos coo upon the *sāla* tree, and the lotus blooms in its youth;
what can the doe do, being tormented by the face [of her husband]?”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍa) He provides a single example for this triad, beginning with the words "kūjanti.

Although the literal meaning is possible here, the intended sense lies solely in the "dropping" and "inserting" of syllables (*cyutadattākṣaratva*), because it consists of a statement that is not useful [to the context].
The nature of a riddle (*prahelikā*) therein consists in the meaning not being apparent upon literal hearing, as for example: "Cuckoos warble in the *śāla* tree;
the lotus blooms in the youth of women;
what can the deer-eyed woman do when she is pressed against by the face?"

This is an example of a statement that is not purposeful (*anupayuktakathana*). However, when syllables are dropped or added, it becomes a purposeful statement—as for example: “The cuckoos warble on the mango tree; in the forest and in the water, the lotus is in bloom.”
"Afflicted by passion due to these excitants, what can the deer-eyed woman do?"—

here, where "rasāle" (mango tree) should have been said, "sāle" is used, and the letter *ra* has been dropped; and where "vane" (in the forest) should have been said, "yauvane" (in youth) is used, and the letters *yau* have been added.
In the phrase "vadanena," [the word] "madanena" [is intended], where the letter "ma" has been dropped and "va" has been substituted.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [examples of] the concealment of action (kriyāgupti), the concealment of the grammatical factor (kārakagupti), and so forth are included. Among these, the concealment of action is as follows:
“Duryodhana arrived in the midst of the assembly hall of the Pāṇḍavas;
to him [the king] gave a cow, gold, and all kinds of ornaments.”
In this context, where one says "Duryodhana," it is [actually] "aduryo 'dhanaḥ. Here, "aduḥ" constitutes the concealment of the verb (*kriyāgupti*).
The same applies elsewhere as well.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍha) Here, he shows the syllables that have been dropped and supplied—“here” (*atra*).
The passage beginning with “of the Pāṇḍavas” (*pāṇḍavānām*) and so forth is clear.

Regarding the concealment of the agent (*kāraka-gupti*) and so forth, as in my own verse: “With notes that have attained harmony with the *ṣaḍja* scale and are enchanting to the ear, he surely triumphs over every peacock perched upon the mountain peak.”
Thus, in this context, in the phrase "the peacock conquers," the agent is elided.
According to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, the meaning is: "The peacock, whose face is like that of a horse, delights all people situated on the peak of the mountain.
An example of the concealment of the object (*karmagupti*) is as follows: "May this person, exhausted by many tasks, ward off [this] coming [danger]."
I shall give a wage to this man for his exhaustion from the journey.
"In this case, [the meaning is] 'this person wards off';
its action is hidden.
But according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), *vāḥ* means water; thus, 'this person causes it to go' (*ayati yāti*)."

O fair-complexioned maiden of Vraja, you truly shine with this bright smile of Mukunda, even though it is dark. [This is an example of] the concealment of a missing syllable (*akṣaralopagupti*) and the presentation of a contradiction (*viruddhapradarśana*).
Here, [the name] *mukunda* possesses contradictory attributes through the words *śubhreṇa*, *hasitena*, and *asitena*.
In this very context, the elision of a certain syllable is concealed;
however, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since the word *mukunda* is devoid of the letter *m*, its meaning is *kundena*.
And thus, the meaning is that she was shining because of that smile characterized by *kundas* (jasmine flowers).

Now, among the figures of speech (*arthālaṅkāras*) based on similarity that are to be defined as they arise in due course, he first speaks of *upamā* (simile), because it is primary as the foundation upon which even those other figures depend—
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṇa) He says "Now" (*atha*) in order to state the figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*).

Regarding the phrase "because of their predominance among those based on similarity": there are many figures such as simile (*upamā*), metaphor (*rūpaka*), and poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that are based on similarity. Because they produce a greater degree of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) than other figures, it is appropriate to define them first.
The meaning is that even there, because it is the basis upon which all others depend, he mentions simile first.
And its status as the basis for all others is due to the fact that, everywhere, simile flashes forth first by virtue of similarity (*sādṛśya*).
— *Locanā* —

(lo, ī) Now, regarding "atha": after the determination of verbal figures (*śabdālaṅkāra*), [the author proceeds] to the figures of meaning (*arthālaṅkāra*), which consist of the definitions of the specific varieties of figures of meaning.
To the word "prādhānyāt" (due to predominance), the word "first" (*prathamam*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
Their status as the basis for subsistence arises from their functioning as the root [of all other figures].

As it has been said: "Simile alone, through its variety of modes, is the seed of all poetic ornaments. "Simile (*upamā*) consists of the similarity between two things expressed in a single sentence, provided there is no absence of common properties (*avaidharmya*). (VisSd 10.14)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta) "Similarity" means the absence of dissimilarity, that is, the non-statement of a difference in nature.
The meaning is that *upamā* (simile) occurs when the similarity between two things— the object compared (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)— is expressed within a single sentence.
In figures such as *rūpaka* (metaphor), this similarity is suggested (*vyaṅgya*),
whereas in *vyatireka* (contrast), there is also the expression of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

In the figure of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison), there are two sentences, whereas in *ananvaya* (self-comparison), there is the statement of similarity of only one [object]; this is the distinction between them.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, tha) In this regard, he states the exclusion of the term *vācya* (the expressed): "In metaphors (*rūpaka*) and so forth. And thus, it should be understood that in the case of suggested simile (*upamā-dhvani*), the word *upamā* (simile) is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*).
He states the exclusion of the term *avaidharmya* (non-dissimilarity): "And in the case of contrast (*vyatireka*)."
He states the application of this term to a single sentence with the word "upamā" (simile).
He states its exclusion from two [sentences] with the phrase "and in the case of ananvaya"; the meaning is that *ananvaya* is the name of a distinct figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*).
In this case, because the object of comparison itself is doubled by being treated as the standard of comparison,
the phrase "similarity" (*sāmyam*) here does not mean "a common attribute" (*samāno dharmaḥ*).

For if it did, there would result the fault of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*), since the attribute is not explicitly expressed in the "omission of the attribute" (*dharmaluptopamā*) which will be discussed later.

Otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because in the metaphor "the moon is a face-pleasing [object]," the property [of being pleasing] is expressed directly (*vācyatva*).

However, in this context, the meaning of the term *sāmya* (similarity) is precisely the relationship between the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), known as the relation of the relatum (*anuyogitā*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*), which consists of a commonality in the form of similarity.

In the expression "the face is like the moon," when there is the cognition that "the face possesses a similarity whose counter-correlate is the moon," it is understood that the similarity has the moon as its counter-correlate and the face as its relatum; thus, it is the relationship of similarity that constitutes the similarity.
This is the meaning of "thus the simile.

Regarding the definition stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*—namely, that "simile (*upamā*) is a connection with a common attribute (*sāmānena dharmeṇa*) among the varieties of simile"—it has been explained there that it is simply a connection by means of a shared quality.
However, particles such as *iva* and so forth convey the relationship just like the genitive case.

Thus, according to that [other] view, because it is written there, the relation called "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitā*) is itself what is termed "the state of being the correlate of the standard of comparison" (*upamānānuyogitā*). However, according to the author of the *Grantha* (Mammaṭa), since he writes later on that [simile] "makes known the relation residing in both the standard and the object of comparison," simile consists of precisely these two relations called counter-correlativity and correlate-ness. Furthermore, in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, because such counter-correlativity is expressed by indeclinable words such as *iva*, the simile is "verbal" (*śrautī*); whereas because it is not expressed by non-indeclinable words such as *tulya*, it is "conceptual" (*ārthī*).

According to the view that indeclinables denote [the object] as being connected [with the action], since words such as *iva* express the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) connected with the moon, whereas non-indeclinable words such as *tulya* do not express it, the author of the present work will state that when *iva* and the like are heard alone, they convey the simile immediately; thus, when these are present, the simile is verbal (*śrautī*). However, non-indeclinable words such as *tulya* convey the simile only after a delay through reflection; thus, when these are present, he will state that the simile is objective (*ārthī*).
Therefore, in his view, there is no *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of the related).
Now, how can such a relation, which constitutes similarity (*sāmya*), be the expressed meaning (*vācya*)?

Even if one accepts its status as the expressed meaning by resorting to the theory of *anvitābhidhāna*, there would still be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases of "elliptical simile" (*luptopamā*) where the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), such as the word *iva*, is not employed; for in those instances, such a relation is not the expressed meaning.
For this very reason, in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, a definition of simile (*upamā*)—which consists of such a relationship—is not formulated as being constituted by its expressibility (*vācyatva*).
It is replied:
even here, a definition constituted by expressibility has indeed been provided.
However, the meaning of the term *vācya* (expressed) is precisely that which is *avyaṅgya* (not suggested).

For this very reason, in cases such as metaphor (*rūpaka*), because similarity (*sādharmya*) is indeed suggested, its exclusion by the word *vācya* is demonstrated therein. But when the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) such as *iva* is not employed, that [similarity] is obtained either through an implied *iva* or from the word expressing the standard of comparison.
The truth is that [the meaning] is not obtained through the literal expression (*vyañjanā*).

However, when particles such as *iva* are employed, if one accepts the theory of "denotation of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*), then such a relation is indeed directly denotable (*vācya*). On the other hand, if that theory is not accepted, then whether *iva* or words such as *tulya* are employed, that [relation] is obtained solely through the force of syntactic connection (*saṃsargamaryyādā*).
In all cases, it is simply that which is not suggested (*avyaṅgyatva*).
*Locanā*:
By the word "metaphor" (*rūpaka*) and so forth, [the author] refers to *dīpaka*, *tulyayogitā*, and other such figures.
In examples such as "His face is stainless, like the moon," the quality of being stainless (*akalaṅkatva*) and so forth constitutes the point of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Furthermore, when there is the repetition of a single form of word (*ekākāraka-pada-āvṛtti*), it is called *Ananvaya* (Non-comparison).
That [comparison] is *Pūrṇā* (Complete) if the common attribute (*sāmānya-dharma*) and the word expressing similarity (*aupamya-vāci*) are present.
When both the object of comparison (upameya) and the standard of comparison (upamāna) are expressed,
that is *upamā*.
The common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is the quality or action— such as loveliness— that serves as the cause of the resemblance between the two.
Words such as "iva" (like) and so forth are the expressors of the comparison (*aupamyavācaka*).
The face and so forth are the object of comparison (*upameya*),
while the moon and so forth are the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) And that [metaphor] is of two kinds: complete (*pūrṇā*) and elliptical (*luptā*).
Among these, he states the complete one with the words: "That is the complete."
"It should be stated" refers to the remainder of the verse following "this, moreover" (*iyaṃ punaḥ*) in Kārikāñcala’s work. He explains it as: "That is the simile" (*sā upamā*).
He states the category of common property (*sāmānyadharmapadārtha*) as "common property" (*sādhāraṇadharma*). To the question "What is that?", he replies: "Of two.
The intention is that even a word with double meaning (*śliṣṭaśabda*) is a poetic quality (*guṇa*).
By this, the inclusion of the passage beginning with "the city [filled] with all arts" is intended.
Locanā:
(lo, ū) He states its subdivisions with the word "that" (sā).

The gloss of the term *sāmānyadharma* is *sādhāraṇadharma*, meaning a common property belonging to both the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*). This, moreover, is as follows: [VisSd 10.15]
The *śrautī* [Upamā] occurs when the words *yathā*, *iva*, *vā*, or *vat*—the latter having the sense of *iva*—are present.
Locanā:
This is the *pūrṇā* [type].

The word *śrautī* (directly expressed) is derived from the etymology "that which is known through direct audition (*śruti*). Therefore, that which is directly stated is *śrautī*. The *ārthī* (implied) consists of terms such as *tulya* (equal), *samāna* (similar), and so forth; it refers to that which has an equal meaning, or where the suffix *-vat* is used in that sense.

Just as words such as *yathā* and others— though common to words like *tulya* which are employed immediately after a standard of comparison (*upamāna*)— convey, by their mere hearing, the relationship characterized as similarity residing between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison,
so too is there a "direct simile" (*śrautī upamā*) when the suffix *vati*,
prescribed by the rule "in that [sense], the suffix *vati* is used in the sense of *iva*" (*tatra tasyeva*), is employed.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, dha) He states its twofold nature—verbal (*śrautī*) and objective (*ārthī*)—with the words "This, moreover...
The meaning is that this complete simile (*pūrṇopamā*), in all its varieties, is both verbal and objective.
The *luptopamā* (elliptical simile) to be described hereafter is of only a few varieties;
for instance, in the example "words such as *ādi*," the word *ādi* itself should also be understood [as being elided].
By this, the same status applies even in cases such as "and he drank up the fame of his enemies" (*śātravaṃ ca papuryaśaḥ*).

"By mere hearing" (śrutimātreṇa) means by mere listening; "quickly" is the intended meaning. Regarding the relationship existing between the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya), it consists of the forms of opposition (pratiyogitā) and non-utility (anupayogitā); this is the meaning of the phrase "characterized by similarity" (sādṛśyalakṣaṇam).
The meaning is that it is a cognition whose definition consists in similarity;

for the relation known as "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitā*) and "correlativity" (*anuyogitā*) is defined by similarity, and thus it is an object of knowledge through the knowledge of that [similarity].
However, the relation itself, in the form of similarity, is not the analogy (*upamā*).

Since words such as *tulya* (equal) and others are also denotable meanings, they are perceived with equal rapidity as *iva* and so forth; thus, there would be no basis for distinguishing between the *śrauti* (verbal) and *ārthī* (implied) types [of upamā]. Furthermore, since Pāṇini has prescribed the suffix *vat*—occurring after words ending in the genitive or locative—in the sense of *iva*, and since that suffix is etymologically derived from *iva* and *tulya*, he states "In this way, there... to show that even when that [suffix] is employed, it is still *śrauti*.

In this context, *tatra tasyeva* is the Pāṇinian sūtra that prescribes the suffix *vat*. Its meaning is that the suffix *vat* is applied after a word ending in either the genitive or the locative case in the sense of "like" (*ivārthe*), signifying "in that very place" or "of that very thing.
*Locanā*:
[The suffix *vat*] is common even to words such as *tulya* ("equal") when they are employed immediately after a term of comparison (*upamāna*).

Now, the meaning is as follows: although words such as *tulya* (equal) and *sadṛśa* (similar), which are employed immediately after the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) in expressions such as "the face is equal to the moon," are common to both [the object compared and the standard] and thus predominant;

nevertheless—[as indicated by the phrase] "by mere hearing" and so forth—the intention is this: from the very use of a word such as "the face is like a lotus," there arises the cognition that the face is the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the lotus is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
"But it is not so in the case of the employment of words such as 'tulya' (equal) and so forth," he will state immediately thereafter with the word "evam" (thus).
By this explanation,
since the employment of the word "iva" (as if) is based on direct audition (śrautī), [the comparison is primary].
Therefore, the point is that even when the suffix *vat* prescribed for that purpose is employed, that same [distinction] is appropriate.
As for words such as *tulya* (equal), in expressions like "the face is equal to a lotus" (*kamalena tulyaṃ mukham*), they refer only to the object of comparison (*upameya*);
whereas in expressions like "a lotus is equal to the face" (*kamalaṃ mukhasya tulyam*), they refer only to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

In examples such as “The face and the lotus are equal,” since the two words find their rest (viśrāmyanti) in both [terms], they convey the similarity only through the contemplation of the meaning (*arthānusandhāna*); thus, when that [contemplation] exists, the simile is *ārtha* (implied).
Likewise, when the suffix *vati*, prescribed in the sense of "equal to that" (*tena tulyam*) and so forth, is employed—as in the *Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, na) But regarding the employment of *tulya* and other indeclinables, he says "tulyādayastu" in order to state their status as having a meaning (*ārthatva*).
The connection with what follows is: "the words *tulya* and so forth rest [upon another].
They "rest" means they convey the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatām*).
For that in which the cognition of the qualificandum (viśeṣyatā) occurs is the object of comparison (upameya), and the other is the standard of comparison (upamāna).

However, when words such as "equal" (tulya) are employed, because the presentation of that [cognition] is not fixed, the status of being the object of comparison and the standard of comparison must be understood through reflective awareness (pratisaṃdhāna);

and since the simile itself—which consists of the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) and the correlate (anuyogin) residing in the object of comparison and the standard of comparison—is also to be understood through reflective awareness, it follows that when such a state exists, the simile is implied by the sense (ārthī).
In this regard, by employing terms such as "equal" (*tulya*) and so forth, he demonstrates the non-restriction of the perception of distinction—namely, with the phrase "by the lotus.

Regarding the expression "the lotus of the face": one should not object that here the face is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the lotus is merely the object of comparison (*upameya*), and thus how there can be a resting upon the standard of comparison;
for even when used in such a manner, it remains so because the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is that the lotus is the standard of comparison.
Even when the meaning is identical, there is another sūtra of Pāṇini, "tena tulyam," which prescribes the suffix *vat*.
He says "in this way, by that" (*evam tena*) to show that [the same sense] occurs even when such a *vati* suffix is not employed, as it is understood through the force of the context (*ārthī*).
— *Locanā*:

The connection with the verb "they rest" (*viśrāmyanti*) is with the locative endings in *upameye* and so forth; they rest precisely upon the object of comparison (*upameya*), because they are employed as its qualifiers. The same applies in the subsequent cases as well.

The similarity consists in the face being the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the lotus being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). "In this way" means according to the principle applicable to the suffix *vat*, which is prescribed in the sense of "like" (*iva*).
There are two types [of simile]— in a derivative formation (*taddhita*), in a compound (*samāsa*), and in a sentence (*vākya*)— namely,
the *śrauti* (verbal) and the *ārthī* (objective).
An example:
“O young girl, your face is like a fragrant lotus, your full breasts are like two jars,
and your countenance gladdens the heart like the autumnal moon.”
In this context, the *śrautī* [metaphor] is of three kinds in sequence.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, pa) Therein, he demonstrates the sixfold nature of the *pūrṇā* [metaphor] with the words "two" (*dve*).
The verse is complete up to the word *vākye*.
The phrase *ṣaḍeva tat* is a supplement to that [verse].
Among those three—beginning with the derivative (*taddhita*)—he states the *śrautī* (direct) [metaphor] with the example *saurabham*.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is "the fragrance of the face.
Here, in the phrase "like that of a lotus" (*ambhoruhasyeva*), the suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the genitive case.

In the phrase "like two jars" (*kumbhāvivā*), because it is joined with the word *iva*, it is a compound by virtue of being an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*). Thus, it is a compound-based [simile].
In the example "Her face is like the autumn moon," it is *śrautī* (expressed by words) because of the presence of "iva" and other such terms that convey that meaning.
It is "threefold" in the sense that it possesses the three forms consisting of being expressed through a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), a compound (*samāsa*), or a sentence (*vākya*).
Locanā:
In examples such as "like fragrance" (*saurabham iva*), fragrance (*saurabha*) is the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

In the case of "like two jars" (*kumbhāv iva*), there is a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*) according to the rule: "With *iva*, there is always a compound, with no elision of the case-ending, and the original accent of the preceding member remains. Thus, it is a compulsory compound.
The utility of this previously mentioned rule regarding the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of a compound is found only in the Veda.
For example: “Her lower lip is sweet like nectar, her hand is like a tender sprout and exceedingly soft, and her two eyes, tremulous like those of a startled deer, are beautiful.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pha) He states the threefold meaning of *amṛta* with the word "sweet" (*madhura*). Here, the suffix *-vati* is used in the sense of similarity (*tulyārthe*), meaning "equal to nectar."
In the phrase "pallavatulya," there is a compound (samāsa);
in the phrase "cakitamṛgalocanābhyām," there is a sentence (vākya).
Here, in sequence, there are three types of implied meaning (ārtha).
The *pūrṇā* consists of all six [figures];
this is clear.
The *luptā* occurs when there is an elision of one or two common attributes (*sāmānyadharma*) and so forth. (VisSd 10.17)
Or, when three [of the four components] are not expressed, the *śrautī* (expressed by word) and the *ārthī* (implied by sense) are also like the previous cases.
*Vijñapriyā* explains the elided [metaphor] with the word "elided" (*luptā*).

A common property (*sāmānyadharma*) is a shared quality (*sādhāraṇadharma*). From the word "etc. (*ādi*), words such as *iva*, *tulya*, and so forth, which convey a simile, as well as the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*), are included.
The meaning is that [the ellipsis occurs] when one, two, or all three of these are omitted.
The meaning is that she (Locanā) also exists, as far as possible, both as direct (śrautī) and as indirect (ārthī);
"as before" means she pertains to the three categories beginning with the secondary derivative (taddhita). — Locanā.

In the phrase "of the common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the object of comparison (*upameya*), and the words expressing the comparison (*upamāpratipādaka*).
That [comparison] is the elided (*luptā*).
He states its divisions:
In the case of the elision of a suffix (*dharmalopa*), it is like *pūrṇā*; however, in the case of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it is without the Vedic form.

That *luptopamā* (elliptical simile), occurring upon the omission of the common property (*dharma*)—which takes the form of a quality (*guṇa*), an action (*kriyā*), or a substance (*rūpa*)—is of six types according to the previously stated method, just like the complete (*pūrṇā*) simile;
however, in this case, because a direct (*śrautī*) expression is impossible when the suffix (*taddhita*) is used, it is of five types.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"Like the full [moon]" (*pūrṇāvat*)—that is, when there is elision (*lopa*), meaning non-mention.
He explains "like the full [moon]" as "as previously stated.
The manner previously stated refers to its application to the three categories beginning with secondary derivatives (*taddhita*).
"Six"—this means six [alternatives] are proposed.
However, he says "but" (kintu) to indicate that in reality there are five;
this is because [the sixth] is impossible according to the Vedic text (śrauti).
When there is a violation of the rule (*dharma-lopa*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) that indicates a relationship with one who is devoted to the rule (*dharma-niṣṭha*) does not exist.
Consequently, since the suffix *vati*—which has the meaning of "like that" (*tad-anta-ādi-vat*)—is also absent, [the formation] is impossible.
— *Locanā*:
In the case of an elided simile (*luptopamā*) involving a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), a verbal (*śrautī*) [simile] is impossible.

This is because, in the example "the beauty of the face is like that of the moon" (*mukhasya candravat śobhā*), the common property in the form of "beauty" (*śobhā*) is not explicitly mentioned; thus, the meaning remains expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) and consequently lacks coherence.
An example [of this] is as follows:
“O beloved, your face is like the moon, your hand is equal to a young sprout,
your speech is like nectar, your lips are like the *bimba* fruit, and your mind is like stone.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ma) "The face is the moon.
In this case, the quality of being delightful is elided.
Because there is no compound with the word *yathā*, it is a verbal (ārthī) simile residing in the sentence;
in the phrase "like nectar of speech" (*vācaḥ sudhā iva*), the attribute of sweetness (*madhuratva*) is elided.
Because of its obligatory compounding with the word *iva*, it is a formal (śrautī) simile.
In the phrase "your lip" (*oṣṭhas te*), the attribute of redness (*śoṇatva*) is elided;
because of the compound with the word *tulya*, this is an implicit (ārtha) compound-based [metaphor].
It is like "the mind-stone" (*mano'śmavat*).
In this context, the meaning is "equal to a stone" (*aśmanā tulyam*); the suffix *vat* is used in the sense of similarity (*tulyārthe*) according to the rule *tulyārthe laddhite vatiḥ*.
Regarding *Locanā*:
in examples such as "the face is like the moon" (*mukham indur yathā*), the aforementioned inversion of the case endings is for the sake of the metrical completion of the verse.
In the two types of denominative suffixes (*kyac* and *kyaṅ*) prescribed for the base object (*ādharakarma*),
as well as in the *ṇamul* suffix used for the object and the agent, it likewise occurs in five ways.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ya) Having thus explained the fivefold [derivation] where the verbal root is elided (*dharmalupta*), he states that same other fivefold [derivation]: "prescribed by means of the substratum and the object" (*ādhārakarmavihita*).
The connection of the term "of two kinds" (*dvividhe*) is only with *kyaci*, and not also with *kyaṅ*.
Regarding "of the object and the agent": the meaning is "of the object and the agent as upapadas.
Locanā says: "by means of kyaṅ."
That is to say, when [the suffix] is prescribed for the agent (*kartṛvihita*).

The phrase “*luptā* [is used] when there is the elision of *dharma*” is supplied [from the previous rule]. According to the Kalāpa school, *kyac*, *kyaṅ*, and *ṇamul* correspond to *in*, *āyi*, and *ṇam* respectively.
The examples in order:
"In battles you act as an inner apartment;
you treat the citizens like your own sons; and your fortune always acts as a beloved wife."
"O Lord of the Earth, you have been seen by your beloved women as one who resembles the moon in appearance and moves upon this earth like Indra."
Vijñapriyā:
"(vi, ra) *antaḥpurīyase*" means that because you are fearless in battles, you behave as if you were in the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*).
In this context, the quality of being a place where one may move about without fear is omitted.
Regarding the word *pauraṃ*:
it means that you behave toward the citizens as if they were your own son.
In this case, the property of being an object of affection is elided; [the suffix] *kyac* is applied to these two bases (*ādhāra* and *karman*).
In the expression "it is always made delightful" (*sadā ramaṇīyate*), the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied in the sense of "acting like one who is delightful" (*ramaṇīvācarati*);
here, the property of being undepressed (*adīnatva*) is elided.
Regarding the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*):
you have been seen by your beloveds through the act of beholding the moonlight;
here, the quality of being "charming" (*manoharatva*) is elided.
And thus, the meaning here on earth is that you move by means of movement performed by Indra;

in this case, the suffix *dharma* (indicating agency) is elided. In both instances, the *ṇamul* suffix is used because the two words (*indra* and *sañcāra*) function as the object and the agent respectively.
Locanā:
(Lo, Ā) You have been seen like the moon, the nectar-rayed one;
you move with the movement of Indra.
The meaning is that you move about like Indra.

Here, in the phrase "you are within [the city]," the common attribute of being the locus of pleasant dwelling is elided; and in the phrase "you are well-pleasing," the common attribute of being full of affection is elided.
The same applies elsewhere;
and here, because there is an absence of [faults such as] *yathāsaṃkhya* and so forth, there is no consideration of specific categories such as *śrautī* and the rest.
— *Locanā*:
"In other cases" means:
as in the case of *ramaṇīyatā* [in the phrase *ramaṇīyate*], where there is dependence;
and in the case of *amṛtadyutidarśam*, where there is loveliness.
In the verse beginning with "indrasāñcāram," the phrase "following the ancients" is to be supplied after "there is not," referring to the excellence of the retinue and so forth.
Furthermore, some cite this as an example of the elision of particles such as *iva* that express comparison.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, la) Here, since the common properties of the performance of that purpose in the three instances beginning with *kyaṅ*, and of the seeing of the verbal root's meaning and the arising of a notion in the two instances of *ṇamul*, exist, these do not constitute examples of the elision of a property (*dharmalupta*); therefore, by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*—

In the section concerning the elision of the indicator of comparison (*upamāpratipādaka*), the elision of suffixes such as *kyaṅ* was cited precisely as an example of the elision of the *vādi* (the comparative particle). However, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, failing to recognize that qualities such as "conduct" (*ācāra*) function as common attributes (*sādhāraṇadharma*), has cited these five cases as examples of the elision of the indicator of similarity (*aupamyapratipādaka*). The author [of this work] now sets forth [his own view] in order to refute that position, beginning with the words: "And some [say] this... (*idaṃ ca kecit*).
That is incorrect; for even suffixes such as *kyaṅ* convey a sense of comparison because they are prescribed for that purpose.

One should not argue that there is no proper perception of comparison in the case of *kyaṅ* and similar suffixes because, being suffixes, they lack independence and because words like *iva* are not employed—this is not to be said.
(Thus says) Vijñapriyā:
(Vi, Va) He refutes [this] with "that is incorrect.
Regarding the phrase "because it is prescribed for that purpose"—the meaning is "because it is prescribed for such conduct.
The meaning is that, by virtue of the cognition "it acts like a son," it is enjoined precisely in that sense.
Now, even if there is a rule for such a meaning, there is no spontaneous cognition of comparison from those [suffixes], as is the case with *iva* and so on;
for suffixes convey meaning only through their connection with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, since *kyac* and the others lack the capacity to convey comparison intrinsically, they do not spontaneously convey comparison.
And so, even though that [suffix] exists, one raises the doubt—beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*)—that the intended elision which conveys the comparison *per se* does not occur:
"But surely, by them the comparison is indeed conveyed *per se*;
however, it is only certain that such a meaning is invariably connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)."

If those [suffixes] were to have such a meaning [of expressing comparison], then there would be no use of the word *eva* as a qualifier for them at all; the sense is: "How could this [word *eva*] be a qualifier of that meaning?

Thus, this doubt—though superficially plausible—is not tenable upon closer examination, because suffixes such as *kyac* and others, unlike words like *iva*, do not inherently convey the notion of comparison.
In this regard, he provides the resolution that "non-intentionality" itself is simply not possible from its own side, stating: "No.
Locanā:
(lo, ī) The suffix -vat has the sense of "for that purpose" (*tadartha*).
Because they lack independence— since isolated words, without connection to a *prakṛti*, lack the capacity to convey meaning—
and because the same consequence would follow even at the beginning of a cosmic age (*kalpa*);
nor is there denotative power in the comparison itself, as it is merely equal to the beginning of a cosmic age and so forth.

However, particles such as *kyaṅ* and others possess the function of illuminators (*dyotaka*); for even in the case of particles such as *iva*, there is no certainty that they are denoters (*vācaka*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
"At the beginning of the eon" means that even those [elements] possess the nature of conditions;
this is an elliptical indication.

It should be understood that even for [suffixes] such as *iva*, there is no inherent usage [of the suffix itself]; furthermore, even if they were present, it would result in the loss of the indicator (*lopa*) that conveys the comparison. He raises an objection at first sight: "Nor [is there a problem] with the *kalpa*-suffixes and so on"—here, "usage" refers to their denotative function (*vācakatva*).
The meaning is that, however, for words such as *iva*, there is only the capacity to suggest (*vyañjakatvam*).
He states the restriction: "even for *iva* and so forth.
Even in the absence of a decisive factor (*vinigamakābhāve*), if by virtue of being independent and primary, one suffix were the denoter (*vācakatvam*) and another suffix [were not], [then...]

If it is argued that they possess the quality of being manifestors (*vyañjakatva*), then particles such as *iva* and others would likewise not be denoters (*vācaka*); for the mere assertion [of their status] does not withstand logical proof, as there is no evidence for it even in that case—this is the meaning.

Alternatively, if they were denoters, then in both of the two views—that "the word as a whole is the denoter" and that "the base and the suffix denote their respective meanings"—the suffixes *vatī* and so on would be exactly the same as *kyaṅ* and so on.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṣa) Is it not the case that this [objection] does not constitute an obstacle here?

For the very fact that words such as *iva* express comparison is itself established by grammatical authority (*anuśāsana*). Therefore, if [you argue] that *iva* and so forth are inherently [expressive of comparison], or otherwise...

If it is maintained that [the suffix] possesses denotative power (*vācakatva*), then for me as well, the denotative power of *kyac* and the other suffixes is exactly the same—whether intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*asvataḥ*) according to different philosophical views. Thus he says: "Or, if there is denotative power," and so forth. The meaning is that just as you have denotative power, so too do I; this is the point of equality.
He shows that it is of two kinds according to different opinions with the words "as a composite" (*samuditam*).
The meaning is: as a composite of its own base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*).
He states another opinion with the words "the base," etc. (*prakṛti*...).
"Expressing their respective meanings by themselves"—the meaning is "expressing their respective meanings inherently.
Regarding the phrase "vatyādi-kyajādibhiḥ":
in your view, suffixes such as *kalpa* and so on are expressers of similarity because they denote equality through their likeness to words like *yathā* and *iva*.
The meaning is that there is a similarity between the two cases because *kyac* and the others likewise [denote comparison].
Thus, it has been stated that since *kyac* and the others have the sense of "like" (*iva*), this is not an example of an elided word used to convey a simile. — *Locanā*.

(Lo, u) He states another refutation with the words "even in the case of *kalpa* and so forth"— the meaning of this is as follows: if, even though *kyaṅ* and other suffixes exist in certain instances, they lack the capacity to convey a meaning because they are dependent as suffixes (*pratyaya*) and thus not independent, and therefore lack the status of being expressers of comparison (*aupamya*),
then the same would apply to *kalpa* and the others, even though they exist.
Furthermore, even though particles such as *kalpa* exist, they do not function as indicators of comparison (*aupamya*),
because the non-existence [of such a meaning] even in the case of *kalpa* is denied by all theorists due to a lack of certainty; for instance,
some accept that particles such as *iva* also function as indicators of comparison.

According to that view, we accept that verbal suffixes (*ky-aṅ* and so on) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*) because they are prescribed for a specific meaning—just like *kalpa* and other such suffixes—whereas nominal suffixes (*taddhita*) are accepted as merely indicative (*dyotaka*). Therefore, he says: "Or, if [the suffix] has denotative power.
"Combined" (*samuditam*) means joined together by both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).
That is the essential nature of the word; before the word "mata," the term "vaiyākaraṇa" is to be understood as an ellipsis.
Thus, there is indeed equality between the suffixes *vati* and *ādi*, and *ky-aṅ* and *ādi*.
This is the intended meaning: if it is accepted that suffixes such as *vat* are expressive (*vācaka*), then suffixes such as *kyaṅ* must also be expressive;
and when those [suffixes] are not expressive, then these [others] are not either.

Since all authorities accept the existence of suffixes like *vat* and *kalpa* as being expressive of similarity (*aupamya*) when they are present, what fault have the similar suffixes *kyaṅ* and others committed by virtue of their being suffixes, such that when they are present there should be an absence of the expresser of similarity?
It may be so.

And as for what some say— that "suffixes such as *vati* are prescribed in the sense of 'like' (ivādi), whereas suffixes such as *kyaṅ* are prescribed in the sense of 'behaving like' (*ācāra*) and so forth."

That too is not correct; for *kyaṅ* and the others do not signify mere action (*ācāra*) alone, but rather action characterized by similarity (*sādṛśyācāra*). Thus, when the suffix is elided, there are ten types of elided [suffixes].
*Vijñapriyā*:

The author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, however, has stated that because there is no grammatical injunction (*anuśāsana*) regarding their meaning as being "and so forth" (*ādi*), they do not have that meaning, since [the suffixes] only enjoin their usage (*ācāra*).
To refute that, he says: "And as for what some [have said]..."—namely, that they do not indeed have mere usage as their meaning.
The point is that the meaning of the grammatical rule *upamānād ācāre* is precisely "conduct similar [to that of the standard of comparison]";

and since the statement regarding the absence of a grammatical rule was made for the purpose of refuting [the view] that the word *iva* has that same meaning, one should understand that there is no tautology with what was stated previously.
Thus, in this way...

The meaning is that there are ten [types of ellipsis]: five— the distinctions between direct (śrauti) and indirect (ārthī) ellipsis— occurring within the three categories beginning with *taddhita*, and five occurring in formations such as *kyac* and so forth.
Locanā:
(lo, ū) "Because they have the sense of similarity and conduct.
This is the meaning: if the *kyaṅ* suffixes and others had only the sense of conduct (*ācāra*), they would not have the sense of similarity; yet that is not the case.
"Because it serves both purposes of similarity and usage.
[This occurs] in two ways—within sentences and within compounds—when a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is not explicitly employed.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ha) "In the non-employment of the standard of comparison" means:
in the case of not employing [the object] by way of its delimitor of the state of being a standard of comparison, such as *candratva* (moonhood).
By this, it should be understood that there is also non-employment when it is not employed by means of words such as *sadṛśa* (similar) or *tulya* (equal).
The example:
“There exists nothing as beautiful as her face, nor anything equal to her eyes.”—
*Vijñapriyā*.
In the sentence "by her face" (*tasyā mukhena*),

and in the compound "neither exists nor is it equal to the eyes" (*na aste na vā nayanatulyam*), the quality of beauty is stated as the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*); thus, in these cases, there is the elision of the standard of comparison (*upamānamātralopa*).

Nor should it be argued: "How can there be an elision of the standard of comparison (upamānalopa) here? For when one says 'similar to the face,' the face itself is understood to be the standard of comparison, and this has already been stated.
[The response is: If the face were the standard of comparison, then the word "similar" (*sadṛśa*) would have to refer to the object of comparison (*upameya*);
and yet, the object of comparison cannot be superior to the standard of comparison.
However, [the word "equal" (sadṛśa)] implies either inferiority or equality.

Thus, when it is stated that there is nothing inferior or equal to her face, the expectation for anything superior is precluded; since the praise of the face would otherwise be untenable, the word "equal" here must refer to the standard of comparison (upamāna).
Consequently, by implication, the meaning is simply that there is nothing superior to her face, because the standard of comparison exceeds the object of comparison (upameya).
Locanā:
(lo ṛ) means "in both the sentence and the compound";
that is to say, in the sentence and in the compound.
According to the grammatical tradition, there is an absence of compound (*samāsa*) in a sentence; for example,
in "tasyāḥ" and so forth, [the upamā] resides in the sentence as in "mukhena sadṛśam," whereas in "nayanatulyam," it resides in the compound.
The meaning is that there is no other distinct object whatsoever.
Here, because two other objects serving as substitutes for the face and eyes are implied, there is an elision of the standard of comparison (*upamānalopa*).
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, kha) [Objection: But if the object of comparison is already expressed by the word "similar" (*sadṛśa*) itself, how can there be its elision? To this, he says: "In this case, 'the substitute for the face'.
A "substitute" (*pratinidhi*) is the object of comparison, such as the moon and so forth.
[The reason for the elision] is "because it is understood" (*gamyamānatvāt*).

The meaning is that because [the moon] is not presented in its form as the delimitor of the standard of comparison (upamānatāvacchedakarūpa), such as "moon-ness" (candratva) and so forth, it must be supplied by the force of syntactic expectancy (ākāṅkṣā).

Thus, since similarity—in the form of being the counter-correlate of resemblance—is to be expressed there through what is obtained by supply, one should understand that the explanation given for the word "vācya" (expressed) in the phrase "sādṛśyapratiyogitārūpasāmyaṃ vācyam" as referring to the "suggested" (vyaṅgya) is appropriate here as well; the same applies to what follows.

And in this very context, in the reading "mukhena sadṛśam" (similar to the face), one may read "mukhaṃ yathedam" (this face as); and in the reading "nayanatulyam" (equal to the eyes), one may read "dṛgiva" (like the eye). Thus, even the verbal (*śrauti*) type of simile is possible here. Although these two types [of upamā] can each be divided into four kinds based on the distinction between the verbal and the implied (*ārthī*), they are stated to have only two varieties according to the tradition of the ancients.
*Vijñapriyā*:
In the two types shown [in the previous section], the quality of being *ārthī* arises due to the presence of words such as *sadṛśa* or *tulya*;
however, if words such as *iva* were placed in the position of those two words, they would instead be *śrautī*. Furthermore, when the upamāna is elided, these two also become *luptā*.
Therefore, there can be four types of *upamānaluptā*.

However, because the ancient authors such as the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* did not mention those two [types], he states that only two varieties were mentioned: "In this very context, moreover... [and so on].
[Verse 10.20: "When the word expressing comparison (*aupamyavācin*) is elided, it is of two kinds: in a compound (*samāsa*) and in the *kvip* suffix."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
gha) "Of that which expresses a comparison" means of that which brings about the understanding of a comparison.
Because it has been shown that [words] such as *tulya* and so forth lack the capacity to denote that [similarity].
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) There is the elision of the suffix *kvip* after [the particle] *iva* and others which express comparison (*aupamya*).
The examples in order are as follows:
“The face of the deer-eyed maiden is as enchanting as the moon.
“Before the great-souled ones, he clearly brays like a donkey, his voice harsh to the ear.”
Vijñapriyā:
"(vi, ṅa) *vadanaṃ* means 'like the moon' (*sudhākara*).
*Gardabhatīti* means that, before great-souled ones, he acts like a donkey, clearly braying with a sound harsh to the ear."

Since both properties—the quality of being heart-stealing and the harshness of sound—are present in both [the elephant and the donkey], there is here merely the elision of the *kvip* suffix used as a marker of comparison, just as in the case of two things that establish a simile.

Because the simile is perceived through the reconnection (*pratisandhāna*) of those two [properties] once they have been elided, it does not follow that the simile is suggested (*vyaṅgya*); therefore, its status as expressed (*vācya*) remains intact.
In this instance, in the word "gardabhati," there is the elision of the *kvip* suffix which expresses the comparison.
And here there is no omission of the instrument and the object either, because they are indicated by the word "ninadan" (roaring) itself.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ca) Regarding the rule "kvip after words expressing comparison":
although it is possible to state that the *lopa* (elision) of the elided *kvip* follows from the rule *kkippare bhāṣā*,
nevertheless, it is stated that the future-elided *kvip* itself possesses the status of *kvip*, and it has already been stated that this very [element] expresses comparison.

By the phrase "by this very [word] ninadan," it is because the agent—the object of comparison—is already expressed by the present participle suffix *śatṛ*, which denotes the agent's action. There are two ways [this occurs]: in a compound and in a sentence, through the elision of both the common property (*dharma*) and the object of comparison (*upamāna*).
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) Having thus shown the *luptopamā* (elliptical simile) through the elision of one [term], she now demonstrates it through the elision of two;
the meaning is that the examples for these two follow in reverse order.
This [type of *śleṣa*] also occurs in four ways, as previously stated, including the sense of "concluding" (*autsargika*).
Examples of these two are found in the passage beginning with "tasyā mukhena," where the reading "loke" is substituted for "ramyam.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, cha) Having thus described the fourteen varieties of *ekaluptā* (single-omission simile)—namely, ten cases where the common property (*dharma*) is omitted, two where the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is not employed, and two where the word expressing comparison (*aupamyavācin*) is omitted—the author states the subdivisions of *dviluptā* (double-omission simile) with the words "of two kinds" (*dvidhā*). Regarding the phrase "in place of 'delightful'": [The text continues: "In place of [the word] 'delightful' (*ramya*), [there is the omission]. This refers to the case where, instead of using the word "delightful," another term is used or the word is entirely absent. This constitutes one type of *dviluptā*. Another type occurs when both the common property and the word expressing comparison are omitted. Thus, there are two types of *dviluptā*. Furthermore, within these, there are sub-varieties based on whether the standard of comparison is explicitly mentioned or not, resulting in four types of *dviluptā*. These are illustrated by examples such as "the face is like the moon" (where the common property is omitted), "the face is like the moon" (where the word expressing comparison is omitted), and so forth. Thus, the total number of similes (*upamā*) is twenty-eight. This concludes the section on similes. Now, the author proceeds to describe the figure of speech known as *rūpaka* (metaphor). As stated: "Metaphor (*rūpaka*) consists in the superimposition (*adhyavasāya*) of the nature of one thing upon another. This is defined as the identification of the object of description (*upameya*) with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) through the imposition of the latter's attributes upon the former. It is divided into two main types: *samastarūpaka* (composite metaphor) and *asamastarūpaka* (non-composite metaphor). Among these, *samastarūpaka* is further divided into three: *mālārūpaka* (garland metaphor), *śliṣṭarūpaka* (pun-based metaphor), and *saviśeṣaṇarūpaka* (metaphor with qualifiers). Examples of these are provided accordingly. Next, *asamastarūpaka* is divided into five: *āvṛttirūpaka*, *saṅkīrṇarūpaka*, *samastaviṣayāvayavarūpaka*, *ekadeśavivartirūpaka*, and *paramparitarūpaka*. Each of these is explained with illustrative verses. Finally, the author discusses *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor), which is defined as the identification of the object of description with the standard of comparison when the distinction between them is obscured. This is further classified into seven types: *vastuviparyaya*, *nimittaviparyaya*, *nimittābhāva*, *niṣedha*, *ākṣepa*, *atiśaya*, and *anyathātva*. Examples for each of these are given. Thus ends the discussion of metaphors. Following this, the author introduces the figure of speech *sahokti* (concomitance), defined as the simultaneous mention of two things that are related to each other. It is divided into two types: *sādharmya-sahokti* (concomitance of similarity) and *vaidharmya-sahokti* (concomitance of difference). Examples follow for each. Next is *vinokti* (description without), which is the description of an object's state in the absence of another related object. It is divided into two types: *praśasta-vinokti* (commendable absence) and *nindita-vinokti* (blameworthy absence). Examples are provided. Then comes *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression), which involves the suggestion of a second meaning through the description of shared attributes (*sādhāraṇadharmokti*). It is divided into two types: *śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇasamāsokti* (abbreviated expression with punned qualifiers) and *kevalasamāsokti* (pure abbreviated expression). Examples are given.
Finally, *parivṛtti* (exchange) is introduced, defined as the exchange of one thing for another
Because of the elision of the *dharma* [suffix] as well;
when there is elision of the *dharmī*, *iva*, and so forth, those ending in *kvip* are of two kinds within a compound. (VisSd 10.21)
The example is:

"vidhavati mukhābjam asyāḥ" (her lotus-face acts like a widow). Here, in the word "vidhavati," there is the elision of both the quality of loveliness and the *kvip* suffix; furthermore, in "mukhābjam," it resides within a compound (*samāsa*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ja) "vidhavati" means "he acts like a *vidhu*";
the suffix *kvip* is simply elided.
Regarding the phrase *mukhābja* ("lotus-face"):
it is a *puruṣavyāghra*-type compound (a "tiger-like man" type), meaning "the face is like a lotus.
And it should not be said here that this is merely a metaphor (*rūpaka*) and not a simile (*upamā*).

According to Pāṇini’s sūtra *upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ sāmānyāprayoge*, the simile (*upamā*) is prescribed by way of precluding the metaphor (*rūpaka*) when there is no employment of a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*); for a metaphor is only possible when a common attribute is indeed employed. — *Locanā*.
"‘Some’—by this, he reveals his own disagreement.
However, some say that here there is the elision of the *pratyaya* [the suffix];
for when the object of comparison (*upameya*) is elided, there would be one [form] in the *kyac* suffix."
Locanā:

(lo, ai) Furthermore, in accordance with the tradition of the ancients, she defines *luptopamā* (elliptical simile) involving the omission of one element within the section on the omission of two elements, stating "of the object of comparison" (*upameyasya*).
For example:
"With eyes wide open at the sight of the enemy's prowess,
and with arms formidable with a sword, he fights as if he were a thousand warriors."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,

jha) Having thus stated eighteen types— four with two elisions and fourteen with one elision— he speaks again of one type with a single elision, beginning with "of the object of comparison" (*upameyasya*) and "the enemy" (*arāti*).
Regarding the expression *sahasrāyudhīyati*:
the meaning is that even though his staff-like arms are formidable with a sword, he behaves as if he were Sahasrāyudha himself.
In this sentence, "he behaves like Sahasrāyudha," there is an elision of the object of comparison (*upameya*), which is the self (*ātman*).
Nor is there an elision of the word expressing the comparison here, for the reason already stated.

On this point, some say: “In the derivation of the word *sasahastrāyudhīyati* from the sentence ‘he acts like one who is accompanied by Sahasrāyudha’ (*sahasrāyudhena saha vartate iti sasahastrāyudhaḥ*, *sa ivācarati*), because the substantive (the object of comparison) is not expressed by the words, there is an elision of the object of comparison (*upameya*) here.”
That is not tenable under scrutiny,
because it contradicts the grammatical rule regarding the suffix *kyac* when applied to an agent (*kartṛ*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
Nor should it be argued that because [the verb] *sahasrāyudhyate* is also possible, the suffix *kyaṅ* could likewise apply here;

for since a verbal form ending in *kyaṅ* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), there is no possibility here of the self (*ātman*)—which would be the object (*karman*)—acting as the object of comparison (*upameya*). Anticipating this objection, he states: "It has already been explained."

The meaning is that the status of being expressive of that [action] has already been stated by the suffix *kyac*. Now, one might object: "Previously, examples such as *pauraṃ sutīyati* were cited as instances of the elision of the common attribute (*dharmalupta*), without considering that the action denoted by *kyac*—namely, 'conduct' (*ācāra*)—is itself a common attribute.
How then can this be cited here as an example of the elision of the object of comparison (*upameyamātralopa*) alone?"
If it is argued that this is not so because [the term] *ācāra* is also omitted due to a failure to recognize its status as a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), we say no;
for in the case of [the word] *arāti* and others, its possession of a common property is indeed recognized,
since even a person with a thousand weapons possesses such eyes.

However, some maintain that there is no elision (*lopa*) of the object of comparison (*upameya*), which is the self (*ātman*) functioning as the subject (*karman*). They argue that because the suffix *kyac* is prescribed here by the rule “*akarmake kartari vā*,” the agent (*kartṛ*) alone is the object of comparison in this instance; and since its form, as delimited by the property that serves as the qualifier (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*), is not explicitly mentioned, there is elision.
He states that opinion: "In this regard, some say...
The meaning is "because it is not conveyed by the word.
According to that view, both the *kyac* suffix and the verb, which are prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*), denote [the object] in the form of the agent.
Therefore, because it is not introduced by means of the form that delimits the qualificand,
and because there is no grammatical rule [to that effect],
the meaning is "in the case of an intransitive verb, [the agent is expressed]."

And thus, it has been stated that such a construction is indeed ungrammatical regarding the meaning already demonstrated; furthermore, it should be understood that in examples such as *puṣyati*, the cognition of the agent arises precisely from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denoting the agent.

Moreover, according to that [opponent’s] own view, it should be noted that there is a flaw: by the word "he" (*saḥ*), the agent is indeed presented in its form as the delimiting property of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*).
*Locanā:*

(Lo, o) The meaning is: "in the context of explaining the sūtra [Pāṇini 3.4.70], which prescribes [the suffix] after the object that serves as a support. Some, such as the scholar Caṇḍīdāsa and others, [hold this view] because it contradicts the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*), since the rule prescribes *kyac* only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is intended.

Furthermore, in the phrase "he acts as one possessing a thousand weapons" (*sa sahasrāyudhīyati*), because the *kvip* suffix expresses comparison (*aupamya*), there is an initial approach (*upagama*).

However, at the final conclusion, because it evokes a possibility (*sambhāvanā*), it is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). For example: "On the forehead-slab, they act as musk-tilakas; on the lotus-face of the Goddess, they act as bees; upon her head, they act as crest-ornaments of tamāla-buds."
May those splendors of Śrīkaṇṭha’s throat—acting as full-blown blue lotuses upon your ears, and as black aloe-wood paste upon the slope of your breasts—spread auspiciousness for you.
In such cases as these;
when both the attribute (*dharma*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) are elided, another type [of simile] occurs—
as follows:
“When your fame spreads, all the oceans act like the Ocean of Milk.

Here, in the phrase "acting like the Ocean of Milk," both the subject (*ātman*)—which functions as the object of comparison—and the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharmma*), namely whiteness, are elided.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ṭa) Regarding the verse beginning with *kṣīrodīyanti*, it was already shown previously that this is an illustration of the omission of the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) because the substratum is not perceived as possessing that common attribute.

However, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* maintains that in such cases, since the act of conduct (*ācāra*) itself is the common attribute, this is cited merely as an example of the omission of the object of comparison (*upameyalopa*).

This is because, through the cognition "just as [he] conducts himself toward the Ocean of Milk, so does he toward himself," the act of conduct possesses the status of a common attribute by virtue of being the object (*karman*) in both instances.
And the trilopa occurs within a compound. (VisSd 10.22)
For example: *rājate mṛgalocanā* ("The deer-eyed woman shines").

Here, in the compound *mṛgalocanā*, which means "she whose eyes are as tremulous as the eyes of a deer," there is an elision of the indicator of the simile (*upamāpratipādaka*), the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭha) He states another variety [of *prahelikā*] with the words "and in the case of a triple elision" (*trilope ca*).
He demonstrates the triple elision in the example "mṛgalocanā."
Regarding the phrase "of the deer" (*mṛgasya*) here:
the reading "like the deer" (*mṛgasyeva*) is a scribal error;
the correct reading is "like the eyes" (*locane iva*).
Because the particle *iva* is restricted to following the object of comparison (*upamāna*),
there are thus twenty-seven varieties of simile (*upamā*). Of these, the complete (*pūrṇā*) simile is of six kinds.
The "omitted" [simile] is of twenty-one kinds; thus, taken together, there are twenty-seven types of simile.

[The author] concludes with the word "therefore" (*tena*).
The *luptopamā* (elliptical simile) is of twenty-one types; for instance, there are ten based on the omission of the common attribute (*dharma*),

There are two types when the particle *iva* and so forth are elided; two types when both the attribute (*dharma*) and the object of comparison (*upamāna*) are elided;
and two types when the attribute (*dharma*) or the particle (*vādi*) is elided.
When the object of comparison (*upameya*) alone is omitted, there is one type; when both the common attribute (*dharma*) and the object of comparison are omitted, there is another;
and when all three are omitted, there is yet another type. Thus, by this calculation, there are twenty-one varieties of the elliptical simile (*luptopamā*).

Furthermore, when the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is not omitted, there are four types—combining those where the attribute is dropped by the proponent (*vādilopa*) and those that are both verbal (*śrauta*) and implied (*ārtha*)—making eight varieties; thus, there are twenty-five types in total.
