(vi, ḍa) "Unobscured" (*alupta*) means when the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is conveyed by words.
A common quality (*guṇa*) is of a single form in some cases, while in others it is distinct. (Viśvavidyāsaṃgha 10.23)
When [the two] are distinct, there is the state of being a reflection and its counterpart, or else the distinction exists merely in terms of the word.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ḍha) The identity of form [is established] because the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for what is conveyed by the single word is one and the same.

Therefore, in the example "You are as sweet as nectar" (*sudhāvan madhura*), although there is an absence of identity in the delimiting factor of the denotable meaning (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), one should understand that there is uniformity due to the identity of the delimiting factor of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), which is "charmingness.
However, if there were a difference in form, a difference in the word itself would be mentioned.
The quality (*guṇa*) is the property (*dharma*). He states the twofold nature of the divided [object] with the words "in the divided" (*bhinne*).
The state of being the original image and its reflection (*bimbānubimbatva*) is the mental superimposition of non-difference between the two individual manifestations (*vyakti*).
— *Locanā*:
(Lo, a) It is twofold: by way of being of a single form, or merely by way of a difference in the related entities.
Of these, the first occurs only in the *vṛtti*—such as "sweet like nectar" (*madhuraḥ sudhāvat*) and so forth;
the second is such as "this city [resounds] with every sound" (*sakalakalaṃ puram etat*) and so forth.
The state of being an image and its reflection is the relationship between an original object (*bimba*) and its counterpart (*pratibimba*).
And this is a similarity to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), just as there is between the quality of having a beard and being covered by bees;
it is a distinction in name only, but not a distinction even in terms of actual meaning.
For example—"smiling," and so forth.
Among these, an example of the single form (ekarūpa) is as previously cited: "The lip is sweet like nectar," and so on.
An example of the mirror-image and reflection relationship (bimbapratibimba) is as follows:
"With their bearded heads severed by his arrows,
he covered the earth as if with honeycombs swarming with bees."
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṇa) *bhalleti*—that Raghava covered the earth with the heads of those Pārasiakas and Yavanas, which were surrendered—that is, cast off—by means of a particular weapon in the form of a *bhallaka* arrow.
Of what kind? *Śmaśrulaiḥ* (possessing beards; the suffix *lac* is used here in the sense of "having" or "possessing").
"By swarms of bees" means by clusters of sweet-tasting honeybees (*saraghā*).
"Like an illustration" (*dṛṣṭāntavat*)—an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntaḥ*) is a similarity (*sādṛśya*); and here, that [similarity] consists in its dark form.
"Like that" (*tadvat*) means the root of the tree is characterized by that [darkness].
Such "reflection" (pratibimbana) means the superimposition of non-difference by the mind.
The similarity between the swarm of bees and the face is indicated by the statement that [the face] possesses a beard inseparable from dark bees.
—Locanā:
(lo, ā) *Saraghā* means honey-bee;
*kṣaudra* means honey.

Here, although there is a difference between the two attributes—namely, the state of having a beard (*śmaśrulatva*) and the state of being pervaded by honey-bees (*saraghāvyāptatva*)—there is a similarity between the two substrata (*dharmin*), the head and the mass of honey, due to their being of one form through the commonality of attributes inherent in each, such as tawny color (*piṅgalatva*).
This is the seed of similarity.
And thus, the non-commonality of qualities is well-established even when two subjects possess contradictory attributes.
The simile by example (*dṛṣṭāntopamā*) and the simile by parallel object (*pratibastūpamā*) will be defined with their respective illustrations.
In this instance, the phrase "by those with beards" (*śmaśrulaiḥ*) is reflected as a simile by the phrase "covered with bees" (*saraghāvyāptaiḥ*).
An example where there is a difference merely in the words is as follows:
"Smiling, she cast her eye upon me like a blossoming blue lotus."
The slender-limbed woman related the entirety of her inner thoughts and intentions.
In this context, some maintain that "smiling" (*smeratva*) and "blooming" (*vikasitatva*) are indicated by the word "prativastūpamā" [in the verse].
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ta) clarifies: "having made it smile" (*smeraṃ vidhāya*) is explicit.
Regarding the phrase "here"— the expression "only one" means "only that which is delimited by a single property.
Although smiliness (*smeratva*) is a property of the face alone and not of the eye, and therefore expansiveness (*vistāratva*) alone is the delimitor of the indicated (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*),

whereas blossoming (*vikasitatva*) is a property of the blue lotus— thus there is a difference even in the delimitors— nevertheless, since blossoming is also a particular kind of expansion, their non-difference should be understood.
"Like the *prativastūpamā*. In that regard, the difference in words for a common attribute delimited by a single property will be explained [in the section on] *Locanā*.
"(lo, i) 'Some indeed'—because there is no distinction between being smiling and being blossomed.
Or, it is a partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivartinī upamā*), where the state of being expressed is understood. (VisSd 10.24)
Where there is equality [between the two], there would be—
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, tha) He states the *ekadeśavivartinī upamā* (partial metaphorical simile)— "ekadeśa" etc.
"Being the object of comprehension" (*gamyatva*) means "being the suggested sense" (*vyaṅgyatva*);
[this refers] to "similarity" (*sāmya*), which consists of the nature of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) and the correlate (*anuyogitā*) in a simile (*upamā*).
— *Locanā*:

(Lo, ī) Since expressibility (*vācyatva*) and suggestibility (*gamyatva*) exist such that expressibility resides in one part and suggestibility in another part, it is appropriately named *ekadeśavivartinī* because it functions through a specific [part]; however, in some cases,
even a simile whose scope encompasses all objects (*samastavastuviṣayā*) is observed,
as in the following by Gopīnātha Kavi:
“O Lord of the World, the universe acts as Your dwelling within Your belly;
the world, shimmering and variegated by the manifold conceptions of sentient beings, acts as the canopy directly above You.
Even in its midst, this river of the dwellers of heaven, which clings to the orb of the earth and possesses a luster like the milk of a pearl necklace, acts as Your girdle.”

Here, because the mansion—the whole (aṅgin)—together with its parts such as the canopy, serves as the object of comparison, this is an instance of *samastavastuviṣaya* (comparison involving all constituent things).
As in:
"With lotuses as if they were eyes, and with swans as if they were faces, the lakes [shone] like the glories of the Goddess."
At every step, they shone with ruddy geese as if with breasts.
Here, the similarity between the lotuses and so forth and the eyes and so forth is expressed (*vācya*), while the resemblance between the splendors of the lake and women is implied (*gamya*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, da): "As if with eyes... and so on.
At every step, in every place, the lakes shone with the beauty of lotus ponds due to their blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), and *cakravāka* birds.
Regarding this, he provides a comparison between the triad of blue lotuses and so forth and the triad of eyes and so forth, saying: "as if with eyes, faces, and breasts.
"In this [regard]" means:
Similarity (*sādṛśya*) is the simile (*upamā*), consisting of the nature of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) and the correlate (*anuyogitā*) of that similarity;
for it is established in the treatises on simile that only the relation consisting of the nature of the counter-correlate and the correlate of similarity is what constitutes simile.
And in this case, that [similarity] is expressed by words such as "like" (*iva*) and is not suggested (*avyaṅgya*).

Since it has already been established that the very state of being non-deficient (*avyaṅgyatva*) constitutes the denoted meaning (*vācyapadārtha*), [the suggested meaning] is the denoted (*vācya*) under the theory of "expression of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*), whereas otherwise it is accessible through the force of syntactic relation (*saṃsargamaryyāda*).
Regarding the phrase "the lake is beautiful":
the meaning is that the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) sense—such as the similarity of lotuses to eyes and so forth—is what is understood by virtue of such resemblance.
The simile of inversion (rasanopamā) has been described;
it occurs when the object of comparison (upameya) is placed above [as] the standard of comparison (upamāna). (VisSd 10.25)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, dha) He states the simile of the tongue—“kathita” (stated), etc.
“Yathordhvam” (as above) means “of the subsequent.”
Locanā:
(lo, u) Just as above, in the sequence of higher and higher; that is to say—

“The swan acts like the moon with its white luster; the beloved acts like a swan with her graceful gait; the water acts like the beloved with the pleasure of its touch; and the sky acts like water through its transparency.”
Vijñapriyā: (vi, na) *candrāyate* means "it acts like the moon" (*candra ivācarati*), and so forth; such is the meaning.
In the phrase "even with white radiance" (*śuklarucāpi*), the word *api* (even) is to be construed with "the swan too" (*haṃso 'pi*).
"Vihāya" means the sky.
This is a *mālā-upamā* (garland simile), wherein many objects of comparison are seen for a single subject.
For example:
"As a lake by its lotus, as the night by the moon,
as a woman by her youth, so is royal fortune made captivating by policy."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pa) He speaks of the "garland simile" (*mālopamā*)—thus, "the garland simile.
The passage beginning with "by the lotus" (*vārijena*) and so forth is clear.
In this instance, the single common attribute (*dharma*) is "manoharatvam" (captivating beauty), which serves as the counter-comparison (*pratyupamāna*).

This [figure] can also occur with distinct attributes (*vibhinnadharma*), as for example: "You are like a wise preceptor, you are like Kandarpa in beauty, you are like the ocean in depth, and you are like Garuḍa in valor."
Thus:
Locanā:
In the phrase "by means of *lo* (*ū*)" and so forth, the quality of being captivating is the single common attribute.
In some cases, there is the *mālopamā* (garland simile), wherein the common attributes are distinct, as for example:
“Like moonlight, she is a delight to the eyes; like wine, she is a cause of intoxication;
like sovereignty, she has pervaded the entire world—such is the woman with shapely hips.”
In this way, the *rasanopamā* (tasting-simile) is also to be understood as being of two kinds: that with a non-distinct common attribute and that with a distinct common attribute.
In some cases, both the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) are contextual (*prakṛta*), as for example:
"The moon shines like a swan; the water is like the surface of the sky."
They were as stainless as white water-lilies and stars at the arrival of autumn.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,

pha) In connection with the discussion of the *mālopamā* (garland simile), he mentions another variety of simile that was previously noted— namely, "in some cases" (*kvacit*) and "laughing" (*hasan*).
In this context, within the description of autumn which is the subject at hand, all the attributes such as the swans, the moon, and so forth, are indeed contextual (*prakṛta*).
Locanā:

(Lo, ṛ) In expressions such as "the swan is like the moon," because the description of autumn is the subject at hand, the swans and the moon, as well as the water and the sky, and the stars and the night-lotuses, are all contextual.
“In this king’s palace shine those riches of monarchs,
like those produced by the wish-fulfilling tree in the abode of Purandara.”

Here, by means of the splendors that serve as the objects of comparison (*upameya*), the splendors that serve as the standards of comparison (*upamāna*)—expressed as "as if born from the wish-fulfilling tree" (*kalpavṛkṣabhavā iva*)—are implied; thus, this is an "implied simile" (*ākṣepopamā*).

Furthermore, because the word "house" (*gṛhe*) here is restated by the word "palace" (*bhavane*), this is a "restated simile" (*pratinirdeśyopamā*); however, these and others have not been formally defined [in the treatises], since such varieties are seen in a thousand ways.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ba) To show the reason why the *ākṣepopamā* (suggestive simile) and *pratinirdeśyopamā* (repeated simile) were not mentioned in the Sūtra, he states those two [cases] with the words "of this king" (*asya rājñaḥ*).
"Brought by the king" (*bhūpānītāḥ*) means brought from kings who had been defeated.
The phrase "produced from the wish-fulfilling tree" implies that the resulting splendors are what follow;
they are drawn forth or attached.
This is an *ākṣepopamā* (implication simile) or an *anuṣaṅgopamā* (consequential simile).
Right here, he also states that [the simile] possesses the quality of being explicitly indicated (*pratinirdeśyopamāvattva*), using the phrase "right here" (*atraiva*).
Locanā:

(lo, ṝ) "Brought by kings" (*bhūpānītāḥ*) means presented as offerings by monarchs; this [term] occurring in the sentence containing the object of comparison (*upameyavākya*) is connected with "in the palace" (*bhavane*), which occurs in the sentence containing the standard of comparison (*upamānavākya*).
"Of such a kind" (evaṃvidhā):

this is the intended meaning. Since one must specifically characterize [such figures] wherever they appear as having the semblance of a striking poetic turn (vicchitti), there would be no result whatsoever—apart from the bulkiness of the text—for such a thing to be possible in a thousand ways.
Even if such a thing were to be described, if there were a distinction from the types already mentioned, then it would have to be characterized as such;
but it is not so.
For *ananvaya* (non-correspondence) consists in the very same thing being both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*). (VisSd 10.26)
By implication, this refers to a single sentence.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, bha) states the figure of speech *ananvaya* (non-parallelism): "The simile... [etc.].
"By implication, it is a single sentence (*ekavākya*).

This is because, if there were a division of sentences (*vākyabheda*), the previously mentioned *rasanopamā* and the *upameyopamā* about to be discussed would apply, and their respective varieties would consequently be included here.
— *Locanā*:
The particle *tu* has the sense of "furthermore. It serves to exclude the application of the term "two" (*dvayoḥ*) when it occurs in the definition of a simile (*upamā*).

The figure of speech called *ananvaya* ("non-connection") is so named because its literal meaning is that there exists no connection—that is, no relation—of the object of comparison (*upameya*) with another object of comparison here; this follows from the sense of the word.
The meaning is that, since the figure of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile) will be discussed regarding these two sentences,
it is as follows:
"A lotus became like a lotus, and water became like water."
Like the moon, he was tireless in his efforts to bring about the arrival of autumn.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ma) "Rājīvam" means [the state of being] "atandra," that is, not asleep, but rather drowsy or reeling.
The autumnal season has arrived; this refers to the onset or commencement of the splendor of autumn.

Here, the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is intended only for the purpose of demonstrating that the lotuses and other elements possess no equal.
Furthermore, the phrase "the lotus is like a *pāthoja*" constitutes a distinct domain from that of *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration).
However, in this case, the use of a single word alone is preferable because it is more appropriate.
As it has been said:
"In the case of *ananvaya* (non-repetition), the identity of the word follows as a matter of course due to propriety."
But in this case of *lāṭānuprāsa*, it is the [repetition] itself that is the direct cause.
Thus [it is said].
Vijñapriyā:
[The term] "vaivakṣika" means "intended by the speaker."
From the word *vivakṣā* (intention to speak), the suffix *kaṇ* is applied.

Just as in the expression "The face is the moon," there is a cognition of the face through the superimposition of non-difference upon difference— where the moon-ness is superimposed despite being in a different locus— so too here, due to the superimposition of difference upon non-difference, the object is understood precisely through a similarity constituted by difference, even though that [similarity] is intended as being in a different locus.
The meaning is that there is no cognition of a simile.
He states the purpose for the intentional desire (*vivakṣā*) for such [a description] as being "artificial" (*āhāryya*)—namely, "on account of having no other likeness.
Here, there is also *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration).
He states this [example] as unconfounded: "pātheyam" (provisions for the journey). Regarding "because of appropriateness" (*aucityāt*):
appropriateness arises from the production of an excellence of beauty through two figures of speech.
"And in the case of non-concomitance (ananvaya)" means that it is established incidentally through the effort directed toward another purpose. "In this [case], however... means:
By the phrase "in this [work]," Lāṭānuprāsa (alliteration) is stated as being expressed through the very verses defining Lāṭānuprāsa; that is to say, it is expressed directly.
The meaning is that there is no effort toward any other purpose.
The connection is that the function of Lāṭānuprāsa is the identity of sound.
Locanā:

(lo, e) [Objection: But how is it not contradictory for one and the same thing to stand in the relation of both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)? To this, he says: "In this case" (*atre*). It is a matter of intention (*vaivakṣika*), for it is not ontological (*tāttvika*).

The intention is that although this ornament may occur in *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration) because the two words "rājīva" have meanings that differ only in their intended sense (*tātparya*), it does not constitute a specific variety of that [alliteration]. In that regard, he demonstrates the distinction between the subject matters: he asks, "How can the single word 'rājīvam' be used, since it would result in tautology? and answers, "But here...
The meaning is that its propriety arises from the fact that the fault of violating the sequence of synonyms must necessarily be overlooked in this context.
Here, he shows the agreement of the ancients with the words "as they say.
The sense is that even though it is incidental and not included within the definition [of *rasa*], it should nevertheless be adopted for the purpose of making the poetry brilliant;
it is so directly, and not merely by way of excluding defects.
The meaning is that it is included within the definition of *tallakṣaṇa*.
By way of synonym, this is considered *upameyopamā* (the comparison of the object of comparison with the standard of comparison);
that is, this state of being both the standard of comparison and the object of comparison.
Or [the simile occurs] by implication within two sentences;
for example:
"The intellect is like a lotus, and the lotus is like the intellect."
His radiance is like his body, and his body is like his radiance; his fortitude is like the earth, and the earth is like his fortitude—he in whom this shines forth perpetually, alas! how wonderful!
The intention here is that there is nothing else comparable to this king’s [qualities], such as his glorious intelligence (*śrībuddhi*) and so forth.
*Vijñapriyā* explains the figure of "mutual comparison" (*upameyopamā*) by stating: "by way of alternation."
The meaning is "of two things, namely the object of comparison and the subject of comparison.
By that, the meaning is the poetic figure *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison).
"Arthāt" means "by implication."
Since it is impossible to express [the meaning] through alternation without two distinct sentences,
[the phrase] "just like a lotus" is used;
here, in every instance, the syntactical connection is with the word "shines forth" (vibhāti).
Locanā:
(lo, o) Upameyopamā (the comparison of the object of comparison).

It is a name derived from its literal meaning: the similarity (*sādṛśya*) of the object of comparison (*upameya*), which is the subject matter of the first sentence, with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) situated in the second sentence.
The result is the exclusion of any comparison other than this;
this very point was stated in the commentary as "of this king.
*Dhṛti* means fortitude.
The recollection of an object arising from a similar experience is called *smaraṇa* (memory). // VisSd 10.27 //
For example:
"Beholding this lotus, beautiful with its sporting khañjana bird,
I remember her lovely face with its flickering eyes."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, la) He states the ornament of recollection (*smaraṇālaṅkāra*)—beginning with "similar" and "the lotus. Regarding "the lotus": [text continues]
The meaning is: "Seeing the beautiful lotus with a wagtail playing upon it, I remember her face with its lovely, flickering eyes.
Here, there is a similarity between the face and the lotus, and a similarity between the eyes and the wagtail.
The recollection of fickleness arises from its similarity to a ball;
however, in passages such as "toward me with hypocrisy," this is not an *alaṅkāra* (poetic figure), because the recollection there is produced without the experience of similarity.
— *Locanā*.
(Lo, Au) He shows what is excluded by the term "from a similar experience" (*sadṛśānubhavāt*) with the words beginning "toward me, feigning... (*mayi sakapaṭam*).

In the example beginning with "the lotus" (*aravindam*), although the memory (*smṛti*) is a means [of the emotion] and falls within the scope of the *preya* ornament as a constituent of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation), it is nevertheless sublated by the *smaraṇa* (remembrance) ornament because of its status as a specific figure of speech.
Therefore, the memory arising from the sight of the object to be contemplated is the province of the *preya* ornament.
It is exactly as [stated] in the verse beginning with "Just as [the moon] toward me with deceit," and so forth.
However, Rāghavānanda Mahāpātra maintains that even memory (smṛti) constitutes the figure of speech *smaraṇālaṅkāra* due to its dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśya*).
Their own example for this is as follows:
Whenever Sītā, as tender as a śirīṣa flower, encountered hundreds of miseries upon the mountains,
at those very moments Rāma, with tears streaming down, meditated upon hundreds of thousands of pleasures in her dwellings.
Vijñapriyā:
[This refers to the verse] beginning with "sakapaṭam" in the sixth chapter, section *va*.
In that context, there is the line: "I remember her smiling face, smiling again and again."
The meaning is that memory is produced precisely by reflection (*cintā*), because it has been stated:

"Similarity, perception, reflection, and so forth, are the awakeners of the seed of memory. This is due to the abundance of factors that awaken the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) which constitute the seed of memory.
Regarding the word *śirīṣa*:

whenever Sītā, who was as tender as a *śirīṣa* flower, encountered hundreds of miseries on the mountain, at each such instance Rāma meditated upon her in his dwellings with hundreds of thousands of joys, so that tears would flow from him;
for the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) states that "meditation on happiness" [is the remedy].
In suffering, there is a lack of similarity to happiness.
*Locanā*:
(lo, a) "Happiness" (*sukha*) itself is "well-being" (*saukhya*).
Herein lies the dissimilarity between pleasure and pain;
it is a metaphor (*rūpaka*) because of the superimposition of the form [of one thing] upon the object (*viṣaya*), which is not denied.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, śa) He states the figure of speech called *rūpaka*: "The *rūpaka*," he says.
Regarding the word *rūpitā*, *rūpaṇa* is the act of forming (*rūpa*); from that, by the addition of the suffix *itac*, the meaning is "possessing the act of forming."
And thus, in this context, the moon and so forth, which are about to be figuratively represented (rūpayiṣyamāṇa), are the objects to be represented (rūpita).
Since the past tense would not apply if the suffixes mentioned were used,
the meaning is that *rūpaka* (metaphor) is the superimposition (*āropa*) of that [moon] upon the face and so forth.

Some here say that the ablative case in the word "āropāt" (from superimposition) indicates the sense of being a "cognizer" (*jñāpakatā*); thus, it should be understood that [superimposition] is the cause for the cognition of the very nature of the metaphor (*rūpaka*) itself, by means of its own cognition.
— *Locanā*.

(Lo, Ā) Having thus determined the figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) based on similarity where non-difference is predominant, he now defines it where difference is predominant—namely, *rūpaka* (metaphor).

It consists in the state of possessing a superimposition (*āropa*) upon that which has been metaphorized (*rūpita*). Nor is there any lack of application here in the present context; for superimposition (*āropa*) is the cognition of identity with another [object] by something whose own nature has not been swallowed up (*anigīrṇasvarūpa*).
Therefore, this also excludes *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and the like, which are rooted in *adhyavasāya* (determination).
*Adhyavasāya* is the apprehension of identity between the object and the subject through the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of the object.
*Apahnava* (concealment) takes the form: "This is not a face, it is the moon."

And thus, when an object that is not denied and not swallowed up [by another] possesses the form of the subject through identity with it, that is the ornament called *rūpaka* (metaphor); the meaning is that one thing possesses the form of another by means of a different form.
This distinguishes it from *pariṇāma* (transformation), as indicated by the term "rūpita" (made to possess form). We shall analyze this further in its proper context.
The term "nirapahnave" (in what cannot be denied) is for the purpose of excluding denial (*apahnuti*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṣa) states the exclusion of other categories: "rūpita" (that which is manifested as form).

In the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation), because the object being transformed (*rūpyamāṇa*) serves as the substratum for the act of representation (*rūpaṇā*), there is a real non-difference (*vāstavābheda*) resulting from that transformation; this constitutes "being represented" (*rūpitatva*), which consists in the absence of superimposition (*anāropa*) due to such a state of affairs.

For example, in the illustration of *pariṇāma*: "An embrace pressing against her breasts was made by her as the stake in the game of dice," the stake (*paṇa*), which is the object being represented, is indeed transformed precisely by virtue of its being the embrace—the substratum of representation—and thus there is a real non-difference between the stake and the embrace. Therefore, the stake does not [merely] represent [itself].
Thus, there is the exclusion of that [superimposition].

Regarding "for the sake of excluding Apahnuti (concealment)": in such cases as "This is not the moon, but the coiled lord of serpents," there is indeed a superimposition of the coiled lord of serpents upon the moon;
however, because this is preceded by the concealment of its moon-nature, there is an exclusion of that [Apahnuti].
That [succession] is threefold: with limbs, without limbs, and paramparita (transferred). // VisSd_10.28 //
Vijñapriyā:
He states its threefold nature with the words "that" (*tat*).
Locanā:
(Lo, i) He states its divisions with the word "na" [in the verse].
Before the word "tridhā" (threefold), the word "first" (*prathamam*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis,
because the other divisions are contained within this one.
That is *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification).
In that regard:
where the superimposition of one thing is the cause for the superimposition of another.
That is the "successive" (paramparita), based on words that are either punned (śliṣṭa) or not punned (aśliṣṭa).
It is of four kinds: individual, solitary, and in the form of a garland.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"In which [verse] 'of someone'... refers to this.

The meaning is that when a certain metaphor (rūpaka) is apprehended, there is the superimposition (āropa) of something upon something else; "parāropaṇasya" means the preeminent superimposition, the primary superimposition; "kāraṇam" means the means of proof.
Regarding the term *śliṣṭa* (punning): when both the literal meaning (*rūpya*) and the superimposed meaning (*āropya*) are presented by means of a single word, it is based on punning (*śliṣṭatva*).
However, when this is not the case, it is based on non-punning words (*aśliṣṭa-śabda*). — *Locanā*.

(Lo, ī) The cause or motive for the superimposition (*āropaṇa*) is that which cannot be established otherwise than by representing the primary object (*para*) as having the nature of another such object. *Śliṣṭa* (conjoined) means that the word itself, which serves as the basis for producing the intended superimposition, possesses a double meaning. *Aśliṣṭa* (unconjoined) refers to a case where the meaning of the metaphorical form is indicated by separate words.
Such a word is the basis, that is, the cause;
the meaning is that it belongs to the primary metaphorical attribution (*mukhyāropa*).
It consists solely of a single instance of figurative description (*rūpaṇā*).
The form of a garland (*mālārūpa*) consists in the superimposition of multiple objects upon a single locus, without depending on a succession of objects;
the same applies elsewhere as well.
It is called *paramparita* (successive) because a succession has arisen for it; thus the term is meaningful.
Among these, an example of pure *paramparita* based on punning words (*śliṣṭaśabda*) is as follows:
“O you who are fierce toward the world in battle,
O you who are the enemy of the circle of kings!”
O illustrious King Nṛsiṃha,
may prosperity attend your arm!
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) "Āhava" means—"O King Nṛsiṃha!
May there be well-being for your *bāhu*, that is, for your hand."

To what sort [of Rāhu]? In the battle (*āhava*), the circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*)—which is itself the circle of monarchs—is like the lunar orb (*rājamaṇḍala*); for that [circle], he is a Rāhu, namely Saihikeya, because he eclipses it. Here, the attribution of the nature of Rāhu to the circle of kings is logically untenable, since Rāhu does not actually eclipse the circle of kings.
Therefore, the superimposition of the lunar orb upon the circle of kings serves as the primary means of establishing that [secondary] attribution.
And by means of the word *rājan* (king), which possesses a double meaning (*śliṣṭa*), he expresses the presentation of both [meanings] with the words "here" (*atra*).

And here, for the sake of establishing the primary metaphor (*mukhyarūpaka*), since both the king and the moon are contextual (*prākaraṇika*), the moon denoted by the word *rājan* is the king alone from the very beginning, and not the moon as a suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*).
For it is only when there is context regarding a single meaning that another meaning can be suggested.

Therefore, there is no possibility here of the "subordinate suggested" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) type known as "that which is an auxiliary to the establishment of the expressed" (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*), wherein the suggested form serves as the means of establishing the expressed. However, in a case where a primary metaphor is established first without any superimposition, and subsequently there arises an incompatibility in the connection of that [metaphorically] determined object with another word-meaning, then— in order to avoid that incompatibility in the connection of the other word-meaning with the primary form of the non-contextual object, which is the secondary meaning of the punning word acting as a restrictor upon that non-contextual object— [the secondary meaning is employed].
When [the suggested meaning] is being manifested, it is indeed the suggested itself; in that case, its status is merely as a factor for establishing the expressed meaning.
For example: “Dizziness, distress, lack of aesthetic sensitivity, dissolution, fainting, darkness, and physical exhaustion...”
And death, forcibly inflicts upon separated women the poison born of the cloud-serpents.

In this context, the metaphorical representation (*rūpaṇa*) of the cloud as a serpent—by virtue of its dark color and its quality of being beneficial—is first established. Subsequently, since the literal meaning of the serpent (as a venomous creature) is incompatible with its function as a producer of the contextual water (rain), that literal sense is set aside; thus, the second meaning of the word "poison" (*viṣa*), namely *halāhala*, becomes the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*).
This is because, within that [metaphorical] framework, the water described in the context of the rain is what constitutes the expressed meaning (*vācya*).

Therefore, since there is no logical inconsistency in the serpent being the producer of the *halāhala* poison, its establishment in the form of a serpent [is valid]; thus, the distinction of the subject matter should be noted by the wise.
And so, when the substantive—which establishes the primary metaphor—is expressed as the literal meaning (*vācya*), it is a "metaphor based on a chain" (*paramparita-rūpaka*);

but when that [substantive] is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), it is a "limb for the establishment of the literal meaning" (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*). This being established, [the verse continues]: "He illumines the hollow between heaven and earth; he blazes everywhere."
"O Indra among kings, your majesty is a forest fire for the lineage of your enemies.

Regarding this, the author's earlier statement—that the superimposition of a bamboo (veṇu) is suggested (vyaṅgya), and thus serves as a constituent part for establishing the expressed (vācya) forest fire—is to be reconsidered.

For even as in the phrase "the Rāhu of the circle of kings," here too the superimposition of the bamboo is actually expressed (vācya), as it serves to establish the primary metaphor of the forest fire.
Locanā:
(lo, u) "Jagaduddaṇḍa" means exceedingly fierce;
"rājamaṇḍala" refers to both a circle of kings and the orb of the moon.

In this instance, the superimposition (āropa) of the circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*)—that is, the assembly of monarchs—upon the orb of the moon serves as the basis for the superimposition of the necklace upon the king’s arm.
An example of the garland form (*mālārūpa*) is as follows:
"The lord of the day, who causes the lotus to bloom; the wind, which is the constant movement..."
"You alone on this earth are the thunderbolt for the range of mountains."
In this context, the rising of the lotuses is nothing other than the rising of Padmā; the arrival of the virtuous is nothing other than the coming of the good;
and the kings, who are the upholders of the earth, are nothing other than mountains—such superimpositions serve as the grounds for superimposing the nature of the sun and so forth upon the king.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, kha) He states a series of *śliṣṭa-paramparita-rūpaka* (conjoined and successive metaphors) beginning with "padmodaya" [the rise of the lotus].
The meaning of this has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) itself.
Thus, the aforementioned superimposition (āropa) serves as the cause for the superimposition of "being the sun" and so forth;
for here, the sun is the object indicated (lakṣya) in its rising,
and the wind in the arrival of the virtuous.

In the series of kings (*bhūbhṛt*), because the thunderbolt (*dambholi*) is of no use, there is the superimposition of the rising of the lotus (*padmā*) and so forth upon it; since that [lotus] is useful for that purpose, it serves as the cause [for the metaphor].
"O learned one, swan of the mind-lake! O you of blazing splendor who causes the closing of the enemy-lotuses!"
O Nīlalohita who traverses difficult paths!
O Vaiśvānara who accepts the fuel!
O you who are skillful in providing true remedies!
O Lord, formidable in your previous state of victory;
O excellent hero, imperial sovereignty!
"O Vatsa! For a hundred years, perform the high rites of the enemy.

This verse was presented by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* specifically as an example of a "successive metaphor based on paronomasia" (*śliṣṭaparamparitamālārūpaka*). Its meaning is indeed: "O excellent hero! [and so forth].
"O Vairiñca, for a hundred Brahmā-years you should perform lofty sovereign rites.
He speaks other forms of address for the King as well—beginning with "O Wise One":
"O Haṃsa, that which is the mind of the wise is itself the Mānasa lake."
O Sun of blazing splendor, the non-contraction and expansion of lotuses is your domain;
O Nīlalohita, the seeking of Durgā consists in not seeking difficult paths— that is, traversing the fortress without [seeking] a path.

The acceptance of battles that have been concluded is indeed the acceptance of fuel; O Vaiśvānara, therein lies the ordaining of pleasure in truth, which is the ordaining of displeasure in untruth; O Dakṣa Prajāpati, victory is indeed the defeat of others, and the manifestation of that victory is Arjuna; O Bhīmasena, this occurs in his prior state, that is, at his initial birth.

In the verse beginning with "he prabho," there are many primary metaphors (mukhya-rūpaka) such as the superimposition of a swan upon the king, each of which is individually supported by multiple metaphors, such as the mind being a lake (mānasa-sarovara).

In the present case as well, there are numerous metaphors—such as the sun and so forth—that support the metaphor of the king, while the rising of Lakṣmī and others serves as the basis for metaphors such as the blooming of a lotus.

An example of a purely *śliṣṭa* (pun-based) *paramparita-rūpaka* provided by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* is as follows: "O you who have illuminated the three worlds with an extraordinary, great light..."
O Lord, by whom are you not praised— you who are a jewel released from a noble lineage?
Thus [it is said].
The meaning of this is: O Lord, by whom would your pearl-jewel not be praised—you who are of a noble lineage?
Here, "noble lineage" (*sadvaṃśa*) refers both to a virtuous family and to a fine bamboo cane; it is from such a source that the pearl-jewel arises. Who would not praise you?

Because pearls originate in his lineage, he addresses the King with another epithet: "O Alaukika... He who possesses the *alaukika*—meaning extraordinary or distinct from other worlds—*mahāloka*, which is a great vision or great light, and by whom the three worlds have been illuminated—that is, adorned with the jewels of liberation (*muktā*)—address him as such.
For here, O Queen, the superimposition of pearls is the primary metaphor, while the superimposition of bamboo upon the lineage is its means of proof;
likewise, the superimposition of light occurs upon the casting of a glance, because in the absence of light, there would be no excellence in the pearls. — Locanā.
(Lo, Ū) Padmā is Lakṣmī and the lotus; the arrival of the virtuous and the arrival at all times; kings who are lords of the earth and those who dwell in the forest.

"Always and ever for Padmā, that is, Lakṣmī. Thus: "O God, you alone are Pātāla; you are the support of the quarters; you are the ground of the winds of Amarāvatī; you are the three worlds in essence."

In this context, the metaphorical representation as consisting of the three worlds and so forth, as well as the metaphorical representation as the netherworld (pātāla) and so forth, serves as the cause.

An example of that which is based solely on the connection of words that are not [semantically] joined is as follows: "May the four arms of Hari protect you— those pillars for the pavilion of the three worlds, dark as rain-clouds and roughened by the striking of the bowstring."
In this instance, the superimposition of the three worlds as a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is the cause for the superimposition of Hari’s arms as pillars.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ga) states that [the following] is merely unconnected (*aśliṣṭa*): "May those dark as clouds protect you."
May the four arms of Hari protect you.
Of what nature are they? They are the pillars of the pavilion that is the triple world itself, because they support it.
Likewise, the harsh twanging of the Śārṅga bow serves as the cause for the attribution of "pillar-ness," because it is associated with pillars throughout the three worlds.
An example of the form of a garland (mālārūpa) is as follows:
“The white parasol of King Manojā, variegated with sandalwood paste, belonging to the lady of the quarter [the West],
shines as a lotus in the lake of the sky— the orb of the moon, possessing the luster of a mass of camphor.”
In this case, the superimposition of kingship and so forth upon Manojāta and the others is the cause for the superimposition of the white parasol and so forth upon the lunar disc.

Regarding this, some maintain that "the superimposition of Rāhu and so forth upon the king’s arms and the like is the cause for the superimposition of the lunar orb and so forth upon the royal circle and the like.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, gha) Regarding "in the form of a garland" (*mālārūpam yathā*)—the ellipsis is "based on non-joined words" (*aśliṣṭaśabdanibandhanam*).
[The example is: "The orb of the moon, possessing the luster of a mass of camphor, shines forth for King Manojara."
In that regard, he states other metaphors (rūpaka) caused by a metaphorical chain (*paramparitarūpaka*): "The mind-born [Cupid] is indeed the king; [the moon] is his white umbrella.
For the woman who has the form of turmeric, there is sandalwood (*śrīkhaṇḍa*).
"The variegated [mark] of sandalwood," "the lotus of the lake whose form is the sky"—

in these four examples, some maintain that the relationship between the cause (nimitta) and the effect (naimittika) regarding the two types of *rūpaka* is exactly the reverse of what was stated; he shows this view with the word "eṣu" ("in these").
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) The sense is that "some [do so], but we do not";
and this he will clarify right here.
If there is a metaphorical representation (rūpaṇā) of the whole together with its parts, that is indeed a "metaphor with parts" (sāṅga).

The *Vijñapriyā* commentary explains that there are two types of *sāṅgarūpaka* (metaphor with parts): one whose scope encompasses all objects (*samastavastuviṣaya*) and the other which manifests in only one part (*ekadeśavivarti*). It states this regarding the "principal element" (*aṅgin*) as follows: "The principal element... [etc.].
"Of that which possesses its limbs and its properties":
the meaning is that if that which undergoes transformation (*rūpyate*) has properties (*dharmas*) that also undergo transformation, then it is "possessing its limbs.
— *Locanā*:
(Lo, ṝ) Of that which is together with its limbs and its accessories;
therein—the first opinion is that all things to be superimposed are expressed by words. (Viṣṇu-sahasranāma-vyākhyā 10.31)
Locanā: (lo,
ḷ) Regarding all limbs and their accessories,
"in being verbal" means in being denotable by a word.
First is that which has all things as its object,
for example:
"With the nectar of his speech, 'He [Rāma] has ended the exhaustion caused by Rāvaṇa’s drought'..."
Having rained down upon the crop of the Maruts, the black cloud vanished.
In this [verse], while the superimposition of "cloud-ness" upon Kṛṣṇa is present, the qualities of "immortality" and so forth are superimposed upon his speech and other attributes.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ca):
"The restraint of Rāvaṇa."

Having refreshed the crop—which was like the wind and exhausted by the drought in the form of Rāvaṇa, which was a hindrance to the rain—Kṛṣṇa, who is Viṣṇu, appeared as a cloud and, having showered upon and drenched the crop, vanished.
Furthermore, another cloud that is being manifested is the subject (*aṅgin*);
its property, water, is metaphorically represented (*rūpita*) as speech.
In this way, even the crop is a limb [of the whole] by virtue of its connection with being sprinkled by its own water;
it is thus represented as such among the winds.
He states this with the words "here."
Locanā:
(Lo, E) Because speech and the other [senses] have black implements, such as nectar and so forth, there is the "cloud" implement;
and here, moreover, is the description of the supreme form.
As they say:
"Upon this stage of your lotus-face, the dancer of your creeper-like eyebrows performs a graceful dance"— this is a charmingly expressed metaphor (*rūpakālaṃkāra*).
Thus [it is said].
For here, after the metaphorical representation (*rūpaṇā*) of the face as a lotus, there follows again the metaphorical representation of it as a stage.

This should be understood similarly in the case of "the creeper-like eyebrows as a dancer. Where one [element] is literal and [the other] is metaphorical, that is *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest).
Locanā:
(lo, ai) "Arthatva" means being understood through the sense.

This type of metaphor has the nature (*śīla*) of functioning (*vartituṃ*) with clarity as something verbal (*śābdatayā*) specifically in one part; thus, it is called *ekadeśavivarti* (partially manifest).
Of something being superimposed;
for example:
"Her blossoming face is filled with the honey of loveliness."
By whom is it not drunk by the swarms of bees that are the eyes of the local women?”
In this case, the superimposition of "honey-ness" and so forth upon the "loveliness" and so forth is verbal (*śābda*), whereas the superimposition of "lotus-ness" upon the face is implied (*ārtha*).

Nor is this a case of "partial metaphorical transformation" (*ekadeśavivartinī upamā*), because the attribute of "blooming," which exists primarily in the lotus that is being superimposed, is only applied figuratively (*upacarita*) to the face.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) He states the *ekadeśavivartirūpaka* [metaphor with partial transformation]— namely, "of whatever" (*yasya kasya*)— meaning, "of some object being described" (*kasyacid rūpyamāṇasya*).
In some cases, the nature [of the figure] belongs to the whole (aṅgin), and in others, to the part (aṅga); this should be understood accordingly.
Therein, he states that the whole possesses the status of being the expressed meaning (*ārthatva*) with the words "lāvaṇya...
etc. By whom is her face—not full-blown and filled with the honey in the form of beauty—not drunk by the swarms of bees in the form of the eyes of the world?
Regarding "the superimposition of a lotus and so forth upon the mouth":
here, being filled with honey and being drunk by bees are the subordinate elements (*aṅga*);
the lotus and so forth, which are the objects of comparison (*rūpyamāṇa*), are the principal element (*aṅgin*).
In some cases, the meaning is merely the form of the subordinate element (*aṅga*).
For example: "The ocean of virtues is [your] state of being.
Here, the quality of the principal element (*aṅgin*), the ocean—namely, its water—is superimposed upon the subordinate quality; thus, it is an implied (ārtha) meaning.

The meaning of the objection beginning with "na ca" (nor indeed) is as follows: since comparisons such as "beauty like honey" are possible, by virtue of those, a comparison of the face to a lotus is also perceived.
The reply begins with "vikasvara" (blooming) and so forth.

The meaning is that "bloomingness" is a property belonging exclusively to a flower; therefore, because it exists primarily and directly in relation to the flower which possesses that property, [the comparison holds].

"And in the mouth" means that in the lotus-like mouth, [the term "lotus"] is applied through a secondary metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) consisting of a transitive relationship, namely the relationship of similarity with its own substratum.
*Locanā*:
"Because it functions as the primary [meaning]."
Primarily, by way of being that which is to be enjoined;
this is the underlying intention:
for here, having concealed the form of this object, [the author proceeds].
When the possessor of attributes (the subject) is endowed with form by means of the form of a lotus, the acceptance of the property known as "blooming" is the establishing proof.
This will become very clear in the context of the discussion on *saṃkara* (commixture), so it is not elaborated upon here.
The metaphorical representation (*rūpaṇa*) of the bare [subject] alone is also of two kinds.
Because it has the nature of the solitary garland—
Locanā:
[the letters] *lo* and *au*, which are solitary, meaning they are not conjoined with any other form of association.
The nature of the *mālā-kevala* (the solitary garland) is to be explained as previously stated.
Among these, the form of the *mālā* that is without parts (*niraṅga*) is as follows:
"The skill of the Creator in fashioning the moonlight, which is the eye of the world."
"This lotus-eyed woman is the pleasure-house of the Bodiless One."
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding "skill in emanation" (*nirmāṇakauśalam*),
this is a metaphorical indication (*sāropā lakṣaṇā*).
The meaning is that they are produced by skill in that [matter].
There is no metaphor (*rūpaka*) here in this respect;
rather, it should be understood as a *mālā* (garland) because of the representation of the two pleasure-houses of Candikā.
Locanā:
Regarding "nirmāṇa" (creation)—here, because multiple objects are superimposed upon a single lotus-eyed woman, it is a "partless" (niravayava) series.
It is simply as follows:

“O beautiful one, when a servant has committed an offense, a kick from his master is considered appropriate; I do not grieve over that. But that which pierces my tender foot with the tips of the thorns of rising, harsh bristles of horripilation—that, indeed, is my pain.”
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
jha) "Upon the servant who has committed an offense"—
the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is with "the tips of the thorns," which take the form of hard, bristling sprouts of horripilation.
Wherein there is merely the throbbing of the throat amidst the sprouts of horripilation;
Locanā says: "O servant! (lo, ā).
O servant, toward one who is under your own control, who has committed an offense, who has committed a transgression,
and who is a master to be served.
I do not grieve over this blow, nor do I feel resentment;
it is broken and pierced.
Here, "only" (*kevalam*) refers to a partless form, because there is no description of a similar internal form, as it is described as being in one place alone.
Here too, following the depiction of the *pulaka* as a sprout, there is a "depiction of what has already been depicted" (*rūpitarūpaṇa*) by means of depicting it as a thorn.
Thus, there are eight varieties of *rūpaka*.
— *Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ña) Therefore, there are eight [types].

For the two kinds of *paramparita-rūpaka*—distinguished as having either a fused (*śliṣṭa*) or non-fused (*aśliṣṭa*) expressive word—there is a fourfold division based on the further distinction between *mālā* (garland-like) and simple (*kevala*).
And that [fourfold type] is twofold, being distinguished by its having all objects as its domain (*samastavastuviṣaya*) or by its being partially transformed (*ekadeśavivartin*).
The meaning is that there are eight types, being twofold by way of being "without parts" (*niraṅga*) and "pure garland" (*kevalamālātva*).
Locanā:
(lo, i) in those respective ways, there are eight.
The intention is that, otherwise, other varieties yet to be mentioned are also possible;
the phrase "stated by the ancients" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
In some cases, there is even a metaphorical (paramparita) type of partial metaphor (ekadeśavivartin), such as:
“The sword of the Indra of Mālava triumphs in battle, acting as the chamberlain to the Earth.”
In this instance, the superimposition of the status of a queen (*mahiṣī*) upon the earth is the cause for the superimposition of the status of a chamberlain (*sauvidalla*) upon the rhinoceros.
Although this variety may also constitute a "garland-superimposition" (*mālāropa*) as in previous cases, an example of it must be sought elsewhere.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṭa) *Khaḍgaḥ kṣmeti*—the sword (*khaḍga*) is the *sauvidalla*, the eunuch of the inner apartments, of the earth (*kṣmā*), which is the forbearance (*kṣamā*) not superimposed as being feminine.
According to the lexicon: "The *sauvidalla* is a *mahallikā* [eunuch].
Regarding the word *atra*:
Because the superimposition of a chamberlain upon a sword is untenable without the superimposition of femininity upon the earth; thus, the example must be sought elsewhere. For instance:
“The moon is the white parasol of the god of love, and from the eastern quarter it is a drop of sandal-paste.”
The lotus-foot of Viṣṇu shines, its pedestal of earth washed by its rays.
In this instance, the superimposition (āropa) of kingship and so forth upon the flower-arrowed god [Kāma] is the cause for the superimposition of the white parasol and so forth upon the moon.

And if the intended meaning is that a "garland" (mālā) consists of several other figures of speech (rūpaka) that establish a single expressed object of comparison (rūpya), then the following should be cited as an example: "The moon is the lotus of the sky on the full-moon night, and [the moon] is the lotus of the hare."

For here, while the moon is being described (*rūpyamāṇe*), the fact that the full moon (*rākā*) is the foot and hand of Lakṣmī, that the sky is a lake, and that the hare is a bee serves to establish the intended meaning (*arthasādhaka*).
Locanā:
(Lo, ī) A *sauvidalla* is a chamberlain or superintendent of the harem.
Regarding this:
the meaning is as follows—here, because the metaphor of the earth (*kṣmā*) being a queen (*mahiṣī*) serves a specific purpose, it is a "partially manifest" metaphor (*ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka*);
and because that metaphor is the cause for the sword (*khaḍga*) being metaphorically represented as a chamberlain (*sauvidalla*), it is a "successive" metaphor (*paramparita*).
Furthermore, in this context, the representation of the sword as a chamberlain is not possible without the representation of the earth as a queen;
however, in the case of a sentence that effects a partial transformation (*vivartana*) of a single part of its constituent members, such a representation is inherently untenable.
The distinction is that while the former implies another meaning through the power of suggestion (*sāmarthya*), the latter does not.
The meaning is that [the quality] is to be sought among the objects of observation (*lakṣya*).
For example:
“Good conduct is the source of well-being for prosperity, the elixir for long-lasting excellence, and the playful manifestation of boundless character; it is beauty itself.”
The sovereign King Bhānu, of the lineage of Gaṅgā, is the presiding deity of the sciences, the manifestation of unconditioned valor, and the auspicious abode of the three Liṅgas.

In this context, the metaphorical representation of Śrī and the others as specific living beings serves as the basis for the metaphorical representation of them as auspicious blessings (*svastyayana*).
Sometimes, in a metaphorical representation that includes its constituent parts (*sāṅga-rūpaka*), the objects to be superimposed are found to be based on wordplay (*śliṣṭa*). (VisSd 10.33)
Vijñapriyā:
"(In the case of) both the *sāṅga* and the *rūpaka*.
This means that there are two types of *sāṅga*, according to whether they revolve around a single part of the subject matter of the praise.
Locanā:

(Lo, u) In some instances, when [the words] are superimposed upon a particular part [of a compound], and are indicated as being suggested (*vyaṅgya*) by the word expressing the locus of that superimposition, there is "partially developed" (*ekadeśavivartin*) punning (*śliṣṭa*), as in my own verse:
“Having placed her upon the breast of the mountain of sunrise, where the garment of the mass of darkness has fallen away,
this nectar-rayed moon kisses the face of the quarter presided over by the Lord of the Immortals, whose eyes are the blooming night-lilies.”

An example concerning all objects is as follows—in this very same passage beginning with "vicumbati," when the reading is changed to "cucumbe haridabalāmukham indunāyakena" (the moon-leader kissed the face of the quarter-elephant).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍa) [This refers to] "karam udaye" (at the time of rising).
This moon is kissing the face of the eastern quarter, the direction of the Lord of the Immortals;
having placed his hand— his very ray— upon the breast of the lofty mountain that takes the form of a woman.
On what kind of breast-tip did that darkness fall? On one where the garment had taken the form of a film. What was the face like?
It was such that its eyes had the appearance of blooming night-lotuses.
Here, the status of heroine (nāyikātva) belongs to the direction of Amareśa, and the status of hero (nāyakatva) belongs to the moon; these are implied meanings.
Their two attributes—the hand placed upon the breast and the wide-open eyes—are expressed by words (śābda).
And the hands and feet are joined.
The example for the second [type] is clear in the reading: "The moon, the leader, kissed the face of the western quarter.
— *Locanā*:
*Lo* and *ū* signify both "ray" (*kiraṇa*) and "hand" (*hasta*);
*mukha* signifies both "the first part" (*ādyabhāga*) and "face" (*vadana*).
Is this not a case of *śliṣṭaparamparita* (successive pun-based metaphor)?

For in cases such as "the thunderbolt that is the mass of the earth's [protective] ramparts," the figurative representation of the king and so forth as a thunderbolt would be entirely inconsistent, as there is no similarity whatsoever in the absence of an attribution of mountainhood and the like to the king.

If that is so, one might ask: how can there be a *paramparita* (transferred) metaphor in examples such as "the lord of the day who causes the lotus to bloom," given that a similarity between the king and the sun based on qualities like brilliance is possible? This objection should not be raised.
For instance, in the case of a king and so forth, the similarity based on causes such as majesty or existence is quite evident;
however, that is not what is intended here, because only the blooming of the lotus and so forth are intended to be the common attributes (*sādhāraṇadharma*) for both.

But here, the similarity between the mountain and the like with the breasts and so forth—by virtue of their being full and high—is indeed very clear; therefore, this is not a case of *śliṣṭa-paramparita* (metaphorical succession based on double entendre).
Vijñapriyā: (vi, ḍha) Nor is it the case here... [etc.]
Because the metaphorical representation of the hand by means of a pun serves as the means for establishing the metaphorical representation of the breasts.
He provides the resolution with the words "for in that case" (*tatra hi*):
it is precisely that metaphor which is "successive" (*paramparita*) that establishes the primary metaphor, and not similarity that establishes it.
However, where a primary metaphor (*mukhyarūpaka*) is established even through similarity (*sādṛśya*), there is no "metaphor by succession" (*paramparitarūpaka*).
Therefore, in the present case, it has been stated by this [author] that the representation of the breasts as such is due solely to their height, which is similar to a mountain.
Now, if it is the case that *paramparitarūpaka* occurs only when similarity is absent, [then...]

Then, he raises the objection that there is an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "the rising of the lotus" (*padmodaya*) by saying "then" (*tarhi*). He demonstrates this over-narrow application by saying "of the king, etc. (*rājādeḥ*).
"But that is not what is intended to be expressed.
As for what *is* intended to be expressed, he says: "Of the very rising of the lotus, etc.
This means: "of the words themselves that are connected with the rising of the lotus, etc."
Locanā:

By means of the punning nature (*śliṣṭatva*) of words such as *kara* and *ādi*, she dispels the suspicion that this might be a "successive pun" (*śliṣṭaparamparita*) with the words "not so" (*na ca*).

Since [the resemblance] is quite evident in the case of a king and so forth when they take on the form of an enemy (*śātrava*) and the like, the ellipsis (*śeṣa*) to be supplied is "it certainly exists" (*asty eva*) prior to that.
In "padmodaya" (the rising of the lotus) and similar cases, the similarity consists precisely in qualities such as the brilliance of light; this is the meaning:

just as in the simile "sakalakalaṃ puram" (the city [resounds] with every sound), where the similarity is the state of being filled with all sounds, as in the case of the rising of the lotus and so forth.
He applies this to the king and the lord of the day (the sun) in the present context, stating: "But here, however... and so on.
In this context, in passages such as "upon the breast-peak of the mountain of rising rays" (*iha kara udayamahīdharastanāgre*), the particle *tu* has the sense of "furthermore.

And thus, in cases such as "bewilderment and discontent" (*bhramimarati*), the superimposition (*āropa*)—that "poison is indeed water, [therefore] poison"—serves as the cause for the superimposition of the serpent, whose similarity [to water] is well-known; hence, this is indeed a case of "metaphorical chain based on word-play" (*śliṣṭaparamparitam*).

Regarding this, those who consider that in examples such as "O swan of the learned man’s mind" (*vidvanmānasahaṃsa*), the superimposition of the nature of a swan upon the king is the cause for the superimposition of the nature of a lake (*mānasa*) upon the mind, say: "In this case, the word 'poison' (*viṣa*) does not possess a double meaning based on its application to a cloud—as in 'O swan of the learned man’s mind'—where it causes the superimposition of a serpent;

rather, it is prompted by the specific eightfold effects of poison, beginning with delusion and ending with death, which are well-known in the medical treatises (*vaidyaśāstra*). For, in this instance, the double meaning is established without the superimposition of identity."
The claim that this is merely the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is incorrect; for,

as in the cases of "the cloud" (*jalada*) being like a serpent (*bhujaga*), or "the city [resounding] with every musical note" (*sakalakalaṃ puram*), the use of the word *viṣa* (poison/nectar) would be untenable without its possessing a double meaning.

Furthermore, it is not tenable to say that "the poison born from the cloud-serpent is water," because the serpent-nature of the cloud is unreal, and because water cannot originate from a serpent. Therefore, the metaphorical description of the actual subject (the rain) is only consistent once one has set aside the metaphorical identification of "poison" with "poison."
Nor is it correct to say that the establishment of the metaphorical representation (rūpaṇā) of the expressed meaning (vācya) occurs through mere punning (śleṣa),
because identity is not perceived through punning.
If there is a fragmented perception brought about by punning, the metaphorical representation of the expressed meaning is inconsistent.
Because of the persistence of that state;
otherwise, there would be the same undesirable consequence even in cases such as "O swan of the learned's mind" (*vidvanmānasahaṃsa*). [For example:
"This line of the dense tamāla forest, thick with the flesh of swords, shines upon your sword, which resembles the night."
Where, having forcibly brought away the fame of his enemies, your youthful valor takes its delight, possessing the luster of the moon.
In this case, regarding a *rūpaka* (metaphor) that applies to only one part, the term *kṣitibhṛt*—meaning both "king" and "mountain"—is a *śliṣṭa* (pun-based) word.

Regarding this, the experts on poetics such as Paṇḍita Caṇḍīdāsa and others accept it as a *śliṣṭaparamparita-rūpaka* (a pun-based metaphorical chain), wherein the superimposition of "mountain-ness" upon the king serves as the cause for the superimposition of "Tamāla forest-ness" upon the sword.
However, that [view] is to be considered.

For instance, because it serves a dual purpose— as in the verse beginning “O swan of the mind of the wise,” where the king’s being a *haṃsa* (swan) is the cause for his being metaphorically identified as such—
the sword’s being described as a grove of *tamāla* trees functions as a subordinate element to that metaphorical identification.

Furthermore, since even in the case of the actions of a forceful lover, the hero and heroine serve as the instruments for [establishing] majesty and fame, we consider it more appropriate here to regard what is stated in the present sūtra as a *sāvayava-ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka* (a metaphor with subordinate parts where one part is based on paronomasia), rather than a *śliṣṭa-paramparita* (a paronomastic chain metaphor). This is because the hero and heroine function as the necessary adjuncts (*upakaraṇa*) for majesty and fame. Thus we maintain.

Furthermore, in cases of "coalesced" (*śliṣṭa*) *paramparita* (successive) metaphor, such as "O swan of the learned man's mind" (*vidvanmānasahaṃsa*), the king’s nature as a swan is not established without the superimposition of the nature of Lake Mānasa upon the mind (*mānasa*).
In this instance, however, the sword’s being the edge of a Tamāla forest is well-established even through its dark blue color and other qualities.

Moreover, in a metaphor with subordinate parts (*sāvayava-rūpaka*), where the similarity of each individual part is sometimes not established, the perception of similarity arises from their becoming one and assisting each other.
For example, in "rāvaṇāvagraha" (the drought that is Rāvaṇa) and similar instances, there is the [superimposition] of the crops and so forth upon the winds and so forth.

Furthermore, because a metaphorical description of the parts (*avayava-rūpaṇā*) is absent in the case of a chain-metaphor (*paramparita*), it is not said to be included within the category of metaphors with parts (*sāvayava*).

In words such as "mānasa" (the mind and the Mānasa lake), the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*)—in this case, the form of the object "lake"—which is merely evoked, serves solely to establish the quality of being a swan and so forth.

For this very reason, even the word *kṣaṇadānibha* (resembling the night) implies the time of night; thus, because the darkness becomes dense, it is suitable for forceful dalliance (*haṭharamaṇa*). This is the interpretation of the ancients as well.
Therefore, since all the objects being described—beginning with "the mountain" (*kṣitibhṛta*)—serve as instruments for forceful dalliance, the aforementioned [interpretation] alone is superior.

In this [previous example], because the denotative function (*abhidhā*) comes to rest after first expressing the meaning of "youth" as "maturity" with respect to the fire of the eyes, the meaning "young man" is apprehended solely through suggestion (*vyañjanā*).

Here, however, in the verse beginning with *kṣitibhṛtaḥ*, because many things are metaphorically represented (*rūpaṇa*), the representation of "valor" (*pratāpa*) as "youth" is verbal (*śābda*). Furthermore, words such as *ramate* serve precisely as supports for the metaphor.
However, in cases such as "he embraced the sky," the embrace and other actions do not serve as the means for establishing *samāsokti* (condensed metaphor), as they do in other instances.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of *samāsokti* occurring in every case of *ekadeśavivartin* (partial) metaphors.
For example, in the verse "He takes [her] by force and enjoys her," although there is a similarity of effect (*kāryasāmya*), there is no *samāsokti*.

For if *samāsokti* were to be accepted on the basis of even a slight similarity of effects (*kāryya-leśa-sāmya*), then the scope of *ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka* (partial metaphor) would be entirely deprived; this is because its specific object, being of such a nature, is not established [otherwise].

Or, where there is no verbal identification (*vācā rūpaṇa*)—as in the examples of *samāsokti* such as "he embraced the sky"—but rather a state characterized by an abundance of similarities of effect, [that too would be subsumed under *samāsokti*].
In that very instance, because of the presence of the complete set of conditions (*sāmagrī*), the identity with the unmentioned heroine is perceived.

Furthermore, in examples such as "it appears" (*ābhāti*) and so forth, since there is a multiplicity of metaphorical descriptions (*rūpaṇā*) of the expressed meaning, the similarity of effects and other factors is minimal and thus merely serves to assist them.

That the identity with the enemy's fame and so forth is the cause for the perception [of the heroine] is established by the experience of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*); it is not the case that *samāsokti* (synthetic expression) depends upon the convergence of conventional usage.

Furthermore, another set of arguments concerning these two—*samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) and *ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka* (metaphor with partial transformation)—will become very clear right here in this discussion of *samāsokti*; so, enough of this prolixity.
In some cases, *rūpaka* is observed even in the absence of a compound:
"O fawn-eyed one, your face..."
"It is a lotus, and not otherwise.
In some cases, even when there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), as for example:
"The Creator has fashioned a row of bees here by means of her creeper-like eyebrows."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ṇa) He elaborates upon the internal distinctions of those very forms already mentioned— beginning with "kvacittu" ("in some cases")—
since in all instances such as "rājamaṇḍalarāhave," that [compound] has been shown to be exclusively a *samāsa* (compound).
"Your face"—
this is clear.
"In a lack of grammatical coreferentiality" means when there is a difference in case endings.
"Vidadhe" (he fashioned):
thus, the meaning here is that the Creator fashioned a swarm of bees by means of the creeper-like eyebrows as the cause.
The ultimate sense is that he fashioned the swarm of bees in order to fashion the creeper-like eyebrows.
Because the creeper-like eyebrows are the cause for the manifestation of desire through its gateway.
Locanā:
Although a metaphor has already been illustrated even in the absence of equality or inequality, she cites "the face" once more for the sake of clear understanding.
In the verse beginning with *vidadhat*, the meaning is that "your creeper-like eyebrows are a swarm of bees.
An example where there is even a contrast (*vaidharmya*) is as follows:
"Goodness is a desert of water; virtuous conduct is a wall for painting; the moonlight of virtue is the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight; straightforwardness is the flickering tail of a donkey;"

For those who have served even this lineage of kings in the Kali age with such evil intent, how much skillful service can they possibly offer to the Wielder of the Trident, who is accessible through devotion alone?
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ta) "Even in some cases of dissimilarity" means that the contradictory property between the material and the immaterial is not the intended meaning [of the term].
However, the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) here is simply the absence of that very similarity which was specified.

Regarding the phrase "the ocean of goodness": in this Kali age, how skillful is the service of those evil-minded ones who have served this lineage of kings—a mere succession of men—when [true devotion] is easily accessible through the Trident-bearer (*Śūlin*) alone?
Of what nature is the lineage of kings? It is a desert for the water that is benevolence.
Here, benevolence and water are indicated as non-different, and thus both possess the attributes of both.
The very non-existence of those two rows of mirage-water is the aforementioned dissimilarity between the two; this should be understood for each subsequent pair as well.
As for the object to be depicted, which consists of good conduct—
Its wall and support are the form of the sky and the form of day;
it is the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight for the moonlight that is the nature of its qualities,
and the flickering of its horse-tail is the application of straightness.
Here, the term *chaṭāpada* signifies its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Likewise, it means the essential nature of the dog’s tail, which is the connection or relation of straightness.
In all cases, the absence of the specified property should be understood.
Locanā:
(lo, o) by way of dissimilarity,
by way of contrariety.
It is by means of that which has not attained the nature of common characteristics;
straightforwardness is the state of being on the true path and the absence of crookedness.
Here, by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), there is a *paramparita-rūpaka* (successive metaphor);
this is my [view].
And here, although some of these metaphors are rooted in verbal punning (*śabda-śleṣa*), they are counted among the figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*) because they are specific types of metaphor.
This should be understood as applying to the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) to be discussed hereafter.
Locanā:

(lo, au) Now, since [ornaments] such as *paramparita* in the verse beginning with "padmodaya" follow the presence and absence of the words, how can they be counted among the "ornaments of meaning" (*arthālaṅkāra*)? To this, he says: "In this regard... (*atrety*).

The sense is that although it is rooted in verbal *śleṣa* (punning), since the duality of meaning depends on following the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the word, it is appropriate—according to the method stated—to regard it as a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*) alone.
"Ornaments to be mentioned" refers to *virodha* (contradiction) and so forth;
the phrase "to be mentioned" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

The remainder [of the sentence] is that this should also be understood to apply to Simile (upamā) when it possesses common attributes expressed by words. That very thing which is a Metaphor (rūpaka) characterized by an elevated distinction is precisely what is designated as "elevated distinction" (adhikārūḍhavaiśiṣṭya).
As in my own verse:
"This face is the moon itself, free from stain; this lower lip is the orb of the sun fully ripened by time, a reservoir for streams of nectar;
these eyes are two blue water-lilies with ever-increasing beauty day and night; and this body is an ocean of loveliness, most pleasant to plunge into."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) He states another variety of *rūpaka*—namely, *adhika*.

The meaning is that it is a specific individual (*vyaktiviśeṣa*) being described as possessing a degree of excellence (*vaiśiṣṭya*) that has ascended above what is commonly known of other members of its own class.
That very thing is what possesses that name;
this is the face.
The absence of a spot is a distinctive quality that has been attributed to a specific individual moon being perceived as such.
Thus, in what follows, the support for the stream of nectar is the lower lip, which has been transformed and ripened by remaining for a long time.
Here, the distinguishing feature of one [the lip] is its long duration;
the latter half is clear.
And thus: "She then attained that age which is beyond childhood—the unadorned ornament of her slender body, the intoxicant known as no-wine, and the flowerless weapon of Love."
In this case, this figure of speech should also be understood as being of the form of a garland (*mālā*),
because of the ascent to specific distinctions consisting in the states of not being accumulated, not being called *āsava*, and being distinct from flowers.
— *Locanā*:

The meaning is: "where there is a distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) consisting of a particularity (*viśeṣa*) that has ascended [to the subject] by virtue of being superimposed upon the object of superimposition.

In the phrase "it is more pleasant to plunge [into the ocean]," the intention is that because of the presence of salt, crocodiles, waves, and so forth, the salt-water ocean does not bring pleasure to those who plunge into it;
thus, there is an additional distinction (*adhikaṃ vaiśiṣṭyam*) in terms of the pleasure and so forth.
In another system of poetics, this is called *viśeṣokti* (peculiar cause) when there is a deficiency of a single quality:
"Then she attained an age beyond childhood— a state that was an unadorned decoration for her slender body, a means of intoxication known as no wine, and a weapon of Love other than flowers."

Regarding this [verse], some say that the ornament called *vibhāvanā* (the description of an effect despite the absence of its cause) is present in the phrase "here, without having prepared her adornment.
That is not so; for it is certainly not the case that the preparation of flowers and the act of adorning are the causes of the adornment, but rather their very nature.
But others say,
"This is a transformation (pariṇāma)";
that too is incorrect.

This is because its effects—namely, the beautification of the body and the kindling of passion—are not being pursued by anyone as the primary subject at hand. However, Rāghavānanda Mahāpātra has stated that this is a *rūpaka* (metaphor) characterized by an excellence based on a superimposed qualification (*adhikārūḍhavaiśiṣṭya*). That too is questionable.

Because the qualification of the object of superimposition by some aspect of that which is being superimposed is the cause of this [superimposition], it possesses the nature of that [superimposition].
Therefore, in such cases as "This king is another Indra" and "The beauty of his limbs is indeed something else," [the superimposition occurs].
My own position is that, as in these examples, it is more appropriate for this to be considered hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) alone;
for the identification (*adhyavasāya*) is experienced as being fully developed,
and because metaphor (*rūpaka*) is rooted in superimposition (*āropa*).
In this case, there is an additional distinction due to the absence of blemish and so forth;
[this occurs] when the object of superimposition, by virtue of being of the nature of the subject, is conducive to the intended meaning. (VisSd 10.34)
Transformation is twofold: having a common locus and having a non-common locus.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, da):
He states the figure of speech "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) with the words "by way of being the nature of the object."

The object (*viṣaya*) is the substratum of transformation (*rūpaṇādhikaraṇa*); it refers to that which is being superimposed (*āropya*) upon something relevant to the subject matter at hand or relevant to the action being performed; the meaning is the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the thing superimposed.
