"Equal and unequal" means that they possess identical case endings (vibhakti) when they are not distinct.
Locanā:

The object (*viṣaya*) is the locus of superimposition; it is by way of being of that nature, that is, by way of having that form, and not merely by way of being colored by it as in the case of a metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*).
And thus, by virtue of its being the very nature of the object and its utility for the task at hand, there is a distinction from *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification).
The intention is that, although identity is perceived in *rūpaka*, there is no desire to go to the ultimate limit [of that identification].
Such a thing exists as the object of description (*rūpyamāṇa*) within the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation), which explains this two-fold transformation as follows:

it is called *pariṇāma* because that which is being superimposed (*āropyamāṇa*) undergoes a transformation (*pariṇamana*) by taking on the nature of the locus of superimposition (*āropa-viṣaya*). — *Locanā*.
"Having superimposed"—this means that by being placed in the locus of transformation, it attains the nature of that [locus].
The sense is not that an existing substratum (*dharmin*) abandons its prior form and undergoes the acquisition of another form; rather, [it is as follows]:
for example—
“A smile was offered as a greeting by her to me when I arrived from afar;
an embrace pressing against her breasts was made by her as the stake in the game of dice.”
Elsewhere, the stakes (*upāyana*) consist of garments, ornaments, and the like;
here, however, they take the form of smiles and embraces within the gambling match of the hero’s courtship (*nāyakasaṃbhāvanādyūta*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding "by means of a smile" (*smitena*):
here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of non-difference (*abheda*).
Here, the gift (*upāyana*) being superimposed upon the smile is transformed into the very nature of the actual smile.
And that [embrace] is useful for the purpose of generating confidence while being performed.
"Stanopapīḍam" means pressing the breasts against each other, that is, an embrace.
Here, in the case of *āśleṣa* (coalescence), the stake being superimposed is transformed into a real coalescence and becomes useful for the gambling being performed.
He demonstrates its utility for the purpose being performed in both cases with the words "elsewhere" (*anyatra*).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the two] are "employed" (*upayujyete*) in the context of "possibility" (*sambhāvanā*) and gambling (*dyūta*).
In the phrase "of the two gifts being mounted [upon the bridegroom] in the form of a smile and an embrace," the word "metaphorical identification" (pariṇāma) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
In the first half-verse, the construction is by way of grammatical discordance (vaiyadhikaraṇya), while in the second, it is by way of grammatical concordance (sāmānādhikaraṇya).

In a metaphor (*rūpaka*), such as "I see the moon of the face," the superimposed moon and so forth serve merely as coloring agents (*uparañjaka*), but have no functional utility for the actual act of seeing and so on.
Here, however, the identity with the object— such as the gift— is established, and it serves a purpose in the context of the hero's estimation and so forth.
Therefore, in a *rūpaka* (metaphor), the superimposed object is construed merely as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*),
whereas here [in *tadrūpa*], it is construed through identity (*tādātmya*).
*Vijñapriyā*:

In the case of *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification), he shows that there is no utility for the object being superimposed toward the purpose being performed—this is expressed by the words "in *rūpaka*" (*rūpake*).
"Merely coloring" (*uparañjakatvamātram*) means merely suggesting beauty; "but not" (*na tu*) [means it does not perform the function].
Utility (*upayoga*) consists in being the means of accomplishment (*nirvāhakatva*), because [the moon] accomplishes the act of seeing.
However, in the present case, such a means of accomplishment certainly exists;
thus he says: "But here... (*iha tu*).

In the phrase "tadātmyam" (identity), the word "is useful" (*upayujyate*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. It should be understood that the demonstration of the utility of identity culminates in demonstrating the utility of transformation (*pariṇāma*), acquisition (*upāyana*), and so forth;
for by means of acquisition, speculation (*sambhāvana*) is carried out, and by means of wagering (*paṇa*), gambling (*dyūta*).
Having clarified that very point, he shows it with the words "and in the case of *prakṛta*.

The meaning is that the application (*upayoga*)—as the means of accomplishing the two [actions] of "conception" (*sambhāvanā*) and "gambling" (*dyūta*)—is construed as non-different from the smile and the embrace, respectively, in the form of the "means" (*upāyana*) and the "stake" (*paṇa*).
And because that construction is not superimposed (*anāropita*), it constitutes the state of being the accomplisher (*nirvāhakatā*).
But [the author] states that it is not the sustainer (*nirvāhikā*) in the case of superimposition (*āropa*), saying "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).
The meaning is: precisely because it is the sustainer only when there is no superimposition.
By way of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*), that is, by way of being unreal (*avāstavatva*).
But regarding the subject at hand, he says "and here" (atra ca) because [the identity] is real (*vāstavatvena*).
Identity (*tādātmyam*) is a real non-difference (*vastavo 'bhedaḥ*). Locanā.

(Lo, ī) Even though there is an identity [of the object] with what is brought forth by the poet's composition, it is only superimposition (*āropa*) that serves as the cause of *rūpaka* (metaphor); thus, [the distinction lies] merely in its being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*).
And "merely coloring" (*uparañjakatvamātra*) means nothing more than the manifestation of an excellence of beauty (*cārutvātiśaya*). The particle *tu* has the sense of "but" (*ca-artha*).

Identity (*tādātmya*) consists in the imposition [of one thing] upon another; in that context, a smile and the like possess the status of being a "gift" (*upāyana*) because they serve as its qualifiers.
The point is that the moon-like nature of the face and so forth is not established in that same way.
In examples such as "When the servant has committed an offense... and so on, there is indeed only metaphor (*rūpaka*).
But it is not a *pariṇāma* (transformation), because the effect of the superimposed thorn— namely, the piercing of the foot— is not the subject at hand (*apratupatatvāt*).
Indeed, that [superimposition] is not employed for the sake of accomplishing any relevant effect whatsoever.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pa) Regarding the metaphor (*rūpaka*) in the verse beginning with "dāse kṛtāgasī," she demonstrates the non-application of *pariṇāma* by saying "dāse. [Objection:

But why is it said here that this is only a metaphor (*rūpaka*), given that the sprouts of horripilation (*pulakāṅkura*) are actually thorns due to their sharp tips and hardness? [Response: She says "āropyamāṇa" (being superimposed) to address this.
The meaning is: "of such a thing as the rising of horripilation (pulaka), which has the effect of piercing the feet"—that is, of that which is being superimposed as thorns (kaṇṭaka).

Here, although the horripilation is indeed the locus for the superimposition of thorns, and thus its being superimposed consists in its being [conceived] as thorns, nevertheless, the meaning is that it is not being superimposed [as such] with respect to the state of producing the effect of piercing the feet.
And so, since it is only by virtue of accomplishing that effect that it is superimposed [as thorns], its status as a thorn is likewise not real.
However, because it is being superimposed [upon something else], the meaning is that it is indeed a metaphor (rūpaka).

Now, one might object: "But the sprouts of horripilation (*pulakāṅkura*) possess the very capacity to effect the division of the feet; so how can they be unreal? To this he says: "Certainly not," and so forth.

The "tip of the sprout of its horripilation" belongs to anyone at all—the meaning is: for the sake of joining together the distinction of anyone whatsoever, whether it be one's own distinction or the distinction of another. In this way, *pariṇāma* (transformation) is established as being non-different from *rūpaka* (metaphor).
Thus: "By her, who had approached Śaṅkara—the teacher of the secrets of love—in private as a disciple, that very skill in the art of lovemaking which she learned was offered as the preceptor’s fee."

In this case as well, since the teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*) results from the skill in sexual union (*suratanaipuṇya*), it should be understood that this is indeed the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation). This too, like *rūpaka* (metaphor), is seen to possess an intensified excellence (*adhikārūḍhavaiśiṣṭya*).
For example:
“There, for the forest-dwellers accompanied by their wives, the medicinal herbs— whose light is fixed within the embrace of cave-dwellings— serve as oil-less lamps for lovemaking during the night.”

In this context, because the lamps possess the nature of medicinal herbs, their utility in destroying darkness—which is conducive to amorous pleasure—is characterized by an excellence that has ascended to a higher degree through their filling the floor.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"Of the forest-dwellers."

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: on that Himalaya, the medicinal herbs themselves serve as lamps for sexual union for the forest-dwellers accompanied by their wives during the night.

He states the reason for their becoming lamps in the phrase "cave-houses" (*darīgṛha*): they are "without oil-filling" (*atailapūrāḥ*), meaning devoid of the pouring of oil, or lacking a collection of oil.

Here, he demonstrates that the state of becoming a lamp is useful for the subject matter at hand with the word "atra. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: in the present context, regarding the destruction of darkness which is conducive to amorous dalliance (*surata*), lamps are useful by virtue of their being of the nature of medicinal herbs (*auṣadhī*).
In some manuscripts, there is also a variant reading: "of the transformation into the nature of medicinal herbs."
Regarding the reading "it is the subject matter by virtue of being the nature of the medicine," this is in some cases a scribal error.
Nor should it be argued that only sexual union (*surata*) is the verbally expressed subject matter and not the destruction of darkness, because the latter is not verbally expressed.

Since that [other object] is also the subject under discussion by virtue of its utility for the poem, "doubt regarding the subject" (saṃdeha) is a doubt concerning something else that arises through poetic intuition. (VisSd 10.35)
This [figure] is threefold: pure (*śuddha*), containing a certainty (*niścayagarbha*), and ending in a certainty (*niścayānta*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ba):
He states the figure of doubt (*sandehālaṅkāra*) with the words "doubt" (*sandeha*).

The meaning is that *sandehālaṅkāra* is the figure of speech consisting of a doubt regarding a relevant subject matter arising from a resemblance (*pratibhā*) to another, irrelevant category of things.
*Locanā*:
*Sandeha* is the figure of speech known as "doubt."
When the subject (*prakṛta*) is being described, something else is superimposed (*āropyamāṇa*).
Thus, when there is doubt regarding the subject, the non-subject (*aprakṛta*) is likewise doubted.
And so, the meaning is that the figure of speech *sandehālaṅkāra* (the ornament of doubt) consists in a cognition of doubt concerning both the subject and the non-subject.
Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a cognition characterized by multiple alternatives (*anekakoṭika*), such as indecision or lack of determination.

Thus, since the definition is complete with the mere statement "doubt," the inclusion of the phrase "of another" in the present context is for the purpose of excluding [other types of cognition], such as that which will be cited from the *Vṛtti* as "the middle is yours," and so forth.
[The term] "arisen from intuition" (*pratibhotthita*)...
*Pratibhā* is the poet’s creative intuition;
that by which [the object] is brought forth and attended to.
Thus, even in the case of a doubt described by a poet such as "Is it a pillar or a man?", there is no status as an *alaṅkāra*.
This very point will become clear in the commentary through the passage beginning with "not brought about by a lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhotthāpita*).
That in which there is a finality consisting solely of doubt is the pure [type].
For example:
"Is this a fresh creeper sprouted from the sap of the tree of youth? Or is it a wave surging from the ocean of loveliness?
Or perhaps it is the very staff of instruction for the God of Love, who confidently imparts his teachings to those filled with intense longing?"
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, bha) What is the use of youth?
Is this heroine a fresh creeper upon the tree of loveliness?
The meaning is that she is like a fresh creeper clinging to the tree of the form of loveliness (*lāvaṇya*).

Of what sort is she? She is "burst forth by the abundance of rasa" (*rasabharodbhinnā*); *rasa* here refers to the water of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) itself, and she has burst forth through its sprinkling, just as a creeper sprouts from the drenching of water.
Alternatively, she is a "surge" (*laharikā*), a wave, of the ocean of the form of loveliness which has surged upward with the tide (*velayā*)—that is, with the water.
The lexicon states: "velā may mean either the shore or the tide.

Alternatively, she is a staff—the direct support for the instruction, that is, the instruction in *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment)—for people who are full of intense longing and bowed down by surging waves of passion, for the sake of the god Kandarpa, the possessor of *śṛṅgāra*.
The instruction is: "Taking hold of this [spring], let the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) be experienced.
The meaning is that the instruction is appropriate for me now because I am confident—that is, trusting—due to the mention of Your Majesty's own season, spring;
"confidence" (viśvāsa) means the very state of being free from doubt.
Locanā: (Lo, Ū) *Rasa* means, in the context of youth, the desire for enjoyment; in the other sense, it means a general fluid.
In the case of Velā-lāvaṇya (the beauty of the shore), it refers to the common boundary; in the case of the ocean, it refers to the coast.
"Ucchalita" means surging upward or transgression.

*Utkalikā* means longing or yearning. It is the direct staff of instruction for one who is confident in presenting their own system and inspires trust when speaking of a matter approved by themselves; it is a direct presentation in the form of a physical staff-like embodiment.
Alternatively, the staff (*yaṣṭi*) is for the purpose of instruction,
while the rod (*daṇḍa*) is for striking with a cane or similar implement.
For it is well known in the world that teachers of any science whatsoever take up a staff for the purpose of striking in order to restrain a restless mind.

That [figure] in which there is doubt at the beginning and the end, but certainty in the middle, is "certainty-in-the-middle" (*niścayamadhyam*). For example: "Is this the sun? But he is surely accompanied by seven horses. Is it fire? But it does not certainly spread in all directions."
Furthermore, upon beholding you in battle, your adversaries entertain doubts as to whether this is Kṛtānta himself, borne by his buffalo mount.
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) It is well known that [the light] does not spread to all directions, but rather blazes only upwards.
In this context, there is a determination of the absence of Mārtaṇḍa and others in the middle,
because once the king has been determined, it is impossible for a second doubt to arise; thus says the *Vijñapriyā*.
"And in the middle, there is certainty" means that there is certainty regarding the exclusion of one alternative. "This" refers to...
In battle, upon beholding you, the opposing warriors— those heroes who stand against you— form such conjectures as these;
he states those conjectures with the words "This one," etc.,
meaning "He has gone from here."
"Regarding the phrase 'all directions':
fire does not spread to all directions,
but this [light] spreads throughout every direction."
Therefore, the meaning is that he is not Kṛśānu (Fire); the grammatical connection is "he is directly Kṛtānta (Death).
The meaning is that because he lacks the vehicle of a buffalo, he is not Kṛtānta (Yama).
In this case, the determination of the absence of Mārttaṇḍa and others occurs in the middle.

Now, one might object that from the determination of the absence of the contradictory alternative (viruddhakoṭi), there is also the determination of the royal alternative (rājakoṭi); to this he says: "the determination of royalty.
That in which there is doubt at the beginning and certainty at the end is called "certainty-at-the-end" (niścayānta).
For example:
"Is that a lotus in the lake over there, or is it the face of a young woman shining forth?
Having hesitated for a moment, someone reached a certainty by means of the gestures of the women dwelling in the temple, which were beyond the perception of others.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ya) "What then?"—
it should be understood that even regarding the heroine, there is a suspicion that she might be a lake.
"From afar"—the meaning is "what is this?"—refers to the *vivvokas*, which are defined as "the disregard for an object of desire even when it is present, due to excessive pride";
the meaning is thus: by means of these particular feminine gestures (*hāva*).

"By what kind [of means]?"—by those beyond the perception (*parokṣa*) of those who dwell with cranes. For cranes, in order to ascertain [the presence of] fish, practice meditation; those who dwell with them likewise learn that meditation from them. Thus, the meaning is that these [objects] are to be known only through extreme meditation, as they are extremely difficult to discern and remain beyond the perception (*apratyakṣa*) of even such people. However, this is not a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) in the case of a doubt such as "Is it a post or a man? which is not prompted by a flash of genius (*apratibhā*).
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) Vivvoka is a particular state of being (bhāvaviśeṣa).
As it has been stated in this very same work: "Vivvoka is a disregard even for a desired object due to excessive pride.

Following the phrase "of the lotuses dwelling with the *baka* birds, by means of things out of sight and beyond their range," the words "even though composed in poetry" (*kāvyopanibaddhe ’pi*) are to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣa*).
“O lotus-eyed one, regarding your waist, which is oppressed by the weight of your breasts,
in whose mind does the doubt ‘does it exist or not’ not arise?”
In this case, there is indeed *atiśayokti* (hyperbole),
because the very subject matter of this ornament is doubt regarding the object of comparison (*upamāna*) with respect to the object compared (*upameya*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(Vi, Ra) He states that even within other types of artificial doubt (*āhārya-saṃśaya*) based on a single point of dissimilarity, there is the figure of speech *nāyaka*—namely, "Your waist...
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "In whose mind does such a doubt not appear?

In this context, the term "hyperbole" (*atiśayokti*) means that although there are five varieties of hyperbole to be described hereafter, the specific variety present here is that which consists in the superimposition of non-difference upon difference.
There is no such category of object; even though it is non-existent, [the figure] consists of the superimposition of identity upon that [non-existent thing].
Now, one might object: "In this way, such a superimposition exists even in the case of the poetic figure *sandeha* (doubt)"; therefore, he says: "The object of comparison (*upamāna*)...
The sense is that, in this manner, the mutual distinction between these two poetic figures must be established.
Locanā:

(lo, ḷ) Hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) alone [is included here], because it is rooted in identification (*adhyavasāya*). Illusion (*bhrāntimān*) is the cognition of one thing as another due to similarity; it arises from creative intuition (*pratibhā*). (VisSd 10.36)
Locanā:
(lo, e) Following the doubt arising from similarity with false knowledge, this [figure] is introduced.
*Bhrāntimān* is an ornament whose name is significant (*anvarthanāmālaṅkāra*), meaning that where a particular state of mental error exists, that mode of delusion is called "possessing error."
For example:

"The simple cowherds place jars [on the ground] with the thought that they are milk; even the beloved women put blue water-lilies behind their ears, suspecting them to be white lotuses; and the Śabara woman gathers the fruit of the jujube tree, thinking it to be a pearl. To whom does this dense moonlight not cause a delusion of the mind?"
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, la) He states the ornament of error (*bhrāntimad-alaṅkāra*)—beginning with "on account of similarity" (*sāmyāt*). "Cognition of that as such" (*tadbuddhiḥ*) means cognition [of it] as being the reality (*tattvena*).
Regarding the word "mugdhā" (the innocent one):
the meaning is that the thick moonlight of the moon causes mental confusion for what person?
He shows those who are deluded by the word "mugdhā."
The cowherds (ballavāḥ), being simple-minded and deluded, place jars beneath the cows with the thought that they contain milk—the meaning being that they do so in order to collect the milk.
In the phrase "by mistaking them for night-lotuses" (kairavaśaṅkayā), the word *śaṅkā* refers specifically to a delusion (*bhrama*).
Regarding the word *karkandhu*: [it refers to the jujube fruit].
The meaning is "the fruit of the jujube tree" (*badaraphala*).
And in this case, the expectancy is rooted in error.
*Locanā*:
(lo, ai) *Karkandhū* is a jujube tree.
An error not prompted by a lack of aesthetic resonance (*asvarasa*) is not a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).
— *Locanā*:
(Lo, o) He shows the exclusion [of other cases] for the defining term "produced by intuition" (*pratibhotthāpita*): "known through its own nature" (*svarasajñata*).
"Own nature" (*svārasa*) means intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For example: "silver in mother-of-pearl."
Locanā:
(lo, au) The meaning is that it is like the illusion of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
From the word "svarasa" (its own essence), the phrase "also in poetry" (*kāvye 'pi*) is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).
Nor is it based on dissimilarity,
as for example:
"In the choice between union and separation, it is better here not to have union with her."
In union, she alone is thus; even the three worlds are composed of her in separation.
Vijñapriyā:
By the words "by its own force" (*svarasena*), he states the exclusion of [the figure] arising from wit (*pratibhā*).
He says "nor by dissimilarity" (*na cāsādṛśyena*) to show that this is not an ornament even when rooted in dissimilarity.
"Saṅgameti" means:
in the conceptualization of union and separation; "varaṃ" means slightly desired, provided there is no investigation [into their nature].

Nor should it be argued that even here, in this threefold world, there is an error regarding that [object] due to an error concerning its similarity; for what is intended to be expressed is precisely the absence of error regarding the aspect of similarity.
Thus, the sense is that because separation exceeds union, this is indeed the figure of speech known as *vyatireka* (distinction).
And thus, even when there is an error due to greed and so forth, one is not a deluded person. As it is said: "The greedy see the world as consisting of wealth; the lustful, as consisting of women;
but the wise who seek the ultimate truth, see it as consisting of Nārāyaṇa."
Thus,

it should not be argued that even here, despite the difference between the two riches, there is only the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) consisting in the superimposition of non-difference upon the riches;
for such [a classification] applies only when the superimposition constitutive of *atiśayokti* is of the nature of being voluntarily assumed (*āhāryya*).
In this case, however, in the first [example] there is a suggestion (dhvani) of the transitory emotion (vyabhicāribhāva) of reflection; in the second, a suggestion of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra);
and in the third, there is only a suggestion of a transitory emotion.
Locanā:
[The commentary on] "sāmyādityasya vyāvṛttirna ca" and so forth begins with:
"In some cases due to the difference among perceivers, and likewise in some cases among objects..."
The multiple delineation of a single [object] in many ways is called *ullekha* (elaboration).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, śa) He states the figure of speech *ullekhālaṅkāra* [with the words] "in some cases due to difference" (*kvacidbhedāt*).
The meaning is that the description (*ullekha*) of a single object in many ways—that is, as manifold—is its being an object of cognition (*buddhiviṣayatva*).
He states two causes for such a cognition: "in some cases due to difference" (*kvacid bhedāt*).
In some cases, there is a cognition of multiplicity in various perceivers by virtue of their respective forms;

in other cases, however, due to the difference among the objects—which consist of the properties that occasion such a cognition—there is the state of being the object of a cognition of that nature for a single perceiver alone. This is the meaning.
Therefore, it is twofold;
the examples in sequence are as follows:
"He is 'the beloved' by the cowherd women, 'the child' by the elders, and 'the sovereign lord' by the gods."
"The God was perceived as Nārāyaṇa by his devotees and as Brahman by the yogis."
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding the phrase "priya iti," the meaning is that the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa accepted [the offerings] together with all of them.
He states that very point in the passage beginning with "the beloved" (*priya*): "The beloved is the Lord.
Due to the distinction between having a form and being formless—specifically, as the one reclining upon the ocean and as the formless one—there is no difference between Nārāyaṇa and Brahmā.
“*Āpo hi nārāḥ*”: He whose abode is that [water] and who resides therein is Nārāyaṇa; the meaning is "the one who lies upon the waters.

Here, although the Blessed One is a single entity, his depiction in various ways due to the association with various attributes is prompted, as appropriate, by the inclinations (*ruci*) of the cowherd women and others.
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding the phrase "in each respective quality" (*tattadguṇe*): the meaning is "each respective quality that serves as the cause for such a cognition.
And in the context of the word "beloved" (*priya*), this [quality] takes the form of beauty (*saundarya*).
In the term "child" (śiśu), there is the state of being an object of affection; in "Lord" (adhīśa), there is sovereignty;
and in "Nārāyaṇa," there is non-difference from the embodied form suitable for meditation.
In the passage beginning with "brahma," there is non-difference from the essential nature as excluded from that [worldly form].
Regarding the statement "desire and so forth are the motivators," it is thus shown that the recipients who possess such desire are distinct [from one another].
As they say:

"Even with respect to a single object, the appearance [of it] varies according to one's inclination, according to one's need, and according to one's proficiency; yet it is established by a unifying synthesis."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ha) He states the consensus regarding the fact that desire (*ruci*) and so forth are the motivators of those cognitions: "according to one's desire" (*yathāruci*).

The meaning is that the manifestation (*ābhāsa*), which is established through the application of the mind (*manoniveśa*) by way of synthesis (*anusandhāna*) toward a single object, is called cognition (*jñāna*), intellect (*buddhi*), and also [desire] and so forth, according to its specific distinctions (*bheda*).
*Ruci* is desire; it is the state of longing, a form of wish for the sake of attaining something. *Vyutpatti* is refinement (or cultivation).
Locanā: (Lo, Ā) Etymological derivation, or habitual impression (*vāsanā*) produced by practice, or cognition.
Investigation (*anusandhāna*) is the fixing of the mind upon that object;
by means of this, [the state] is accomplished, meaning it is carried through after excluding other objects.
And thus, in the case of "beloved" (*priya*) and so forth, the triad beginning with desire (*ruci*) is the cause for the Lord’s being beloved by the cowherd women.
In childhood, there is the comprehension of the elderly;
among yogis, there is the comprehension of Brahman as being Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), and so on in other cases.
Here, because the Lord’s qualities such as being "dear" (priyatva) and so forth are real, and because of the difference among the perceivers, this is not a "garland-metaphor" (mālārūpaka).
Nor is this a case of mere error,
nor is it the poetic figure of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consisting in the notion that there is a difference where there is no difference.
For instance, in such examples as “The beauty of the limbs is indeed something else,” there is a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the object— such as beauty— as being distinct.

And here, in the case of the Blessed One, [qualities such as] being beloved are not superimposed by cowherd women and others, because at that time, being beloved and so forth are real in the Blessed One.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ka): Here, he refutes the possibility of a "garland-metaphor" (*mālārūpaka*)—namely, "here, in the case of the Blessed One."

Because it is real, there is no possibility of *rūpaka* (metaphor) consisting in an imposition of non-difference that cannot be sublated; and because of the difference between the perceivers, there is no possibility of its being a *mālā* (garland) [of metaphors], since in the case of a *mālā*, the difference between perceivers is precisely not intended to be expressed.

Although the impossibility of *rūpaka* due to its reality already excludes the possibility of *mālārūpaka* for that very reason, the demonstration of the difference between perceivers is nevertheless intended to indicate the exclusion of the possibility of *mālāpariṇāma* (transformation into a garland).
The reason is that even if there were a possibility of that [superimposition] by virtue of reality, the difference between the perceivers serves as its sublation.
To clarify, he sets aside a specific variety of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) even though it was not previously raised: "And this is not non-difference.
He then demonstrates an example of that variety.
He states that there is no such over-extension [of the definition] with the words "for in that case" (*tatra hi*).

"In that case" refers to a specific variety of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole); "as distinct from that" means as something other than that very same variety; and "not here" means not in this present context.
In this example from the *Priyāhatī* section,
"priyatānyathā" means "other than [the state of being] dear to my father."
However, the reading "but because of its being [regarded as] dear (*priyatva*), it is determined (*adhyavasīyate*)" is an occasional scribal error.
This must be justified through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by interpreting "it is determined" as "it is rejected.
The term "because of its reality" (*tāttvikatvāt*) means "because it is not cognized as something other [than itself]."

And it has been stated that there is no *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) in the form of a superimposition (*āropa*) based on a non-figurative (*āhārya*) cognition, because [the object] is real (*tāttvika*) at that time for the Blessed One and because of the difference in perceivers.
*Locanā*:

(Lo, i) For these two reasons—the reality of the object at that time and the distinction between perceivers—there is a distinction between both *mālārūpaka* (garland-metaphor) and *bhrāntimān* (the appearance of error).
For, in reality, that state of being is possible as a factual matter;

likewise, in the case of the *mālārūpaka* (garland-metaphor), the sole operative factor is the superimposition of identity brought about by the poet's construction and the reader's mental appropriation.
And in the case of *bhrāntimān* (illusion), the very cause is false cognition itself.

The sense is that even though the distinction between the two types of perceivers is possible, the ornament called *ullekha* (multiple description) is not the governing factor because it functions as an exception (*apavāda*).
It is not apprehended through superimposition;
rather, it is apprehended precisely as its own true nature.
*Adhyavasāna* (poetic identification) is the apprehension of non-difference between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*) through the swallowing up of the former by the latter.
Some say: "This ornament is invariably rooted in the strikingness (*vicchitti*) of another ornament;

and in the example cited, because there is an intention to restrict [the qualities] such as childhood, and because there is an apprehension of difference regarding [qualities] such as dearness, there is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole)."

Even when that [object] exists, the specific excellence (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) consisting in the perception of multiplicity due to the difference among perceivers is the cause for the employment of the distinct figure of speech called *ullekha*. Regarding this, some say: "Because of its commingling with other figures of speech, this figure is necessarily rooted in its particular stylistic charm (*bhaṅgi*). He shows this by saying "some. *Vijñapriyā*: (vi, kha) Some say that because of its commingling with other figures of speech, this figure is necessarily based on its particular stylistic charm (*bhaṅgi*). He demonstrates this by saying "some."
*Vicchitti* is a striking arrangement (*bhaṅgi*).
He demonstrates that *vicchitti* in the examples mentioned with the words "in the examples mentioned.
[He says] "due to the intention of restriction."

The meaning is that the child was grasped first by the elders precisely because of this intended restriction (*niyamābhiprāya*). The phrase "there is hyperbole" (*atiśayokti*) connects with what follows.

Thus, although the Lord is young and distinct from a [literal] child, because a child is necessarily superimposed upon him despite the difference, the hyperbole consisting of the superimposition of non-difference upon a difference is demonstrated.

In this context, it should be understood that the demonstration of the restriction is solely for the purpose of showing the excellence of their cultivation (*bhāvanā*) as such, and not for the purpose of constructing a poetic exaggeration (*atiśayokti*).
He demonstrates that very same exaggeration even in the portion beginning with "dear" (*priya*), by saying "of [the words] beginning with 'dear'."
And here, even though there is a distinction, only the figure of speech known as *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), which consists in the superimposition of non-difference upon difference, is possible.
Thus, in the phrase "the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of distinct objects," the meaning is "the determination of that which possesses distinctness.
To the question "of what is there this determination? he says: "of [qualities] such as dearness (*priyatva*), etc."
And thus, the meaning is that the superimposition of ownership upon a king who is not actually the owner is precisely the superimposition of non-difference from the owner.
By the phrase "here some [say]," there is an indication of dissatisfaction.

This is because, although the word "king" expresses the locus of the superimposition (*āropaviṣaya*), the general definition of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*)—which consists in the act of swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*)—is absent here.
It should be noted that there is no lack of aesthetic flavor (asvārasya) in the passage to be cited, beginning with "in the region of Śrīkaṇṭha," and so forth.
Now, one might object: "If hyperbole (atiśayokti) is indeed present here, let that alone be the ornament (alaṃkāra), and not ullekha"; to this, he replies: "even though that [hyperbole] exists."
The meaning is: "even though there is hyperbole (atiśayokti).
The meaning is that a specific excellence in the form of aesthetic suggestion (*pratīti-rūpa-vicchitti-viśeṣa*) is the cause for an ornament other than the hyperbole known as *ullekha*.
In the description of the Śrīkaṇṭha region: "It is a 'cage of diamonds' by those who have sought refuge..."
The passage beginning with “the opening of the sky, as [said] by the Vātikas” and so forth is a distinct domain of hyperbole (atiśayokti);
and here, there is the application of the figure of speech known as metaphor (rūpaka).
However, in reality, in cases such as “the opening of the sky,” they maintain that it is indeed an instance of error (bhrāntimān) and not a metaphor.
For it is only superimposition (*āropa*) preceded by the cognition of difference that serves as the basis for figurative usage (*gauṇī*), primary metaphor (*mūlarūpaka*), and so forth.
As the venerable Vācaspatimiśra stated in his commentary on the *Śarīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya*:

"Furthermore, where a word denoting one thing is applied to another because of its connection with qualities perceived in that other—provided there is agreement between the speaker and the listener—that is figurative (*gauṇa*)."
"And that [superimposition] is preceded by the cognition of difference.
However, in this case, regarding the description of the region of Śrīkaṇṭha by the Vātikas, the attribution of sky-cavities and so forth is caused solely by error.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(Vi, Ga) He demonstrates that there exists a domain for *ullekha* (multiple description) even when it is not confounded with *atiśayokti* (hyperbole)—namely, the verse beginning with "Śrīkaṇṭha. The meaning is as follows:

a specific king named Śrīkaṇṭha had a city which was perceived by enemies who had sought refuge there out of fear of him as a "thunderbolt-cage" (*vajrapañjara*). Since the city is similar to a thunderbolt-cage because it acts as a protector for those who have entered it, this is simply a case of *rūpaka* (metaphor) consisting of the superimposition of identity.
Because of the difference in the perceiver, there is a representation that appears as mixed with that [other object].
Nor should it be argued that this is merely *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) consisting of the superimposition of a relation where no relation exists;
for that [hyperbole] finds its occasion only when it is rooted in similarity to something else.
Regarding the term "child" (*śiśu*), it has already been stated that this is not a metaphor (*rūpaka*) precisely because of its ultimate reality (*tāttvikatva*).

As for the phrase "the cave of the Asuras," the meaning is "a cavity" (*vivara*), based on the perception of a similarity in form with those who are insane (*unmatta*) due to their [doctrinal] discourses (*vātika*), which are of a non-luminous nature.

The phrase "distinguished from hyperbole" (atiśayokti) means that since the city—the object of superimposition—is expressed by its own word, there is no swallowing up (nigaraṇa) of it; therefore, the point is that hyperbole does not apply here.
The phrase "based on secondary metaphor" (gauṇīmūla) [is used].

The meaning here is not that [the figure] is based on metaphorical indication (*gauṇī-lakṣaṇā*), as in the case of "The Vāhīka is an ox" and so forth; for there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in a metaphor (*rūpaka*),
because from the word "moon" the face is understood through its own primary power (*śakti*) precisely by way of the moon-ness residing in a different substratum.
When the basis of superimposition is mentioned first, it is *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification), as in "This is the moon.
However, when the superimposition itself is mentioned first, it is *gauṇī lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication),
as in "The Vāhīka is an ox."

However, the meaning of the term *gauṇī* (secondary/metaphorical) here is precisely that cognition which consists of a similarity characterized by the connection of the qualities of the superimposed object (*āropyaguṇa*) with the locus of superimposition (*āropādhikaraṇa*).

This is because [the secondary usage] serves as the motivator for metaphors (*rūpaka*) and other figures based on such cognition; the meaning is that it involves a superimposition preceded by the perception of a distinction [between the two objects].
By the phrase "metaphors and so forth" (*rūpakādī*), there is the inclusion of numerous other ornaments (*alaṃkāra*) rooted in similarity, such as poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

In this context, the demonstration of being the root is for the purpose of showing that suchness does not exist in the poetic figure of transformation (*pariṇāmālaṅkāra*) which is preceded by that [root].
Regarding the phrase "the word *para*," and so forth:
the meaning is that the word *para* refers to words such as "moon" (*candra*) and words such as "cow" (*go*).
"In another [place]" refers to the face and so forth, or to the Vāhīka and so forth.

"Being indicated" (lakṣyamāṇā) means: by connection with that quality (guṇa), which is the property of the superimposition (āropa) being indicated—that is, being known—of the locus of the superimposition; such is the meaning.

Furthermore, in the case of *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification), the function [of the word] toward another object occurs through its primary power (*śakti*) itself by way of a non-co-referential mode; however, in instances of figurative indication (*gauṇī-lakṣaṇā*), such as "The Vāhīka is a cow," the distinction is that it occurs through indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
This is what is meant by the phrase "it functions."

The meaning is that a word is secondary (*gauṇa*) when there is a common understanding between the speaker and the listener regarding it. And "that" refers to the connection with a quality (*guṇayoga*).
He states that the cognition of such a connection with qualities is not present in the case of "asuravivaram" by saying "iva tu.
Locanā:
(lo, ī) The sense is that its cause is the distinctiveness of another poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "childhood and so forth," qualities such as being beloved are included.
This is the meaning: although various distinctions such as childhood exist in the Blessed One, he is perceived by the cowherd women simply as "the Beloved" (*priya*), and not as a child.
Just as, even though qualities such as being beloved are present, he is perceived by the elders simply as a child.

In this case, although the recipient is manifold in form, there is a restriction [of him] to the singular form of each individual recipient; thus, because there is a determination of difference within non-difference, it is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). However, if this were merely the existence of *atiśayokti* due to the difference among the perceivers when there is actual difference, then it would simply be a particular variety of *atiśayokti*. But it is not so, for it is possible even in other figures of speech. Thus he says: "Śrīkaṇṭha... and so forth.
The region named Śrīkaṇṭhajanapada is a land presided over by the deity Śrīkaṇṭha.
"Asuravivara" refers to a cave of the Siddhas; "vātikās" are those who practice the yoga of wind (pavana).
Alternatively, "asuravivara" may refer to a certain specific disease that brings about the pacification of wind-related ailments (vātaroga).
"By those suffering from wind-diseases" means by those afflicted with *vāta* disorders.
Here too, he demonstrates that this is rooted in the charm of another figure of speech (alaṅkāra), stating "and here.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "those who know the truth so desire."
The phrase "the application of the figure of speech *rūpaka*" is stated according to the opinion of some; this is the meaning.
To the question "How is it not *rūpaka*?", he says: "by the cognition of difference" (*bhedapratīti-puraḥ*).
By the word "only" (*eva*) in the expression "of the lake itself" (*sara-syaiva*), there is an exclusion of error (*bhrānti*) and the like.
Even at the initial stage of the cognition of difference, there is an absence of error and the like;

for in examples such as "the foolish woman with the notion of milk," since the false cognition is brought forth by the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*) and is thus composed by the poet as residing in the cowherd and others, it is presented as true. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "metaphor (*rūpaka*) and so forth," the inclusion of concealment (*apahnuti*) and other figures is intended.
To the question of how such a superimposition (*āropa*) can be the instigator of metaphors and the like, he says: "based on secondary [signification] (*gauṇīmūla*)."
The meaning is that [the cognition] regarding a form and so forth is secondary (*gauṇī*), because it is caused by indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Nevertheless, as to how superimposition (*āropa*) therein is preceded by the perception of difference, [the author cites] the consensus of the Teacher found in the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda:

"In cases such as 'The boy is fire' (*agnirmāṇavakaḥ*), the word 'fire' (*paraśabdaḥ*)—which is the word for the boy (*māṇavakaśabdaḥ*) and so forth—is indicated (*lakṣyamāṇaḥ*) in another object, namely the boy; and according to that view, the quality (*guṇa*) is sharpness, tawny color (*piṅgala*), and so forth."
The "speaker" (prayoktā) is the one who employs the sentence;
the "comprehender" (pratipattā) is the knower of its meaning. And that [comprehender] is the "person to be informed" (bodhya) in the sense of a figurative application (gauṇīvṛtti).
He applies this to the present case with the words "But here...

The sense is that, according to the view of the ancients, it is only when produced by error (*bhrānti*) that [the figure] exists; however, in the absence of being produced by error, there is still *rūpaka* (metaphor).

Although this is a figure consisting of error (*bhrāntimad*), its status as a distinct figure does not lose its foundation in aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*); thus, there is no deficiency whatsoever in the present context.

And in this very context, in such passages as “The sages call it Capovana, while the courtesans call it the abode of love,” there is the employment of the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation).
Locanā:
In this very description of the region of Śrīkaṇṭha, there is the employment of the figure of speech *pariṇāma*.

Some maintain that in the region of Śrīkaṇṭha, because the superimposition (āropa) of being a penance grove (*tapovana*) and so forth upon the sage and others is useful for the actual practice of austerity and the like,
this is not a metaphor (*rūpaka*), as such a superimposition lacks a basis in similarity;
rather, since the sages and others— whose true nature is distinct from that of a penance grove— are perceived as having that very form, this is the figure of speech "Illusion" (*bhrāntimān*).

They say this is their intention: even though a certain portion of the Śrīkaṇṭha region consists of penance groves and the like, because of the non-difference between the part and the whole, the perception here that the entire collection is such [i.e., a penance grove] is not ultimate;
thus, it is not a *pariṇāma* (transformation).

Likewise, although there is the possibility of the distinctness of other figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) among all these cases, the multiple delineation (*anekadhā-ullekha*) occurs due to the difference in the perceivers.
The meaning is that because a specific distinction is possible, it is impossible to deny the figure of speech *ullekha* (multiple description) employed therein.

Furthermore, in cases such as "By your profundity you are the ocean; by your majesty you are the mountain," where there is a multiple description (*anekadhollekha*), the differentiating factor is the distinctness of the objects, such as profundity and so forth.
And here there is the application of metaphor (*rūpaka*);
*Vijñapriyā* says: "And right here."
In the verse beginning with "taponam" (the penance-grove), the syntactical connection is that there is a *pariṇāma* (transformation) figure of speech.
This is because the status of being a penance-grove and the status of being a temple of the God of Love (*Kāma*) are both real in that context, thereby making the *pariṇāma* ornament possible.
Nor should it be asked how the status of being a penance-grove can be real in that context.

Because the term *vanapada* (forest-word) is used here with the intention of being indicative (*lākṣaṇika*) of the hermitage, it is stated that this constitutes the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation).
Having thus illustrated *ullekha* (multiple description) as constituted by a difference in perceivers, he illustrates it as constituted by a difference in objects with the words "By its depth," etc.
The "difference in objects" refers to a difference in objects consisting of attributes (*dharma*).
In this case, there is indeed identity with the grasper alone: "The Guru [resides] in his speech,
Pṛthu in his chest."
And in passages such as "Arjuna in fame," its scope is distinct from that of metaphor (*rūpaka*);
for here there is a connection with hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) based on paronomasia (*śleṣa*). *Vijñapriyā*: [End of commentary].
(vi, ṅa) He shows its scope, which is not confused with metaphor (*rūpaka*), by saying "the teacher" (*guru*).
In the sense of the subject matter, which is speech in the form of instruction, the meaning is "the instructor";
and by way of pun (*śleṣa*), the meaning is Bṛhaspati.
"Pṛthu" means broad; by the cutting away of the chest, he is broad and expansive, and through punning (śleṣa), he is King Pṛthu.
"Arjuna" means... [the rest of the sentence is omitted in the source].
In this instance, in the phrase "in fame" (*yaśasi*), the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental;
the meaning is that Arjuna is white by means of his fame.
Furthermore, through *śleṣa* (paronomasia), he may be either Pāṇḍava-Arjuna or Kārttavīrya-Arjuna.
Regarding the phrase "distinct from form" (*rūpakād vivikta*):

because there is no mention of either of these two—namely, "you" (*tvaṃ*) or "your lordship" (*bhavān*)—due to this swallowing (*nigaraṇa*) of the forms, it falls within the domain of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) alone.
Furthermore, in this case, it takes the form of an attribution of non-difference despite the existence of difference.

If, however, there is an indication of either one of these two— *tvaṃ* (you) or *bhavān* (your lordship)— then it is indeed a metaphor (*rūpaka*), for this alone is the distinction between metaphor (*rūpaka*) and hyperbolic metaphor (*rūpakātiśayokti*).
Regarding the phrase "for here":

Nor should it be argued that this is a case of suggested simile (*upamā-dhvani*), as in the example "whose form has not been crossed by Durgā" (*na ca durgālaṅghitavigrahaḥ*). For in that instance, there is a pun on the substantive word *umāvallabha* (the beloved of Umā), whereas here there is no such substantive word. Even though the word *tvam* (you) exists, it is merely a metaphor (*rūpaka*) and not a suggested simile, because it lacks the quality of being a pun (*śliṣṭatva*). — Locanā.
(Lo, Ū) Having thus illustrated [the figure] in the case of a difference in gender, he illustrates it in the case of a difference in object with the words "by profundity" (*gambhīryeṇa*).
This is an *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) based on paronomasia (*śleṣa*).

Because there is an identification of difference as non-difference—namely, that the teacher (*guru*) who is the instructor is none other than the teacher (*guru*) Bṛhaspati—this is an *atiśayokti* based on paronomasia.
Pṛthu is both "broad" and the son of Viṇā;
Arjuna is "white," or else refers to Kārtavīrya or Pārtha.
Nor is there here a suggestion (*dhvani*) based on the power of words,
nor is there a metaphor (*rūpaka*), because qualities such as being a teacher are not identified with qualities such as being Bṛhaspati.
Apology (*apahnuti*) would occur if, after negating the subject at hand, something else were established in its place.
Locanā:
(*lo*, *ṛ*) Superimposition (*āropa*) consists in establishing something else upon the subject of superimposition (*āropaviṣaya*), which is the actual state of affairs (*prakṛta*).
This is twofold.
In some cases, there is superimposition preceded by concealment; in others, concealment preceded by superimposition.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ca) He states the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment): "the subject at hand," etc.
"The subject at hand" (*prakṛta*) means that which has been introduced; "establishing something else" (*anyasthāpana*) means establishing what is not the subject at hand (*aprakṛta*).
"And thus" (itthañca) means:

when there exists that which is distinct from these two alone—namely, the denial of the subject at hand (prakṛtāpahnavah) and the establishment of something else (anyasthāpanam). By the phrase "in some cases" (kvacid), he shows that there is a twofold division based on the reversal of the sequence between the denial of the subject at hand and the establishment of something else.

Nor should it be argued that because the term "having negated" (*niṣidhya*) does not specify the object of negation, only a negation preceded by concealment (*apahnava*) is obtained, and thus how there can be a twofold division;
for its meaning is simply "having made [the object] the content of the cognition of negation," and such making it the content of that cognition is possible in both ways.
The examples in order are as follows:
“The sky is not the orb of the heavens, but an ocean; these stars are not fragments of fresh foam;
this is not the moon, but the coiled king of serpents; and that is not a dark spot, but the reclining Murāri.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) "This is not the sky.
By negating the sky and so forth, this establishes the Enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu) reclining upon the serpent in the ocean with its foam.
In all instances beginning with "amburāśi" (ocean), it should be understood that the word "kintu" (but/however) is implied.
"This orb of the cool-rayed moon, kissing the peak of the western mountain, shines like a mass of foam;
it bears the smoke of the fire of love kindled throughout the night under the guise of its manifest dark spot."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ja) Having first established something else, he states the negation with the words "this appears.
This refers to the reflection (*bimba*), which by implication is that of the moon.
"Hiṇḍīra" means camphor. "Of that which has been ignited" means of that which has been extinguished.
The rising of smoke from the extinguishing of the fire of passion due to the night’s intense enjoyment with her beloved is [the mark].

By the word "kaitavena" (by way of a pretext), there arises the subsequent cognition of a negation: "This is not a [natural] mark, but rather the aforementioned smoke," as indicated by the term "kaitava."
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) *Hiṇḍīraḥ* means foam.
Here, by the word *kaitava*, meaning "deceit," there is an implied denial (*apahnava*) based on the understanding that it is not a manifest mark.
This verse is my own:
"The ocean, whose body is the sky, shines forth; and therein, the stars are like fragments of foam."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, jha) He states "it shines" (*virājati*) even by way of another mode of expression to convey the negation.
Here, through the word *vapuḥ* and the suffix *mayaṭ*, there is the cognition of the negation of space (*vyoman*) and so forth.
The negation of the subject at hand should be understood through such forms as these;
having somehow indicated the meaning that is to be concealed, [one should speak]. (VisSd 10.38)
If one should alter [the meaning] through a pun or otherwise, that too is *apahnuti* (concealment).
Locanā:
"One should alter" means...
One should employ it for another purpose;
"someone" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]; "even with" (sapīti).
The meaning of the word "api" (even/also) is that this is a form of *apahnuti* (concealment/denial) distinct from the type just mentioned.
An example by way of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is as follows:
"At this time, it is simply not possible to remain without the falling of rain from the clouds."
"You are longing, O fickle one! No, no, my friend;
the path is slippery."
In this context, regarding the phrase "by not having fallen" (*apatitayā*), having first stated "without a husband," it was subsequently changed to "by the absence of falling.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ña) states the second type of concealment (*apahnuti*)— namely, that which is to be hidden— with the words "it is to be concealed" (*gopanīyam*).
Illumination by means of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) occurs through *śakti* (denotation) alone;
otherwise, illumination occurs through *vyañjanā* (suggestion).
Furthermore, it should be understood that "speaking of another [meaning]" occurs through *śleṣa*, namely, by means of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) of the paronomastic words.
Regarding the word "kāle" (at the [proper] time):

here, by stating that the time for the streams of water—because it kindles passion—is such that staying [there] is impossible due to being bereft of her husband, she expresses a meaning that must be concealed; then, following the question of the clever women, she refutes that [objection] with "nahi...
nahi" (it is not so... it is not so).

In the rainy season, because the paths are slippery and prone to being broken by falling [objects], the statement is altered through a pun (*śleṣa*); this is what is meant by "here. An example of non-punning (*aśleṣa*) is as follows:
"In this city, which creeper does not meet with the tree, its form shaken by the wind?"
"Do you not remember, friend, the festival of dalliance with your lover? The manner of the arrival of the clouds has not been described [as a mere natural phenomenon]."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) "In this place, before me" means:
in this location, what creeper is directly in front?

Through the power of the word *vanaspati* (tree), there arises by means of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) the cognition of a hero associated with a heroine who is filled with trepidation; this is *samāsokti* (synecdoche). Upon that cognition, when a question such as "Do you remember? is posed, the speaker subverts it by means of the expressed meaning itself, saying: "Not indeed, at the arrival of the clouds. In *vakrokti* (paronomasia), there is a transformation of another's statement.
But here, the distinction lies in the fact that it is [the concealment] of one's own statement itself;
furthermore, because even that which is to be concealed is stated first by the author of the concealment, this constitutes *vyājokti* (disguised speech).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṭha) He states its distinction from *vakrokti* (indirect speech): "In *vakrokti*...
He also states its distinction from *vyājokti* (disguised speech): "By concealment...
In *vyājokti*, the speaker does not first state the matter that is to be concealed.
For example: "This labor with the large water-jar causes me to pant;
therefore, O friend, I shall rest for a moment in your presence."

"In this [verse], although the fatigue resulting from the encounter with a handsome man on the path while fetching water was not initially mentioned by the speaker, it was concealed out of fear that her female friend would perceive it.
This is the distinction [of this figure] as a *vyājokti* (concealed speech)," such is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*).
*Locanā*.
(Lo, e) "Apatitayā" means that for her there is no husband (*pati*) because she has not fallen; thus, "apatitā" signifies the state of being free from falling.
He expresses this very same thing as "alteration" (*anyathākaraṇa*) in the case of indirect speech (*vakrokti*), as in the example beginning with "Who are you? Just on dry land! and so forth.

In the case of *vyājokti* (concealment), as in the verse beginning with "being led by the Lord of Mountains," there is no mention of the horripilation and so forth produced by the touch of the Daughter of the Mountain’s hand.
Furthermore, *niścaya* (ascertainment) is the establishment of the subject at hand after having negated something else. *Viśvavidyānidhi*, 10.39.
Locanā:
(lo, ai) is called "certainty" (niścaya),
because it is the opposite of "concealment" (apahnuti).
This is the poetic figure known as *niścaya* (certainty).
"The other" refers to that which is being superimposed.
As in my own verse: "This is a face, not a lotus; these are eyes, not two blue lotuses."
O bee, why do you wander joyfully near this lovely-eyed woman?
Or as it is said:
"This is a necklace of lotus fibers upon my heart, not the lord of serpents; this is a garland of blue lily petals around my neck, not the luster of poison;
this is sandalwood dust, not ashes. O Anaṅga, do not strike me—who am bereft of my beloved—with the delusion that I am Śiva!"
"Why do you run away in anger?"
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ḍa) He states the figure of speech *niścaya* (certainty): "by negating one thing... In *apahnuti* (concealment), there is the establishment of another through the negation of the subject at hand. In *niścaya*, however, it is the establishment of the subject itself by means of its own certainty. Thus, there is a distinction between the two. This is what is meant. Furthermore, this [figure of speech] is not merely a variety of *apahnuti*. For in *apahnuti*, the negation of the subject is for the purpose of establishing something else; whereas here, the negation of the subject is for the purpose of establishing that very subject. Therefore, it is a distinct figure of speech. Moreover, this is not a case of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). For in *utprekṣā*, the object of comparison (*upameya*) is presented as if it were the object of comparison (*upamāna*), based on a perceived similarity. But here, the object of comparison is established as being none other than itself, by means of the exclusion of all other possibilities. Therefore, it is a separate figure of speech. This is the meaning. Furthermore, this is not a case of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). For in *atiśayokti*, there is a superimposition (*adhyavasāya*) of the object of comparison upon the object of comparison itself, based on a perceived similarity. But here, there is no such superimposition. Rather, the object of comparison is established as being none other than itself, by means of the exclusion of all other possibilities. Therefore, it is a separate figure of speech. This is the meaning. Moreover, this is not a case of *bhrāntimān* (error). For in *bhrāntimān*, the object of comparison is presented as the object of comparison itself due to a mistaken cognition. But here, there is no mistake. Rather, the object of comparison is established as being none other than itself, by means of the exclusion of all other possibilities. Therefore, it is a separate figure of speech. This is the meaning. Furthermore, this is not a case of *ullekha* (multiple description). For in *ullekha*, a single object is described as many things by different perceivers. But here, there is no such multiplicity of descriptions. Rather, the object of comparison is established as being none other than itself, by means of the exclusion of all other possibilities. Therefore, it is a separate figure of speech. This is the meaning. Moreover, this is not a case of *sandaṃśa* (the pincers). For in *sandaṃśa*, the subject at hand is established as being none other than itself by means of the exclusion of other possibilities, while simultaneously being compared to something else. But here, there is no such comparison. Rather, the object of comparison is established as being none other than itself, by means of the exclusion of all other possibilities. Therefore, it is a separate figure of speech. This is the meaning. Furthermore, this is not a case of *samādhi* (ingenious solution). For in *samādhi*, a certain action is accomplished by means of a different cause, while the original cause is excluded. But here, there is no such substitution of causes. Rather, the object of comparison is established as being none other than itself, by means of the exclusion of all other possibilities. Therefore, it is a separate figure of speech. This is the meaning. Moreover, this is not a case of *parivṛtti* (exchange). For in *parivṛtti*, a small thing is exchanged for a great thing, or vice versa. But here, there is no such exchange. Rather, the object of comparison is established as being none other than itself, by means of the exclusion of all other possibilities. Therefore, it is a separate figure of speech. This is the meaning. Furthermore, this is not a case of *vibhāvanā* (specification). For in *vibhāvanā*, an effect is produced even in the absence of its usual causes. But here, there is no such production of an effect. Rather, the object of comparison is established as being none other than itself, by means of the exclusion of all other possibilities. Therefore, it is a separate figure of speech. This is the meaning. Moreover, this is not a case of *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation). For in *viśeṣokti*, an effect is not produced despite the presence of its causes. But here,
But here, the meaning is that it is the opposite of that.
Regarding the phrase "this face":
O bee, do not wander in vain here in the presence of this lovely-eyed one.
In the phrase "bhrāmya," there is the optional addition of the suffix *śyan* belonging to the *divādi* class;
the meaning is that it is in vain that you wander with the notion that [the face] is a lotus and so forth. He establishes its futility with the words "this is the face."
"The lotus-stalk necklace upon her heart," and so forth, is the utterance of one separated from his beloved.
Likewise: "This is a fresh rain-cloud, not a haughty night-stalker;
this is a rainbow drawn far back, not his bow."
"This too is not a succession of arrows, but a sharp-edged essence; she is not my Urvaśī, but lightning, as smooth as gold on a touchstone"—
in such passages as these, this ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is also to be understood.
Locanā:
(lo, o) "Of the one with charming eyes" means of the one with beautiful eyes.
Since this ornament has not been elucidated by previous teachers, he provides another example for the sake of demonstrating its full scope, saying "or for instance."
Vāsuki is the leader of the serpents.
For this is not a doubt that culminates in certainty, because in that case, doubt and certainty would have to reside in a single locus.
In this case, however, there is doubt on the part of the bee and others, while there is certainty on the part of the hero and others.
Furthermore, even for the bee and others, there is no doubt in the sense of a cognition exceeding a single alternative (ekakoṭyadhika),
because approaching [the woman] closely would be impossible [if such doubt were present].
In that case, let it be an illusion;
indeed, let there be an illusion regarding the moon and so forth.
However, in this context, that [illusion] does not possess the quality of producing aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*).
Rather, such speech arises solely from the words of the heroine and others; this is to be understood by those of sensitive taste (*sahṛdaya*).
Furthermore, even if the falling of the bee and so forth, or its wandering, were not intended [as literal facts], such speech is possible only in the form of the heroine's flattery and the like.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ḍha) For "na hy ayam" [is used]; here the particle *hi* has the sense of "for" (*hi*), meaning "certainly not this" (*na vai ayam*).

By the phrase "of the bee, etc.," the word "etc. includes the lover (*anaṅga*) and so forth; by the phrase "of the heroine, etc.," the word "etc. includes the man who makes her known. Now, one might object: in a doubt that ends in certainty, their identity is not intended [to be expressed]. To this he says: the meaning is "in a cognition that does not exceed a single alternative" (*ekoṭi*).
And such a cognition occurs when there is a certainty regarding the very alternative that resides in that [cognition] by virtue of its intensity (*utkaṭatva*) within that single alternative.
And since such a certainty is indeed an error, he raises a doubt by taking up that alternative with the words "then" (*tahi*). The response is "let it be so" (*astu nāma*).
[The reason is] "precisely because of the statement of the leader and others of that kind."

The sense is that the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) arises precisely from the presentation of the excellence of the heroine’s pleasure in the second verse, as well as the excellence of the speaker’s *vipralambha* (love-in-separation). He states "by those with sympathetic hearts" (*sahṛdayaiḥ*) to indicate that connoisseurs are the authority regarding this matter. [An opponent might argue: "In examples such as 'The innocent girl, with the thought that it was milk...'," the charm likewise arises from the presentation of the moon's excellence; thus, the case is the same. To this he replies: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
In that case, "delusion" (*bhrānti*) refers to an action such as the falling of a jar dependent upon error;

however, in this instance, it is the bee itself—not an action of falling dependent upon error—that is intended. Although a resolution could thus be reached, the author addresses those who would argue for the presence of the *bhrāntimad* ornament even in the absence of such an action by stating: "even when not intended to be expressed."
According to the maxim "let it be satisfied," he says "not from the heroine's coaxing" upon accepting that state of affairs;
thus, it is accepted that the figure of speech *niścaya* (certainty) is indeed intermingled with the figure of speech *bhrāntimat* (error).
Nor is this a case of *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification), because the face has not been determined as being a lotus;
nor is it *apahnuti* (concealment).
Because there is no negation of what has been presented, this figure of speech is distinct from those mentioned by the ancients.

When a person falls upon a mother-of-pearl shell with the cognition that it is silver, the statement by someone else, "This is a mother-of-pearl shell, not silver," is not this figure of speech, due to the absence of poetic charm (*vaicitrya*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṇa) Although the status of being a suggestion of metaphor (*rūpakadhvani*) was not even under consideration, it is refuted for the sake of clarity: "And it is not a metaphor...
[and so on]. Regarding the phrase "because there is no determination as a lotus":
there is no determination because of the mention of its opposite, namely, "it is not a lotus."
He states that concealment (*apahnuti*) is simply not possible here, saying "and not" (*na ca*).
Regarding the term "ancient" (*cirantana*):
this is not merely a poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*), but rather— "Him whose splendor was like a thousand rays [of the sun], who was renowned in all ten directions by his fame..."
The wise know him as Daśapūrvaratha by name, and as the preceptor of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa.
This is the figure of speech known as *ekasaṃkhyā* (the ornament of unity).

I bow with a prostration of eight limbs before the one Viṣṇu, his two eyes, those three gods, the four arms of Viṣṇu, the five faces of Śiva beginning with the one adorned by Agni, and the seven flames of fire.
Thus ends the figure of speech known as *kramika-saṃkhyā* (sequential enumeration).
Other figures that bring about variety, even if not explicitly mentioned here, should be inferred by oneself.

Since, for almost all figures of speech, the status of being an "ornament" (*alaṅkāratva*) exists only when they are objects of a consciousness involving an artificial superimposition (*āhāryyāropabuddhi*), and not when they are merely factual, he says: "In the case of mother-of-pearl," and so forth.
Locanā:
(lo, au) Because they exist as having a single substratum, the very one who doubts becomes the one who ascertains, as for example in "Is this perhaps a lake? and so forth;
here, one alternative is "a lotus pond" and so on.
Likewise, the possibility of approaching [the object] and so forth is established by both scripture and reasoning.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is an inclusion of such things as the striking [of the object] in cases like "a lotus-fiber necklace upon the heart. Thus it is said.
If the meaning is that false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) does not exceed one limit— that is,
if such a kind of error is accepted in some way as a qualification for the speech of a heroine or others, such as "Your face is indeed like a lotus"— then [it follows that]...

Regarding this, he asks: "What is the authority [for this]? He replies: "It is to be known by those with aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdaya)," which means the experience of those who possess such sensitivity.

Whether or not there is an actual occurrence of falling and so forth on the part of bees and the like, if their delusive cognition is grasped by the hearts of those sensitive readers, it would be appropriate to speak of the figure of speech *bhrāntimad* (the Delusory).
But that is not the case here.
He further confirms its non-existence by showing another logical argument, beginning with "Moreover" (kiñca).
This speech, which is of such a kind, has the nature of a lotus;
and thus, because of the absence of the very essence of error.
And in the absence of that [determination], how could there be the figure of speech *bhrāntimān* (the appearance of error)? This is the meaning.
Because there is no determination [of the object] as being a lotus, the phrase "even of the two suggested meanings" (*vyaṅgyayoḥ*) is to be understood as a supplement (*śeṣaḥ*) prior to this.
This figure of speech called *niścaya* (certainty) has been elucidated by us.
Vividness is a transcendental distinctiveness that serves as the seed for poetic ornamentation.
"Utprekṣā (Poetic Fancy) occurs when there is a supposition of the subject at hand as having the nature of something else.
Vijñapriyā (vi, ta) states the ornament of Utprekṣā: "It would be," etc.

The meaning is: the imagining (*sambhāvanā*) of the subject (*prakṛta*) as being identical with the non-subject (*aprakṛta*) through its supreme self-nature (*parātmanā*), which is a doubt whose alternative is predominant (*utkaṭakoṭika*).

By this, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases of doubt where the alternatives are not predominant, nor to certainty, nor to metaphors (*rūpaka*) and the like. — *Locanā* The meaning is that the imagining of the subject (*prakṛta*) as being identical with the non-subject (*aprakṛta*) by means of its supreme self-nature (*parātmanā*) constitutes a doubt in which one alternative is predominant (*utkaṭakoṭika*). Consequently, there is no over-extension to cases of doubt where the alternatives are not predominant, nor to certainty, nor to figures such as metaphor (*rūpaka*).
— *Locanā*

(Lo, a) Having thus defined the figures of speech involving superimposition (*āropa*) by emphasizing non-difference, he now defines those involving identification (*adhyavasāya*) with the words "it may be" (*bhavet*).

The "other" is one similar to the subject at hand (*prakṛta*), which is possible and intended to be described; it is "impossible" in the sense that it is another object. The "conception" (*sambhāvanā*) is the imagining of that [subject] in the form of that [other], that is, in its own nature (*tatsvarūpeṇa*).
The meaning is that the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is a specific type of false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).
That [fancy] is considered to be first of two kinds: the expressed (*vācyā*) and the implied (*pratīyamānā*).
When words such as "as if" (*iva*) are employed, it is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy); when they are not employed, it is *parā* (the other).
Furthermore, that which is to be fancied—whether it be a genus (*jāti*), a quality (*guṇa*), an action (*kriyā*), or a substance (*dravya*)—is present in both types.
Then, each of those eight [types of conceptualization] is further divided into eight by way of the conceit of existence and non-existence,
and again by way of the cause being a quality, an action, or an essential nature.
They reach thirty-two varieties—
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, tha) In order to establish that this [poetry] consists of one hundred and seventy-six varieties through the multiplicity of its divided sub-divisions, he first states its twofold nature with the words "vācya" (the expressed), etc.
And what is being perceived here is not a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*),
because that would result in its being a case of *utprekṣā-dhvani*,
as will be shown in the example beginning with "mahilāsahasra... and so forth.
However, the meaning is simply "being supplied" (*adhyāhriyamāṇā*).
In the phrase "the other [types] are being supplied for both," this means they apply to both *vācyotprekṣā* (expressed fancy) and *adhyāhriyamāṇotprekṣā* (fancy based on what is supplied).
Therefore, the meaning is that there are eight types, consisting of the fourfold *utprekṣā*—based on genus (*jāti*) and so forth—which are either expressed (*vācyā*) or supplied (*adhyāhriyamāṇā*).
He states that the conceptualization (*utprekṣā*) of the non-existence of the fourfold set beginning with birth is likewise eightfold, saying: "That [non-existence] is also eightfold.

This means that because one conceives of the non-existence of each member of the fourfold set of entities—namely birth and so forth—the conceptualization is eightfold; that is, there are eight modes of that conceptualization.
The particle *api* ("also") is to be construed according to the manner shown by shifting its position [to after "eightfold"].

Thus, the eightfold set of *utprekṣā* regarding the existence of birth and so forth, together with the eightfold set regarding their non-existence, result in sixteen varieties; even though the number sixteen was not explicitly stated, it is established by implication.
By doubling that, he states the number thirty-two: "guṇākriyā" (quality and action).
Since the cause (*nimitta*)—the basis for the *utprekṣā*—consists of the nature of qualities and actions, those sixteen types of *utprekṣā* further become thirty-two-fold. This is the meaning.

The meaning is that these sixteen types—consisting of eight *utprekṣās* (poetic fancies) of existence regarding genus (*jāti*) and so forth, based on the distinction between the expressed (*vācya*) and the implied (*pratīyamāna*), and eight *utprekṣās* of non-existence thereof—become thirty-two through doubling due to their possession of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*) as causes; and the "cause" (*hetu*) is that which generates the *utprekṣā*. — *Locanā* The meaning is that these sixteen types—consisting of eight *utprekṣās* (poetic fancies) of existence regarding genus (*jāti*) and so forth, based on the distinction between the expressed (*vācya*) and the implied (*pratīyamāna*), and eight *utprekṣās* of non-existence thereof—become thirty-two through doubling due to their possession of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*) as causes;
and the "cause" (*hetu*) is that which generates the *utprekṣā*. — *Locanā*
