He states the divisions of that [suggestion]: "The expressed" (*vācya*), etc.
The *vācya* is understood immediately due to its dependence on words such as "as if" (*iva*) which indicate it.
The *pratīyamāna* (the suggested) is to be connected through reflection upon the expressed meaning in the absence of any indicating word.
He states that very point: "In the denoted [object], of 'vā' and so forth.
The object to be compared (upameya), which possesses various properties like a single property, is the *jāti* (universal).
A *guṇa* (quality) is a property that is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and is to be indicated as something already accomplished.
Action (*kriyā*) is a property (*dharma*) that can be indicated by its state of being accomplished;

substance (*dravya*) is a property that can be indicated by pointing it out directly, as if seizing it by the horns; and the object of conceptual determination (*adhyavaseya*) is that which is to be imagined.
Even though this [figure] belongs to the subject matter at hand, it is not counted as a distinct variety because, despite its connection with difference, it does not bring about diversity;

for this ornament, whose very life is imagination (*sambhāvanā*), receives its specific character solely from the particularity of that which is being imagined. This refers to the two aforementioned varieties.
Existence (*bhāva*) is precisely birth (*jāti*) and so forth;
non-existence (*abhāva*) is the mere absence of those very things.
These aforementioned sixteen types are the characteristics of the object (*viṣayadharma*), which serve as the cause for the conceptualization of signs (*nimitta*).
It is "imagined" (utprakṣyate) or "made manifest" (prakāśyate);
that is to say, by this [mental faculty], even though it is very slight, many similar things are manifested—this is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
Among these, an example of *vācyotprekṣā* (expressed poetic fancy) is given merely as a direction: [Example follows]
“The thigh of the fawn-eyed woman, with its fluttering hem of her garment,
shines like a golden pillar of victory belonging to Smara, complete with its banner.”
Here, because the victory pillar (*vijayastambha*) has many meanings, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on genus (*jāti*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
"A mere indication" (*diṅmātra*) means a very small amount.
"Ūru" means the part of a garment;
"cañcalacelāñcalaḥ" refers to a portion of a moving cloth.
The meaning is that the thigh of the deer-eyed woman shines like a golden victory-pillar of the God of Love, adorned with a banner.
The pillar is a golden shaft;
the banner is the cloth placed upon it, located there in place of the fluttering ends of a garment.
Here, [the author] makes it understood that this is a case of *jātyutprekṣā* (genus-based poetic fancy) by saying "here. Regarding the phrase "of the victory pillar" (*vijayastambhasya*),
the meaning is "of the word expressing that [pillar]."
Because that which has been introduced denotes many things— that is, it expresses multiple individuals—
the nature of "pillar-ness" as a universal (jāti) is thereby established;
and since the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the pillar possesses that [universal] as its qualifier, that too is a poetic fancy.
This principle should be applied everywhere.

This example is not an instance of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*) as its cause; rather, it is an instance of *utprekṣā* with an unstated cause (*anuktanimitta-utprekṣā*), which will be discussed later.
Therefore, in this case, the cause for the poetic fancy of the "pillar of victory" (*vijayastambha*), namely its being an excitant of passion (*kāmoddīpakatva*), remains unstated.
Locanā:
(lo, i) This is a genus-based poetic fancy (jātyutprekṣā), because it consists of a poetic fancy regarding the essential nature of a genus.
“Silence in the face of knowledge, forbearance in the face of power, and the absence of self-praise in the face of renunciation—
these virtues of his seem to be in full bloom, as they are bound up with virtue itself.”
In this context, "being accompanied by offspring" is the poetic quality (*guṇa*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, dha) states the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the expressed quality: "silence in the case of knowledge," and so forth.
The meaning is that because of Dilīpa’s being connected to both virtues and non-virtues, they were as if accompanied by their offspring.
He demonstrates that virtues are connected to other virtues with the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*);
the meaning is that when knowledge and so forth exist, there is silence (*mauna*) and so forth—"here" (*atra*).
"Procreation" (prasava) is the emergence from the womb.
While the act of "producing" (utpādana) is the subject under discussion, this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding something not so subject.
Since the word *prasava* ends in a *kṛt* suffix and thus functions as a noun (*nāman*), its meaning is not an action; therefore, it is merely a quality (*guṇa*).
In this context, the fact that [the object] is connected with qualities (*guṇa*) has already been stated as the cause for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
Locanā:
(Lo, ī) Thus, after the word "quality" (*guṇa*) which is about to be mentioned, the words "is fancied" (*utprekṣyate*) are to be supplied.
Likewise elsewhere:
"O Protector of the Faith, the sound of your laughter resounds upon the waters of the Gaṅgā."
He is as if bathed, though he is a sinner who has caused the fetus of a pregnant woman to fall.
Here, "bathes" is the action (*kriyā*).
Vijñapriyā says: he expresses a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the action by means of the phrase "in the waters of the Gaṅgā."
"Suratrāṇa"—this is a specific term in the Karṇāṭaka language (Karṇāṭabhāṣā) signifying the preeminence of Western kings; it is a corruption of the word *sulatāna*.

O such [king], the sound of your battle-drums, which are free from the whetting-stone (*niḥśāṇa*), is a sinner (*pātakī*) for causing the miscarriage of the fetuses of the wives of your enemies; therefore, the meaning is that [the sound] seems to bathe in the waters of the Gaṅgā in order to expiate that sin.
The implication is that because the army of the Western king is far from the Gaṅgā, the sound of the army has reached as far as its very limits.
The author himself will demonstrate the reason for this:
"The face of the deer-eyed woman shines like another full moon.
— *Vijñapriyā*.
(vi, pa) He states the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding a substance (*dravya*)—namely, "the face" (*mukham*).
This too has an unstated cause (*anuktahetuka*).
Here, the word "moon" (*candra*) is a term denoting a substance because it refers to a single individual entity (*ekavyakti*).
These [examples] concern the conceit of existence;
as for the conceit of non-existence, it is as follows:
"Alas, those two cheek-plates of hers, having become such [as they were],..."
"Beholding each other as if they were mere shadows, they have both come to such a state of emaciation."
In this context, "not seeing" signifies the absence of the action;
the same applies to other cases.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, pha) Regarding the conceit of non-existence (*abhāvābhimāna*), when there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) concerning the non-existence of [physical] birth and so forth, he states therein a poetic fancy regarding the non-existence of action (*kriyābhāvotprekṣā*): "The two cheek-boards...

The meaning is: "Alas! Her two cheek-boards—the expansive regions in the form of her cheeks—having been of such a nature, that is, full and well-nourished, have now reached such a state of emaciation and thinness.
This attainment of thinness results from the sight of her beloved.
Here, while separation is the actual cause of emaciation under discussion, the absence of the act of mutual beholding is poetically imagined (utprekṣita) as being that very cause.
The statement of this cause will be shown by the author himself later on—“and so it is with other cases.
Here is an example of the poetic fancy of the absence of a genus (*jātyabhāvotprekṣā*): “Does the sun not perform the *saṃdhyā* [twilight rite] because of his lack of ‘twice-born’ status?”

Thus, when the heat-exhausted state is mentioned as the cause for performing the *sandhyā* (twilight ritual), and slow movement is the subject at hand, the absence of the "twice-born" (*dvijatva*) caste is poetically imagined (*utprekṣita*) as the cause for performing the *sandhyā*, which is a word associated with the non-contextual;
and the performance of the *sandhyā* is stated as the cause for the poetic imagination.
An instance of poetic fancy (utprekṣā) based on the absence of birth, where the cause is not stated, is as follows: "Even as he approaches, it is perceived that this man is not a Brahmin."
Thus [it is said].
Here, however, the absence of the configuration indicative of brahminhood is the unstated reason (*hetu*).
In this manner, the presence or absence of the statement of a reason in other cases should also be understood.

In the verse, "Has your fame, O illustrious one, gone far away as if out of disrespect? fame is poetically imagined (utprekṣita) as having the quality of disrespect; its status as a rival wife is the basis for this, and being "illustrious" (śrīmattva) is stated as the reason.
“The night came to an end, as if due to the death of its lord, the moon.”
In this [verse], the absence of the substance—the moon—is imagined;
its cause, the departure of the night, is stated.
(Locanā)
(Locative, ablative): "Of such a kind" means possessing form.

Regarding the cause (*nimitta*) of an action consisting of perception—when that cause takes the form of a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*), as for example in "in the waters of the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgambhasi*) and so forth—the sinfulness (*pātakitva*) which serves as the cause for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) "as if she were bathing" is a quality (*guṇa*).
In the passage beginning with "apaśyantau," the action consisting of the attainment of emaciation is the *nimitta* (cause).
The same applies to other instances.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ba) Among these, whether the causes (*hetu*) possess the nature of an action (*kriyā*) or a quality (*guṇa*) should be determined by oneself. In the case of [the verse], "The cause is the state of being a sinner," and in the case of "At dawn, she seems as if laughing," the cause— namely, the sight of the beloved sun— is not explicitly stated.
"Similarly with others": in the verse,
"As if eager, this night-lily laughs at the moonlight of the moon," the moonlight is the *guṇa* (the quality) upon which the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of eagerness is based.
An example of suggested *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is as follows:
"The slender-limbed woman did not reveal her face because of the shame [felt] that no place had been given to the virtuous pearl necklace."
Here, because of the absence of words such as "as if" (*iva*), there is a suggested (*pratīyamāna*) poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), as in the phrase "as if out of shame.
The same applies to other instances.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, bha) "By the slender-limbed one":
the non-revealing of the face is due to its being covered by a garment;
the taking up of the necklace from its place is due to her being in close proximity and the absence of any gap between them.
In this context, the taking [of the object] from its place is stated to be the cause for the [acquisition of the] quality;
"and so it is with the other.
"Having sold [it], the fools [act] with a clear face..."
The garland-maker, desiring to sell the blossoming lotuses, covers her face with the hem of her garment while holding the lily buds.
In this case as well, since the desire to sell the lotus is not the cause for covering its face, one must supply the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that she is "desirous of selling" [it].
The sense is that at that very moment, because the moon-like face is no longer visible, the closing of the lotus is prevented.

However, if one supplies a *kriyotprekṣā* (fancy regarding an action), it would be "the lotus laughs at the rising of the sun"; and if one supplies a *jātyutprekṣā* (fancy regarding a genus or class), it would be "this other twice-born man is a sinful outcaste."

In the case of the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) involving the superimposition of a substance (*dravyotprekṣā*) and ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*): in the two instances "the moon" and "this woman’s other face," because of the presence of the word *anya* ("other"), there is no metaphor (*rūpaka*).
Locanā:
(lo, ū) "Face" (*mukha*) is synonymous with "breast-nipple" (*cūcuka*) and "mouth" (*vadana*).
The thread (*sūtra*) consists of the qualities (*guṇa*), such as discernment and discipline;
here, the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) based on these qualities is implied.
Furthermore, there is the attribution of a living being (*bhāvābhimāna*) elsewhere, as in my father’s [verse].
Beholding before him the eastern quarter— with its face blossomed by the attachment of passion, its dark garment of gloom falling away, and touched by the rays of the sun— the moon,
his complexion pale as a ripened lavalī fruit and his inner being deeply troubled, takes refuge at dawn in the northern direction.
Here, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) consisting of the act of "looking" (*nirīkṣaṇa*), expressed as "as if looking," is suggested (*pratīyamāna*).
The same applies elsewhere.
Now, it was stated during the discussion on *dhvani* that all poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) can indeed possess the status of being suggested.
Now, however, how is it that *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is understood as being suggested (*pratīyamāna*)?

It is said: in the case of suggested *utprekṣā*, such as in the verse beginning with “*mahilāsahasra-*,” the sentence reaches its full meaning even without an explicit act of imagining. Here, however, because shame is impossible for breasts, the phrase “as if by shame” functions solely through *utprekṣā*. Thus is the distinction between the suggested *utprekṣā* and the *utprekṣā* that is directly expressed.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ma) The objection beginning with "nanu" is indeed clear.
Since the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is untenable without the supply (*adhyāhāra*) of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), when that is supplied, there is a suggested (*pratīyamāna*) poetic fancy.

Since the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is possible even without supplying that [word], he shows the scope of the suggested simile (*utprekṣādhvani*) in order to establish the doctrine that it is a "suggested simile" when the simile is manifested by the force of *tātparya* (intentional implication) subsequently; thus he says: "It is said:
'O woman' (*mahileti*)."
This has been explained previously.
This is a statement made by the heroine’s friend to her husband, informing him of the condition of his wife, who is wasting away due to the hero’s infatuation with many other women.
That wife of yours, unable to find space for herself (*amāntī*), stretches out the day—that is, she makes it seem long—by thinning it out.
This is the form of the word *tanu* at the end of a compound whose function is based on its name;
[this applies] in such cases as "ity-ādau.
"Resting" (*viśrānti*) means comprehension (*bodha*).

Since the non-attainment of a place [in the heart] is not itself an object of cultivation—given that it is the very absence of the attainment of a place—it is possible for it to be understood through the relation of being that which is cultivated (*bhāvyamānatva*).

However, by reflecting on the intention (*tātparya*) of attenuating the limbs (*aṅga-tanūkaraṇa*), the non-attainment of a place in the mind through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is perceived as the cause for the attenuation of the limbs.

And since that [non-attainment] is sublated [by the fact that it is not actually cultivated], there is here a suggestion (*dhvani*) of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the non-attainment of a place.
But [the author] says that it is not so in the case of "tanvaṅgayā," stating "here, however" (*iha tu*).
In the phrase "as if by this very poetic fancy" (*ityutprekṣayeva*),
the word "resting" (*viśrānti*) is to be supplied as a grammatical connection (*anuṣaṅga*).

"The distinction between the two types of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy)" means that the difference between the two types of *utprekṣā* consists in their being respectively brought about by the speaker's own effort (*āhāryya*) or manifested (*vyaṅgya*). —
*Locanā*.
And thus, desiring to demonstrate the distinction from the suggested metaphor (*utprekṣādhvani*), he raises an objection with "Now, [is it not the case]?
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with "It is said.
[This refers to] the case of a suggested metaphor, where the metaphor that constitutes the suggestible (*vyaṅgya*) is the factor that causes the poem to be a *dhvani*.
The meaning of the verse has already been explained as resting upon the sentence even without poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
This is the intended sense:
because the word *amānti* (“do not fit”) rests upon the expressed meaning, namely, “without attaining the status of being a vessel for the passion of your heart.”
In this present example, there is a distinction between the suggested (vyaṅgya) and the implied (pratīyamāna) poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
This is the underlying intention:

just as for many other figures of speech their status as specific varieties of *alaṃkāra* is established by such statements as "because the implied is a factor in the accomplishment of the expressed" (*vācyasiddhyaṅgatvāt*), so it is also for poetic fancy; thus, there is no deficiency whatsoever.
However, where there is suggestiveness (*vyaṅgyatā*) as the cause for the status of poetic resonance (*kāvyadhvani*), it is not proper for there to be the status of a figure of speech (*alaṅkāratā*).
Thus, the sense is that the example cited by some regarding the suggested metaphor (*pratīyamānotprekṣā*) in the verse beginning with *mahilāsahasra-* is incorrect.
Here, he states a distinction among the sixteen varieties of expressed metaphor (*vācyotprekṣā*):
Vijñapriyā:

Regarding the sixteen types of expressed *utprekṣā* (*vācyotprekṣā*), there are eight kinds of expressed *utprekṣā* based on the fourfold set beginning with genus (*jāti*) and the absence of that same fourfold set; these become sixteen by being twofold, since each of those eight is caused by either a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*).
Even though it is understood in this way, one should remember that the number sixteen was stated previously.
Regarding that, the further divisions of the denotable meanings are as follows:
"Excluding substance, all [the remaining categories] are threefold, pertaining respectively to the essential nature, the fruit, and the cause. (Viṣṇu-siddhānta 10.43)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ra) "Therein, the expressed" means the varieties— that is, the distinctions— of the expressed *utprekṣā*.

Since the fourfold set beginning with *jāti* (genus) possesses a twofold nature by way of both existence and non-existence, and each of these is further doubled by being caused by both quality (*guṇa*) and action (*kriyā*), it must be stated that there is a fourfold variety; thus, regarding the sixteenfold nature previously mentioned for *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), he says "except for substance" (*vinā dravyam*), because apart from the fourfold set of *dravya-utprekṣā*, there is a threefold nature for only the remaining twelve types.
The meaning is "without the fourfold [types] of substance-poetic fancy (dravyotprekṣā). Regarding "svarūpa" (essential nature):
when the cause of some fancied object is stated as its effect, that poetic fancy whose object is its own essential nature is "svarūpotprekṣā" (poetic fancy of essential nature).
But when they are stated as being either of those two, they pertain to either of those two;
[thus] Locanā (lo,
ṝ) pertains to the essential nature, the fruit, and the cause.
Namely, simile of essential nature (svarūpotprekṣā), simile of result (phalotprekṣā), and simile of cause (hetūtprekṣā).
The essential nature [of the object] is a distinct attribute (*dharmāntara*),
and the attribute is stated as being equal in number to the objects [of comparison].
Among the aforementioned varieties of expressed (*vācya*) and suggested (*pratīyamāna*) poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*), regarding those sixteen varieties of expressed conceit:

Furthermore, regarding the twelve varieties of the three [categories] beginning with birth (*jāti*), since each of these possesses twelve varieties by way of being categorized as essence, fruit, and cause, there are thirty-six varieties.
Since only the imagination of the essence of a substance (*dravya*) is possible, there are four [varieties for that]; thus, taken together, there are forty varieties.
Here, an example of *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature) is as in the previous illustrations: "the victory pillar of Smara.
Expressions such as "as if with offspring" (*saprasavā iva*) and so forth are instances of *svarūpagā* (pertaining to the essential nature) based on genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*).
Vijñapriyā:
He explains [the word] "therein" (*tatra*) as follows:
"those which are the twelve divisions."
Because there are twelve [factors] in each of the three tetrads;
the meaning is that each of them has twelve divisions.
Since each tetrad possesses a threefold nature, there are twelve—thus making thirty-six.
Because three times twelve makes thirty-six;
"from forty" means because the fourfold examination of substances amounts to thirty-six.

In this regard, he shows the two types of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) concerning the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*), which have already been mentioned before, with the words "here, the essential nature" (*atra svarūpa*).

In the phrase "having the essential nature of genus and quality" (*jātiguṇasvarūpāḥ*), the meaning is "having the essential nature of genus, quality, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *utprekṣā* regarding action (*kriyā*) and substance (*dravya*) is intended.

In this very context, the reading "jāti-guṇa" [etc. is correct; the variant reading "kriyā-guṇa" found in some places is merely a scribal error. This is because, since the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on action has not been explicitly mentioned, it must necessarily be included by the word "etc. (*ādi*). Thus, the poetic fancy regarding the essential nature of that action is expressed as "she seems to bathe" (*snātīvety*).
The *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the essential nature of a substance (*dravyasvarūpotprekṣā*) consists of exactly the two types mentioned previously, such as "like another full moon.
The *utprekṣā* regarding the fruit (*phalotprekṣā*) is, for example:
"Even Rāvaṇa’s heart, pierced by Rāma’s swift arrow..."
He entered the earth as if to announce pleasant news to the serpents.
Here, "to tell" is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣita*) regarding the fruit of the entry into the earth in the form of an action.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, va) Thus, since a fancy of essential nature (*svarūpotprekṣā*) is possible even with respect to a substance (*dravya*), it occurs only in the four [categories] beginning with genus (*jāti*), together with those included by the word "etcetera."

Having demonstrated the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) based on the result and the conceit based on the cause, [the author] now states the conceit regarding the result as it pertains to action—in order to show it in the three categories beginning with genus (*jāti*), excluding substance (*dravya*)—in the verse beginning with "Even Rāvaṇa’s... The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: even the swift arrow (*āśuga*) discharged by Rāma, having pierced the heart of Rāvaṇa, entered the earth as if to announce pleasant news to the serpents.
Regarding this:
the meaning is that the fruit of the entry is poetically imagined (utprekṣita) as having the form of the action of narration;
for it is understood that the object of a desire [expressed] with an infinitive suffix (tumun) functions as a fruit.
Locanā: (lo,
ḷ) "The lover was struck by the lover," is the connection,
as if [the arrow] were to announce what is dear.
An example of *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause) is as follows: “This is that very spot where, while searching for you, a single anklet was seen by me fallen upon the ground;
it remained silent, as if bound by the sorrow of separation from your lotus-like foot.”
Here, the quality of having a harsh nature is poetically conceived as the cause;
other instances are to be understood in the same way.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, śa) "This is that very spot"— this is Rāma’s speech addressed to Sītā as she stands upon the Puṣpaka chariot.
"While searching for you— that is, while reflecting on you— I beheld here a single anklet which had fallen, meaning it had slipped from your foot."
He imagines the cause of the silence of the soundless anklet with the words "at thy feet.
Here,
the meaning is that [the anklet] lacks the status of being a cause.

"Thus, the other [types] are likewise. It has been stated that in the case of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of action, it pertains only to the result (*phala*) and not to the cause (*hetu*); in the case of the poetic fancy of quality (*guṇa*), it pertains only to the cause and not to the result;
whereas in the case of the poetic fancy of genus (*jāti*), it has been stated that it may pertain to either.
The meaning is that it should be inferred in this manner.

In that regard, an example of the cause being the basis for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of action is as follows: "O Protector of the Earth, [your fame] is stainless, as if from the act of wiping [it clean]."
In this instance, the act of wiping is poetically imagined (*utprekṣita*) as the cause of stainlessness.
An example of a quality serving as the result is: "The lotus, the gateway to fame, remains as if for the sake of merit.
Here, both the quality (*guṇa*) and the merit (*puṇya*) are poetically imagined as the result.

An example of how a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) leads to a result is as follows: "In the act of love, the beloved woman, afflicted by the arrows of the God of Love, seems to desire the pain caused by the nail-marks for the sake of pleasure itself."
In this instance, the fruit of the desire—consisting in the superimposition of the genus *sukhatva* (the nature of pleasure) even upon suffering—is poetically imagined (*utprekṣita*).

An example of the cause-based nature (*hetugāmitva*) of the poetic figure of genus-poetic-imagination (*jātyutprekṣā*) is as follows: "Even when seized by Rāhu, the cool-rayed moon [shines] as if he were a twice-born who has performed meritorious deeds.
Here, the genus of being twice-born (*dvijatva-jāti*) is poetically imagined as the cause for the production of merit.

Although, in instances such as "The mental distress of the young Kokila bird has arisen as if from the moon," it is possible for even a *dravotprekṣā* (liquid-like poetic fancy) to possess the quality of being based on a cause (*hetugāmitva*), nevertheless, because such cases are rare and do not produce a particular variety of charm, their impossibility [in that specific sense] has been demonstrated.
— *Locanā*.

In the phrase "this very [silence]," the silence of the anklet arises from the absence of contact with moving substances; thus, it is identified (*adhyavasita*) with the absence of silence caused by suffering. Alternatively, the very absence of contact with moving substances—which is the cause of the anklet's silence—is identified with suffering itself. In that case, as in the figure of *atiśayokti*, the object [of identification] is merely implied; and this will be discussed further below.
It will become clear:
there, the two types [of causes]—the expressed and the unexpressed—reside in the essential nature of the cause.
*Vijñapriyā*:
The forty-fold nature of expressed *utprekṣā*, as constituted by the two types of causes—namely, qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*)—has already been demonstrated.

Now, however, in order to show its fifty-six-fold nature through the inclusion of sixteen varieties based precisely on the sequence of the causes, he says: "of expression and non-expression" (*uktyanuktyoḥ*).

Since it will be stated later that for the triad beginning with genus (*jāti*), there is no possibility of the non-expression of the cause because they function as either effects or causes, and since for the triad [beginning with genus] in relation to the *utprekṣā* of substance (*dravya*), the non-expression of the cause is possible only when they pertain to the essential nature (*svarūpa*), he says: "in two ways" (*dvidhā*).
The phrase "residing in the essential nature" (svarūpagā) means that they do not reside in the cause or the effect.

Among those forty varieties, the sixteen varieties residing in the essential nature become thirty-two varieties through the inclusion and exclusion of the cause of the poetic conceit (utprekṣā-nimitta). Thus, when combined—
There are fifty-six varieties of expressed *utprekṣā*.
Among these, an example of the mention of the cause (*nimitta*) is the aforementioned *utprekṣā* "as if bathing," where the cause—being stained with sin—is explicitly mentioned.
An example of its non-mention is "like another moon," where such an excellence of beauty and so forth is not mentioned.
However, in the case of cause and effect, there is necessarily the employment of a *nimitta* (grounding factor);

for instance, in the phrase "as if from the pain of separation," the *nimitta* is the state of observing silence (*baddhamauṇatvam*), and in the phrase "as if to tell," it is the entry into the earth (*bhūpraveśa*). If these two were not employed, the sentence would indeed be incoherent.
(Vijñapriyā)
He explains [the verse] with the words "among those" (*teṣu*).
Those sixteen divisions which reside in their own nature (*svarūpa*) consist of four that pertain to genus (*jāti*),
and eight that pertain to existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāva*) by virtue of having them as their objects.
It should be understood that the sixteenfold nature of *svarūpotprekṣā* (intrinsic poetic fancy) arises from the twofold nature of its causes—qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*).
Regarding the phrase "by way of being based on [a material cause] or not being based on one":
those sixteen types that involve a material cause (*upādāna*) are indeed included within the forty varieties [of *utprekṣā*].
It should be understood that there are sixteen varieties [of *vṛtti*] formed by excluding the *anupādāna*.
Nor should it be argued: "If the *nimitta* (cause) is excluded, how can there be sixteen varieties formed by including the two types [of *nimitta*], since eight would be more appropriate"?
For in some cases, the *nimitta*, being an action (*kriyā*), is simply not mentioned.
In some cases, there is no mention of such a quality;
for even when it is not mentioned, the possibility of a twofold division remains.
"Combined" means...
The meaning is that [the number] is obtained by adding together the sixteen types where the cause is not stated.

Thus, since the non-statement of the cause is possible only in the case of *svarūpotprekṣā* (conceit regarding the essential nature), there are fifty-six varieties, but not in the case of *phalayogotprekṣā* (conceit involving the connection with a result); this he states with the words "But in the case of cause and result" (*hetuphalayos tu*).
In the phrase "entry into the earth" (*bhūpraveśe*), the construction is "that which is the cause" (*yannimittam*).

"Incoherence indeed" means that incoherence is simply the non-fulfillment of the syntactic expectancy between the word ending in the suffix *tumun* and the word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). —
Locanā:
"Expression" (*ukti*) is the employment of words that convey meaning; "non-expression" (*anukti*) is the state of being obtainable through implication even in the absence of such words.
[The opponent claims] that this is simply inconsistent.
The meaning is that this is because of the state of expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*).
Locanā states the distinction regarding the sixteen varieties of the implied sense (*pratīyamāna*):
In the sixteen—those just mentioned—the non-differences that are being perceived each reside within both the fruit and the cause. (VisSd 10.44)
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ha) Regarding the phrase "among the sixteen of the suggested meaning"—it has already been shown that there are eight types of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) concerning the four categories such as genus (*jāti*), etc., by virtue of having both existence and non-existence as their objects; and because of the two causes, namely quality (*guṇa*) and action (*kriyā*), there are sixteen.
Regarding the phrase "going by way of fruit and cause":
it will be explained that this does not refer to their intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).
And thus, because of the two-fold division of going by way of fruit and going by way of cause, it will be explained that there are thirty-two types.

Just as in the example cited, "nanvaṅgyāḥ stanayugmena," where the cause "as if out of shame" (lajjayeva) is poetically imagined (utprekṣita), here too, the non-mention of the cause is not possible; for if the particle *iva* and so forth are not employed and the cause is not stated, the cognizer (pramātṛ) would be unable to ascertain that a poetic imagination is occurring.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ka) [Objection: But why is the sixteenfold increase (*paraṣoḍaśavṛddhi*) not demonstrated here, which is produced without taking a formal cause (*nimitta*)? To this he says: "In this too" (*asyām api*).
The meaning is: "in this case of suggested poetic fancy (*pratīyamānotprekṣā*)."
The meaning is that, just as [the cause] is to be expressed in *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the result, it is likewise so here.
He demonstrates the impossibility of that [cause being unexpressed] with the words "in the absence of *iva* and so forth.
For instance, in the verse beginning with "tat-taṅgyāḥ," the taking up of the necklace from its place is the cause for the poetic fancy of shame.
The meaning is that, if that [shame] were not apprehended, since no cause for shame would be perceived, the postulation of shame by the cognizer—the knower—would be impossible to ascertain.
Since shame could not arise in that pair [of body and mind] if it were insentient, their concomitance would be strictly sublated;
and one should not argue that the postulation should be ascertained on the strength of such sublation.

In the absence of a cause, how could there be shame? Because there is a desire for [an explanation], certainty is impossible. Furthermore, even *svarūpotprekṣā* (imagination of the essential nature) does not occur here;

for this [type of imagination], which is based on the identity with another attribute (*dharmāntara-tādātmya*), is accepted as being a case of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) when it is employed without words such as *iva* and so forth, provided there is a connection with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
For example: “This king is another Indra” (where the metaphor exists due to the presence of a distinguishing attribute).
And [as for] the metaphor in the absence of a distinguishing attribute, for example: “The king is Indra.”
Thus, there are thirty-two varieties of suggested *utprekṣā*.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, kha):
Only its occurrence with respect to cause and effect has been stated here.

To the question, "Why is the increase of other sub-varieties not shown by way of [the figure] residing in its own nature (svarūpagāmin)? he says: "The utprekṣā (poetic fancy) of its own nature also occurs here. He establishes the impossibility of that [other variety] with the words: "In another substratum" (dharmyantare).
This refers to where the identity with another, non-contextual substratum is established in the contextual substratum.
The meaning is: "in such a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) which has that as its basis.
"Connection with a qualifier" means the employment of qualifiers such as "otherness" (aparatva) and so forth for the moon and other objects that are the subjects of the fancy.
He demonstrates the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) in that case with the example "as this king.

Here, there is hyperbole consisting of the superimposition of non-difference upon what is actually different. He states "of the qualifier" because, in the absence of that [qualifier], one would instead accept a metaphor (*rūpaka*).
He demonstrates this by saying "the king" and "of thirty-two kinds.
It should be understood that when combined with the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) based on the expressed meaning (*vācya*), there are eighty-eight kinds.

Locanā: [The letters] *lo* and *au* do not [constitute a fault], because another figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) is admitted in that case; this is the meaning. He states that very point: "in another substratum" (*dharmyantare*), etc.
Each of those [two] is also twofold, according to whether the subject at hand is expressed or not expressed.
Locanā:
"Of the subject at hand"—that is, of the object of the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*).
Those—referring to the types just mentioned—are the poetic conceits (utprekṣās). An example of these as expressed in speech is:
“The broad [hips] of the deer-eyed woman... and so forth.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,

ga) By doubling these eighty-eight types, [the author] states that there are one hundred and seventy-six forms, based on the presence or absence of explicit expression (*ukti*) and non-expression (*anukti*),
regarding the subject at hand (*prastuta*), that is, the topical matter (*prākaraṇika*).
By combining all the expressed (*vācya*) and suggested (*pratīyamāna*) forms, eighty-eight types of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) are declared.

Nor should it be said that when the contextual subject (*prākaraṇika*) is not explicitly stated, this is merely the figure of speech known as *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) consisting of "swallowing" (*nigaraṇa*); for such a case occurs only within the scope of *svarūpotprekṣā* (fancy regarding the essential nature).

In the case of suggested (*pratīyamāna*) poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), however, it is precisely because the impossibility of a fancy regarding the essential nature (*svarūpotprekṣā*) has already been demonstrated.

In the case of expressed (*vācyā*) poetic fancy, since words such as "as if" (*iva*) are present, there is no possibility of it being an exaggerated statement (*atiśayokti*). He shows the expression of the subject matter (*prakṛtokti*) in the case of expressed poetic fancy with the verse beginning "the thighs" (*ūru*):
"As for example, in my *Prabhāvatī*, [Pradyumna says]: 'It is as if, at this very moment, the mass of darkness were covering the quarters of the sky...'"
The world seemed as if fashioned from heaps of collyrium, filled with powdered musk,
spread over with tamāla trees, and enveloped in dark blue garments.
In this instance, the pervasion of the object by the suggested quality—such as being "fashioned" by collyrium—is not explicitly stated.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, gha) "As if fashioned," etc.—the meaning is: "as if it were done in such and such a manner by the mass of darkness itself."
He demonstrates the respective instrument [of this perception] with the words "as if fashioned" (*ghaṭitamiva*).
The meaning is that the world appears as if it were fashioned or constructed from masses of collyrium.
That [world] is pervaded by it.
"Enveloped" means covered.
"Object" refers to the form under discussion.
Or, for example:
“Darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain collyrium.
Here, the substratum (*viṣaya*) of the darkness’s smearing—namely, its pervasion—is not explicitly mentioned; [likewise], the substratum of the raining of collyrium is the falling of darkness.
The grounds for these two poetic fancies (*utprekṣā*) are, respectively, the extreme density of the darkness and its contact with the surface in the form of a stream.

However, some say: "Even though darkness is not the agent of smearing, it is fancied as the agent of smearing, and its spreading is the ground [for this fancy]; likewise, the sky is also [fancied] as the agent of the action of raining."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ṅa) She also shows a verse by another author— namely, "limpatīva" (as if smearing)—
where the connection is that "the falling of darkness" is what is not explicitly mentioned (*anupātta*).
And *sampāta* is the action (*kriyā*) that causes conjunction with the downward direction, but it is not the conjunction with the downward direction itself.
Therefore, there is a distinction here from the conjunction with the downward direction which will be described later as the efficient cause (*nimitta*).
He shows the unstated cause for these two with the words "of these two.
This is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the nature of an action; however, some call this a poetic fancy regarding the nature of the agent-substance (kartṛsvarūpadravyotprekṣā).
He demonstrates this with the words "But some...
Here, the phrase "some" indicates a lack of consensus (or a lack of naturalness).
Furthermore, it is because the particle *iva* following the verb, as well as the sky (*nabhas*), cannot be conceived of as having actual reality.
If it is argued that the agency of smearing and raining is unreal, then the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) would terminate in the mere acts of smearing and raining themselves.

For a specific type of fancy is recognized as a variety of *utprekṣā* when there is a conceptualization of form based on the equality of attaining an excellence called "pervasion" (*vyāpti*), just as in the case of a particular conjunction.
In the two types of fancy—namely, those concerning cause (*hetu*) and effect (*phala*)—the status of being the object (*viṣaya*) is accepted as being implied.
And if that were to occur only in the case of *svarūpotprekṣā* (intrinsic poetic fancy), then what fault would there be? Enough of this prolixity.
*Locanā*:
"With *kṣodas*" means with powders.

In the two examples beginning with "as if joined together" (*ghāṭitāmiva*) and "as if smearing" (*limpatīva*), the basis for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is, prior to this, the "pervasion" (*vyāpana*) [of darkness], with the word "due to the application of collyrium" (*añjanaghaṭanāt*) being the ellipsis.
Furthermore, in the verse "the sky seems to rain collyrium," the meaning is "conjunction with the downward direction in the form of a stream.
The connection is that some, such as the author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva*, say thus.

The intention [of the author] is as follows: because "he smears" (*limpati*) is imagined through the agency of the act of smearing, and because that agency is expressed, and because its co-referentiality with darkness leads to the cognition of its residing therein.
This is their reasoning: when the agency of the action of smearing is imagined as residing in darkness, the cause for the smearing and so forth is understood [as being inherent].
If, however, pervasion (*vyāpana*) and the like were the objects of the imagination, another cause would have to be sought.
Moreover, it is not logical for the object to be that which is being understood (*gamyamānatva*),
because it is more appropriate to designate that which has been introduced as the basis of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
By the phrase "here some [say]," he reveals his own lack of approval.
For instance, as in the case of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) such as "the lotus is not in water," here too both the object (*viṣaya*) and the cause (*nimitta*) are merely implied.

Furthermore, since there is an absence of similarity between darkness—which is the agent of pervasion—and the agent of smearing, the attribution of the agency of smearing to darkness constitutes a distinct poetic figure (*alaṅkāra-antara*), which would possess greater aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*). (VisSd 10.45)
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ca) "Arising from another ornament" means that if it arises from another ornament—such as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy)—in which all its varieties have been demonstrated, and is thus produced by another ornament, then it possesses an additional degree of aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*). This is the meaning.

Among these, an *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) involving concealment is as in my own verse: “Under the guise of tears, from the beautiful-eyed woman whose eyes were clouded by the smoke of the sacrificial fire,
a flood of the water of her loveliness seems to flow away from her body, unable to find a place within it.”
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
cha) "Under the guise of tears" means this is a description of the flow of tears from the heroine who stands near her husband while he is making an oblation.

The meaning is that, upon the body of the beautiful-eyed woman whose eyes are clouded by the smoke of the sacrificial fire, the flood of her beauty-water flows forth under the guise of tears, finding no room for pride.

Here, the word "guise" (chala) serves to establish a *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature of the object), wherein the flood of beauty-water—which is the actual subject—is the basis for the conceit;
for without the concealment of the tears, such a conceit would be impossible, as it would otherwise result in the tears themselves being merely a metaphor for beauty.
And here, the phrase "a being filled with water" does not constitute the actualization of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*);
for even if one were to say "even without its loveliness," the poetic fancy would still be fully realized.
— *Locanā*:

By the phrase "sāpahnavotprekṣā" (a poetic fancy involving concealment), the subordinate status (*aṅgabhāva*) of the concealer (*apahnuti*) is indicated through its connection with the meaning of "together with" (*saha*).
This is because only the intensification of the imaginative possibility (*sambhāvanā*) is manifested.
The fire offered was the one [lit] at the time of the wedding.
An example of a *śleṣa-hetugā* (a cause based on double entendre) is as follows:
“The heap of pearls emerging from the narrow interior of her oyster-like shells— lovely-eyed lady—
we know that it has acquired its quality of excellence through dwelling upon her beautiful, conch-like neck.”

Here, the quality of being possessed of [auspicious] marks (*guṇavattva*)—as in the case of [the description of] "dwelling upon a shell-like neck" (*kambugrīvādhivāsa*) and so forth—is the cause for the poetic fancy (*hetūtprekṣā*).
In this instance, the word "we know" (*jānīmahe*) is the indicator of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣāvācaka*).
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ja) "A heap of pearls" (*muktotkara*): having emerged from the oyster-shell—the narrow and painful vessel—due to being constrained by its covering, this heap of pearls possesses a quality [of excellence] solely because of its dwelling upon her lovely conch-like neck;
we know, that is, we imagine, that its possession of quality consists in the attainment of an abundance of luster. This is the meaning.
The meaning is that for one who has crossed over the suffering of dwelling in an improper place, there is the attainment of excellence as if from residing in a virtuous place.
The neck distinguished by three lines is called *kambu*.

Since the threads here are real, a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding them as the cause for attaining that [excellence] is not possible; therefore, because of the pun on the word *guṇa* (meaning both "thread" and "virtue"), this is a poetic fancy regarding the attainment of a particular kind of light as the cause, and thus this *utprekṣā* is sustained by a pun (*śleṣa*).
Locanā:
(lo, ī) "Guṇa" refers to a thread, as well as qualities such as great value and so forth.
In this context, the fact that [the figure] is caused by paronomasia (śleṣa) follows precisely from the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of the paronomastic words.
In this way—
*manye*, *śaṅke*, *dhruvam*, *prāyaḥ*, *nūnam*, and so forth [are used as particles expressing certainty]. —
Locanā.
The meaning is that words such as *jānīmahe* ("we know") and *manye* ("I think") should also be understood as expressers of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), words such as *kim* ("what") and so forth are included.
Regarding the usage of the word *kim*, there is, for example, Gopīnātha’s description of the Gaṅgā:
“Carrying far away for her devotees a garland of blossoms from her forehead with the waves as her hands—
having sold this liberation for its price, which is but the number of cowries, what is she doing?”
In some cases, there is a combination of simile (*upamā*) and poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), as for example:
“On the far shore of the ocean, Murāri beheld rows of forests with dark foliage,
which bore the appearance of moss rising up at every moment by the thousands of their budding sprouts.”
In this passage, because the word *ābhā* (appearance) functions as a term expressing comparison (*upamā*), there is a simile (*upamā*) at the outset;

however, since the existence of moss upon the shore of the ocean is impossible, the resulting suggestion of a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) constitutes a "production of a poetic fancy" (*sambhāvanotthāpana*) at the conclusion.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, jha) "In some cases, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) introduced by a simile (*upamā*).
This means that the poetic fancy is actually based on a simile that has been commenced.
Regarding the phrase *pārejalam*: Murāri—that is, Śrī Kṛṣṇa—beheld rows of forests on the shore (*pārejala*), which is the bank (*kūla*) beyond the water (*jala*) of the ocean (*nīranidhi*).
Of what kind? Those in which there is a dark-blue mass of *palāśa* leaves.
Again, of what kind?
The meaning is: those possessing the luster of moss that rises up at every moment due to thousands of ripples, that is, thousands of waves.
Here, he causes one to understand that the very simile gives rise to the poetic fancy (utprekṣā), as indicated by the phrase "of the word *ābhā* here.
By virtue of the *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that in which there is a luster (*ābhā*) like that of *śaivala*"—it is the indicator of a simile;
by this, the commencement of the simile is shown.
Next, he establishes the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) for that simile with the words "But in the final conclusion" (*paryavasāne tu*).

Since the completion of the simile is possible by the phrase "having the luster of *śaivalā* grass" alone, the mention of "rising up" (*utkūla*) would be superfluous; therefore, the connection is that in the final conclusion, there is a poetic fancy: "as if having *śaivalā* grass rising up."
He establishes the emergence of such a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) with the words "on the shore of the ocean" (*jaladhitīre*).

Since it is impossible for moss (*śaivala*) to be washed up on the edge of a forest, no such fancy could arise there. However, because the presence of moss on the shore of the sea is possible, and thus there is no lack of justification (*anupapatti*), the fancy arises; that is to say, the fancy of the moss being washed up emerges.
Regarding the statement "it is like that appearance" (*tadābhā iva*), [the author] says "it is a poetic fancy" (*utprekṣā*).

The meaning is that if there were no arising of such a possibility (*sambhāvanā*), the use of the intensified adjectives (*utkūlita-viśeṣaṇa*) would be purposeless. Thus, since the poetic fancy has been introduced as the domain of the simile (*upamā*), the meaning is that this poetic fancy is produced by the simile.
— *Locanā* —

(Lo, Ū) *Upamopakramotprekṣā* (Metaphorical Conception introduced by a Simile): That [conception] is so called because, at the time of syntactic integration (*padārthānvaya*), the word expressing that [object of comparison] is employed at the outset of the simile. It is a *utprekṣā* because it comes to rest (*viśrānti*) upon the emergence of the mental operation of the conceiving subject’s imaginative identification (*abhimāna-vyāpāra*) following the comprehension of the sentence.
*Utkalikā* refers to waves.
*Utkūlitāni* means those that have overflowed their banks.

This should be understood in the description of separation—as in the verse beginning with "The curved side-glance of the deer-eyed one acted as an armlet at her ear"—and also in such passages as "The blooming blue lotus at the ear [was surpassed] by the curved side-glance of the deer-eyed one.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, jha) Regarding "keyūrāyitam":
it means acting as if with armlets;
*keyūra* refers to an armlet or bracelet.
The meaning is that due to the emaciation caused by separation, [the arms] have reached the position of armlets (*keyūra*).
Even there, because of the force of the suffix, a simile is suggested; however, since an armlet lacks the capacity for such action, it is treated as a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
Having thus shown the verbal simile-fancy (*autyupamotprekṣā*), he demonstrates the nominal simile-fancy (*ārthyupamotprekṣā*) with the word "vikāsī" (expanding).
Here too, due to the elision of the *kkip* suffix, a meaning involving an elided simile (*luptopamā*) is suggested as a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
Locanā:
Now, he provides an example of the suffix itself functioning as the indicator of the simile—namely, "keyūrāyitam" (it acted like an armlet).
He provides an example for the elision of the causal suffix (*pratyaya-lope*) with the word *vikāsī*.

In the figure of speech *bhrāntimad* (the presence of error), as in the verse beginning “*mugdhā dugdhadhiyā*,” there is no cognition at all of the object— such as moonlight— for those who are deluded, such as the cowherds, because the poet himself has constructed that basis for the illusion.

But here, there is a distinction between the two because there is knowledge even of the object of the person performing the imaginative attribution (*saṃbhāvanā*). Although a distinction is possible based on the fact that in the ornament of error (*bhrāntimadalaṅkāra*) there is certainty (*niścaya*), whereas here there is a doubt with a predominant alternative (*utkaṭakoṭikaḥ saṃśayaḥ*), he states another point of distinction by saying "in the ornament of error. *Vijñapriyā:* (vi, ña) [The commentary explains: In the ornament of error, there is certainty; here, however, it is a doubt with a predominant alternative—thus, while such a distinction exists, he states yet another distinguishing factor by saying "in the ornament of error."
The meaning is that knowledge itself does not exist;
for if it did exist, it would be untenable to give jars to cows when one has the cognition of milk. Knowledge itself does not exist as moonlight.

Now, one might object: since it is said, "Whose mental confusion does this moonlight not cause?", there must be a cognition [of the object] as being moonlight; to this he replies: "of its attribution [to them].
This means: of the attribution of confusion regarding the cowherds to the moonlight.
Thus, by the poet's statement, the meaning is that for the listeners—the cowherds and others—there is no cognition [of the object] as being moonlight.

Regarding this poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), he states its distinction [from other figures] with the words "But here... This means: because the poet, who is the creator of the possibility, has composed it in such a way;
and because the object itself is not prominent, [the cognition] pertains even to that alternative possibility (*tatkoṭi*).
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) "Of the object being described" refers to moonlight and so forth; by the word "etcetera," moonlight-mottled water-lilies and the like are included.
Regarding its formulation in poetry through words:
here, in *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), there is the perception of two alternatives consisting of the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*);
whereas in *saṃdeha* (doubt), there is the perception of two alternatives as being of equal status.
In this case, however, one extreme possibility that was previously conceivable has become predominant.

The distinction is this: in *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), the unreality of the perceived subject (*viṣayin*) is realized after its prior establishment; here, however, it is realized at the very moment of perception.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) In that case, [one might argue] that this is not distinct from the figure of speech *saṃdehālaṃkāra* (the ornament of doubt); therefore, he says: "In *saṃdeha*...
The meaning is that the distinction lies in the intensity (*utkaṭatva*) or the equality (*tulyatva*) of one of the alternatives.

He states the distinction from *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) with the words "in *atiśayokti*": at the conclusion—that is, at a subsequent time—the superposed object (*viṣayin*), such as "how [could there be] a plumage upon a peacock? [is not possible].

In this context, the meaning is that the unreality of the *kalāpa* (the bundle) is established precisely because, immediately after the error regarding the *kalāpa*, one perceives the specific nature of the hairs (*keśatva*).
As for "here, however" (*iha tu*)—it means at the time of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) beginning with "as if giving birth" (*saprasavā iva*).
And this statement was made merely as a prima facie view, having in mind the difference from actual experience.

In reality, however, there is complete equality between the two cases, since in both instances there exists a superimposed cognition (*āhāryabuddhi*)—just as there is a superimposition of the act of giving birth in the form of emerging from the womb, so too is there a superimposition of a mass of hair upon the heroine's head.

Nevertheless, the distinction lies in this: *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) consists of a doubt with a predominant alternative (*utkaṭakoṭika-saṃdeha*), whereas *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) consists of a certainty (*niścaya*).
In the phrase "How [is it] above?", the doubt understood by the word "how" is precisely a forced conviction (*āhāryaniścaya*) regarding the cluster [of qualities].
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) It is called "intense" (*utkaṭā*) because it is perceived through the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of the object.
Having the form of a single-pointed object:
"Are the various trees stained [red], or is the sky bent down, or is it covered? Is the earth filled in its uneven places, or have the quarters been withdrawn by darkness?"
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭha) Regarding the very domain of the poetic figure *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), some claim that the figure *sandeha* (doubt) occurs in certain verses;
to refute that, he cites the verse beginning with “rañjitā nu” and so forth.
This is a description of the deepest darkness. "As if dyed"—the meaning is that it has been made black in color.
The connection with "by the gloom" applies to every instance.
"Sthagita" means covered or concealed. "Viṣameṣu" refers to uneven places—regions consisting of deep hollows and high elevations.
"Saṃhṛtāḥ" means these have been destroyed.

Regarding this, some say that because the state of being pervaded by darkness in the trees and so forth is doubted in the form of "coloring" (rañjana) and the like, this is the figure of speech *saṃdeha* (doubt);
but that is not correct—because doubt consists precisely in the flashing forth of multiple alternatives (*koṭi*) with equal strength regarding a single object.

Here, however, there is a difference in the counter-correlatives (*pratisaṃbandhin*) of the pervasion [of darkness], and the flashing forth of "coloring" and so forth occurs through the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of the act of pervading and the rest.

Others, however, have said: “Because it serves as the basis for a poetic figure (*vicchitti*) consisting of the determination of multiplicity, this type of doubt is distinct [from ordinary doubt], even though it exceeds a single alternative.

That too is incorrect—for *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic probability) is the cognition of identity with something else when its own nature has been swallowed up, and since that exists here clearly, and since it is indicated by the word *nu* just as it is by the word *iva*, it is proper that this should be considered *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) alone.
Enough with this elaborate imagining of a type of doubt never before seen.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍa) Regarding this, some have said that [the author] demonstrates the figure of speech *sandeha* (doubt)—thus [it is said] "here" (*atra*).
"In a single object" means in a single substratum (*dharmī*).
"Pervasion by trees and so forth" means pervasion by [the action of] coloring trees and so forth as its objects.
The meaning is that the object to be qualified (*viśeṣya*) has the form of the word "pratibimba" and so forth.

Now, one might object: "In that case, there would indeed be many doubts regarding each individual object to be qualified. To this, [the author] replies—by stating "due to pervasion, etc. (*vyāpanādeḥ*)—that there is also a specific cause that brings about the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*).
The meaning is: "due to the pervasion by cataracts (*timira*) and so forth."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipada*), the non-perception of high and low [objects] caused by cataracts is included;
its "swallowing" here refers to making it non-prominent.
Others, however, say that this is a specific variety of the figure of speech *sandeha* (ambiguity).
He shows this with the words "But others...
Here, in order to establish *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) itself, he says: "That too is incorrect.

The identity of that whose own nature has been swallowed—that is, whose nature has had its specific aspect rendered non-prominent—is the non-difference from another [object] whose other aspect is non-prominent.

Now, one might object that because there is such a swallowing (*nigaraṇa*) [of the object], it would follow that this is a case of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*); to this, he says: "and by the word *nu*, just as by the word *eva*.
Locanā:
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "coloring, etc.," actions such as bowing and so forth are intended.
The object is one:
in cases such as "Is it a post or a person? it is the post and so forth;
in cases such as "Who is this sun? it is the king and so forth.
"By way of equal strength"—that is, by being on the same side; "here"—in the present example;
"but" (tu)—has the sense of "furthermore."
Regarding "pervasion by trees and so forth": trees, the sky, and so on are the correlates of the pervasion of darkness over trees, the sky, and so on;
due to the non-difference [of the locus], there is also a difference in the pervasion itself.
Therefore, because of this difference in the objects, how can there be a doubt of the form described? This is the meaning.
Nor is there a flashing forth of multiple alternatives due to their being of equal strength; thus he says, "because of pervasion and so forth.
"Others" refers to the *ekadeśins* (partialists).
"Non-determination" is a partial element of the seed of doubt.
To explain how it is improper, he says: "swallowed," etc.;
that is, distinct from the object.
Of that [notion], there is the possibility.
The meaning is: "by those who do not know the method [of reasoning].
The nature of doubt resides in multiple objects and takes the form of a mental manifestation in which one side predominates.
"That which displays the grace of a water-lily leaf within the moon, the world calls a hare; it does not speak thus to me."
But I consider the moon to have its body marked by the scar of a wound from the falling meteor-like glances of young women overcome by separation from their lovers.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ḍha) Regarding the verse beginning with "yadetaccandrāntaḥ" and so forth, he says "yadetad... etc., in order to refute the possibility of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) involving concealment (*sāpahnavā*) and to establish that it is merely the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment).
O Queen, this is the saying of someone:
that thing which exists within the moon spreads a grace (*līlā*) consisting of a resemblance to a fragment of a cloud, a piece of a rain-cloud.
The world says, "It is a hare";
let him say so to other people, but he does not say so to me— this is the meaning.
The meaning is: "because there is a certainty for me that [the state] is not so.
To the question, "In what manner, then, is your certainty? he says: "āhantv iti" (let them strike).

This refers to the scar—the visible portion at the site of the wound—produced by the wounds caused by the falling firebrands of the side-long glances of those young wives of yours who have been seized as captives and are overcome by separation.
That very stain is the defect; [the body] is such that its form is marked by that.

In this case, even though the word "bhanye" (O others) is employed, since the aforementioned kind of imaginative supposition (*sambhāvanā*) is not perceived, this is merely a conjecture (*vitarka*), and not the figure of speech known as "concealed poetic fancy" (*apahnava-utprekṣā*).
Vijñapriyā: "(vi,
ṇa) Of the expectation of a superior form" means of that which consists of two extremes, the intense and the non-intense.
And the meaning is that for me, there is no such non-apprehension of that [absence];
for by that, the speaker’s ascertainment of the non-existence of ten million rabbits is apprehended.
Thus, this is not a denial—such is the sense that here there is merely a denial.
Locanā:
(lo, ai) *Lavaḥ* is a portion of the cloud (*jalada*).
*Kalaṅkāṅkitam* means marked by a spot (*kalaṅka*).
I think the word *manye* (I think) is, in various instances, an indicator of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
Of the aforementioned form— that which is to be designated by the term "accomplished through identification" (*adhyavasāya*)—
*vitarka* means conjecture (*ūhana*).
When the identification (*adhyavasāya*) is established, it is called *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).

Identification is the apprehension of non-difference between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*) through the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of the object. *Vijñapriyā*: [This is the definition.]
(vi, ta) He states the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (hyperbole): "When there is the established nature," etc.
The meaning is that *atiśayokti* occurs when there is the establishment—meaning the nature of certainty—of *ādhyavasāya*, which is superimposition (*āropa*).
And thus, there is the exclusion of the figures of speech *sandeha* (doubt) and *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), which are of the nature of uncertainty.

However, over-extension (*ativyāpti*) remains in the case of the figures of speech *niścaya* (certainty), *apahnuti* (concealment), and *rūpaka* (metaphor), because in those three figures the object of superimposition (*āropya*) takes the form of certainty.

To exclude these, he provides the qualification "preceded by the swallowing up of the object" (*viṣayanigaraṇapūrvakatva*) and, establishing that the focus is on the superimposed object (*āropaviśeṣya*), explains [the definition] with the words: "by the swallowing up of the object" (*viṣayanigaraṇena*).

The meaning is that what is intended here is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding the object (*viṣaya*), which follows from the cognition of non-difference (*abhedapratipatti*) with respect to the subject (*viṣayin*). That upon which something is superimposed is the object; that which is superimposed is the subject.
Swallowing (*nigaraṇa*) and "making downward" (*adhahkaraṇa*) will be explained [later].
That too is of unclear meaning; therefore, without a word possessing a specific sense, "making downward" is the cognition of the negation of an object through suggestion (*vyañjanā*) alone.
And that will be demonstrated on the occasion of all types of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole).
In the figures of speech *apahnuti* (concealment) and *niścaya* (certainty), there exists only a word with a negative sense; therefore, there is no suggestion (*vyañjanā*) of negation therein.

In a *rūpaka* (metaphor), however, the face is perceived precisely through its identity with the moon, and not through the perception of a negation of the face. If *apahnuti* were suggested, it would not be that figure of speech, but rather a *dhvani* (suggestive poetry) based upon it.
In this regard, the application of the term "ornament" (alaṅkāra) is merely figurative, according to the logic of the Brahmin and the laborer;
however, there is over-extension (ativyāpti) of the definition to mere concealment (apahnuti) within the case of suggested concealment (apahnutidhvani).
But as for hyperbole (atiśayokti), it consists in the superimposition of identity with something else preceded by concealment; thus, there is a distinction between these two.
Furthermore, because the subject of this poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is indicated as being uncertain, it possesses the quality of being "to be established" (*sādhya*);

however, here [in the case of *atiśayokti*], it is perceived precisely as certain, and thus possesses the quality of being "established" (*siddha*). Moreover, in a poetic fancy, the swallowing up of the object (*viṣayanigaraṇa*) occurs merely by the subordination of the object.
In this context as well, [the distinction applies] in cases such as "The face is the second moon.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, tha) shows the exclusion of the term "because it is established" (*siddhatve*) with the words "And of that... (*tasya ca*).
The state of being "to be established" (sādhyatva) is the state of non-certainty;
the state of being "established" (siddhatva) is the state of certainty.

By the very intention of [defining] certainty, he shows that this excludes poetic fancy (utprekṣā), and not because of the intention of [defining it as] preceded by swallowing (nigaraṇa)—as indicated by the phrase "and the swallowing of the object."
The category of *adhah-karaṇa* (subordination) has already been explained.

Furthermore, in the case of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), there is the suggestion of a negation (*niṣedha-vyañjanā*) due to the non-mention of the delimiting factor of the object (*viṣayatāvacchedaka-koṭi*) in some instances, and in others, even when it is mentioned, because of its lack of prominence (*anutkaṭatva*).
For example: "His virtues, being bound to his own virtues, are as if they have offspring."

In this case, there is the suggestion (*vyañjanā*) of the negation of that very same category of birth—which consists in emerging from the womb—that has been described as having two aspects: the intense aspect and the non-intense aspect associated with qualities.

However, in examples such as "He bathes, as it were, in the waters of the Gaṅgā," there is the suggestion of the negation of the category of connection with the Gaṅgā, which has not been explicitly stated.
Since this is not impossible even in a specific type of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), he says: "Here too, [in the example] 'the face is a second [moon],' etc."
The meaning is that, precisely by virtue of the expression "second moon," there is the suggestion (*vyañjanā*) of the negation of its being a face;
for when there is no second moon, one perceives: "This is not a face; this is indeed a second moon.
However, in the absence of the word "second," such a perception of negation does not occur; therefore, in that case, it is merely a metaphor (*rūpaka*).
As they say:
"Whether the object is not taken up or even when it is taken up,
the wise declare that it is 'swallowed' (nigīrṇa) merely by its being cast down."
Thus [ends the citation].

*Vijñapriyā* (vi, da): Regarding what they say—"the subordination (*adhah-karaṇa*) of that which is not swallowed but taken up, and of that which is swallowed but not taken up, is indeed already explained."
Even when there is difference, there is non-difference; even when there is connection, there is non-connection, and their respective opposites as well.
The inversion of the sequence of cause and effect is fivefold;
from that [arise] their two reversals: [the fallacy of] difference where there is non-difference, and [the fallacy of] connection where there is no connection.
That is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, dha) states its fivefold nature: "non-difference even where there is difference," and so forth.
If non-difference is being superimposed, then that superimposition is *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole); such is the meaning.
The same applies to what follows.
Regarding effect and cause: the "reversal of sequence" means the inversion of their temporal order.
In this regard, non-difference within difference is as in my own verse:
“How is it that above the peacock’s plumage there shines a crest, beneath which is a fragment of the eighth-day moon;
below that, a pair of restless blue lotuses; beneath those, a sesame flower; and below that, a sprout?”
In this case, there is an identification (*adhyavasāya*) of the beloved’s mass of hair and so forth with the plumage of a peacock and so forth.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, na) How is it "above"?—the meaning is "above the heroine."
It should be understood that [the water] exists there in the form of its constituent parts.
Therefore, in the phrase "tremulous" (*vilola*), the word "that place" (*tatsthāna*) is to be supplied;
likewise, in the phrase "sesame flower" (*tilakusuma*), the word "that place" is also to be supplied.
"Pravāla" means a fresh sprout.

Here, because the objects of superimposition (the locus of the metaphor), such as the mass of hair and so forth, are not explicitly mentioned, there is the subordination [of the primary meaning] through the manifestation of negation (*niṣedhavyañjana*).
The same should be understood for each subsequent instance where the objects [of superimposition] are not mentioned.
But in the case of *upādāna* (metaphorical transfer), it should be understood that it is indeed a matter of form (*rūpaka*).
For example: “As if bound by silence due to the pain of separation.
Here, the silence residing in a sentient being is one thing, [while the silence attributed to the object is another].
And "the other is insentient"—thus, despite the difference between the two, there is non-difference.
Likewise:
"In his youth, his beloved became possessed of passion along with the lower lip."
Here, "passion" (rāga) refers to redness in the case of the lower lip, while it refers to love in the case of the beloved; thus, there is an identity between the two.
Vijñapriyā:

"And another [type] pertains to the insentient"—the meaning is that it is other than the silence consisting in the non-performance of speech, even though there is the capacity for subsequent action; and that [silence] consists in the non-production of sound.
And that object is not explicitly mentioned here;
the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is "in her youth" and "in her very lower lip.
Thus, there is non-difference between the two.
The intended meaning is "due to the contact with the locus of passion.

For if there were merely the cognition of concomitance (*sāhitya*) in the form of arising at the same time, then the experience of a distinct excellence (*vaicitrya*) beyond what is expressed by "possessing passion along with the red lower lip" would result in an inconsistency.
An example of difference within non-difference (*abhede bheda*) is as follows:
“The loveliness of her limbs was of one kind, and the abundance of her fragrance another;
in that lotus-petal-eyed woman, there was a world-transcending freshness.”
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
pha) "It is something else indeed" means that because of the distinctness from the beauty of the limbs and so forth, there is the superimposition of its difference upon that very [beauty].
"Sarasatvam" means "rasikatvam" (the state of being a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor).
It is the superimposition of a transcendental distinction upon that which is mundane.
Here, although the beauty that is the object [of the superimposition] was not explicitly mentioned, its negation is suggested through the superimposition of otherness (*anyatva*) and so forth.
An example of non-connection where there is a connection is as follows:
"In the act of her creation, was the Creator the moon, the bestower of luster? Or was he Love himself, whose sole essence is passion? Or was he the month of spring, the source of flowers?"
"How indeed could that ancient sage, rendered dull by the study of the Vedas and with his curiosity turned away from sensory objects, be capable of fashioning this enchanting form?"
Locanā:
(lo, o) The ancient sage is Brahmā.
And here, in the first half-verse, because the word *nu* excludes the established nature (*siddhatva*) of the determination (*adhyavasāya*), there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
In this context, although there is a connection with the creation by the ancient Prajāpati, there is also a lack of connection [to her].
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ba): "In the act of her creation... [is the meaning].

Now, regarding the conjecture: in the act of her creation, Prajāpati was the creator, yet it was the Moon who was the true fashioner, since he is the bestower of beauty; for it is only through his possession of splendor that his status as a bestower of beauty can be conceived.
Or perhaps it was Madana himself, since he alone has the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) as his sole flavor.
For she is indeed full of passion (*śṛṅgāriṇī*);
even in the month of Caitra, the source of flowers, there is a connection with the singular essence of passion (*śṛṅgāra*).
To the question, "How do you destroy the state of being the original creator?", he says: "By the study of the Vedas," and so forth.
"Antique" means worn out or ancient;
"muni" means one who follows the dharma of a sage, that is, an ascetic.
Here, because the moon and others are described as being the Creator (vidhātṛ), there is a suggestion of the negation of the connection with the Creator, which is the locus of the superimposition.
An instance of a connection where there is no [actual] connection is as follows:
"If there were two blue lotuses attached to the orb of the moon,
then her beautiful-eyed face might be compared to them."
In this context, if there is a connection by way of possibility through a relation brought forth by the force of the meaning, [it is expressed as] "if it were so" (*yadi syāt*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, bha): "If it were so."
In place of beautiful eyes, there are two blue lotuses; in place of a face, there is the orb of the moon.
Regarding the phrase "by means of a brought-about connection":
it is the possibility of a connection such that there would indeed be a connection between the orb of the moon and the blue lotus.
Here too, by the very possibility of a relation, there is the suggestion of the negation of the non-relation that serves as the locus of superimposition.
Locanā:
(lo, au) "If [the meaning]... etc.

In this case, although a connection between the lunar disc and two blue lotuses is not possible, nevertheless, the meaning is that such a connection exists either as something composed by the poet or in the form of a poetic conceit (*sambhāvanā*).
By this, the distinction of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) stated by some— namely, "conception [is present] when there is an expression of the word 'if' (*yadyartha*)"—
as well as the depiction of a single thing as having multiple forms, are illustrated.
In this regard, the first [type] has been illustrated by the author himself in the passage beginning with "something else indeed" (*anyadeva*);
in the second, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the mass of hair and so forth," there is an inclusion of the forehead, eyes, nose, and lips.
Thus, her face is a second moon.
And so it is said:
"The male cuckoo, its throat reddened by tasting the mango sprouts, sang with such sweetness."
