That very speech of Smara has become skilled in destroying the pride of high-minded women.”

In this case, there is no metaphor (*rūpaka*) based on superimposition (*āropa*), as in the expression "her face is the moon," because the nature of *adhyavasāya* (poetic identification) arises only when there is a firm conviction of identity.
For here, the meaning is that the world fell under the power of Madana even without his exertion, merely by the sound of the cuckoo's call.

For example: "The passion of women is indeed excessively ascendant and knows no [proper] time. Likewise, in the verse "One whose conduct is driven by desire does not heed what is censurable," there is a statement of non-difference between the instrument (the passion) and the agent (the state of being driven by desire), despite their difference as action and its performer.
Furthermore, in such cases as "This beloved woman is the means for subjugating the minds of young men," the figure of speech called *hetu* (cause/reason) will be discussed later.
The meaning is that this [feeling] is subsumed under a distinction characterized by a relation, even though there is no actual relation with that very [object].
Here, a pure example occurs in the description of separation: "Burning is water; spreading heat is cooking; rising vapor is a glance," and so forth.
In this case, although there is no relation between burning and the like with water, spreading, cooking, and so on, a relation is stated as if it were established.
Furthermore, the reversal of the sequence between cause and effect occurs in two ways:

Vijñapriyā:
To illustrate the fifth variety of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), he says: "Of cause and effect... even before..."—*utkalikā* means longing; *bakularasālayoḥ* is a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
The meaning is: "after the beauty of the blossoming buds of those two."
Here, because the cause—the sight of the beauty of the flower bud—is described as being established subsequent to its effect—longing—it is a case of *viparyaya* (inversion).
Through that [sight], which is the object of an artificial cognition (*āhāryabuddhi*), the swiftness of the cause's operation is suggested.
Here too, because it is established subsequently, there is a suggestion of the negation of the previously arisen object of superimposition (*āropa*).
The same should be understood for what follows as well.
Locanā:
(lo, a) longing.
“Longing and the rising of the buds were both simultaneously overcome by him who moves with the gait of an elephant.”

"At the very same time"—by this [phrase], Raghu [is meant].

Because it is stated that the cause, which is the ascending to the father’s throne, and the effect, which is the ascending to the circle of the earth's rulers, occurred simultaneously, there is a reversal of the sequence [of cause and effect].
Regarding this, some say: "The worldly excellence residing in things such as a mass of hair is determined (*adhyavasīyate*) as being non-worldly (*alaukika*).

[If the definition were restricted to this], there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the definition in cases such as ‘Another indeed is the beauty of the limbs (*aṅgalāvaṇya*)’ when a mass of hair and so forth is determined as a cluster and so forth.
This is not so; for even in that case, another beauty of the limbs is determined as being something else.

For instance, in the place where "anyadeva" (something else indeed) occurs, the reading "anyadiva" (as if something else) implies that the identification (*adhyavasāya*) is not established as a fact, and thus it is accepted as a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

In the verse beginning with "prageva hariṇākṣīṇām—" (At dawn, for the deer-eyed women...), although the beauty of the *bakula* trees and others actually exists first, it is identified as occurring later;
therefore, because of the connection with the word "iva" here as well, it is a poetic fancy, and so it is in other cases too.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ra) Some say that there is an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) of the general definition of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) stated by the author of the treatise in such instances as "the beauty of the limbs is something else entirely" (*anyadevāṅgalāvaṇyam*). To refute this, he says: "In this regard, some...
For the meaning of the definition composed by you is indeed the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the object (*viṣaya*) as non-different from the subject (*viṣayin*).

Furthermore, the relationship between object (*viṣaya*) and subject (*viṣayin*) is constituted by difference. Thus, while in the example "How [is there] above the peacock? the relationship defined by that [difference] is possible because a difference exists between the hair and the mass of feathers, in the case of "The loveliness of the limbs is quite another," there is an absence of the object-subject relationship constituted by difference when one superimposes that very [loveliness] upon that same [limb]. Consequently, some argue that this results in an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*). He shows this view with the words: "residing in the mass of hair and so forth."

"Excellence" (*atiśaya*) refers to beauty that is worldly yet common to the hair of other worlds; the meaning is that it is determined as being "extraordinary," that is, as a beauty residing in a collection distinct from the world.

He states—"of the mass of hair and so forth"—because the superimposition of non-difference is possible between those two distinct collections of hair, which are rooted in the superimposition of non-difference between the two beauties.
After the word "in the determination" (*adhyavasāye*), the phrase "is also possible" (*sambhavaty api*) should be supplied.

Nevertheless, he states "it is something else" (*anyadeva*) and so forth, because there is an over-extension (*avyāpti*) in such cases; the intended meaning is that there is no difference between the beauty of the object superimposed (*āropyamāṇa*) and the locus of superimposition (*āropa-viṣaya*).
He provides a resolution by stating: "That is not so," asserting that even here, the superimposition of difference upon identity exists within the sense of the definition we have stated.
Regarding the phrase "for there" (*tatra hi*):
the meaning is that the beauty of the limbs, which is non-different [from the whole], is determined (*adhyavasīyate*) as if it were different—that is, as distinct.

And thus, because of this determination as distinct, since difference is superimposed upon the non-difference that is the locus of the superimposition (*āropa-viṣaya*), the relationship of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) consisting of difference exists here as well; this has been established.
In *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), you also accept a superimposition (*āropa*) constituted by the distinction between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*).

Since *utprekṣā* is possible only here [where such a distinction exists], he states "for instance" (*tathā hi*) to show that even in your own view, the superimposition is constituted by a distinction; thus, he demonstrates that there is a relationship of object and subject constituted by a distinction even in the verse "even before [the arrival of the spring]... (*prāgeva hariṇākṣīṇām*), in order to show that this is distinct from *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).
Here too, he demonstrates the possibility of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), stating "for this very reason.
This means: precisely because there exists a relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) constituted by difference.
— *Locanā* —
"Supramundane" (*alaukika*) means natural (*svābhāvika*).

By the term "supramundane excellence," which results from the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of something as being supramundane, there is an inclusion [of such cases] by phrases such as "the beauty of the limbs" and "dear to the cowherd women.

The intention behind the phrase "of the definition characterized by non-pervasion" (*avyāpti-lakṣaṇasya*) is this: the emergence of the form of determination occurs precisely when the object of comparison (*upameya*) attains identity with the object of comparison (*upamāna*).
In this case, there exists no other substitute entity for loveliness and the like that could be designated by words such as "another" (anya) and so forth.

Thus, he states the established conclusion—that there is an over-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition in such instances—as "That is not so. To the question, "How can there be a determination [of identity] through difference? he replies, "For instance... (*tathā hi*).
When there may be [the perception] of objects currently presented or of others, // VisSd_10.47 //
When there is a connection with a single attribute, then there is *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, la) states the ornament of *tulyayogitā*: "Of the things... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "or of others":
by means of the word "or" (vā), which indicates independence from the preceding, one should understand the prohibition against mixing the subject at hand with that which is not subject at hand.
However, if such a mixture occurs, it will be described as the figure of speech *dīpaka*.
Locanā:
Regarding the phrase "of things" (*padārthānām*),
the plural number is not intended as restrictive.
By this, it should be understood that the same applies to the two types of objects:
those under discussion (the contextual) and those not under discussion (the non-contextual).
Of others that are not relevant;
dharma consists of qualities and actions.
An example—
By that means— the unguents, the flowers, and the lamp-wicks used by women who had become angry with their husbands— they awakened for a long time the god of love who had been asleep.
Locanā:
(lo, ī) "Anulepanāni" means that she awakened Smara, who had been lying for a very long time, and made him conscious; this is the meaning.
In this context, since the description of the twilight is the subject at hand, there is a connection between the subjects—the ointments and so forth—and a single act of cognition.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"The ointments," etc.
This is a description of the objects of that time in the *tamisrā* (the dark night) as they arouse desire in the lover.
"By him who had slept for a very long time, awakened—that is, aroused—by such a night-form; [the ointments and so forth] 'awakened' means they roused him for the sake of play.
This refers to the description of darkness.

The sense is that because darkness is an excitant (*uddīpaka*) of passion, when it is introduced as the subject, other excitants of that same time—such as ointments and the like—are also considered introduced.
[As the verse says: "In whose heart does the softness of her limbs not appear to one who beholds it?
For the hardness of the *mālatī* flower, the crescent moon, and the plantain tree [is well known]."
In this [verse], there is a connection with a single quality—namely, hardness—among the irrelevant objects such as the *mālatī* flower and others.

He states the connection with a single quality among irrelevant objects in the verse beginning "The softness of your limbs for one who beholds..."
In the mind of which person who perceives this would the hardness of the *mālatī* and other flowers not appear?
For here, due to the excellence of their softness, hardness appears [only by contrast].
In this case, the *mālatī* and others are "non-contextual" (*aprakṛta*) because they serve as points of comparison for your limbs.
Thus:
"One should extract the essence from what is essenceless: charity from wealth, truthfulness from speech, fame and dharma from life, and service to others from the body."

Here, the connection of the qualities—such as giving (*dāna*) and so forth—which function as the objects of action, with a single quality consisting of the act of crossing over, and their connection with a single action consisting of the act of taking away, is [the subject].

Although the connection of the subjects (*prakṛta*) with a single quality and the connection of the non-subjects (*aprakṛta*) with a single action were not illustrated by the preceding verse, they are now illustrated by the verse beginning, "In this way, giving from wealth... and so on.

In this case, there is also a connection with the quality of "lack of essence" (*aisāratā*) regarding those things under discussion which serve as the *apādāna* (starting points); however, it has not been demonstrated here for fear of making the work overly prolix. — *Locanā*.
(Locative, Universal) He provides an example even with a different grammatical factor—namely, "giving" (*dāna*).
Here, there is not only a connection with the act of extraction for giving and the other [virtues], but also a connection with the single quality of worthlessness for wealth and the other [objects].

And here, in the case of *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing), although both members are contextual—as in "the moon shines like a smile"—the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is determined by intention (*vaivakṣika*).
Because there is no explicit mention of the object of comparison, the simile is to be understood by implication;
however, that which serves as a common attribute for both the irrelevant and the relevant is called *dīpaka*.

He states another kind of *dīpaka*: "Now" (*atha*).
Locanā:
(lo, ū) The meaning is that there is a connection through a single attribute between the irrelevant (*aprastuta*) and the relevant (*prastuta*).
And here, because there is no speaker asserting that two things are respectively the subject and the non-subject, the suggestiveness of the simile is indeed clear.

(vi, ha) "On account of the arrogance of power" (*balāvalepāt*); *avalepa* means egoism (*ahaṅkāra*).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: just as in his previous birth [as] Hiraṇyakaśipu, the world was oppressed by Śiśupāla, who desired victory, as before.

[this refers to] in other existences (*bhavāntareṣu*), that is, in other births (*janmāntareṣu*).
Here, there is a connection through the single action of following [the lover] between the subject at hand, the perfectly steady nature, and the subject not at hand, the woman:

(vi, ka) He states the connection of a single agent with multiple actions in the verse beginning with "dūram" (far).
This is a description of the state of separation from her husband, spoken by the friend of the heroine's wife once the hero has returned from his journey abroad.
"Having arrived"— that is, having come.
That ascetic woman, your beloved, was filled with sorrow due to her expectation of attaining you upon entering your bedchamber.
"This is mine.

In this type of *dīpaka* (the "illuminator"), since actions are the subject under discussion, the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is incidental.
Within this, there are three varieties—namely, the initial, middle, and final *dīpaka*—based on whether the common attribute (*dharma*) occurs within the initial, middle, or final sentence.
Among these, an example of the initial *dīpaka* is as follows:
“O Lord of Men, by you this world has been sustained: the sky by your majesty, poetry by your passion, youth by your voice, and the snowy mountain by your nectar.
This is an example of *madhyadīpaka* (middle illuminator), as in the previously cited verse beginning with "balāvalepāt" and so forth.
The same applies to other cases.
That is *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism) when there is a similarity to be understood between two sentences.
Even when a single common property is indicated separately [in each case], [it constitutes the ornament].
Vijñapriyā comments on the *prativastūpamā* ornament as follows: "Regarding the term *prativastu*..."

In this context, by virtue of the statement regarding the similarity of what is implied (*gamyasāmya*), it is understood that [the similarity pertains] to the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: that ornament in which even one common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) of those two—the object of comparison and the standard of comparison—which appear in two separate sentences, is indicated by distinct words, is *prativastūpamā*.
It should be understood that "of the object and the similarity" means "of the two similarities.

Furthermore, this state of being made known occurs sometimes through two words by means of both primary signification (śakti) and indication (lakṣaṇā), and sometimes through the power of the word denoting the object of comparison (upameya) regarding another attribute, by means of its dissimilarity [to the standard], through suggestion (vyañjanā).
This he will demonstrate in the examples.

(Lo, Ṛ) "The meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārtha*).

Thus, because the meaning of the sentence is compared with another meaning of a sentence by means of this [definition]—"that in which there is a similarity of the meaning of the sentence"—it is called *pratīvastūpamā* (simile based on the comparison of things), as its name is derived from its own meaning (*anvarthā*).
"Common" means shared.

It is indicated—that is, explained—by various synonyms and so forth, for the purpose of avoiding tautology; this is because, by relying on the metaphorical application of each individual term, they do not terminate in a single identical meaning.
For example:

What praise indeed can there be for the moonlight, since it causes even the ocean to tremble?
In this context, both "summoning" (*samākarṣaṇa*) and "making superior" (*uttaralīkaraṇa*) are in fact a single action; they are indicated by different verbal forms only to avoid tautology.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ga): [She says,] "You are blessed."

"here" refers to Damayantī as the object of comparison (*upameya*) and moonlight as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*); the common attribute (*dharma*) shared by both is their powerfully captivating nature.
Regarding the phrase "it is drawn":

by the power of the word, in the expression "it makes tremulous," the meaning is that it is rendered characterized by a drawing that produces tremulousness. And as for "the act of making tremulous": [this refers to the result].

"only one" means it consists solely of the form of attraction.
"By way of having different expressive bases" means by way of having different nominal stems (*prātipadika*).

(vi, gha) "Vimala" means pure;
"Śivagiri" refers to Kailāsa.

The single quality of stainlessness is presented through various verbal expressions.

In the passage beginning with "vimala eva" and so forth, the fourth quarter-verse is the subject under discussion.

By way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), for example:

(vi, ṅa) "As in the case of dissimilitude" (vaidharmyeṇa yathā)—the meaning is: by means of a property residing in the object of comparison (*upameya*) that is the opposite of the property mentioned [in the standard], and by means of a property mentioned in another object (*dharmin*) which is obtainable through suggestion (*vyañjanā*), there is a similarity (*sādharmya*) residing in the object of comparison; for example, "only the *cakora* birds... and so forth.

An illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), however, is the reflection of an object possessing common characteristics. (VisSd 10.50)
Locanā:

(lo, e) "Of that which possesses common attributes" (*sadharmasya*) refers to an object or the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) that is accompanied by common qualities and actions. By the term "of that which possesses common attributes," the figure *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism) is excluded.
This [type of simile] is also twofold, by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ca) states the ornament of the example (*dṛṣṭāntālaṅkāra*): "The example, however... and so forth.
"Of the similar" (*sadharmasya*) means of that which possesses a common or identical property (*sādhāraṇaikadharmasya*).
"Reflection" (*pratibimbanam*) means the manifestation of one of those two through the two properties mentioned in both [verses], which are mutually identical; this is the meaning.
Since the "similar object" (*sadharmah*) is intended to be well-known in this way, its explicitness will be evident in the figure of speech *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Praise of the Irrelevant).

In *prativastūpamā* (the simile based on parallelism), however, the property predicated of the object of comparison (*upameya*) is directly expressed (*vācya*), whereas the property predicated of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is understood either through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or, in some cases, through primary denotation (*śakti*); this is the distinction.
When that [property] is understood through suggestion (*vyañjanā*), it is a *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration), which occurs by way of both similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
The meaning is: by means of the two types of similarity already mentioned—namely, through similarity alone and through both similarity and dissimilarity.
The examples in order are as follows:

For even a garland of jasmine, though its fragrance has not yet been perceived, captivates the eye.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) "Even though its qualities are unknown" means that it is [attractive] solely due to the sweetness of its phonemes; this is the intended sense.
In this verse, the two attributes of "pouring streams of honey" and "stealing the eyes" are distinct yet mutually equal in their quality of producing delight.
A single attribute, namely the state of being a producer [of pleasure], is suggested by both.
"When you are seen, the deer-eyed woman's pain of love falls away."
When the moon does not rise as expected, the cluster of night-lotuses suffers exhaustion.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ja) She states the suggestion (*vyañjanā*) by means of both similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): "When you were seen" and "when [the moon] did not rise after being seen."
The meaning is: "it being present" refers to that which was seen not to have arisen in the moon; for even when there is an actual rising, it may not be seen due to clouds.
The word "seen" (dṛṣṭa) is used for the purpose of demonstrating exhaustion.
In this instance, *klānti* (exhaustion) is the opposite property of *vyathā* (distress) and *astraṃsana* (falling away).

Through these two properties residing in the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), a single common property is suggested: the attainment of one's own desired object upon seeing that which is dear to oneself.
Nor should it be asked what the distinction is between this and the *prativastūpamā* (parallelism) suggested by contrast (*vaidharmya*).

This is the distinction.

In this regard, he cites his own verse: "The unique Vasantalekhā"—where *Vasantalekhā* is a particular heroine.
And this is the King’s statement:
"This verse is mine.

*Vijñapriyā*:

"Because it culminates in a single form" means that because the various women—the objects of comparison (*upameya*)—and the other many women—the standards of comparison (*upamāna*)—are reduced to a single form through the superimposition of unity by virtue of being the object of a single attribute consisting of the question regarding the nature of the object to be expressed.

For here, the other woman is the object of comparison, while the others are the many standards of comparison; their culmination consists in the superimposition of unity upon them by virtue of being the object of a single attribute, namely the question which serves as the cause for both their being objects of the mind and objects of desire.
However, in the phrase "even though its qualities are unknown," there is no conclusion regarding identity;
rather, it is simply the manifestation of a single common property shared by both through two similar properties. Thus he says: "But here... (Locanā).
(Lo, Ai) Because the conclusion is reached through an identical form;

for the conclusion of the question "Why not [love] the mind? has the meaning "I do not desire any other beloved," whereas in this present example, there is once again the relationship of the original image and its reflection.

In this case, the distinction is that between the statement of the "supported" (samarthaka) and the "supporting" (samarthya), there exists the relationship of general and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*), which constitutes *arthāntaranyāsa*;
however, such is not the case for *prativastūpamā* and *dṛṣṭānta*. Thus is the difference.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ṭa) He states the distinction between *arthāntaranyāsa* on one hand and *prativastūpamā* and *dṛṣṭānta* on the other by means of the words "sāmarthya" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the two sentences," the meaning is "of the two sentence-meanings.

Since, in these two [figures] as well, the object of comparison (*upameya*) is the capacity (*sāmarthya*) and the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is the corroboration (*samarthana*), there arises the contingency of non-distinction [between them].
"Not so" means that there is no relationship of universal and particular. Whether a real-world connection exists or does not exist in some cases, [it remains as such].
Where the state of being an original image and its reflection is made known, that is *nidarśanā*.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ṭha) He states the figure of speech *nidarśanā*— beginning with "sambhavan"—
[referring] to two things, in some cases [being] an action and its agent.
The meaning is that, in some cases, the relationship between the referents of the words *yat* and *tat* being impossible,
and in other cases, [the relationship] being possible,
the two expressive words may indicate similarity in the form of a reflection and its counterpart (*bimbānubimbatva*) anywhere.
Locanā:
(lo, o) The meaning is that the relation between things is the state of being a property and its locus (*dharmadharmibhāva*).
The meaning is that [this relation] is impossible because of the appearance of sublation (*bādhapratibhāsa*).
The state of being an image and its reflection;
the relationship between the original object and its reflected image;
the illustration; the act of producing a reflection.
Therefore, when there is the statement "it exists in this," it is *nidarśanā*.
Among these, *sambhavadvastusambandhanidarśanā* (illustration by showing a possible connection between things) is, for example:
"Who in this circle of the earth, causing people to suffer in vain, attains prosperity for long?"
Thus making himself known, the sun reached the western mountain by the end of the day.
Vijñapriyā: (vi, ḍa) "Who is it here? [The answer is: Who in this circle of the earth, tormenting people in vain and for no purpose, attains prosperity for a very long time?
"Bhānumān" means "the sun.
The sense is that, making known—that is, signaling by day—he reached the western mountain from the middle of the sky.
In the expression "dinena," the third case ending denotes the cause (*kāraṇatā*) consisting of the state of being antecedent to the day.
Locanā: (lo, au) "By day" (*dinena*) [indicates] completion; the third case [ending] expresses the sense of the third case, which consists of the misfortune encountered by those who are tormented.
In this context, the connection of the sun as the agent (*vaktṛ*) with the action of knowing such a meaning is indeed possible.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"In this [context]" (*atra*).

In this context, the connection with agency (kartṛtva) is the connection with being a producer (janakatva), because [the word *svasti*] produces such a cognition in the form of an inference by means of its own auspiciousness (*svastigamana*).
This is because the following inference is possible: "A person does not attain prosperity for a very long time, because he causes suffering to others, like the sun that is about to set.

He demonstrates that it possesses the capacity to convey a reflection (*pratibimba*) and a counter-reflection (*anubimba*) through the manifestation of similarity (*sādṛśya*), stating: "And that... (*sa ca*).
And that is the meaning of "connection.

It is because [the sun] possesses the property of reaching the western mountain—which is capable of making known such a fact—that other oppressors as well meet with calamity, just like the setting of the sun which oppresses others; for such is the nature of the case.
This is because it possesses the characteristic of reaching the final mountain, which is capable of making known this kind of meaning.
And this [simile] makes known the relationship of reflection between the sun’s setting behind the western mountain and the onset of calamity for those who suffer;
however, *asambhavadvastunidarśanā* (the indication of an impossible thing) is of two kinds, according to whether it occurs within a single sentence or across multiple sentences.
Among these, an example occurring within a single sentence is as follows:
“Her curved glance possesses the charm of a garland of blue lotuses;
her lower lip has the playfulness of a young sprout; and her face bears the splendor of the moon.”

In this context, since it is impossible for one person to possess the gracefulness and other qualities found in Kuvalayamālā and others— such as side-long glances and the like— on the grounds that "how could another bear the dharma of another?",

the [description] conveys a sense of gracefulness and so forth similar to that [original] gracefulness; thus, it makes known the relationship of prototype (bimba) and reflection (pratibimba) between the side-long glances and the like, and Kuvalayamālā and the like.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṇa) "She fashions" means that her crooked casting of sidelong glances takes on the graceful arrangement of a garland of blue lotuses; she assumes its beauty.
The syntactical connection of the phrase "it conveys one [element] even further" is as follows:

here, by means of the qualities (*dharma*)—namely, the casting of side-glances and so forth, which are the agents—and the graceful gestures (*lalita*) and so forth, which are the objects, he demonstrates the reflection and counter-reflection (*prativimbānubimba*) of the two substrata (*dharmin*) as well;
that is to say, by means of the casting of side-glances and so forth, it makes known the graceful gestures and the like.

In this instance, there is a reflection of the reflected between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison contained within a single sentence; the same applies in subsequent cases as well. — *Locanā*:
(lo, a) It causes understanding—that is, it brings about comprehension.
Because [the manifestation] is of the same class as the graceful (*lalita*), there is an absence of absolute incompatibility, and thus there exists a state of not being too remote.
This should be understood in the same way regarding *līlā* and so forth.
Or as it is said:
"O Indra among kings, at your departure,
the deer-eyed wives of your enemies were released [from their grief]."
With her gait like that of a royal swan, she possesses the luster of the moon in her face.
In this case, since it is impossible for the feet to possess the gait of a royal swan—which is not naturally connected to them—their connection with that gait is postulated;
and that [connection], being otherwise impossible, makes one perceive a gait as if it were the gait of a royal swan.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ta) "At your departure": when your departure—that is, your journey—takes place, the gait of royal swans is abandoned by the feet of the deer-eyed women of their enemies because they flee swiftly; and the splendor of the moon is abandoned by their faces because they have withered away. [The term] "unconnected" means: (vi, tha) "O King, the lotus-stalks of the fame of your enemies are severed at their roots by the wind of your majesty. Your majesty is the wind; by that, the lotus-stalks of the fame of your enemies are severed at their roots. Why? Because it is said: "The root of a lotus-stalk is called 'nāla'. Since the stalks are severed, the fame itself is destroyed. This is the meaning. (vi, da) "O King, the moonlight of the faces of the wives of your enemies has been eclipsed by the brilliance of your majesty. Your majesty is the sun; by its brilliance, the moonlight of the faces of the wives of your enemies has been eclipsed. Why? Because it is said: "The moonlight is the radiance of the moon. Since the moonlight is eclipsed, the faces themselves are eclipsed. This is the meaning. (vi, dha) "O King, the pride of the wives of your enemies has been crushed by the weight of your majesty. Your majesty is the elephant; by its weight, the pride of the wives of your enemies has been crushed. Why? Because it is said: "Pride is the arrogance of the heart. Since the pride is crushed, the wives themselves are crushed. This is the meaning. (vi, na) "O King, the lotuses of the faces of the wives of your enemies have been closed by the heat of your majesty. Your majesty is the sun; by its heat, the lotuses of the faces of the wives of your enemies have been closed. Why? Because it is said: "A lotus is a flower of the day. Since the lotuses are closed, the faces themselves are closed. This is the meaning. (vi, pa) "O King, the lotus-stalks of the arms of the wives of your enemies have been cut off by the sword of your majesty. Your majesty is the sword; by that, the lotus-stalks of the arms of the wives of your enemies have been cut off. Why? Because it is said: "The lotus-stalk is called 'nāla'. Since the stalks are cut, the arms themselves are cut. This is the meaning. (vi, pha) "O King, the fragrance of the breath of the wives of your enemies has been scattered by the wind of your majesty. Your majesty is the wind; by that, the fragrance of the breath of the wives of your enemies has been scattered. Why? Because it is said: "Fragrance is the scent of the mouth. Since the fragrance is scattered, the breath itself is scattered. This is the meaning. (vi, ba) "O King, the luster of the faces of the wives of your enemies has been stolen by the brilliance of your majesty. Your majesty is the moon; by its brilliance, the luster of the faces of the wives of your enemies has been stolen. Why? Because it is said: "Luster is the radiance of the face. Since the luster is stolen, the faces themselves are stolen. This is the meaning. (vi, bha) "O King, the beauty of the bodies of the wives of your enemies has been taken away by the majesty of your majesty. Your majesty is the god of love; by his majesty, the beauty of the bodies of the wives of your enemies has been taken away. Why? Because it is said: "Beauty is the loveliness of the body. Since the beauty is taken away, the bodies themselves are taken away. This is the meaning. (vi, ma) "O King, the lineage of the wives of your enemies has been broken by the power of your majesty. Your majesty is the lineage; by its power, the lineage of the wives of your enemies has been broken. Why? Because it is said: "Lineage is the succession of progeny. Since the lineage is broken, the wives themselves are broken. This is the meaning. (vi, ya) "O King, the sovereignty of the wives of your enemies has been lost by the glory of your majesty. Your majesty is sovereignty; by its glory, the sovereignty of the wives of your enemies has been lost. Why? Because it is said: "Sovereignty is the state of being a ruler.
