Because the abandonment [of a thing] is only possible for that which is related,
a relation is postulated;
for the apprehension of non-existence is preceded by the superimposition of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
It shows the reflection with the words "And that" (*sa ca*).
Locanā:
The word "first" (*prathamam*) is to be supplied as the remainder before the phrase "is conceptualized" (*kalpyate*).
And this is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*);
it should be understood that the same applies to the phrase "the moon’s radiance by means of its face.
An example occurring across multiple sentences is as follows:
“Indeed, that sage who desires to achieve through ascetic toil this body, naturally so enchanting,
is surely attempting to cut down a thorn bush with the edge of a blue lotus petal.”
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, tha) "This, they say"—this is the speech of Duṣmanta upon seeing Śakuntalā in the hermitage, dressed in attire appropriate for asceticism; *avyājena* means "without artifice," that is, according to reality.

The meaning is this: that sage who desires to accomplish penance suited to this charming body will surely—meaning, with certainty—endeavor to cut the hard *śamī* creeper with the delicate edge of a blue lotus petal. Here, the connection between the two sentence-meanings indicated by the word "ca" (and) as a non-difference (*abheda*) being untenable, [the intended sense is] that such a body is [unfit for] penance.
The desire to effect the removal of fatigue by means of holding a blue lotus petal results, in the relationship of *bimba* and *pratibimba*, in a desire to cut a *śamī* creeper;
thus it is said, "here [the words] 'yat' and 'tat'... in the *Vijñapriyā*.
Regarding the phrase "of the two sentence-meanings," the meaning here is "of the meanings of the two poems.
The two sentence-meanings, however, are [respectively] "one desiring the means for the practice of austerity and forbearance" and "one desiring the cutting of the *śamī* creeper.
Since the verbal root √*iṣ* (to desire) also signifies "determination" (*vyavasāya*), the sense is that a relation of identity between those two is untenable.

The meaning is that, because the two words [icchā] denote a single substratum (dharmin), their syntactic relation as non-different (*abhedānvaya*) is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*);
however, since there is no non-difference between the two desires (*icchā*), that relation would be untenable. *Locanā*.
(lo, i) This body desires to accomplish what is possible through austerity; the sense is that it wishes to carry out penance by means of this very form of Śakuntalā.
Not only when both "yat" and "tat" are explicitly stated is there *vākyanidarśanā*, but also when one of them is implied, as for example:
“If this body, so difficult for those dwelling in the inner apartments to obtain, belongs even to people living in a hermitage,
then surely garden creepers have been surpassed by forest creepers in their virtues.”
Thus: "If a funeral rite (śrāddha) were the cause of satisfaction even for deceased beings, then oil would increase the flame of an extinguished lamp."
“That arrow of Rāma, which made a breach in the solid rock when it struck his chest,
became the gateway for Death, who had not yet entered the realm of the Rākṣasas.”
In this case, however, the figure of speech is *nidarśanā* (illustration),
for there is no capacity here for [the word] "as" (*iva*) to signify "being a means" (*dvāratā*).
The great scholar Rāghavānanda maintains that because the object of comparison (*upameya*) and other factors are possible here, this is *pratīyamānotprekṣā* (suggested poetic fancy):
"When the Sage’s mind was difficult to penetrate—though desired by the gods—the side-long glances of the deer-eyed woman thus became the very arrows of Love," and so forth;
however, in such cases, there are indeed *pariṇāma* (transformation) and other figures.
As it is said:
"This birth has been rendered fruitless by the desire to obtain the enjoyments of worldly existence;
alas! it has been sold for the price of glass."
It is made of wish-fulfilling gems.
In this context, the conclusion is that by greed for worldly enjoyment, one brings about the futility of birth, which is like selling a *cintāmaṇi* jewel for the price of glass.
Thus—
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, dha) "This birth" and so forth.
The bringing of futility and the selling of a *cintāmaṇi*—it should be understood that even this birth is like a *cintāmaṇi*.
"Where is the lineage originating from the Sun, and where is my intellect of such limited scope?"
"Out of delusion, I desire to cross the ocean that is so difficult to traverse by means of a mere raft."
In this regard, according to my own opinion, the description of the Solar dynasty results in the conclusion that it is like crossing the ocean by means of the moon.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, na) Where [is] "the Solar"?
This is the statement of Kālidāsa, who desires to describe the lineage of Raghu; the word "mine" (*mama*) is to be supplied as the object of "intellect" (*matiḥ*).
Here, in the first half-verse, there is the poetic figure *viṣama* (the incongruous), which will be explained later.
The subsequent half-verse, however, provides the illustration under discussion.
It causes that [meaning] to be understood by saying, "by my mind" (*manmatyā*).
Nor should it be asked why there is not merely a metaphor (*rūpaka*) of a person desiring to cross over.
Because such a person is not well-known;
and even if some such person were to exist who was insane, he would not enter into the mind [of others];
rather, the desire to cross over (titīrṣā) is clearly manifested only in the speaker himself.
Through the understanding of that [simile], a similarity is perceived between the two who desire to cross over by means of describing the lineage of Raghu.
Locanā:
(Lo, ī) Following the phrase "like crossing the ocean," the remainder is that there exists a relationship of original image and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*).
And this [type of simile] occurs even when that which resides in the object of comparison (*upameya*) is impossible in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*),
as for example:
"The sweetness experienced on the lip of that deer-eyed woman..."
He was tasted by those expert in flavors as being like the juice of the *mṛdvīkā* grape.
Vijñapriyā: (vi, pa) "And this" means:
this is an *nidarśanā* [simile], because the property residing in the object of comparison (*upameyavṛtta-upameyadharma*)—namely, "it bears the blue water-lily"—[is transferred to the subject].
In passages such as these, however, [the figure] is shown because the attribute belonging to the standard of comparison (upamāna) simply cannot exist in the object of comparison (upameya).
Regarding the phrase "even though there is impossibility":
the meaning is that even when that which was stated as residing in the standard of comparison is impossible [in the object of comparison], the similarity between them is still communicated.
"That which has been experienced" refers to sweetness;
*mṛdvīkā* means grape.

In its juice, which is liquid; here, since the quality of sweetness belonging to the subject under discussion—the lower lip—is impossible in the juice of the grape, it results in similarity, as in the previous case. —Locanā:
As before, that is, like the previous example;

thus, in the verse "Even the moon abandons the luster of your face," this is indeed an instance of *nidarśanā* (illustrative simile), just like the example "O Indra among kings, at your departure," because the defining characteristic of the *nidarśanā* ornament— namely, the relationship between the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) as established in such a manner— is possible here.

Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even in the immediately preceding example, "That which was experienced... and so forth, there would be an absence of illustration (*nidarśana*).

Thus, in the definition—"The possible connection between real entities (*vastu*) is the cause of the conceptualization of an illustration (*nidarśana*)"—the word *upamā* signifies mere similarity (*sādṛśya*) and not the poetic figure of simile (*upamālaṅkāra*).
For this very reason, the author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva* also stated that "illustration (*nidarśanā*) is the cause of a reflected image (*pratibimba*)."
Even in the form of a garland, as it is said by me:
"You cast the parrot into the mouth of a cat; you offer the deer to the fangs of a predator;
you bestow the horse upon the horns of a buffalo—thus you fix your mind upon the expanse of worldly enjoyment."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
pha) "You cast aside"—
this is a statement by a peaceful person directed toward a man attached to worldly enjoyments.
O man! By directing your mind toward the expansion of enjoyments—that is, toward the multitude of pleasures—you are casting a parrot into the mouth of a *vṛṣadaṃśaka*, a cat.
Just as a cat destroys a parrot, so too will the expansion of enjoyments destroy you by causing a fall into hell.
Therefore, the meaning is that directing the mind toward enjoyment is like casting a parrot into that [mouth].
The same applies in subsequent cases as well;
for example, "the tiger is the devourer of deer.
In this instance, the meaning of the sentence remains incomplete without the implication of the relationship between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).

In the case of the simile (*dṛṣṭānta*), however, the communication of the relationship between the original and its reflection occurs through the power of the sentence-meaning once it has reached its conclusion.
Nor is this a case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because in instances such as "This necklace of the deer-eyed ones... there is no finality in the similarity.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ba) He demonstrates the difference between a *dṛṣṭānta* (illustrative example) and a *nidarśana* (exemplification) with the words "here, the original object" (*bimba*).
The sense is that there is no completion of the sentence-meaning because it would be contradicted.
"By being concluded" means that there is no sublation (*bādhā*) therein. "By implication" (*sāmarthyāt*).
The capacity [of the word] lies precisely in avoiding the fault of stating what has already been stated or what is not relevant;
as in: "This necklace belongs to the deer-eyed women," which means: "This necklace rolls upon the circle of the breasts of the deer-eyed women."

"Even for those who are liberated, such is their state; where are we, the servants of Smara?"—the final implication of this verse is that it is indeed most fitting for us to roll about upon the circle of her breasts, and not that there is a similarity [between our state and theirs]. This is the meaning.

Because, by the principle of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpanyāya*), when one thing is mentioned, the conclusion regarding another follows as a matter of course through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*).
*Locanā*:
(lo, ū) A "deer-eater" (*mṛgādana*) is a hyena (*tarkṣu*).

The sentence-meaning does not reach completion because the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is untenable; for once the meaning has reached completion, there is no further untenability of connection, as both the sentence regarding the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the sentence regarding the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) each rest upon the communication of their own respective meanings.
Thus, the lack of completion is absent in the case of similarity (*sādṛśya*).
However, by the principle of fixed similarity, merely through the occurrence of another attribute—
whether there be an excess of the object compared (upameya) over the standard of comparison (upamāna), or its deficiency—
it is *vyatireka* (distinction).
And that [unestablished reason] is of one kind when the reason is stated, and of three kinds when it is not stated. (10.52)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, bha) He states the figure of speech *vyatireka* [contrast]: "Excellence" (*ādhikya*), etc.

The meaning is that when the excellence or, alternatively, the inferiority of the object of comparison (*upameya*) over the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is described, that is the figure of speech *vyatireka*.
Its division into forty-eight types is through the further subdivision of those [categories].
Regarding the phrase "and that":
in some places, however, there is a verse stating that when one [type of] reason is mentioned or not mentioned, it is again threefold.
The phrase beginning with "eva" functions as the instigator [of the comparison].
The term "in the cause" (hetau) means that there are two types of causes, by virtue of being either superior or non-inferior.
Furthermore, although it is fourfold, it is understood through both word and meaning because it conveys similarity.
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) "In the sense of cause" means that the singular number is used in view of [the individual] *jāti*.
Regarding what was stated in the *Vṛtti*: "The cause [of comparison] resides in the object of comparison (*upameya*)," and so forth;
and regarding the phrase "by means of words," it was stated in this very same work: "The *śrautī* [metaphor] consists of the words *yathā*, *iva*, and *vā*."
Regarding the phrase "by way of meaning" (*arthataḥ*):
as stated right here—“The *ārtha*, *tulya*, *samāna*, and so forth [occur] by the logic already mentioned”;
and because of implication (*ākṣepa*), there are twelve types even in the case of *śleṣa*, thus making twenty-four in total.
Taken individually, there would be forty-eight types when combined.

Furthermore, the cause for the excellence of the object of comparison (*upameya*) over the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) consists of a ground for superiority residing in the *upameya* and a ground for inferiority residing in the *upamāna*.
When both of these are stated, it is one type; [when only one is stated, it is another].

When [the distinction] is not stated either individually or collectively, there are three types; thus, even within these four types, because the relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is communicated through word, through meaning, or by implication, there are twelve varieties.
By the inclusion of the word "also" (*api*), it is understood that this occurs even in the absence of *śleṣa* (pun), resulting in twenty-four varieties.

Since there are likewise twenty-four varieties when the standard of comparison is inferior [to the object of comparison] by this same method, the *vyatireka* (distinction) consists of forty-eight varieties in total.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ma) He clarifies the meaning of the verse himself with the words "of the object of comparison" (*upameyasya*) and "each one" (*pratyekam*).

He says "threefold" (*trividha*) to indicate the three types of non-statement: two for the non-statement of either the reason for superiority or the reason for inferiority, and one for the non-statement of both together.
He says "even in this fourfold [classification]" because of the combination with the statement of the two reasons.
"Announcement" means making known.
"By means of a word" means when the simile is based on direct verbal expression (*śrautī*).
"By means of the sense" (arthena) means:
when the simile is based on the sense (ārthī). "By way of implication" (ākṣepeṇa) means: [by way of suggestion].
The meaning is: "by means of the absence or the [explicit] mention" of particles such as *iva* and words such as *tulya* which express comparison (*upamā*).
Regarding the phrase "thus it is of twelve kinds":

since there are four types of simile based on the presence or absence of the two causes (the explicit statement of the common property and the particle), and each of these four is threefold according to whether the comparison is suggested by the word (*śabda*), the sense (*artha*), or both, it is thus of twelve kinds.

He demonstrates the possibility of that twelvefold [classification] occurring both in cases of *śleṣa* (paranomasia) and its absence, based on the word "also" (*api*) mentioned in the verse—namely, "even in *śleṣa*" (*śleṣe 'pi*).
"By way of" (*bhaṅgyā*) means by means of a particular mode.
An example follows:
“Her face is stainless, like the moon which is not stained. Regarding the word *akalaṅkam*: [it means] "stainless. *Vijñapriyā*: (vi, ya) "Stainless," etc.
Her face is not like the moon which is stained with a spot;
rather, it is superior to it,
because [her face] is "spotless" (akalaṅka).
Here, both causes—the spotlessness residing in the object of comparison (the upameya) and the spottedness residing in the standard of comparison (the upamāna)—are stated;
and because it is conveyed by the word "yathā," the comparison is verbal (śābda).
In this very context, with the reading "na kalaṅkividhūpamam" (not comparable to the spotted moon), the comparison is implied (ārtha).
In the reading “He conquers the spotted moon,” however, because words such as *iva* or *tulya* are absent, [the excellence] is merely implied (*ākṣipta*).

In this very same case, if the word *akalaṅka* (spotless) were omitted, there would be a failure to state the cause for the excellence of the object of comparison; and if the word *kalaṅkin* (spotted) were omitted, there would be a failure to state the cause for the inferiority residing in the standard of comparison.
When two [factors] are not mentioned, both are not mentioned.
*Vijñapriyā* (*vi*, *ra*): In that very context, he demonstrates the possibility of various modes by saying "in this very [case]."
"The non-mention of both" means that the formulation is such as:
"Her face is not the moon.
This is the sense.
Locanā: (lo,
ṝ) In the case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), it occurs when there are two words— one stainless and one stained— and two causes [for their respective states], as for example:
“And for one whose virtues are exceedingly profound, the virtues do not break like lotus fibers.
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) *guṇa* refers to qualities such as beauty, as well as a thread.
The suffix *vati* is used in this sense [of "like"], thus it is a verbal simile (*śābdamaupamyam*).
There is a statement of both causes for excellence and deficiency.
The word "quality" (*guṇa*) is a pun (*śliṣṭa*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, la) He states that there are likewise twelve types even in the case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) by means of this same method, beginning with "atigāḍha" etc.;
here, the sense is "in this very [context]."
Because it is expressed by a word ending in the genitive case, as in "of the lotus" (*abjasyeva*).
Regarding "excellence" (*utkarṣa*):
the intensity and non-interruption found in the qualities are the causes of excellence and inferiority, respectively.
Other distinctions are to be inferred as before.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"Other distinctions" refers to those [previously mentioned].

In that regard, when neither of the two causes is mentioned individually or collectively in a verbal simile (*śābdopamā*), as for example: "The qualities of the deer-eyed woman, whose face is like the moon, are not fragile like a lotus"—this is an instance where the cause of excellence is not mentioned;
and: "And her qualities, possessing exceedingly firm virtues, are not like those of a lotus."
Thus, when the cause of inferiority is not mentioned,
as in: "The eyes of that woman with lashes like blue lotuses are not red like a lotus," there is a non-mention of both [the object of comparison and its quality].

In the case of an implied simile (*ākṣiptaupamya*), as for example: "The young girl possesses exceedingly firm virtues; she is not one whose virtues falter like those of a lotus"—this occurs when both [the common property and the object of comparison] are mentioned.
Or: "The young girl possesses exceedingly firm virtues; her virtues are indeed equal to those of a lotus."
Thus, when the grounds for disparagement are not mentioned— as in "that girl with the moon-like face indeed does not possess qualities equal to the lotus"—
there is the non-mention of both.

An example of *ārthopamā* (implied simile) occurs when both [the common property and the object of comparison] are expressed, as in: "The young girl possesses exceedingly firm virtues (*atigāḍhaguṇā*), yet her virtues do not falter like those of a lotus (*nābjatulyaskhaladguṇā*). Or, when only the object of comparison is expressed: "The young girl possesses exceedingly firm virtues; her virtues are indeed like those of a lotus (*nābjatulyaguṇa*)."
Thus, when the grounds for disparagement are not mentioned—
such as, "That girl with the moon-like face does not have faltering virtues equal to those of a lotus"— and when the grounds for praise are not mentioned;
‘That young girl with the moon-like face does not indeed possess qualities equal to those of a lotus’—this is an example where neither [of the two] is mentioned.
As for an implied simile (*ākṣiptaupamya*), it is as follows: ‘Her qualities are exceedingly firm, while the qualities of the lotus are fragile.’
Thus, when both [the general and specific qualities] are included, as in:
"The lotus is truly virtuous; let its virtues, however, be fragile," there is no mention of a cause for inferiority.

"The lotus, though possessing qualities, was surely surpassed by her who possesses qualities"— this is an example when neither [of the two] is mentioned. And these are examples of the excellence of the object of comparison over the standard of comparison.
An example of brevity (nyūnatva) as a mere indication is as follows:
"Though the moon wanes again and again, it grows full once more; this is true.
Cease, O beautiful one, and be gracious!"
But youth, once gone, does not return."
Here, there is a superiority of the instability of youth, which serves as the object of comparison (*upameya*).

Therefore, regarding the definition of some who state that "the *vyatireka* [figure] occurs when the object of comparison exceeds the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), or in the reverse case," the claim made by certain others that "the phrase 'or in the reverse case' is redundant" is not withstands critical examination.
For instance, in this context, what is intended by "excess" and "deficiency" is precisely existence and non-existence. Locanā: (lo, e) existence and non-existence.
Regarding beauty and ugliness:
in this case, the non-existence of youth in relation to the moon is quite evident. Or, let there be some manner of pleasure in this example however it may be.
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding "deficiency" (*nyūnatva*),
the word "of the object of comparison" (*upameyasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
"Exhausted, exhausted!"—
this is a lover's address to his indignant beloved;
the words "cease" are to be supplied, meaning "cease from your indignation."
The construction is "youth, however" (yauvanaṃ tu).
"Gone" (yātam) means departed.
"An excess of instability" (asthairyyasyādhikyam) refers to this.
And thus, since instability is a cause of diminution, I explain that there is inferiority in the object of comparison (the face) and superiority in the moon alone;
therefore, whatever some have said regarding this is not withstands critical examination—this is what he means by "Therefore, here...
Some refers to certain authors of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
Regarding what they say here, he states: "from the analogy" (*upamānāt*).
This is an ancient verse ending with "in the case of exclusion" (*vyatireke*). In its definition, [it says] "or in the case of the contrary" (*viparyaye vā*).
They say that the word "pada" (foot/step) is meaningless; this is the sense.
Regarding existence and non-existence as being "there" or "not there," he states the non-locality of youth with the words, "here, in relation to the moon."

Now, it might be argued that in the present context, what is intended to be expressed is precisely the superiority of the subject (uddeśyārtha), and since the purpose here is to demonstrate the instability of youth in the proud woman, that superiority is nothing other than the superiority of the object of comparison (upameyādhikya); to this, he says: "Or let it be so"—"The path of the messenger was whitened by the fame of Hanumān and others, but by me, it was whitened by the laughter of my enemies."
Regarding such passages as these, what is the solution? It has been well stated: "Or else, there is deficiency.
[The commentary] *Vijñapriyā* explains: "By Hanumān and others."
This is a statement of despondency by Nala, who has become a messenger of the gods, because the fruit of his mission has not been achieved.
The meaning is that his fate is such that he exceeds even the standards of comparison— Hanumān and others— who made the path of messengers cool with their fame.
This is an illustration:
“You repeatedly touch her trembling glance with its flickering corners; moving close to her ear, you hum softly as if whispering a secret.
While she waves her hand, you drink from her lower lip, the very essence of pleasure. O bee, we are ruined by our search for the truth, while you, indeed, are successful!”

Thus it is said in the Abhijñāna: "It is better for the dust kicked up by a foot to rise and settle upon the head of an embodied being—even when he is in a state of well-being—than for him to suffer dishonor."

Thus, in the *Māgha*, since the superiority of the bees and the pollen is expressed by the very words *kṛti* and *varapada* through their status as the objects of comparison, the opinion of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* on this point is simply not to be accepted.
*Locanā*:
(Lo, Ai) "By Hanumān and others," etc., is the speech of Nala, the divine messenger, addressed to Damayantī.

The sense is that, having abandoned the role of a messenger due to the laughter of his enemies, he himself accepted the status of a leader. "Where, by the force of the meaning of 'together' (saha), there may be a single expressive word for two [things]. (VisSd 10.54)

When that [figure] becomes a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) which serves as its foundation, it is *sahokti*. [The author] states the figure of speech *sahokti*: "of the sense of 'together' (*saha-artha*)," and so forth.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, sa). He explains the *sahokti* ornament: "of the sense of 'together' (*saha-artha*)," etc.
"Expressive of both" means that it conveys the connection of its own meaning in both cases.

Even a word with a different case-ending, by the force of its inherent connection (*sāhārtha*), conveys the connection of its own meaning through non-difference between the meanings of words with both identical and different case-endings.
Locanā:
(lo, o) [The term] *saha* refers to the word that is a synonym for "together" (*sahārtha*);
it denotes either a single action or a quality.
It is the root and the seed.

Furthermore, the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) found here is based on the identification of two things as non-different (*abhedādhyavasāya*), and it takes the form of an inversion of the temporal sequence between cause and effect.
Even that which is based on the identification of non-difference is further divided into that which rests upon a pun (*śleṣa*) and that which does not.
He provides an example in sequence:
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ha):
"It has its root in the identification [of the object] with the subject (*abhedādhyavasāya*)."
Nor should it be said that since the determination of difference (*bhedādhyavasāya*) itself constitutes hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), how can that [hyperbole] have that [determination] as its basis;
for it is the verbal expression of the determination alone that is the hyperbole, and thus it has as its basis the speaker and their determination.
"Wall" means the support; the meaning is that it rests upon a pun (*śleṣa*).
“In her youth, her beloved partook of passion along with her lower lip.
Here, there is *śleṣa* (paronomasia) in the word *rāga*.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ka) "sahādharā" and so forth: here, with respect to the referent of the third-case term, namely the lower petal (*adharadala*), and the referent of the first-case term, namely the beloved (*priya*), the word "possessing passion" (*rāgavān*) conveys its own meaning through non-difference (*abheda*); for there is the cognition that the lower petal also possesses passion.
And the basis is the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consisting of the superimposition of non-difference between the passion and the object.
Locanā:
[This is] otherwise based on *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
*Rāga* means redness as well as passion;
*śleṣa* consists in having two meanings.
In this case, the relationship of the standard of comparison and the object compared is determined by intention (*vaivakṣika*),
because both are the subject matter (*prakṛta*).
And both are the subject matter because they are both specific types of wisdom (*prajñā-viśeṣa*).

Here, there is an intention to express the object of comparison (*upamāna*) as subordinate (*guṇabhāvena*), since it is indicated by the third case ending. Furthermore, in this example, there is also an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) associated with the simultaneity of cause and effect, because the lover's passion is observed immediately after the lower lip has begun to take on its redness.
Thus, two types of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) are established here.
[This occurs] due to the difference in the related entities and the difference in the substrata.

As stated by Rāghavānanda: “Even if a single attribute, by resorting to superimposition, becomes connected to another substrate through the force of the word ‘together’ (saha), that is then called *sahokti*”; this is incorrect.
For they themselves have admitted that this [figure of speech] is rooted in hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).

In a hyperbole based on identification (*adhyavasāya*), there is no possibility of a separate seed in the form of superimposition (*āropa*). As Caṇḍīdāsa and others have said: "Superimposition is the cognition of the identity of one thing with another, wherein the object [of comparison] is not swallowed up [by the subject]."
Regarding the phrase "but [it is] *adhyavasāya* (determination) of that which has been swallowed":

the author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva* has made the distinction that when there is *āropa* (superimposition), it is *rūpaka* (metaphor) and so forth, whereas when there is *adhyavasāya*, it is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and so forth.
"Causing the night to bloom along with clusters of white water-lilies, and driving away steadfastness along with the masses of thick darkness..."
Together with clusters of lotuses, the rays of the moon move in every direction, causing the hearts of all to close.
"This is mine.
Here, the distinction between "exultation" (ullāsa) and the others arises solely from the difference in their respective relations,
and not through punning (śliṣṭatā).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, kha) Without employing *śleṣa* (paronomasia), he says: "Together with the night-lotuses...
The rays of the nectar-rayed moon spread in every direction.
He states the qualifiers of the rays: "together with the night-lotuses.
*Kadamba* means a cluster or a multitude.
*Āmīlayantaḥ* means causing to close or contract.
The contraction of the internal organ (*svānta*) is precisely its turning away from other objects.
Regarding the word "here" (*atra*):
after the word "difference," one must supply the words "the determination of non-difference."
And thus, the connection is that his resolve was such, but not through any physical attachment:
“Simultaneously with the king, she— her consciousness utterly lost through profound delusion—
went to the surface of the earth along with a drop of oil, like the flame of a lamp.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ga) He states [the following] based on hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consisting in the inversion of the temporal sequence of cause and effect: "At the very same moment" (*samameva*).
With her consciousness utterly lost through profound delusion, that Indumatī went to the surface of the earth together with Aja, the lord of men.
The meaning is "like the flame of a lamp together with a drop of thin oil.
Here, the fact that the lord of men also went to the surface of the earth is understood through the force of the word *saha* (together) as expressing the sense of simultaneity.
The fall of Indumatī is the cause (*kāraṇa*), and the fall of the lord of men is the effect (*kārya*).
The inversion of sequence consists in stating the simultaneity of two things where such is not the case;
this can also occur through a string of instances (*mālā*), as in the example cited: "Together with the clusters of night-lotuses... and so forth.

In such passages as, “Rāma went to the dense forest together with Lakṣmaṇa,” this is not an ornament [of poetry], because there is an absence of the basis for hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). “*Vinokti* (description by contrast) is when something is neither good nor bad without another thing. (VisSd 10.55)
"It is not that it is non-virtuous (asādhu) or unlovely (aśobhana).

And thus, although the ultimate conclusion concerns loveliness itself, this statement of "loveliness" is nevertheless intended by way of the absence of unloveliness; for the unloveliness of any object worthy of description is merely a defect arising from the proximity of something else.
Furthermore, its beauty lies precisely in its inherent nature.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, gha) states the figure of speech *vinokti*: "It is called *vinokti*..."
He explains: "It is not incorrect.
Having stated it by means of two negative particles (*nañ*), he says "And if this is so" in order to express the positive sense.
[The meaning is: "The fault lies precisely in the proximity of another."
The meaning is that the very fault which arises from proximity to another constitutes its lack of excellence (*aśobhanatvam*).
Locanā:
(lo, a) The ultimate conclusion is indeed "lack of excellence," as in the statement: "But the non-existence of non-existence leaves only existence remaining."
The meaning is "according to this principle.
For example:
"Without the season of the clouds, the moon has attained fullness."
"Even without the heat of summer, the beautiful forest grove came into being."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ṅa) "Without the rainy season" means [the attainment of] alertness and purity.
For here, from the very fact of the rainy season, the moon is perceived as soiled, and during the summer season, the forest groves are perceived as not beautiful.
*Locanā*:
"Nistandratām" means stainlessness.

In this context, the lack of clarity and lack of beauty in the moon and the forest king are caused respectively by the rainy season and the summer season; however, their clarity and beauty, on the other hand, are due to their innate nature—this is the intended meaning. An example of what is improper and unattractive is as follows:
“O noble lady, you have done well by following your beloved who has transcended the world;
for what is the beauty of day without the sun, and what is the night without the moon?”
Vijñapriyā:
"They follow after" (anuyāntyeti).
This is Anasūyā’s speech directed toward Sītā.
"Janānītam" means devoid of attendants.
Locanā:
(lo, i) "Janātītam" means having gone to a secluded place beyond the world (*lokāntika*), that is to say, a place free from people.
“The birth of the lotus was in vain, by whom the orb of the moon was not seen;
likewise, the rising of the moon was indeed fruitless for him who did not behold the lotus awakened from sleep.”
Locanā:
(lo, ī) "vibhātā" means blossomed;
here, through the stylistic device of mutual inseparability (*avinokti*), there is an excellence of aesthetic wonder (*cākacikyātiśaya*).
Even in the absence of the use of the word *vinā*, if there is an intention to convey the meaning of *vinā* (without), this is indeed *vinokti*.
Likewise, it should be understood that *sahokti* also occurs when there is an intention to convey the meaning of *saha* (together), even in the absence of the use of the word *saha*.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(Vi, Cha) He states "nirarthakam" [meaningless] to show that this is an *alaṃkāra* even in the absence of the word "vinā," provided its meaning is fully realized.
Regarding the word "atra":
the sense is that the attainment of the specific form of *vinokti* arises precisely from their mutual non-perception.
"Thus, even the mention together [is established]" means by the force of the instrumental case alone. —
Locanā:
Anticipating the objection that how there can be *vinokti* here in the absence of the word *vinā*, he says: "In the absence of the word *vinā*...
When the word *saha* is absent, there is still the intention to convey the sense of "together," as in: "Then, by the sprout of Bhārgava’s mature arrogance, the bow of Śiva was suddenly broken."
Whose heart is not pained upon seeing the beauty of the forest deserted by spring, the moonlight deserted by the cool-rayed moon, and a beloved deserted by her husband?
In this context, since "it is not grieved" already implies its lack of propriety, this is simply a *vinokti* (figure of speech based on absence).
*Samāsokti* (synecdoche) occurs where, through the similarity of effects, signs, or adjectives, the behavior of another thing is superimposed upon the subject at hand. (VisSd 10.56)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ja) He states the figure of speech *samāsokti* [as follows]: "The figure of speech called *samāsokti*.

This means the superimposition (*samāropa*) of another object—that is, of an irrelevant (*aprastuta*) thing or its conventional behavior (*vyavahāra*), which is by implication suggested (*vyaṅgya*)—upon the relevant (*prastuta*) object.

"And that indicative mark (*vyañjana*) [is conveyed] by means of equal [words], meaning by those words—whether related to the subject at hand or not—that are common to both the relevant and the irrelevant, through their objects, attributes, or qualifiers.
— *Locanā*:
"This is called *samāsokti* (condensed expression)."
By "equal" (*sama*) is meant identical; it refers to a transaction (*vyavahāra*) performed, and not to itself as in the case of a *rūpaka* (metaphor), nor to another unrelated thing.
Here, through an equal effect (*kārya*), there is the superimposition (*samāropa*) of an unstated transaction upon the subject at hand.
For example:

"O breeze from the Malaya mountain, you alone are blessed, for you forcibly embrace every limb of that lotus-eyed woman, shaking off the garment from her breasts which possess the grace of golden jars."
Here, there is a superimposition of the behavior of a forceful lover upon the wind.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, jha): "Having shaken... [and so on].
"Having shaken off," that is to say, having cast far away, the garment from her breasts;
here, an embrace is to be performed.
The Malaya breeze is the subject under discussion by virtue of being addressed.
Or as it is in my own verse: "O you whose limbs are exceedingly beautiful, who raise up your pair of broad thighs—the abode of dance—and toss up your creeper-like arms;
salutations to you, O meritorious one, purifying in the cool season, whom women with longing minds attend."

"In this case, the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), which is purifying, is to be treated as the object of address (*saṃbodhyatvena*) because it serves as the locus for the superimposition (*āropa*) of the behavior of a heroine.
Locanā:

In the verse beginning with *vyādhūya*, although the similarity of gender (*liṅgasāmya*) is also a factor in the superimposition of the behavior of a forceful lover (*haṭhakāmuka*) upon the wind (*gandhavāha*), this is another example [of superimposition] because the primary factor is the similarity of actions such as the shaking off of clothes (*vasanavyādhūnana*)."
The same should be understood regarding other examples of *samāsokti* (synecdoche),
where there may be a combination of two or even all three— effect, mark (*liṅga*), and attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*)— as the case may be.
An example by way of similarity of marks (*liṅgasāmya*) is as follows:
“What concern for women can there be for a high-minded man who has not yet achieved his desire for conquest?
The sun does not resort to twilight without having traversed the entire world.”
Here, by means of the mere masculine and feminine genders, the behavior of the hero and the heroine is attributed to the sun and the twilight respectively.
*Vijñapriyā*:
[The phrase] "not yet completed" [is used].
The meaning is clear. The example is given for the higher half [of the aeon]. "Sandhyām" means the evening twilight.
In the expression "the conduct of the hero" (*nāyakavyavahāra*), there is an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one term from a pair).
Although here the sun alone is the subject of comparison (*upameya*) by virtue of being the contextual topic (*prakṛta*), and thus the non-contextual (*aprakṛta*),
nevertheless, with respect to the suggested heroine (*vyaṅgyanāyikā*), the expressed sun is relatively contextual (*prakṛta*).
The equality of qualifiers (viśeṣaṇasāmya), however, is threefold: by way of punning (śliṣṭatayā), by way of commonality (sādhāraṇyena), and by way of containing a comparison (aupamyagarbhatvena).
As for "by way of being double-entendre," it is as in my own work—
*Vijñapriyā*: "(vi,
ṭa) 'By way of being double-entendre'."
The meaning is that [the word] itself, being a "śliṣṭa" (double-entendre) word, serves as a qualifier for both.
By the phrase "by way of commonality," the meaning is that the qualifier consisting of the expressed form (ārtharūpa) is common to both.
The state of containing a comparison (*aupamyagarbhatva*) is the superimposition of the designation "irrelevant" (*aprastutatva*) even after the perception of the comparison;
its threefold nature will be explained [later].
— *Locanā* —
"Merely by virtue of being masculine and feminine genders" means by way of being the primary cause; that is,
by way of being connected and having two meanings.
By way of a commonality, through the possession of a single attribute distinguished by a difference in relation:
"Beholding before him the eastern quarter— its face blossomed due to attachment to passion (the sun), its veil of darkness dispelled by the touch of the sun's rays— the man,
his complexion as pale as a ripe lavalī fruit and his inner heart deeply troubled, alas, takes refuge in the green direction (the west)."
But the moon [shone] upon the daughter of the ocean."
In this context, there is the punning nature (*śliṣṭatā*) of words such as "mukharāga" and others.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṭha): [The phrase] "with her face blossomed."
This is a description of the dawn.
Alas, in grief!
Having beheld before him—the eastern quarter—touched by the rays of the sun, like a ripe and hard *lavalī* fruit...
Having become pale in hue, the moon—its interior turbid and its core stained by the dark spot—takes refuge in the western quarter, which is green with *prāyeta* grass.
This is because when the *lavalī* fruit reaches full ripeness, it becomes hard and pale;
and this is observed from the paleness of the moon.
What kind of Aindrī is she? One whose face is blossoming, having come face-to-face with the light,
due to her attachment to passion.
"Due to contact with the redness of the rays, the veil of the form of darkness falls away.
By the word "hanta," there is an expression of distress.
The intended meaning of the sentence is that, seeing his own occupied direction taken over by an adversary, he becomes pale with grief and takes refuge in another quarter of the sky.
Through suggestion (*vyañjanā*), there is the superimposition (*āropa*) of the sun and moon upon the eastern and western directions;
for instance, having seen another hero touching his own heroine— who has a smiling face and whose body-coverings have slipped away due to passion— with his hand,
the hero, pale with grief, abandons her and resorts to another heroine— such is the behavior [suggested].
There is a superimposition (*āropa*) of the eastern wall and the western moon;
and therein, the words *mukha*, *padarāga*, and *kara*—meaning "face," "redness of the feet," and "hand"—are used in their double meanings (*śliṣṭa*). To this he says: "here, *mukha*... —Locanā.
"Vikasita" refers to the beginning of the face and the mouth;
"rāga" refers to redness and attachment.
*Kara*, *kiraṇa*, and *hasta* all mean "hand.

The intention behind the term "conjunction" (*śliṣṭatā*) is that, due to this wordplay (*śleṣa*), the seed for the conduct of the hero—which serves as the purpose for the poetic figure of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*)—is established.

For in this very context, even when there is a metaphorical representation (*rūpaṇa*) of this region by reading "timirāśukam" (a dark garment) instead of "timirāvṛtim" (an envelopment of darkness), it is still simply "suggested complete description" (*samāsokti*).
However, this is not a case of partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka*);

for in that instance, the relationship between the object of comparison (*rūpya*) and the object compared (*rūpaka*)—namely, the darkness and the garment—is such that, because both function as concealers and their similarity is so manifest, they rest solely within themselves even without depending on mutual assistance. Thus, it is not capable of subverting the perception of *samāsokti*.
Locanā:
(lo, e) means "due to manifest similarity," as in the case of the face and the moon;
[it refers to] the assistance of another.
It provides assistance—that is, aid—for the imposition of another word or meaning;
it depends on itself alone and not on another word.

However, where the similarity between the object of comparison (rūpya) and the object compared (rūpaka) is indistinct, that [similarity] would be inconsistent without the imposition of another part; therefore, even when not expressed by words, the imposition of another part necessarily depends on the implied (ārtha) sense.
In that case, it is indeed a *rūpaka* with partial transformation (*ekadeśavivartin*), but not a *rūpaka* with partial transformation [in the sense of the other definition].
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ḍa) It is not, however, a *rūpaka* with partial transformation.
The suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is the delineation of the principal heroine as being [the goddess] Aindrī.
It should be understood that the possibility of this [suggestion] arises because a part of her nature—namely, her garment or the darkness—is expressed as the literal meaning (*vācya*).
He states the reason for its existence here with the words "for in this case" (*atra hi*).
When there is the implication of another metaphor (*rūpaka*) precisely where the relationship between the object of comparison (*rūpin*) and the thing compared (*rūpaka*) is expressed,
and not through its own explicit similarity, that alone is *ekadeśavivartin-rūpaka* (metaphor existing in part) by virtue of implying another expressed metaphor.
An example of this will be shown in the verse beginning with "jassa raṇante."

In the present case, however, because of the clear similarity between the garment (*aṃśuka*) and darkness (*timira*), there is an inherent relationship of the objectified and the objectifier independent of a formal metaphor (*ārtharūpaka*). Therefore, the meaning is that this is not a "partial manifestation" (*ekadeśavivartinī*). "Independent" means resting solely within itself.
[The author] now shows the scope of the "partial manifestation."
The meaning of the gloss "non-verbal" (*aśābda*) is "the suggested" (*vyaṅgya*). For example:
"In whose inner harem of battle, while he was making a circle with his sword-blade..."
"Even the enemy army, though facing toward passion, suddenly turns its back."
In this case, the similarity between the battlefield and the inner apartments is indeed not explicit. *Vijñapriyā* (vi, ḍha): "Of him, at the end of the battle... etc.
“In whose inner palace of battle, as he wields the blade of his sword,
the enemy army— even when facing him with passion— suddenly turns its back.”
Thus it is observed:
the creeper at the edge of the mandala is the sword-creeper;
the essence is indeed the essence of battle.
In the context of the suggested rival heroine (*pratināyikā*), there is the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*).
She turns her face away out of fear;
that very shyness causes the turning away of the face by making it dependent upon another.

The battlefield itself is the harem (*antaḥpura*), because it suggests a heroine who is metaphorically represented as a dagger (*maṇḍalāgra*) by virtue of being the referent of a word in the feminine gender. Even for the king who wields it in his own hand, his role as the hero (*nāyaka*) is suggested.

Furthermore, when the enemy army has been defeated, the opposing heroine (*pratināyikā*)—metaphorically represented as the referent of a word in the feminine gender—is also suggested. In this context, the metaphorical representation of the battlefield as a harem is a "partial metaphor" (*ekadeśavivartin*).

Locanā: (lo, ai) Anticipating the question, "In that case, what then is the scope of the *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest) metaphor? she says: "In that regard, however... [and quotes: “jassa raṇantaura” (of whom the shore of the battle...).

In such passages as this, the partial metaphorical identification (*ekadeśavivartinī rūpaka*) of the battle and the inner apartments—where the sword-blade and the creeper are respectively the object of comparison (*rūpya*) and the object of superimposition (*rūpaka*)—is indeed not explicit without the superimposition (*āropa*) of the status of queen and so forth upon the sword-blade and the creeper.
As for the verse beginning with *jassa*: "Of him who, in the inner apartments of battle, holds the creeper of the sword-blade in his hand..."
Even when facing the enemy, the hostile army suddenly turns its back.

The *rasas* are enthusiasm (*utsāha*) and affection (*anurāga*). Furthermore, in cases where there is a verbal representation (*rūpaṇa*) of many things that possess clear similarity, and where the representation of one part is achieved through the sense (*artha*), there it is indeed *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest) *rūpaka*. Vijñapriyā: [Commentary] *Rasa* refers here to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) consisting of enthusiasm and affection. Moreover, when there is a verbal depiction (*śābda-rūpaṇa*) of numerous objects despite their having a manifest similarity, and the depiction of a single part is understood through the power of the meaning (*ārtha*), in such instances it is specifically the *ekadeśavivartin* type of *rūpaka*. This occurs when the metaphorical identification of the whole is not explicitly stated, but is instead inferred from the description of its constituent parts. Thus, it is distinguished from other types of *rūpaka*.

(Vi, ṇa) But if it is the case that partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivartitva*) occurs only when there is an unmanifest similarity, then how [is this to be explained]: "Whom does her blossoming face, filled with the honey of loveliness, not intoxicate, like a swarm of bees that are the eyes of the world?"
"Thus has an example of partial transformation (*ekadeśavivartin*) been provided.

In that instance, because the similarity between the sweetness of the honey of loveliness—which culminates in its being desirable—and the eyes, as well as the similarity in the form of flickering between the eyes and the bees, are explicit, [the author] says: 'Where...'"—thus [ends] Locanā.
In cases such as "filled in some places with the honey of loveliness" (*kvacillāvaṇyamadhubhiḥ pūrṇām*) and "the hand on the mountain of sunrise" (*karam udayamahīdhare*),
because the perception of *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) is all-pervasive, it obscures the perception of *samāsokti* (condensed expression).
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ta) To the question, "What is the reasoning for the claim that when there is a multiplicity of clear similarities and so forth, there is 'partial transformation' (*ekadeśavivartin*)?", he says: "Because of the cognition of *rūpaka*.
Due to its pervasiveness and multiplicity, and by virtue of that multiplicity, its arising first constitutes a contradiction to *samāsokti*.
Locanā:
(lo, au) The meaning is that it is because [the word] pervades and rests upon multiple words.
Now, one might object: "Is there not also a clear similarity between the end of battle (*raṇānta*) and the inner apartments (*puraya*), insofar as both are places where one can move about with ease?"
Locanā:

(Lo, a) Because it is a place for effortless dwelling due to its ease of movement, it is by its very nature the abode of the central deity of the mandala and so forth; thus, without depending on the superimposition of the status of a heroine and so on, what you have said is true.
It certainly exists, but it is dependent upon a thorough consideration of the meaning of the sentence, and not independent of it;
for, unlike the loveliness of the moon-like face and so forth, there is no inherent ease of movement within the garden or the inner apartments.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
tha) She anticipates the objection that there is indeed a clear similarity even between the harem and the inner apartments— namely, "But it exists"—
and states that [the objection] depends upon a thorough consideration of the meaning of the sentence.

The meaning is that by seeing the king, the enemy army turns its back; by observing the king’s intent toward the adversary, one gains knowledge of his heroism and, consequently, his fearlessness in battle; and from that very fact, one gains the ability to move about freely.
This is because, otherwise, there would be no natural freedom of movement between the battlefield and the inner apartments.

The point is that, unlike the charm of the moon-like face [of the king], the ease of movement in battle cannot be understood through perception or other means without the notion of fearlessness on the part of the king.

In this context, regarding the phrase "due to the lack of movement between the battlefield and the inner apartments," the reading "due to the absence of the state of being a movement" found in some places is merely a scribal error.
An example by way of commonality (sādhāraṇya) is as follows:
“Adorned by the song of bees wandering about her natural fragrance,
the lotus plant blossomed with a smile when the lord of the day had risen.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) Regarding "by nature" (*nisargataḥ*): here, the heroine who is not the subject of the context (*aprastuta-nāyikā*) is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
And according to that interpretation, the compound is: "she who is both one whose [face] is bewildered by the natural fragrance of her face and one who is endowed with song.
Likewise, *vāsaram* means the day itself;
the meaning is: "when the master of that house—the lord of the home—has risen."
In this context, according to the manner shown, the heroine does not fall [into the category of *nāyikā*] because of the qualifying term "by nature" (*nisarga*).
Locanā:
"Smiling" (*smerā*) means possessing a slight smile.

In this case, because of the similarity of the qualifiers beginning with "nisarga" (natural), the cognition of the behavior of a heroine (*nāyikā*) in the lotus plant (*sarojinī*) is caused by the superimposition (*samāropa*) of the attribute of "smiling," which belongs to women in general.
*Locanā*:
[This is so] because the attribute of "smiling," which pertains only to women, is applied to the lotus plant only through figurative usage (*upacāra*).
The *kāraṇa* (cause) is the primary factor,
while for the others, it is merely the assistance of its power;
for without that, the cognition of the heroine's behavior cannot occur through the mere similarity of attributes.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, dha) Since that [the smile] is established even by its merely conveying the incident concerning the heroine, the lotus, it is necessary to state that the qualification "smiling" (*smera*) is specifically intended to convey that; therefore, he says:
"In this [verse], *nisarga*... and so forth.
"Merely a woman"; by the word "merely," Sarojinī is excluded.
Likewise, [it excludes] Sarojinī.

The meaning is that, by virtue of the superimposition of the state of being smiling upon the blossoming of flowers, that [state] becomes a common attribute (sādhāraṇadharma); and such a superimposition is the cause for the perception of the heroine's behavior.
"By the mere similarity of the adjectives" means: by the mere similarity of the adjectives beginning with "naisargika" (natural) and so forth.
"Because it is impossible" means that this is established by the very example of the sun and the lotus.
Furthermore, the state of containing a comparison occurs in three ways.
Because it contains within it a confusion between simile and metaphor.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, na): "Upamārūpaka" [means]...

The meaning is: [this occurs] when there is an internal simile (*upamāgarbha*), an internal metaphor (*rūpakagarbha*), and when there is a combination based on doubt (*sandehasaṅkaragarbha*) between simile and metaphor.
Furthermore, "having it as its core" (*garbhatva*) means being preceded by the cognition of that [simile or metaphor].
Nor should it be asked how a figure containing a metaphor can be a sub-variety of one containing a simile; [for they are not mutually exclusive].
Since even a metaphorical representation (*rūpaka*) produces similarity, it must first be understood before that similarity is produced; for this reason, he says:
"In that regard, an example of its being pregnant with a simile (*upamā*) is as follows:
'Adorned with the flower-like luster of her teeth, beautified by sprout-like hands...'"
The deer-eyed woman was beautifully attired with a mass of hair like a swarm of bees.

Here, because of her exquisite beauty, there is first a compound based on a simile, namely that "the luster of her teeth is like flowers. Subsequently, by resorting to another compound—namely, "covered with flowers resembling the luster of her teeth"—and through the power of these identical adjectives (*samānaviśeṣaṇa*), the conventional designation of a "creeper" (*latā*) is perceived in the gazelle-eyed woman.
*Vijñapriyā*:

Regarding the phrase "tadantaprabhā" (the luster of those teeth): here, the compound is an *upamā-samāsa* (simile compound) based on the rule for compounds such as *puruṣavyāghra* (tiger-like man), following the pattern "the lusters of the teeth are like flowers," and so forth.
It should not be argued that this is merely a *rūpaka* (metaphor) based on the pattern "the luster of the teeth is itself the flower," and so forth.
Because there exist two subverting factors against *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification).

To explain: first, by Pāṇini’s rule, “That which is compared with [words such as] *vyāghra* and others occurs when the common property (*sāmānya*) is not employed,” the compound of *rūpaka* is subverted when the common property is not employed; thus, since the compound of *upamā* (simile) alone is established in that case, this constitutes one subverting factor.
The author himself states the second [point]: "here, by virtue of being well-dressed.
This is the intended meaning:
dress consists of those properties that are superimposed [upon it].

Because the bracelets, earrings, vermilion, and so forth, as well as the luster of the teeth and so forth, are superimposed as attributes residing in the attributes of the heroine; and because the perception of a beautiful appearance cannot be established by those [ornaments] distinct from the flowers and so forth, he states that first, in the case where the luster of the teeth and so forth are the subjects, there is indeed a *vyāghrādi* compound— namely, "by way of containing a simile" (*upamāgarbhatvena*).

"Is it not the case that even so, the same inconsistency remains, because it is impossible for [the word] to possess its own qualities as a well-attired [subject]? To this, he says: "And immediately thereafter.

The meaning is this: since it is impossible for words uttered only once to produce cognition through both primary signification (*śakti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*) more than once, this meaning of the compound of comparison—having "flowers" and so forth as the qualificand—is shown to be purely suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Either by virtue of *tātparya* (intentional meaning) or through its own expressive power (*śakti*), it brings about the understanding of the sentence.

Furthermore, the possession of "fine attire" (*suveṣatva*) and "possibility" (*upapattikatva*) serves as the indicator of the intention behind the two compounds. By means of that, he states the justification for the possibility of fine attire: "by the power of the common qualifiers" (*samānaviśeṣaṇamāhātmyāt*).
Because both [compounds] consist of two members, there is a similarity due to their shared qualifiers.
The meaning is that each individual qualifier is formed by a single compound.
The conventional usage of the term "creeper" (latā) refers to such things as her graceful movements (*lāsya*) and so forth. — *Locanā* —
(Lo, ī) Because of the power of the word *suveṣā* (well-attired), which arises from the necessity of being well-attired;

for that [quality] resides primarily in the heroine (*nāyikā*) and not in the creeper (*latā*). Thus, it is only the attributes of the heroine—such as the luster of her teeth—that serve as the basis for the object of comparison (*upameya*), and not the employment of the term *hariṇekṣaṇā* (deer-eyed one).
This is because the application of a compound is established solely in relation to a word other than the one being expressed [as the subject];

otherwise, even in cases such as *dāse kṛtāgasī* ("the servant who has committed an offense"), where a metaphorical compound (*rūpaka-samāsa*) is traditionally accepted, there would instead have to be a comparative compound (*upamā-samāsa*) in the phrase *pulakāṅkurakaṇṭakāgraiḥ* ("by the tips of the thorns of hair-pores") due to its conformity with the mentioned heroine.
In another type of compound, due to the force of the collection [of parts] being rendered intolerable,
there is the presence of an internal metaphor (*rūpakagarbhatva*), as in:
"filled with the honey of loveliness," and so forth.

Vijñapriyā: (vi, pha) Regarding the phrase "the honey of loveliness"— it should not be argued that since only an example of a partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivartin-rūpaka*) was previously mentioned, how can there be a case of synecdoche (*samāsokti*) here?
According to the traditional view, in cases of partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivartin-rūpaka*), the status of *samāsokti* is accepted everywhere regarding the suggested element of similarity;
however, as will be clarified later, this is not accepted in instances where a specific [common] attribute is involved.
In the present case, even though a common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) is not employed, there is no *upamā-samāsa* (compound based on simile).
It cannot be argued that because drinking is impossible for that which possesses a beauty equal to honey,
whereas drinking is indeed possible for honey if it were a metaphorical representation—
and furthermore, since it is the mouth itself that is said to drink here, drinking is impossible for it in either case. This is not a valid objection.
"Affirmation and negation accompanied by qualifiers apply to the qualifier when there is no cognition of the qualified object"—
according to this maxim, because the connection occurs with the honey itself [as the qualified],
as in the example containing *saṅkara* (commixture), such as "The flowers of the luster of her teeth... and so forth.
In the reading "parītā" for "suveṣā," since there is no evidence to establish either simile (upamā) or metaphor (rūpaka), one must resort to the figure of commingling (saṅkara).
The compound is to be analyzed as before.
Through the power of this alternative analysis, the perception of a creeper arises.
Vijñapriyā:

Regarding the reading "parīta," since being well-dressed cannot occur through one's own inherent nature (*nijadharma*), it is shown that its existence is possible only through the two successive compounds; therefore, there is no confusion between *rūpaka* and *upamā* based on doubt in that instance.

However, in the reading *parīta*, the sense is that since pervasion (*vyāpti*) by flowers and lovelinesses is possible through the state of being *parīta*, there indeed arises a doubt between the simile (*upamā*) and the metaphor (*rūpaka*) via two distinct compounds.

Nor should it be argued that the absence of the application of a common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) precludes the metaphor in favor of the simile; for when a metaphor is possible, it is not thus precluded.
Because the sublation of the *rūpaka* (metaphor) occurs due to the force of its being well-dressed (*suveṣatva*), and because such sublation has already been demonstrated previously;
[the author] causes one to grasp the mixture (*saṅkara*) with doubt, stating "for here...
and "another compound."

The syntactical connection is as follows: due to the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamakābhāva*), there is the cognition of a creeper (*latā*) from either of the two compounds, just as before.
He states the reason for this: "by the power of the other compound" (*samāsāntaramahimnā*).
In this context, the "other compound" is the metaphorical compound (*rūpaka-samāsa*).

In the example of a "partial metaphor" (*ekadeśavivartirūpaka*)—namely, "filled with the honey of loveliness"—the presence of *samāsokti* is likewise demonstrated according to the traditional school's doctrine.
*Locanā*:
[This is so] because there is no evidence [to the contrary].
Because the quality of being "limited" (parītatva) applies equally to the fawn-eyed woman and to the creeper,
it is said to be "based on a combination" (saṅkarasamāśrayeṇa).
Here, "combination" (saṅkara) refers to the combination of simile (upamā), metaphor (rūpaka), and doubt (sandeha).
Based on that [metaphor], the compound has its form determined;
it is of the type previously described as "strewn with flowers resembling the luster of teeth.
In the expression "the perception of a creeper," the word *latā* (creeper) emphasizes the state (*bhāva*).

Furthermore, in the opinion of those for whom partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivartin*) does not exist within the categories of Simile (*upamā*) and Conflation (*saṅkara*), the first and third types [of *samāsokti*] are considered *samāsokti*;
however, the second type pertains exclusively to the domain of partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivartin-rūpaka*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, bha) However, some do not accept *samāsokti* in this case of *ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka*, but rather maintain that it exists only when it contains an *upamā* or its *saṃkara*.
Since the sublation of the *rūpaka*-compound has not been demonstrated therein, he presents their view with the words "And in these... (*eṣu ca*).
The first [example] begins with "the luster of his teeth" (*dantaprabhā*) and so forth;
the third is distinguished by the reading *parītattva*.

Thus, the second example, stated as "by the honey-like loveliness" (*lāvaṇyamadhurair*) and so forth, pertains exclusively to the domain of metaphor (*rūpaka*) and not to the domain of synecdoche (*samāsokti*).

In the case of *vyaṅgyarūpaka* (implied metaphor), such as in the verse beginning with "dantaprabhā" (the luster of teeth), the lotus-nature of the face is suggested, while the honey-nature of its attributes like beauty (*lāvaṇya*) and so forth is expressed; thus, it is a *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest) metaphor due to the presence of the qualifier "well-dressed" (*suveṣatva*). However, upon careful consideration, it is more appropriate to accept that in the first type [of this category], it is actually a *ekadeśavivartin* simile (*upamā*) that should be admitted. *Vijñapriyā*: [This is the commentary on the above.]

(Vi, Ma) Regarding the thorough investigation [of the verse], however, the author states his own view: "But upon thorough investigation," and so forth. He asserts that there is neither *samāsokti* nor *ekadeśavivarttirūpaka*, but rather only *ekadeśavivarttyupamā*.
In the compound (*samāsa*), because the particle *iva* is elided, the comparison of honey and so forth with loveliness and so forth is expressed (*vācya*).

However, the comparison with the heroine is suggested (*vyaṅgya*); thus, by the use of the restrictive particle *eva* ("only"), he excludes *samāsokti* and establishes that it is indeed only *ekadeśavivarttyupamā*.
He states that "the exclusion of that [other meaning], however, arises from the close consideration of it" with the words "But upon close consideration.

Regarding what was said—that *samāsokti* (condensed expression) occurs when there is a similarity of qualifiers—the qualifier possesses two types of characteristics: commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*) and punning (*śliṣṭatva*).
Thus, these two varieties alone are appropriate.
The third type, consisting of that which contains a simile within it (*aupamyagarbha*), is not appropriate.

In that case, once the understanding of the compound *dantaprabhāpuṣpam iva* (like the flower of the luster of teeth) as a simile is established, the understanding of *hariṇekṣaṇā latā iva* (the deer-eyed woman is like a creeper) follows even without the fabrication of two separate compounds; such is the consideration.

Thus, since the method of the first type is also possible in the third type, the intention here is that there is no instance of *samāsokti* (speech by means of a compound) characterized by an internal simile (*upamāgarbhaviśeṣaṇika*) in that [third] case either, but rather it is simply a case of *ekadeśavivartinī upamā* (a simile residing in one part).
The phrase "in the first type" is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Locanā:

(lo, ū) And here, although there is thus a possibility of threefold division for that which contains a comparison (*aupamyagarbha*), the second example pertains exclusively to the domain of *ekadeśavivartin* metaphor; therefore, there is no contradiction between what preceded and what follows. Thus he says: "Among these..."
And thus: the first [verse] is the stanza beginning with "The luster of her teeth" (*dantaprabhā*);
the third is that same [stanza], but here it is joined with the reading *parīta* in place of *suveṣā*.
The second [type] is established in verses such as "Filled with the honey of loveliness" (*lāvaṇyamadhubhiḥ pūrṇam*).
He states that the first and third types are not *samāsokti* (condensed expression) by saying:
"But upon close examination," meaning upon a thorough investigation or discernment according to reality, because there is the cognition: "She is like a creeper with gazelle-like eyes."
Otherwise—
Vijñapriyā:
"Otherwise" means [as follows].
The meaning is that the assumption of two compounds is merely a forced construction when *samāsokti* (speech of compounding) is accepted in instances where a comparison is inherent.
To the question, "How can there be *samāsokti* in cases where the assumption of two compounds is impossible due to being a forced construction? he says:
"The autumn, bearing a rainbow upon her pale cloud-breast, resembling a fresh nail-mark..."
While delighting the spotted moon, she increased the heat of the sun beyond measure.”
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ra) "The rainbow of Indra"—

bearing the rainbow of Indra, which resembles fresh nail-marks due to the comparison with her pale cloud-like breasts, she propitiates the spotted moon, making it clear and stainless, surpassing the autumnal sun.
The meaning is that it spread heat;
for in autumn, because the clouds are pale, the moon is stainless due to the absence of cloud-obscuration, and the sun’s heat is excessive.
Here, by means of the "pale-cloud-breasted" [woman], there is the implication of a rival woman with a fair bosom bearing fresh nail-marks, acting as the one who departs.

Through *samāsokti* (synecdoche), there is the perception of a heroine who, while conciliating her lover who is stained [by jealousy], causes her husband to experience an intensification of his distress by pointing that out; and through that same figure, there is the perception of the autumn season, which shares those same characteristics.
— *Locanā*.
(Lo, ṛ) "Aindram" refers to the cloud and the breast. "Prasādanam" means the act of making clear or purifying.
And *paritoṣaṇa* means satisfaction;
*kalaṅka* means a mark, as well as a defect such as one's lineage.
"Torment" refers to heat, sunlight, and mental fever.
It has been stated that there is the perception of the autumn season as the heroine (nāyikā),
because it is precisely its specific qualities that have ascended to the stage of deliberation.
When the sun and the moon function as the hero (nāyaka) and the antagonist (pratināyaka), that very [moon] occupies the primary position as the cause.
Because the words "stained" (sakalaṅka) and "heat" (tāpa) describe the primary entities— the sun and the moon— and because they are not restricted to the subject of the hero,
their status as objects of comparison (upamāna) is understood through the word "ābha."
It must be correctly understood through the examination of the object and its investigation;
the sense is that [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of the subsequent arising [of the cognition], as in the case of the "bow-like" [form].
Thus, in this context, how can there be the perception of the conduct of a heroine in autumn?
Because it is impossible for the heroine’s breast to bear the rainbow of Indra appearing as a fresh nail-mark;

[the meaning of] *Vijñapriyā* is: if one accepts the presence of a *samāsokti* containing a simile (*upamāgarbha*), and if there is a restriction to two compounds when that [simile] is contained within them, then how could such a figure exist?

In the phrase "resembling a fresh nail-scratch," since the word *ābhā* (resembling), which indicates a simile (*upamā*), is present, a metaphor (*rūpaka*) is impossible. Furthermore, in a compound expressing a simile (*upamāsamāsa*), the rainbow (*aindraṃ dhanuḥ*) cannot attain similarity with a fresh nail-scratch. Moreover, since the heroine lacks that specific attribute, and because that attribute does not possess the quality of being common to both the autumn season and the heroine, how can there be a "similarity of attributes" (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*), and how can it [the compound] contain a simile within itself?
Or, considering how there could be the conception of two [meanings] contained within a compound, he says: "by the heroine’s breast.
Thus, there is no *samāsokti* (metaphorical identification) containing a simile (*upamā*) at all;
rather, this is simply a *samāsokti* with punning adjectives (*śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇikā*), involving the words *payodhara*, *prasādayantī*, *sakalaṅka*, and *tāpa*.

By this, it has been stated that [the figure] is characterized by a unique internal simile (*naupamyagarbhaviśeṣaṇikā*). Now, one might object: although the status of being a standard of comparison (*upamānatva*) resides in the phrase "resembling a fresh nail-scratch," it must, upon consideration of the actual subject matter, be transferred to Indra’s bow (the rainbow). Vijñapriyā: [This is not so. For in the case of "resembling a fresh nail-scratch," the status of being a standard of comparison is indeed established; however, because the primary subject under discussion is the rainbow, the status of being the object of comparison (*upameyatva*) is transferred to the fresh nail-scratch. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the definition of *Rūpaka* (Metaphor), which consists in the imposition of the nature of the object of comparison upon the standard of comparison. Furthermore, since the status of being a standard of comparison is already present in the phrase "resembling a fresh nail-scratch," its transfer to the rainbow is merely a restatement of what is already established. Consequently, the status of being a standard of comparison does not need to be transferred to anything else. Thus, the objection is refuted. Moreover, the status of being a standard of comparison is not transferred to the rainbow because the word "resembling" (*-ābha*) is used as a qualifier for the fresh nail-scratch. If the status of being a standard of comparison were transferred to the rainbow, the word "resembling" would have to be construed with the rainbow, and the compound would have to be analyzed as "that which resembles a fresh nail-scratch" (*ārdranakhakṣatam ivābhātīti*). However, since the word "resembling" is used as a qualifier for the fresh nail-scratch, the compound is analyzed as "that which resembles a fresh nail-scratch" (*ārdranakhakṣatam ivety ārdranakhakṣatābham*). Therefore, the status of being a standard of comparison remains fixed in the fresh nail-scratch and is not transferred to the rainbow. Hence, the objection is refuted. Furthermore, the status of being a standard of comparison is not transferred to the rainbow because the word "resembling" is used as a qualifier for the fresh nail-scratch. (Vi, Va) Now, in the phrase "resembling a fresh nail-wound," the fresh nail-wound is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the rainbow of Indra is the object of comparison (*upameya*).
Since the connection with the act of bearing is understood only in relation to the standard of comparison, its impossibility [in the case of the object] has been demonstrated.

However, one should understand that the state of being the standard of comparison (*upamānatva*) belongs to the fresh nail-mark with respect to the bow, while the state of being the object of comparison (*upameyatva*) belongs to the wound.

Thus, since the bearing of such a wound is indeed possible for the breast, this too is simply a *samāsokti* containing a simile; so how can there be a loss of the *samāsokti* containing a simile? With this in mind, he raises the objection: "But surely... (*nanu*).
"Even though it remains" means even though it remains on the nail-scratches;
this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).
It should also be understood that the state of being the object of comparison (*upameyatva*), which resides in the bow, must likewise be transferred to the nail-marks;
for it is precisely that transfer which serves the purpose of supporting the breasts under discussion.
This is [the meaning] by way of thorough consideration (*paryālocanayā*).
The meaning is: "by means of reflecting upon such a sense through the punning connection (*śleṣa*) of words such as *payodhara* (cloud/breast).
For example, in cases such as "He offers oblation with curds" (*dadhnā juhoti*), since the act of offering could otherwise be accomplished, the injunction is transferred to the curds.
If it is argued that, in the same way, there will arise the cognition: "She bears a fresh nail-mark resembling Indra’s bow (the rainbow)"?
No; for rather than postulating a difficult creation [of meaning] through such an interpretation, it is more appropriate to accept the *ekadeśavivartin* type of simile.
In the *Vijñapriyā*, [the author] provides an example of the transfer of a meaning conveyed by a word in one place to another, stating: "Just as with *dadhnā*... (Vi, Śa).
By means of the verb, it is understood that the act of offering (*havana*) is relevant to the context of holding the breast;

for the act of offering is already established by another statement in the form of a sentence, namely, "one offers with the oblation" (*haviṣā juhoti*). And considering that what is already established cannot be the object of an injunction (*vidheya*), that alone is the object of the injunction which is not yet established.
Therefore, the meaning is that [the quality] is transferred to the curd;
for otherwise, the status of the curd as the instrument of the oblation would not be established from any other source.
