And thus, by this method, the bearing of nail-marks—which are the counter-subjects—upon the breast becomes possible.
Thus, there certainly exists the figure of speech known as *samāsokti* (speech of compendium) which contains an internal simile (*upamā*).
To the question "How can there be its [the simile's] elision?", he says: "In such a resolution.
This means: by means of such a resolution.

The meaning is that since only the acceptance of *ekadeśavivartin* (partial manifestation) simile is [valid], there is no such thing as a *samāsokti* (speech of condensation) containing a simile (*upamāgarbha*). — *Locanā*.

(Lo, ṝ) He provides an example for the case where the meaning obtained through the power of the word’s expressive capacity (*śabdaśakti*) is found to be otherwise upon further reflection—beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*).
A "prescription" (*vidhi*) is an instruction regarding what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*).

For here, although the instruction prescribing the oblation (*homa*) is understood from the root *juhoti* in the sense of "one should offer," nevertheless, in that which is obtainable from another sentence...

In that case, according to the principle that "the scripture is meaningful only when [the matter] has not already been established," the instruction would be as futile as grinding what is already ground; therefore, the instruction culminates precisely in the aspect of curd being the instrument (*karaṇatva*), which had not yet been stated.
He demonstrates the mechanism of transference in the present example: for comprehension arises from thorough reflection.
"Of such a kind" means this:
it is improper to transfer a comparison to a rainbow in the manner just described, as one would transfer the injunction for offering curd into the fire.

For it is established by logic that words possess the status of being "in the process of being accomplished" (*sādhyamānatā*) due to their connection with their own actions which bring about the primary action;
therefore, there is a transference of the injunction (*vidhi-sañcaraṇa*) to the curd.

In the case of the phrase *ārdranakhakṣatābham*, because the meaning of the word *ābha* (resembling) and the comparison itself are connected through their relation to the "fresh nail-mark," if one were to transfer them to the rainbow—which is connected [to the mark] by abandoning that [relation]—there would be a disparity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*), and thus the construction would fail.

In cases such as "Aindraṃ dhanuḥ" (Indra’s bow), there is *arthāpatti* (presumption). For in "Aindraṃ dhanuḥ" and similar instances, while the [word] primarily functions in its literal sense, there exists the presence of actions such as "pleasing," which serve as the illuminators (*uddīpaka*) for the *samāsokti* (speech of compression) through the specific feature of mere comparison. Since this is established without effort—being superior to the conceptualization of that difficult process of transference (*sañcāraṇa*) which is not natural—it is more excellent. Thus, in "Aindraṃ dhanuḥ" and so forth, there is *arthāpatti*. In "Aindraṃ dhanuḥ" and the like, although it functions primarily in its direct sense, there is the existence of the act of pleasing and so on, which specifically serves as the stimulus for the *samāsokti* based on mere comparison.
This is due to its power;

or rather, let there be a *samāsokti* (synecdochic metaphor) here in some way or another, as in the case of "with eyes as it were with blue lotuses, with lotuses... and so forth, because no other interpretation is possible.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṣa) [Objection: "Surely, because it has been stated by the ancients, one must also accept the conception of a 'painful creation' (*kaṣṭasṛṣṭi*).

However, since the 'partially transformative simile' (*ekadeśavivartyupamā*) was not mentioned by the ancients and is not seen in their examples, it should not be accepted. To show that it *is* seen in examples, he says: "Or let it be," etc.
“In ‘netrorivotpalaiḥ’ and so forth: ‘At every step, the beauties of the lakes shone with blue lotuses like eyes, with lotuses like faces, and with ruddy geese like breasts.’”
In this context, regarding the example of *ekadeśavivartin* simile, the meaning is that there is no other possible way [to classify it] than as a "difficult creation" (*kaṣṭasṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, since a *samāsokti* (speech of ellipsis) containing a simile is impossible here, the remainder must be supplied as follows: "it is indeed nothing but an *ekadeśavivartin* simile."

Nor should it be argued that here too one might transpose the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison—saying "with eyes like lotuses"—and ask how there could be any other alternative. For in that case, since the beauty of the lake would be understood through its eyes and so forth, the final meaning would result in "the heroine is like the beauty of the lake," which would lead to the failure of the intended description of the lake's beauty.
Furthermore, since there is no cognition of a conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) in a simile (*upamā*), how can there be an entry for *samāsokti*, which depends upon that [simile]?
As they say:
[Vijñapriyā] (vi, sa):

But if this is so, then how is there no loss of the figure *samāsokti* based on a simile in the case of "dantaprabhaiḥ" (with the luster of teeth), and how is there no loss of the *ekadeśavivartinī upamā* (simile with partial manifestation) in the case of "netrairivotpalaiḥ" (as if with lotuses that are eyes)?
To this he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
Locanā:
On the contrary, because there exists a valid means of establishing the simile in the phrase "as if with lotuses for eyes" (*netrairivotpalaiḥ*), [the objection does not hold].

Furthermore, as for what was stated by the *Rāghavānandas*—that similarity of gender (*liṅgasāmya*) residing in the lake (*saraḥ*) is the cause for the figure of speech *samāsokti* (speech through ellipsis)—that is incorrect, because there is no means to establish the cognition of the conventional usage [required for such a transfer].
If *samāsokti* were to be perceived through mere similarity of gender, then [in the verse]: "O friend, it is seen... [the figure would apply inappropriately].
Because there would be an over-extension [of the definition] even in cases such as "the cool-rayed moon" (śītāṃśu) and so forth;
for it has been stated by you yourself immediately thereafter that *samāsokti* is employed only with reference to what is under discussion.
Therefore, if one asks: "How then, even in your own view, can there be the cognition of *samāsokti* when there is a similarity of gender?"

Regarding the presence of two or three [conditions]— namely, similarity of function (*samānakāryatva*), similarity of mark (*liṅgasāmya*), and a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*)— among the objects of description (*lakṣya*), linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) occurs primarily based on that [specific condition].
Furthermore, as for what they themselves have stated— that there is also poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) in examples such as "as if with eyes that are blue lotuses"—
that is utterly inappropriate.
Because a determination [of identity] does not arise in the absence of a cause [for such identification].

Furthermore, if this were the case, then in instances such as "The deer-eyed woman shines with her face as if with a lotus," there would be a coalescence of *samāsokti* and *utprekṣā* through the superimposition of the conventional designation of a lotus upon the deer-eyed woman. Subsuming all of this within its core meaning, he shows the consensus of the ancient masters by stating: "As they say."
“Whether it be conventional usage or reality, that which is perceived through comparison is not true comparison; rather, it is clearly *samāsokti* (synecdoche) or *ekadeśopamā* (partial simile).”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ha) Regarding the phrase "or [it is] usage":

having stated the fault consisting of a laborious construction due to the mention of a transposition of the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison in examples such as *aindraṃ dhanuḥ* ("the rainbow of Indra"), he states another fault in accepting the presence of a simile (*aupamya*) within a *samāsokti*.
"Give!"—this is the verse.
Therefore, the phrase "or else" (athavā) indicates that this is a distinct type of refutation.

For, whereas in *samāsokti* based on the cause of similarity with *kāvyaliṅga* and so forth, a superimposition (*samāropa*) is perceived according to worldly convention, in this case, such an essence of comparison (*aupamyagarbhatva*) is not perceived from that [superimposition].
Therefore, it follows that the *samāsokti* (condensed expression) based on comparison should not be accepted;

rather, in such cases, it is clear that only the *ekadeśopamā* (partial simile), specifically the *ekadeśavivartinī upamā*, applies. Thus, it has been stated that there is no *samāsokti* containing a comparison at all.
Locanā: (Lo,
e) If worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) is understood through comparison (*aupamya*)— as in *samāsokti* it is through ellipsis, and as in *rūpaka* it is through metaphorical identification—
then that would not be *samāsokti* containing a comparison (*aupamyagarbhaka*).
For this very reason, the author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva* has also stated:

"In such cases as 'with eyes like blue lotuses,' the perception of the lake's splendor as a heroine does not arise through *samāsokti* (synecdoche), because there is an absence of similarity in the adjectives;
therefore, in this instance, the heroine is perceived only as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*)."
However, since the lake is not perceived as the heroine by virtue of its being the *dharmatva* (essential nature) of Śrī,
it is simply a case of "partial manifestation" (*ekadeśavivartin*) simile that is being employed.

By this [analysis], in examples such as "the flowers of the luster of her teeth," because there is the possibility of compounds consisting of either similes or metaphors for the words, [there is no contradiction] between the deer-eyed woman and the creeper.

Even though it is possible for [the word] to function as a qualifier, and even though the aforementioned reasoning applies to cases such as "Indra’s thunderbolt" (*aindraṃ dhanuḥ*), one must necessarily accept the figure of speech known as *ekadeśavivartinī upamā* (partial metaphor) according to the method described; therefore, its usage is properly accounted for by this alone.
Thus says the traditional saying: "If one should find honey on an arka tree, why would one go to the mountain?"

Thus, if one accepts that both simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*) involve the partial manifestation (*ekadeśavivartin*) of their constituent parts, then even when there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of those two bases, its non-inclusion within *samāsokti* (speech of compendium) is established by logic alone; therefore, being "elicited by a qualifying attribute containing a comparison" is not the province of this [figure].
— *Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ka) Since the same logic applies when both simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*) are "partially transformed" (*ekadeśavivartin*), *samāsokti* does not enter into either case; thus, he states that *samāsokti* is also absent in instances where there is a "blend of doubt" (*sandehasaṅkara*) between those two—namely, "And so," etc. [He says] "This is not its domain."
The meaning is: "of this concise statement" (*samāsokti*).
Locanā:

(lo, ai) Regarding the mixture based on that [concise statement] in examples such as *dantaprabhā* ("the luster of teeth"), some have remarked that it is redundant if the reading is *parīta* ("surrounded").

Regarding the claim that "in the case of a confusion of doubt (*sandeha-saṅkara*), because there is no fixed determination due to being a locus of doubt, there is an absence of both metaphor (*rūpaka*) and simile (*upamā*)," that is not correct.

For the figure of speech called "confusion of doubt" occurs when two [possibilities] persist at the end [of the process] as neither deficient nor excessive, due to the absence of any evidence for or against either.
It does not occur, however, in a state where one knows there is no doubt—such as "Is it a post or a man?"—where one of the two might be false in some cases, or both might be false in others.
Otherwise, the similarity between the crown and other ornaments mentioned by the ancients as being in contact with necklaces, rings, and so forth would be untenable.
Furthermore, it is not correct to say that the resolution of the "confusion of doubt" (sandehasaṅkara) is impossible to achieve,
because its aesthetic charm (vaicitrya) is established by experience, and that alone constitutes its status as an ornament.
Furthermore, the ancients maintain that *saṅkara* (admixture) occurs through the blending [of figures] according to the analogy of milk and water;
and by such blending, there arises the existence of one or both [figures].
However, in this context, the designation of *sandeha-saṅkara* (admixture of doubt) is used merely on account of the absence of certainty regarding either one; enough of this prolixity.

He summarizes with the words "by that" (tena). This concise expression (*samāsokti*) is of two kinds: that which is produced by punning epithets (*śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇotthāpitā*) and that which is produced by common epithets (*sādhāraṇaviśeṣaṇotthāpitā*).
Since both the effect and the mark are equal [in status], there are two types; thus, *samāsokti* (synecdoche) is of four kinds.
In all these cases, the superimposition of conventional behavior (*vyavahārasamāropa*) is the cause.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, kha) Having set aside the view that *samāsokti* contains a comparison (*aupamya*), he establishes its form as being fourfold by summarizing it: "When there is similarity of adjectives, [it is] *śliṣṭa*," and so forth.
He says "and in all cases" in order to state that the superimposition of behavior (*vyavahāra-samāropa*) is also fourfold.
And that [superimposition] is, in some instances, the superimposition of the behavior of a worldly object upon a worldly object.

It is fourfold: the superimposition of the conventional usage of a scriptural entity upon a scriptural entity, the superimposition of the conventional usage of a scriptural entity upon a worldly entity, or the superimposition of the conventional usage of a worldly entity upon a scriptural entity.
Locanā:
(Lo, O) In the worldly [level], which is common to all paths;
and in the scriptural [level], which is accessible through the specific development of knowledge.

In this regard, even worldly objects are of many kinds due to the distinctions of taste (*rasa*) and so forth; likewise, even scriptural objects are of many varieties, being well-known through the sciences of logic (*tarka*), medicine (*āyurveda*), and astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*). Thus, the *samāsokti* (condensed expression) is manifold. To give a mere indication: in such passages as "Having shaken off her garment... and so forth, there is the superimposition (*samāropa*) of a worldly matter—such as the behavior of a forceful lover—upon another worldly object.
“I believe that those who perceive You as a single form, though You proceed in an infinite number of ways across all Your manifestations,
have indeed composed Your definition by applying the grammatical elision of case-endings for the sake of the supreme.”
In this case, there is the superimposition of the linguistic usage of a thing well-known in grammar upon a thing well-known in the scriptures and treatises;
so it is elsewhere as well.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ga) "By those for whom [Thou art] of one form":
this is a statement addressed to the Supreme Lord by certain people.

By those people who perceive You—the non-dual One of a single form—amidst all states of existence within saṃsāra, the elision (*lopa*) of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) denoting distinction, which expresses otherness, has been effected.
The meaning is that, because of this [perception], the cognition of difference was not produced.
I consider that by those very [factors], its permanence (*dhruvatva*) has been definitively established as its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The term "permanence" (*dhruvam*) is an indication where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary referent.

Of what kind are you? You are the imperishable and undecaying one, who have proceeded by way of being "innumerable" (asaṃkhya) because of the impossibility of counting you due to your infinite nature, since you follow upon countless words.
Here, by the power of the punned adjectives, there is the perception of the indeclinable *api*.

For indeed, since those [particles] exist within their functions (vṛtti) through the conjunction with all words, they possess a uniform nature due to being devoid of modification; thus, there is an absence of number in their meaning.
Furthermore, I consider it certain and settled that the elision of the subsequent case-ending (sup-vibhakti) has been performed.

The sense is this: by those who see you as such and effect the elision of the case-ending, this very state—namely, the elision of the case-ending—has been established as the definition or mark (lakṣaṇa) of particles such as "ca" and so forth.
In this context: "āgama" refers to the Vedic scripture;
"vastu" refers to things well-known in grammar, such as the letter *ca* and so forth.
In the same way, linguistic usage consists of the nature of sound;
for even the superimposition of that [usage] upon the Lord has the nature of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman).
Thus it is in other cases as well.
In that regard, there is the superimposition of the conventions of other treatises upon a subject well-known from the Vedic scriptures, such as the Lord (Īśvara), as in my own verse:
“His splendor is exceedingly radiant with the brilliance of his forms; even one who falls at the end of his feet, though humble, attains great dignity.
[This is] *chandas* (meter).
May he, whose body consists of perfected syllables, who possesses virtuous qualities, who is the embodiment of sound, and whose fame is holy, ever abide within my mind.
In this sentence, the subject under discussion is as follows: may that Puṇyaśloka, the Supreme Lord, ever abide within my mind;

in whose physical form there is an exceeding brilliance through the luster of the ornaments, the Kaustubha gems, and at whose feet even one who falls—though light and lowly—attains dignity, weight, and excellence.
Of what nature was that one of virtuous fame?
He was one whose body—consisting of perfected syllables and free from error—in the *chandas* (Veda), and who possessed true qualities in the form of sovereign power.
For the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states: "These [kings] are portions of Viṣṇu, who bears the form of sound."

Here, through the power of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) by means of punned adjectives (*śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇaiḥ*), there arises the perception of the "One of Excellent Fame" (*uttamaśloka*) as being like a poet (*kavi*). For that [poet] too, in his composition (*vigraha*), there is an exceeding brilliance due to the splendors—that is, the beauties—of poetic ornaments (*alaṅkṛti*) such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and simile (*upamā*). Furthermore, because it is stated in the treatises on prosody (*chandaḥ-śāstra*) that even a light syllable (*laghuvarṇa*) falling at the end of the fourth part of a foot becomes heavy (*guru*) if it occurs at the end of a word (*padāntaga*).
He is perfected through the *anuṣṭubh* and other meters; his form consists of phonemes (*varṇa*);
he possesses qualities such as sweetness (*mādhurya*) and so forth; and his essence is sound (*śabda*). — Locanā.

(Lo, au) It is of a single form (*ekarūpa*) because it is nothing but pure existence (*sanmātra*), or because it is devoid of specific modifications such as the grammatical suffixes (*pratyaya*). By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that which exists, functions, or manifests within," it refers to things (*vastu*) or to gendered characteristics (*liṅga*) such as femininity; it is indeclinable (*avyaya*) because it is free from decay, and includes [the vowels] beginning with *ca* (the *cavarga*). It functions as the innumerable (*asaṃkhya*) because it evolves (*vivartana*) in the form of infinite categories of objects.
And because it is well-known that in one case there is an absence of the first number (the singular),

the elision— that is, the determined non-existence— of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) has been made for the individual (*vyakti*), which is to say, for the entity (*vastu*) that possesses otherness and partakes in difference.
By means of its status as a condition (*pratyayatva*), it conceals—that is, hides—the future case-ending (*vibhakti*).
"Unconcealed nature" (*anavacchādita-svarūpa*) means having an unrevealed nature (*agūḍha-svarūpa*).
The "prior state" (*pūrvāvasthā*) is that which is well-known in the world.
As it has also been stated by Caṇḍīdāsa Paṇḍita: "Where there is a cognition of the subject (*prakṛta*) through identification with the non-subject (*aprakṛta*), there is *rūpaka* (metaphor);
where there is a cognition of the subject as independent, possessing the activity of the non-subject, there is *samāsokti* (synecdoche)—this is the clear meaning.
Thus, the claim that *rūpaka* also involves the superimposition of behavior (*vyavahāra-samāropa*) has been refuted by Rāghavananda."
In a metaphor (*rūpaka*), the form of the subject (*prakṛta*) is concealed by the imposition of the essential nature of the non-subject (*aprakṛta*).
Here, however, by the superimposition of its own state, it distinguishes that very object—whose true nature is already concealed—from its previous state.
For this reason, they say that here there is a superimposition of function (*vyavahāra-samāropa*), but not a superimposition of essential nature (*svarūpa-samāropa*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, gha) He states the distinction between *ekadeśavivarttirūpaka* and *sāmāsokti* with the words "in the case of *rūpaka*";
the meaning is "in the case of *ekadeśavivarttirūpaka*."
Regarding the phrase "the non-primary form of the self-nature": the non-primary form is the suggested (vyaṅgya) form, and that is the agent [of the action].
"By means of the arrangement of the self-nature" means...
The meaning is that, by superimposing non-difference upon the essential nature of the self (*ātmasvarūpa*), it conceals the subject under discussion— that is, it renders it the object of negation—
as in the example “full with the honey of loveliness,” and so forth. But here, however...

The nature of that which is manifested by its own state is its own form; through the superimposition of that [other state], its own form remains unobscured and unimpaired. That is the subject at hand, the expressed (vācya). It distinguishes [the subject] from its previous state—that is, from the state of being a metaphorical figure (*rūpaka*) where the manifestation is superimposed—meaning it effects the treatment of the manifestation as something superimposed.

In the case of *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifesting) metaphor, the object of comparison (*rūpya*) is manifested when it is superimposed upon the expressed, as in "shaking off the garment" (*vyādhūya vasanam*), etc., where there is a superimposition of non-difference between the wind and the lover in the expressed sense.

However, the meaning here is that there is only a superimposition (*āropa*) of the behavior of lovers—specifically behaviors such as the casting off of garments and embracing—for the sake of sexual pleasure.
He states the corroboration: "Therefore, in this case, [it is called] *vyavahāra* (behavior).

In reality, however, the two factors—the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) and the nature of the metaphor (*rūpaka*)—are what differentiate *ekadeśavivartin* (partial metaphor) from *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation).

In the suggestion of simile (upamādhvani) and in paronomasia (śleṣa), there is similarity even of the substantive (viśeṣya), whereas here [in aprastutapraśaṃsā], there is similarity of the adjectives (viśeṣaṇa) alone;
furthermore, in aprastutapraśaṃsā, that which is relevant (prastuta) is what is implied.
But here, the distinction lies in the fact that [the subject] is irrelevant (*aprastuta*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṅa) states the distinction of this from suggestion based on simile (*upamā-dhvani*) as follows: "In the case of suggestion based on simile... and so forth.

In this context, the reading should be "by means of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) alone," because in the form of *śleṣa*, since both [the subject and the object] are expressed (*vācya*), there is an absence of anything suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
The meaning is that by means of *śleṣa*, there is a similarity even of the substantive (*viśeṣya*).
However, if there is a pun (*śleṣa*) due to a careless reading, then the meaning is that there is a similarity between the qualificand and so forth;
even so, the word "ca" (and) is redundant.
Furthermore, the distinction from *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) is indeed clear.
Locanā:

(Lo, a) Furthermore, in this case of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), it would be logical for the subject at hand (*prastuta*) to be understood by means of the description of something not at hand; however, since such a description of the non-subject would otherwise be nothing more than an incoherent prattle lacking a basis, and because here—despite the fact that the context restricts the meaning of the adjectives to the object being described—the perception of a second meaning is established by experience.
The *parikara* (periphrasis) is considered to consist of the aforementioned epithets used with specific intention (*sābhiprāya*).
For example:
"O King of Aṅga! O General! [and so forth].
"O Karna, you who mock Drona,
protect this son of Duḥśasana from Bhima!"
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ca) He states the *parikara* ornament: "the expression" (*ukti*). Its state of being "intentional" (*sābhiprāyatva*) consists in its capacity to nourish the meaning by strengthening the sense that is intended to be conveyed.

And although that [ornamentation] could be obtained simply by avoiding the defect of an insufficient meaning, nevertheless, because many [qualifiers] are intended here in the phrase "by means of qualifiers," the state of being an ornament arises from the experience of specific varieties within that multiplicity.
The passage beginning with "O King of Anga" is a speech by Aśvatthāman, who is mocking Karṇa.
Here, the object to be established is the mockery of Karṇa, and these vocatives serve to nourish that [mockery].

The mockery is explicit: it is a derision that, while Duḥśāsana was being directly bound by Bhīma, his status as king of Aṅga, his role as commander-in-chief, and his being ridiculed by the great hero Droṇa were all "fit for a hero" at that time. (Locanā)

(Lo, Ā) Even at the occasion of defining the figure of speech based on similarity (*sādṛśyamūla*), he defines *parikara* immediately after *samāsokti* because it is caused by the strikingness of the adjectives (*viśeṣaṇa-vicchitti*). He says: "The expression... (*uktiriti*).

Regarding the plural number in the word "by adjectives" (*viśeṣaṇaiḥ*), the sense is that this aesthetic charm does not arise from a single or two adjectives; rather, it is precisely the avoidance of the fault of "meaningless adjectives" (*apuṣṭārtha-doṣa*).
[The verses] contain intentional meanings that are implied within the literal sense;
and here, because the implied meaning is not concealed (*agūḍha*), it constitutes *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion), and therefore this ornament does not possess the status of *dhvani*.
"O King of Aṅga!"—
this is the speech of Bhīma.
Aṅga is a specific region.
Here, by virtue of being the King of Aṅga, his status as a sovereign for the sake of others' wives is indicated;
by virtue of being the commander-in-chief, he receives honor from the king;
and by virtue of being mocked by Droṇa, his pride in his own heroism is perceived.
śleṣa (paronomasia) is the expression of multiple meanings by means of words that, by their very nature, possess a single meaning. VisSd 10.57.
The exclusion [of other types of poetry] is due to the verbal pun "having the same meaning as its own nature" (svabhāvādekārthaiḥ),
and the term "recitation" (vācanam) excludes *dhvani*.
An example follows:
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) He states the figure of speech *arthaśleṣa* [with the words] "by words," etc.
"By words having a single meaning" means by words whose power (*śakti*) resides in a single meaning alone.

"Having multiple meanings" (*anekārtha*) means that the meaning which is distinct from what is possible [for the primary sense] is another meaning; its "denotation" (*vācana*) refers to its being made known through *lakṣaṇā* (indication).
"Exclusion from *śleṣa*" means that *śleṣa* is the poetic figure of verbal punning (*śabdaśleṣālaṅkāra*).

In this context, by the phrase "because of the word’s own nature and its single meaning," [the author] states through the term *vācana* (verbal expression) that it excludes *vyañjanā* (suggestion)—namely, "of *dhvani*.
This is also an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion). — *Locanā*.
(i, lo) Here, *śleṣa* (paronomasia) occurs because of the context of *śleṣa*. "Vācana" means making known by way of non-determination.

Thus, the meaning of the words of the verse (*kārikā*)—having become unified and having entered into a state of mutual sublation—is due to the capacity of many distinct word-meanings, when combined, to convey such a meaning.
Furthermore, no word possesses the power [to denote] a meaning qualified by another category of entity.
For example: "Setting virtuous actions in motion, removing impurity, and blazing with abundant splendor, the Maker of Light shines forth."
In this case, because there is no restriction from context or other factors, both types of *rājasūya* are to be expressed.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"Setting it in motion."

The sun, named Vibhākara, and a particular king also named Vibhākara, both shine forth. He states the qualifiers for both with the word "pravarttayan" (setting in motion): [these are] actions accomplished by light.
In one sense, it refers to the ritual activities of the social classes, such as the Brahmins; in another sense, it refers to the "darkness" of the green directions—
that is, the impurity, the gloom, and the blackness of the worlds situated in those directions.
And [he saw] the lack of brilliance due to the poverty of his side;
by "splendor" (mahaḥ) is meant light, and in the other sense— heroism.
In this case, regarding the word *kriyā*, there is no polysemy;
however, for the three words beginning with *mālinī*, there is expressive power (*śakti*) regarding one meaning and indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding another meaning,
while in the portion concerning the sun, there is verbal punning (*śabdaśleṣa*).
Here, [the author] excludes the nature of suggested simile (*upamā-dhvani*) by stating: "When a word with multiple meanings is restricted by [factors] such as association (*saṃyoga*), etc.

It should be understood that the mention of suggested simile here is intended to include multiplicity of meaning (*anekārthatā*) through both primary denotation (*śakti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*). *Locanā*.
(Lo, ī) Ritual actions such as the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) and so forth, as well as sacrifices and charitable works (*iṣṭāpūrta*) and so forth;
*mālinya* is the state of being composed of darkness,
or the association with improper conduct.

The sun (*vibhākara*) is one whose great splendor is a festival, who is radiant, illuminated, and purified. According to its etymology— as in "he who makes (*karoti*) or manifests (*vyanakti*) light (*vibhā*)"— the king too should be understood as such, because he is the cause of light (*vibhā*) or the locus of it, being determined as the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
In some cases, the particular is [inferred] from the general, or the general from the particular;
the cause from the effect, or the effect from the cause; and likewise, the equal from the equal. (VisDh 10.58)
If the relevant subject is understood from the irrelevant, then there is Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description), which is of five kinds—
thus says the *Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, jha) He describes the fivefold figure of speech Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description): "In some cases, a particular...

The meaning is that when, from all the objects denoted by words ending in the fifth case (ablative)—which are *aprastuta* (not the subject at hand)—the object denoted by all the words ending in the first case is understood or perceived as being *prastuta* (the subject at hand), then there is the fivefold figure of Aprastutapraśaṃsā.
This technical term *anyāpadeśa* is also used elsewhere.
Locanā:
For the object-words such as "viśeṣa" (particularity) and so forth, the qualifier is "prastuta" (the relevant);

for the words ending in the fifth case, such as "sāmānyāt" (from the general), the qualifier is "aprastutāt" (from the irrelevant), meaning from that which is irrelevant by virtue of its sense, though not explicitly stated.

In this very case, because there is a description of something irrelevant (aprastuta) by way of its being expressed as praise, it is by implication the figure of speech called Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Praise of the Irrelevant).
Thus, the general definition is: Aprastutapraśaṃsā is the cognition of the relevant (prastuta) from the irrelevant. The sense is that, according to the method already stated, it has five varieties.
The examples in order:
"It is better for the dust that, when kicked by the foot of a living being, rises up and settles upon his head,
than for that very dust to remain indifferent even when he is being insulted."
In this case, while a specific point—that even dust is better than us—is being introduced, a general statement has been made.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ña):
Regarding that, he explains how a specific matter under discussion is suggested by a general one that is not under discussion, with the verse beginning "pādāhatam" (struck by the foot).

Even in the face of insult, it is better—that is, superior—for an embodied being to remain composed; for that dust which, when struck by the foot, rises up and ascends—meaning climbs—onto the very head of the striker.
Here, "here" refers to the general state of all embodied beings.
The meaning is that because of the mention of that [word], there is a suggestion (*vyañjanā*) of the subject at hand, namely "from us" (*asmattaḥ*).
Locanā:
"Struck by the feet" (*pādāhatam*).
Thus, according to the statement in Māgha’s poem, this is Balarāma’s speech addressed to Śrī Kṛṣṇa in order to incite him toward marching against Śiśupāla.
Regarding the word "asmat" (our): those denoted by the term "we" are indeed Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the others who are the expressed subjects.
“If this arrow, which takes away life, were placed upon my heart, would it not kill me?
By the will of the Lord, even poison might sometimes become nectar, or nectar might become poison.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) He states that there is the suggestion (*vyañjana*) of a general subject at hand through a specific subject not under discussion—namely, "this garland" (*strag iyam*).
This lamentation of Aja is made while holding in his heart the Pārijāta garland given by Nārada to the husband of Indumatī.

In this case, while the general principle was under discussion—that by the will of the Lord, even those who cause harm may become benefactors, and even benefactors may cause harm—a specific instance has been stated.
Thus, here we have an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) based on *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
In a *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration), however, a well-known object is employed as a reflection.
But here, since the transformation of poison into nectar or of nectar into poison is not established, its existence [as a distinct entity] does not occur.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṭha):
"Here" means in this context.
In the general category of "causing benefit or harm," there is a specific instance;
the specific instance of causing harm is [the consumption of] nectar (amṛta).

Since the figure of speech *arthāntaranyāsa* is here established by means of this *aprastutapraśaṃsā*, there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) between these two in the form of a relationship of the assisted and the assister (*anugrāhyānugrāhaka-bhāva*). Thus he says: "And so... (*evaṃ ca*).
The *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) is [defined] as "by way of a generality.
Its specific variety here is accomplished through *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
For instance, by the phrase "what does it not kill?", a distinction is stated regarding the absence of killing despite the existence of the power to kill in the specific agent, namely the garland.

And that [similarity] consists precisely in the absence of being harmful while being subject to the will of the Lord, by virtue of the commonality of "being harmful" which is obtainable through *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
Because of the identity of meaning, it is constituted by the non-killing of the garland;
for there is the cognition that even for one who acts for the benefit of the Lord's will, there is an absence of being harmful.

Now, one might object: "Since the non-injury and the state of immortality residing in the two [the body and the soul] possess the capacity to cause harm, yet they are reflected as the probans in the form of 'not being harmful,' does this not entail the presence of the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (simile) here as well? To refute this, he says: "*dṛṣṭānta*" (simile).
It is only that which is well-known—that is, already established—as a reflection (*pratibimba*) of the original image (*bimba*) through the suggested commonality (*vyaṅgyasādharmyeṇa*).
The meaning here is that because of the word "tasya" (of that), there is no presence of the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (simile).
And thus, in the rule "the *dṛṣṭānta*, however, [is] of that which possesses common properties," the intended meaning is "of that which possesses well-known common properties. — *Locanā*.
Poison is a specific instance of that which causes harm, while nectar is a specific instance of that which causes benefit;
this is the seed for the emergence of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise),
because it serves as the corroborative support for an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) through the relation of the general to the particular.
In that [previous] example,
however, because there is a determination (*adhyavasāna*) of poison as nectar, it is indeed *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole);
for between those two, a specific charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) is possible by way of the relationship between the general and the particular.
“Alas! Before Sītā, the moon seems as if smeared with collyrium; the gaze of the does is as if dulled;
the coral leaf has lost its ruddy glow; the luster of gold has turned dark;
and even a trace of harshness has begun to manifest, as it were, in the throats of the female cuckoos.”
The plumage of the crested birds was as if possessed of splendor.

In this case, from the possible effects residing in Indra and others—such as being smeared with collyrium—the contextual cause, which consists of the specific beauty residing in the face and so forth, is perceived.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ḍa):
He states the suggestion of the contextual cause from the non-contextual effect with the verse beginning "The moon is indeed smeared... and so on.
The collective meaning is that the moon and other celestial bodies are inferior in the presence of Sītā, who possesses the beauty of her face and so forth.
In this regard, compared to Sītā’s face, the moon— [is inferior].
In comparison with the tremulous eyes of the fawn-eyed woman, [the eyes of others appear dull];
in comparison with her coral-red lips, [the color of coral appears pale];
and in comparison with the golden luster of her limbs, [the radiance of gold seems dim].

The adjectives expressing the inferiority of the cuckoo’s throat— which utters such a sound— compared to a throat that is soft and capable of uttering sweet sounds, and the inferiority of a peacock’s plumage compared to [beautiful] hair, are to be understood as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
For instance, in the phrase "the moon as if smeared," and so forth.
"Stupefied" means devoid of agility;
"withered like a faded dawn" means like a dawn that has lost its luster.
"Roughness" refers to a hardness that renders one incapable of uttering sweet sounds.
It was presented, established, or produced by her alone;
and even by a mere fraction, even by a small portion, even by a cuckoo, through the utterance of some sweet sound,
the peacocks were rendered despicable and subject to reproach.
"Hanta" expresses either dejection due to the disparagement of Indra and the other gods, or joy due to the exaltation of Sītā;
from these [emotions] which are either inferred or imagined,
a cause is perceived.
Thus, causality should be understood as the cause for the production of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
*Locanā*:
"Induḥ" and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" in "the face etc.," the eyes, the luster of the lower lip, the speech, and the hair are included.
Having uttered "I am going," that gazelle-eyed woman let fall a deep sigh and cast a sidelong glance at me with one eye clouded by tears;

then, her affection for me having increased, she addressed the fawn with a playful taunt: "Today, let your love for me, which was bestowed upon you, be transferred to this circle of dear friends. Thus was the young deer spoken to.
In this instance, the cause for a certain effect consisting of non-going has been stated.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ḍha): He states the manifestation of the contextual effect from a non-contextual cause: "I am going."
This is the speech of one who has set out on a journey, addressed to someone asking, "Have you turned back from your departure?
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Having let out a heavy, forceful sigh, and having glanced askance at me with a single eye clouded by tears.

This is an adverbial modifier for the act of my speaking, which arose with a sigh to signal death, serving as a reproachful instruction to the circle of dear friends regarding the affection bestowed upon me by the fawn—affection that had increased through love—and which was directed toward myself.
Regarding the phrase "of someone here":
it means of the hero who has desisted from going.
Regarding the word "presented" (*prastuta*): [it refers to the subject at hand].
The meaning is that the subject has been introduced by someone's question.
The cause is the heroine's indication of her own death.
Locanā:
Regarding "here" (*atrei*):

when someone is asked by another for some reason, "Why have you not come?", it is inappropriate to state [the answer] with something irrelevant; the meaning is that this refers to the cause of one's not having gone.
When the subject matter presented is similar and the expression used is also similar, *śleṣamūlā* (based on punning) is of two kinds: that based solely on similarity, and that based on punning.

Even within the category based on punning, there are two types: like *samāsokti*, when only the adjectives are punned; and when the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is also punned, as in *śleṣa* itself. Thus it is twofold.
*Vijñapriyā*: [This is the commentary.]
(vi, ṇa) Regarding the phrase "equal to the equal":

in order to state the threefold nature of the fifth variety, he first states its twofold nature—namely, that which is rooted in *śleṣa* (punning compounding) and that which is rooted in similarity (*sādṛśya*).
He further states that the one rooted in *śleṣa* is itself twofold, by saying "as in *samāsokti*."

For in *samāsokti* (synecdoche), since even the application of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) to the substantive would result in it being classified as a suggestion of simile (*upamādhvani*), there is no *śleṣa* in the substantive.
He states another way [of classifying it]: "like *śleṣa*" (*śleṣavat*).
This means: like a particular type of verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*) that resides in the substantive.
In the phrase "for when fate has turned adverse," there is also a pun (*śleṣa*) upon the substantive word (*viśeṣyapada*).
Locanā:
[This is] based on *śleṣa*.
Paranomasia (*śleṣa*) is the appearance of verbal punning (*arthaśleṣābhāsa*), because the intended meaning is understood through implication. Examples in order:
“The mango tree, ever-fragrant and endowed with the beauty of spring...”
Possessing a brilliantly radiant luster, glorious, and agitated by abundant longing.
Locanā:
(lo, ai) *Āmoda* is an exceedingly intense fragrance and joy;
*utkalikā* is a sprout that has emerged and longing.
Here, by virtue of the pun on the mere adjectives (*viśeṣaṇamātraśleṣa*), there arises the cognition of a certain relevant hero from the irrelevant mango tree (*sahakāra*).
Regarding the pun on the mere adjectives here, [the author] says: "The mango tree."

The *sahakāra*, the mango tree, having taken refuge in the splendor of spring, being crowded—that is, pervaded—by many abundant, emerging buds and flower-buds (*mukula*), possesses constant fragrance, that is, an existing supreme scent; for that very reason it has a brilliantly blazing luster, and for that very reason it is glorious.
Regarding the word "here" (*atra*): [it refers to this state].
The hero too, being attended by the splendor of spring, was one whose taste was fixed upon the perfectly radiant *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) through its fragrance—that is, its joy;
for Amara states, "the *śṛṅgāra* is pure and radiant. He was illustrious, and for that very reason, filled with *utkalikā*, that is, longing.
The lexicon states: "Utkaṇṭhā and utkalikā are synonyms. Regarding the phrase "of someone," the meaning is "of one possessing the aforementioned qualities."

“Even if he were to lose his manhood, even if he were to fall to the lowest depths, even if he were not great in the art of persuasion—even so, he would uplift the entire world; such is the direction shown by that certain Supreme Person.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) Regarding the pun on the substantive word (*viśeṣyapadaśleṣa*), he says: "Because of his manliness," and so forth.
This is the speech of someone instructing a certain king on how to recover a kingdom seized by a rival by any means whatsoever.
By some ineffable Supreme Person, Nārāyaṇa, this very direction and this very manner have been manifested and shown.
To the question "What kind of direction? he says: "From manhood.
If one should deviate from manhood—that is, from the state of being a person—even then he would uplift the entire universe, the cycle of worldly existence.
For in the past, when the kingdom had been seized by the Asuras, Nārāyaṇa, having assumed the form of Mohinī, rescued it;
likewise, the meaning is that even if he were to go below—that is, because he went to the netherworld (pātāla) in the form of a Boar and raised up the earth.
Likewise, the meaning is that even if, in the matter of "praṇayana"—that is, in a request or on account of a request—he were not great but small.
Just as he [Viṣṇu] attained a state of lightness by assuming the form of a dwarf in order to recover the kingdom seized by the Daityas,

so too should you, O best of men, even by moving from your manhood and prowess, by falling into a state of degradation, and by attaining a state of lightness through begging, recover the kingdom stolen by your rival— this is the suggestion of the contextual meaning.
Locanā:
(lo, o) "Because of masculinity," etc.; this refers to the context of Vāsudeva, who is not the subject under discussion.

At the time of stealing the nectar, there was a deviation from masculinity; by assuming a female form, there was a downward movement, that is, the attainment of a low state. If he had not been the "Supreme Person" (Puruṣottama), the most excellent among men, in the matter of affection (*praṇayana*).

Here, although the word *puruṣottama* is used as a substantive (*viśeṣya*), because it is a *śliṣṭa* (double-entendre) term, Viṣṇu alone is understood first due to its greater conventional renown. By that [initial understanding], a certain man who is the subject of description is perceived. Vijñapriyā: In this context, even though the word *puruṣottama* functions as the substantive, because it is a *śliṣṭa* (punning) term, Viṣṇu alone is first understood due to its widespread fame. Through that, a certain man who is the object of description is apprehended.
(Vi, da) "First" is said because of its abundant renown;
by that, there is no designation for a connection with a cognition of equal time.
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
It should be understood that this is because the Lord alone was first made known, and because of the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Locanā:
(lo, au) By means of a word with a double sense (*śliṣṭa*) [possessing two meanings].

The phrase "by means of abundant renown" means that, according to the principle that the renown of a whole is more authoritative than the renown of a single part when the context is set aside by the force of the totality of circumstances, [the Lord is the intended meaning].

Furthermore, as for what was stated by Rāghavānanda— that words such as *puṃstva* (masculinity) and so forth possess a connection with the Blessed One as their primary referent here— that is not correct.
Because there is a lack of authoritative evidence;
on the contrary, because there is a restriction regarding the subject matter to be described in the context.
An example based merely on similarity is as follows:
Locanā:
[The figure] *lo* (*lo*, *a*) is based solely on similarity and is not caused by the double meaning of qualifiers and so forth.
"A single young pigeon; hundreds of hawks rush toward it, driven by hunger."
The sky is devoid of cover; alas, alas! The compassion of Brahmā is our refuge.
In this case, from the dissatisfied pigeon, a certain [other] subject is understood.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"One" (*eka*).
*Potaḥ* means a child;
*kṣudhā* is in the instrumental case;
*atra* means "in this."
Someone here, surrounded by many robbers and unable to flee, having sought refuge in the compassion of Fate, should be understood [as the subject].
And this [comparison] may also occur through dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*):
"Blessed indeed are the winds in the forest, cool with the touch of the *kahlāra* lily."
Those who touch Rāma, dark as a blue lotus, without being restrained."
In this instance, by means of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the subject under discussion is understood through the contrast: "The winds are fortunate, while I am unfortunate.
This [type of *vyatireka*] is threefold, according to whether the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is possible, impossible, or both.
Among these, the examples for the case of possibility are precisely those already stated.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi,
na) "Blessed one" refers to this speech of Daśaratha, who is distressed by the grief caused by Rāma having been sent away to the forest.
"Sambhaveti" refers to the three positions: possibility-possibility, possibility-impossibility, and impossibility-possibility. Locanā.
(Lo, ā) This ornament consists in a dual nature, arising from being possible in one respect and impossible in another.
An example of impossibility is as follows:
“I am a cuckoo and you are a crow; our blackness is the same.
However, those who are experts in the nuances of song will tell the difference.”
In this instance, the dialogue between the crow and the cuckoo is impossible without the superimposition (*adhyāropaṇa*) of the subject at hand.
*Vijñapriyā*:
When the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is impossible, there is a superimposition upon the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
"I am a cuckoo. *Kākalī* refers to a sweet yet indistinct sound;
as the lexicon states: "The term *kākalī* applies to a subtle, sweet, and indistinct tone."
Regarding the term *vākovākya*:
this is indeed the speech of the cuckoo itself.
How so? This *vākovākya*, consisting of statement and counter-statement, serves for internal discourse by relying upon a mediator.
This is because, upon the attainment of the state of quarreling, there is an implied comparison (ākṣepa) even of a crow with a cuckoo.
"Without the superimposition (adhyāropa) of the subject at hand" means:
without the superimposition of the suggested subject at hand upon the non-contextual cuckoo which is the expressed object.
Nor should it be argued: "If the literal meaning (vācyārtha) is already understood, how can there be a superimposition (āropa) of that [meaning] upon a non-literal subject?

For since a cuckoo is incapable of speech, one recalls a man who is capable of speech as being suggested (vyaṅgya) by that [cuckoo]; thus, the superimposition is possible. Furthermore, even when a specific person is understood through suggestion (vyañjanā), there is no lack of logical consistency. An example of this dual nature is as follows:
“There are many holes within and many thorns without;
how can the fibers of the lotus stalk not be fragile?”
In this case, without the superimposition of something relevant [to the subject], it is impossible for the holes within the lotus stalks to be the cause of the breaking of the string;
however, for others [the causes such as wind], it is possible. Thus, there is a dual nature [of both the possible and the impossible].
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, pha) "Internal cavities" means:

here, regarding that which is to be expressed as the lotus stalk's possession of internal cavities and so forth, it is impossible for the internal cavity to be the cause of the breaking of the fibers; thus he says: "of the cavities."
"But for others," that is to say,
for thorns;
for it is possible to cut fibers with thorns.
Thus, the superimposition of the "thorn-like" attendants upon the person under discussion occurs only upon that part which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*);
the point is that it does not occur upon the part consisting of the thorns themselves. — *Locanā*.
(i) Internally there are cavities, in the middle there are hollows, and there are the very wicked deeds of the family;
there are subtle thorns and members who are envious;
they are fragile, prone to breaking, and perishable.
The "threads" (sūtra) are the qualities;
these include craftsmanship and so forth, as well as gravity and so forth.
Their status as instructions on impossible threads arises from their distinctness.
For when a thread is being drawn out, its breakage is observed at that boundary;
and here too: "O friend, give me [the cloth]; do not tear it while you are painting it, for it is very thick.
Even though it is unadorned, O cucumber-seed [cloth], you carry it straight away."

In this case, there is no *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), because the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) possesses a greater aesthetic relish (*āsvādya*) than the expressed meaning (*vācya*), and thus constitutes *dhvani*. This poetic figure is accepted only when the suggested meaning is subordinate to the expressed meaning. Furthermore, regarding the acceptance of *aprastutapraśaṃsā*, the great scholar Rāghavānanda Mahāpātra [states] that where the suggested meaning is the unrelevant matter itself, it is the suggested [meaning].

Thus, the collection of works by the masters beginning with Dhvanikāra and extending to Caṇḍīdāsa Paṇḍita, who have repeatedly declared this, has been demonstrated right here in this *Sāhityadarpaṇa* during the examination of *dhvani* based on *lakṣaṇā*:
"In some cases, it appears as something to be sublated."

Having disregarded the statements of those who know the scriptures beginning with the *Rigveda*, and having asserted that [the term] "life" (*jīvitam*) is a case of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), he has cited "sulakṣyaḥ lakṣyaḥ" as an example for them.

Thus, the opinion of certain dull-witted individuals— who have been deceived by mere prattle— has been written down as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in an exceedingly trivial manner, solely to reveal his own lack of intelligence.

In this context, regarding the verse beginning with "That which was kicked by the foot, having risen," etc., according to the previously stated principle that "in some cases there is an appearance as something to be sublated," [this is like] the example "O righteous man, wander! and so forth, as well as "O neighbor, cast your gaze! and so on.
And let there be no metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in such cases as "I am a cuckoo" (*kokilo 'ham*).

For if metaphorical indication does not apply when the literal meaning is impossible—as in "I am a cuckoo"—how could it fail to apply in cases like "an internal hole," where a part [of the body] is impossible?

To this it is replied: In cases such as "I am a cuckoo," where there is indeed a comprehension of the sentence-meaning, how can there be metaphorical indication caused by the sublation of the intended connection (*anvaya*) that was about to arise?
And as has been shown by those very [authorities]:
"Because it follows from what was heard, there is no expectancy," and so forth.

Furthermore, in this example, or in the case of "interior holes" (*antaśchidrāṇi*) and so on, if there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it must be either pure (*śuddhā*) or figurative (*gauṇī*); it cannot be the first [pure].
Because that [superimposition] is rooted in either similarity or another type of relationship;
if it were the second [type], it would also be either superimposition (*sāropā*) or identification (*sādhyavasānā*).
It cannot be the first, because the object (*viṣaya*) would not be suppressed (*nirgorṇatva*).
If it is the second [type], let it be hyperbole (*atiśayokti*); what is the use of postulating a separate ornament?
Or else, how could that which causes the understanding of the meaning of a single word enter into the understanding of the sentence?
For here, in the case of [words] such as "lord" (*prabhu*) and so forth, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is the object to be accomplished by some intention.
Through concealment, there is the communication of a desired matter;
for this very reason, the ancients maintain that here, as in the figure *samāsokti*, there is a superimposition (*samāropa*) of behavior.
For instance: "This ocean is a mine of jewels; it was resorted to with the hope of wealth."

In such cases, the designation "ocean" applied to the king under discussion is for the purpose of conveying—through the primary expression of the word *su* (well) residing in that [king]—the excellence of qualities such as profundity (*gāmbhīrya*) belonging to the indicated object (*lakṣya*), which is the fruit of the metaphorical function (*lakṣaṇā*). However, this is not so in instances such as "I am a cuckoo," where one does not obtain the literal meaning for the sake of serving that [object], but rather encounters an undesirable result;
thus, in some cases, the designation "cuckoo" applies to the composition of beautiful words itself.

In order to demonstrate that it is improper for an inferior person to feel envy toward a certain great man who is under discussion, even when there is a mention of a similar subject not under discussion (*aprastuta*)—

as in the well-known example accepted by them, such as "jaṃ de lihiṇa mā asī" (Do not be proud because of your [fine] body)— there would have to be indication (*lakṣaṇā*), despite its being the domain of suggestion (*vyañjanā*).

If it is asked, "In cases such as 'interior holes' (*antaśchidrāṇi*), since it is impossible for interior holes and the like to perform actions such as breaking the fibers of a lotus stalk, how can there be a logical connection (*anvaya*)?"—regarding this, the scholar Caṇḍīdāsa says: "Because the external [meaning] here is subordinate to the contextual subject (*prastuta*), and because from the very beginning it is surrendered by its own nature at the moment of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*), its cognition is not defective.
For this very reason, the author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva* has also stated that in all varieties [of this figure], the expression of the contextual subject is appropriate.
“Here, describing that which is irrelevant is indeed improper because it is irrelevant;
however, it might perhaps be appropriate if it were subordinate to the relevant subject.
This would be the case if [the phrase] ‘there are holes within’ [were intended as such].”

If there is metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in such cases, then when the primary meaning is sublated, what exactly is being indicated that serves to establish the connection with the sentence-meaning? If it is an irrelevant matter, such as "the misdeeds in the family," then even for that, the breaking of a lotus stalk—so fragile—is not set aside.
Furthermore, although much that is unerring has been determined according to the opinion of these venerable scholars, some slight defect or other is nevertheless proclaimed.

In this matter, O wise ones of unimpaired intellect, may you forgive me for my fear of shattering the mass of most pure objects of knowledge so laboriously established by the eminent teacher Paṇḍita Caṇḍīdāsa, beginning with the author of the Dhvanyāloka;
and as for that which was stated by those very same [authorities]—

“Who are you? You are the fame of Kuntalamalla; alas, where are you? Nowhere at all. Where are those friends of yours? Tell me, where are your speech, fortune, and splendor now? Having thus imagined [the situation] through a questioner who is superior in inquiry, and having written the definition of a specific figure such as *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) according to the rule: “The [subject] being described is perceived through a slight indication,” he provides this as an illustration thereof: “Speech has reached the face of the Four-faced One (Brahmā); Fortune has reached the chest of Murāri (Viṣṇu); but as for my own beauty, that circle of ornaments has not yet found a place of rest.”
That which has been shown by us is to be disregarded;

for here, due to the absence of a listener who asks questions, the speaker does not employ *samāsokti* (condensed expression) through the superimposition of conventional usage upon things in their state of becoming.
The expressed meaning (*vācya-artha*) is of two kinds:
It is well known that [the suggested meaning] is either inherently possible (*svataḥ-sambhavī*) or established through bold assertion (*prauḍhokti-siddha*).

In that regard, if the meaning established through bold assertion were considered a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*), then meanings such as "The month has arrived" (*sajjai surai māso*) would also result in being poetic figures.

In this instance, there is the figure of speech *nidarśanā* (illustration), as in the verse beginning "That which was experienced by the deer-eyed one," where the King of Kuntala’s speech and other qualities are shown to have gone to the Four-Faced One (Brahmā) and so forth.
Since the identification (*adhyavasāya*) is established without being explicitly stated, some propose the figure of *śabdamūlātiśayokti* (hyperbole based on words).

Nevertheless, regarding the analysis of *nidarśanā*, it has been stated here that in the definition "the conceptualization of a comparison is *nidarśanā*," the word "comparison" (*upamā*) signifies mere similarity (*sādṛśyamātra*).
For this very reason, the author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva* has also stated:
"Nidarśanā is the production of a reflection that is understood through a connection between two things, whether such a connection be possible or impossible.
Thus, in examples such as "the gait of a swan by her feet" and "that [moon] the luster of whose face," there is also the creation of a mental image (*pratikalpanā*).
“Upon the emerald grounds, the rays of the sun, falling through the gaps between the branches of the trees and shimmering with networks of fine dust,
here bear the beauty of the throats of downcast peacocks.”

And in this case, since there is the possibility of the occurrence of those whose necks are bowed before the blue-throated one (Śiva) on such grounds, if one were to conceive of it as a *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), the present example would fall under that; whereas if one conceives of it as *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), it would fall under *nidarśanā* (illustrative simile).

Furthermore, because each individual [attribute]—speech and so forth—occurs both in the king and in the four-faced one (Brahmā) and others, and because this [figure] has its life-force in the superimposition of behavior (*vyavahāra-samāropa*) just like *samāsokti*, it is distinct from *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact) based on the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*).

In the case of suggestion through simile (*upamādhvani*), the subject not under discussion is suggested; likewise in the case of "speech of condensed meaning" (*samāsokti*). But in the case of paronomasia (*śleṣa*), both subjects are expressed as the literal meaning.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,

ba) But surely, in examples such as "O traveler" (*panthia*), regarding that suggestion of a fact (*vastudhvani*) based on the power of words which was mentioned— where, while there is the capacity for enjoyment, there is the suggested fact consisting in the inference of [the traveler's] staying— is it not that very thing which is the subject at hand (*prastuta*) by virtue of being the speaker’s intended object?

The expressed meaning (vācyārtha), however, is irrelevant to the context; thus, it would follow that this is merely *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise). Therefore, he states its distinction from that: in the case of *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact), there is an admission of such a state [of the expressed meaning] as being suggested (*vyaṅgya*).

The meaning is that it is because the superimposition (*samāropa*) of the expressed conventional usage onto the suggested person and so forth constitutes its very life-force (*prāṇatva*), and because it brings that about.
Furthermore, in this context, the phrase "rooted in the power of the word" (*śabdaśaktimūla*) is illustrative;
for even in such cases as "O neighbor, [look at] my sight," there is a suggested meaning—the concealment of future nail-marks.
That too was introduced by the speaker as the intended subject.
It should be understood that the objection—that the expressed meaning (*vācya-artha*) is irrelevant there—and the response are exactly the same in this case.

He states "in the suggestion of simile" (*upamādhvanau*) because there is no possibility of such an objection at all in the figure of speech known as *samāsokti* or in the ornament of verbal pun (*śabda-śleṣa*).
For here, the non-contextual (aprastuta) is the expressed (vācya);

whereas in the case of suggestion of simile (upamādhvani) and concise expression (samāsokti), the non-contextual is exclusively suggested (vyaṅgya). Thus, there is no possibility of this [figure] occurring in those two. He states that there is also no possibility of its occurrence in the case of paronomasia (śleṣa): *atra hyaprastuto vācyaḥ / upamādhvanisamāsoktau cāprastuto vyaṅgya eveti tayornāsyāḥ prasaktiḥ / śleṣe 'pi nāsyāḥ prasaktirityāha /*
For *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) occurs when there is the suggestion of an irrelevant matter through *śleṣa* (paronomasia);
however, in the case of *śleṣa*, the meaning is that both matters are equally expressed as the literal sense (*vācya*). — *Locanā*.

(Lo, ī) Now, [the author] demonstrates the distinction of this [figure] from suggestion based on the power of words (*dhvani*) regarding the matter, which is to be understood by those of good intellect—starting with the words "asyāśca" ("and of this").

"Of this" refers to *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise). Its distinction from suggestion based on the power of words regarding the matter (*vastudhvani*) is as follows: in such instances as "The sole means for enjoyment and liberation," when the word "āgama" occurs, the conventional usage of the meaning "coming of the virtuous" (*sata āgamanam*) is superimposed upon the sense of "sacred scripture" (*sacchāstra*).
However, the employment of redundant words is solely for the purpose of concealing the secret; therefore, the intended meaning is that this constitutes a distinction.
The phrase "the state of being expressible" is to be understood as "by way of not being definitively determined."
The figure of speech known as *vyājastuti* (feigned praise) has been explained once more.

When praise and blame are implied by words that express either censure or eulogy, it is the figure of speech called *vyājastuti* ("disguised praise"), as noted in the *Locanā*. (Lo, u) This is the name of the poetic ornament.
Following *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), the definition of this [figure] is given because of its similarity to the variety caused by what is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Its distinction from *aprastutapraśaṃsā* lies in the fact that it lacks the relationship of general and particular, cause and effect, or identity, which exists between praise and blame in the former.
When praise is understood through blame, it is called *vyājastuti* (disguised praise) based on the etymological derivation "praise by means of a pretext" (*vyājena stutiḥ*).
When censure is understood through praise, it is "disguised praise" (*vyājastuti*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, bha) states: he describes the figure of speech "disguised praise" with the words "it is called *vyāja*."

Regarding the phrase "by the two expressible [meanings]": although in the examples to be cited neither the censure nor the praise is directly expressed (*vācyatva*), nevertheless, the meaning is "by the two meanings that are expressible and which serve as the motivators for the censure and the praise. Since the suggested sense (*gamyatve*)—that is, the implied sense—is present, there is the possibility of the application of the term *vyājastuti* (ironic praise) because praise occurs under the guise of censure, or *vyājanindā* (feigned censure) because censure occurs under the guise of praise. Thus, by means of the two compounds, he establishes the referent of that term in both cases with the words "by censure" (*nindayā*).
For example, in sequence:
"O King, even when you were angry, the wives of your enemies became as trusting as before— their pearl ornaments fallen from their breasts and their slender bodies covered in thorns."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ma) Here, under the guise of censure, he utters praise with the words "the breasts," etc.:
O Lord, those well-known wives of your enemies, when you were formerly angry with them, were as trusting as ever.

He describes the state of unity even during the state of anger, as if it were the state of non-anger, beginning with the words "stanayuga" (pair of breasts). [The women] had ornaments fashioned from pearls.

In the state of non-anger, their slender bodies were seen to be covered with thorns; however, in the state of anger, because they entered the thorny forest out of fear, they appeared just like that—[the same] as in the state of non-anger.
"Trusting" means fearless; however, in a state of anger, they possess "excessive trust" (viśiṣṭa-śvasta), meaning their breathing is particularly labored due to long sighs caused by anxiety.

Since they are expressed by the same word in every respect, they are previously considered equal; yet, because there is no distinction from their state during non-angry times even when in anger, this constitutes a censure.
But the praise is by means of the second sense of the compound word *śliṣṭapada*. Regarding *Locanā*:
(lo, ū) in the word *muktā*, it means "released" or "abandoned."
In the alternative sense: she in whom there are ornaments made of pearls; where there is a *kaṇaṭaka* (a thorny plant), it is well known to be found upon a creeper, as is horripilation (*lomāñca*);
and "trustful" (*viśvastā*) refers both to a widow and to those endowed with trust (*viśvasa*).
This is mine.
“O cloud, this ‘praise by artifice’ has been uttered by me regarding you: that your waters are for the very life of the world. But this, O rain-cloud, is truly a great hymn to you!
That you acquire the assistance of the King of Dharma by slaying travelers on the road!
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ya) He expresses censure through praise—this is *vyājastuti* (feigned praise).
O cloud (*payoda*), that which is for the life of the world (*jagat*)—your lives, your waters—is this feigned praise (*vyājastuti*) of yours that has been uttered by me; it is indeed a false praise.
The meaning is that when the praise exceeds this [limit], even this praise is no praise at all.
He speaks of a further praise: "But your hymn...
O Cloud! In that you destroy the travelers who are separated from their lovers, you acquire the greatness of being an assistant to Dharmarāja, Yama.

This, however, is a great hymn to you; because your deeds are equal to those of the King of Dharma (Yama) in causing the destruction of the world, there is an excess of majesty in your performing the opposite of his function—namely, the sustaining of the living beings of the world—but it is not that [same] kind of majesty.
Here, there is censure for being a slayer of travelers.

In this context, although praise (*stuti*) is the expressed meaning, the fact that the word for praise has been explained as being directed toward the purpose underlying the praise is for the sake of including other examples. For instance, in the speech addressed to Karṇa by Aśvatthāman: "O Karṇa, you obtained praise through your generosity; but now, from battle, having retreated and given away your fame to the enemy, you have obtained even more than that," there is no literal expression of praise.
Locanā:
(Lo, Ṛ) "Jīvana" refers to waters and vital breath;
"ghana" means without interval.
Yama is the King of Dharma;
*paryāyokta* (indirect expression) occurs when that which is already implied is stated by means of a figurative turn of phrase.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ra) He states the figure of speech *paryāyokta*—namely, "paryāyoktam" [is as follows].

The "suggested" (*gamya*) is the *vyaṅgya* (the implied meaning), and that should be understood as being of the nature of the cause of the subject at hand (*prastuta*). By a particular turn of expression (*bhaṅgyā*), even the subject at hand, in the form of its effect, is expressed—that is, it is communicated.
The ellipsis is "only by means of suggestion" (*vyañjanayā eva*).
The meaning is that it is not understood through [direct] denotative power (*śakti*).
The meaning is: when the relevant cause is manifested by means of the relevant effect.

However, in the case of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), where the form consists of a cause, a manifestor, and an effect, the distinction will be stated as follows: by means of the non-contextual effect, the contextual cause is manifested—as in the verse beginning with "The moon is as if smeared with collyrium.
(Locanā)
(lo, ṝ) Now, in connection with the section on the varieties of suggestion (*vyaṅgyavicchitti*), he defines *paryāyokta* [with the words] "paryāyoktam":

by means of a particular turn of phrase (*bhaṅgyā*)—that is, by resorting to another striking figure of speech that is skillful in producing aesthetic wonder—the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is expressed or made known through the medium of an effect (*kārya*) and so forth; this is the sense.
An example follows:
The flower-clusters of the Pārijāta tree, which had been cherished by Śacī as she enjoyed them in the Nandana grove, were touched with disdain by his soldiers.

In this case, the fact that "Heaven has been conquered by Hayagrīva" is the very cause already under discussion; however, for the sake of conveying a particular strikingness (*vaicitryaviśeṣa*), it is expressed through its effect—namely, the army's disdainful touch upon the *pārijāta* blossoms.
Thus says the *Vijñapriyā*: "They were touched."
The meaning is that those famous clusters of *pārijāta* blossoms, accustomed to being fondled by the hair of Śacī, were touched with contempt in the Nandana grove by the soldiers of King Triśaṅku.
Here, the implied suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*)— which takes the form of a cause— is the aforementioned touching of the clusters with contempt, as it is communicated through suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
"Of the one to be described" means of King Hayagrīva;
it is by his power alone that [Añjanadevī] touched Mañjarī with contempt.
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) [The letters] *lo* and *ḷ* are those cherished through the enjoyment of hair and those accustomed to the binding of hair.
This is stated by way of function (*kāryadvāreṇa*), because the touch of a cluster of blossoms from the Pārijāta tree is not distinct from the conquest of heaven.
And here, the specific excellence of variety is obtained from the demonstration that "Heaven has been conquered," a fact attested by direct experience.
Thus, having seen him, even the long-established love for dwelling was abandoned:
pride left the face of Airāvaṇa out of intoxication, and the heart of Indra [left it] out of respect.
In this passage, the very destruction of pride and arrogance is expressed as their abandonment of the pleasure of their dwelling; this is *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
Thus, the sense is that *paryāyokta* occurs when that which is actually implied is itself stated.

As stated by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* in his explanation of the definition of *paryāyokta*: "That which is expressed is the same as that which is suggested, but it is not expressed in the same manner as it is suggested."
And this [type of *aprastutapraśaṃsā*] is possible even when the effect is understood through a cause that is explicitly expressed;
nor is this the same as the *aprastutapraśaṃsā* consisting in the cognition of a cause from an effect, because in that case the effect itself is the irrelevant subject (*aprastuta*).
In this case, however, the effect is presented as being like the cause, because it serves to make known the extraordinary power of the subject being described.
Thus:
“By him, who was shedding teardrops as large as pearls upon their breasts...”
The necklaces of the wives of the enemies have returned, even without the strings used for their fastening.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, va) Now, by means of another verse concerning the matter at hand, he demonstrates the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) known as *prastutakāraṇavyañjanā* (the suggestion of the relevant cause), beginning with "In this way" (*evam ca*).
This is the speech of the nurse to Indumatī, who was choosing her own husband.

By this king, who caused the largest drops of tears— like pearls— to fall upon the breasts of his enemies' women, necklaces were returned even without the string for tossing them or the string for threading them; the meaning is that the very drops of tears were made into necklaces.

In this case, just as the cause—the killing of the enemy who is to be understood—is described through the king who is the subject of description, so too the effect—the weeping of the wives of such enemies—is worthy of description because it makes known the excellence of his power;
thus, this is indeed *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
"O King, the princesses do not teach me; the queens also remain silent. O Kubja, feed me! Why is nothing yet being eaten by the princes and ministers?"
Thus, having been released from his cage by travelers in the palace of your enemy, the royal parrot gazes upon the figures in the paintings and addresses each one individually from the empty turret.
Vijñapriyā:
