Regarding the figure of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), which consists in the suggestion of a relevant cause through an irrelevant effect, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* has provided the example beginning with "O King, [are these] princesses...
Some say that even in that case, the effect is indeed the relevant subject (*prastuta*); to demonstrate this, he says: "O King," etc.
This is the speech of a minister addressed to a king intent on conquering Śatruñjaya: "Your enemies have fled;
the path has proceeded right through the middle of their city."
The meaning is that the royal parrot, having been released from its cage by travelers, saw the king and others depicted in a painting and addressed each one in this manner.
To the question of what he said, [the author] replies: "O King!"—addressing him as "O Queen," the implication being that you too remain silent.
However, this statement was not made by the king, because it is impossible for him to speak to each person individually.
A certain hunchbacked woman, a princess appointed to feed the parrot, asks "O Princess" during the time of the minister's meal, due to her own rule of eating at that same time.
Locanā:
(Lo, E) The hunchbacked women are the elderly ladies of the inner apartments;
the "princes' ministers" are children who have become childhood friends of the princes.
In this case, the reason presented is that upon hearing you were intent on setting out, the enemies fled immediately;
some say that "the effect is also presented as being worthy of description.
Others, however, say: "By means of the account of the royal parrot, some power of the subject at hand is made known; therefore, this is indeed *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description)."
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṣa) According to the view of some, here the effect of the contextual cause—which consists of the enemy’s flight—is precisely the parrot’s speech, which is also the subject at hand; thus he shows this with the words "here" (*atre*).
He then shows the intention of the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* with the words "others, however" (*anye tu*).
Regarding the phrase "by means of the story of the royal parrot":

the meaning is that, unlike the shedding of a tear-drop during the act of killing an enemy, the parrot's speech lacks the certainty of causing the enemy's flight; therefore, it does not serve to awaken the king to his own power.
The underlying intention is that the city could have become empty even due to the force of a great pestilence (*mahāmārī*).
The statement made by the minister is indeed justified by the intention that fleeing was the course of action;
however, in reality, the topicality of the minister’s speech remains entirely unassailable.
Whether it be the general qualified by the particular, or the particular by the general—[the context is established].
And this effect is established by means of its cause, and the cause is established by means of the effect.
"Then, by means of similarity and its opposite, the *arthāntaranyāsa* is of eight kinds. [The author] states the eightfold *arthāntaranyāsa* ornament: "Or the general," and so forth.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, sa) He states the eightfold *arthāntaranyāsa* ornament—namely, "or the general," etc.
Having understood it generally, one understands it specifically;
likewise,
having understood it specifically, one understands it generally.
In this way, the effect is supported by the cause, or the cause by the effect; that is to say, it is established as being appropriate.
What has been stated—that which is general is understood as appropriate because its suchness is seen in the particular—is the method of support (*samarthanarīti*).

Thus, there are four kinds of support, based on the similarity between the supported (*samarthya*) and the supporter (*samarthaka*), or otherwise through their mutual dissimilarity; therefore, the meaning is that there are eight types.
The examples in order are as follows:
"Even one who is very small reaches the completion of his task when aided by a great companion;
a mountain stream, having united with a great river, reaches the ocean."
Here, the general meaning contained in the first half [of the verse] is supported by the specific meaning found in the second half through a logical justification.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ha):
In that regard, he states the support of the general by the specific through similarity (*sādharmyeṇa*) as follows: "It is vast... (*bṛhat*).
"Kāryāntam" means the end of the task intended to be accomplished;
"kṣodīyān" means minute or small;
"sambhūya" means having come together or united with a great river.
"Nāgāpagā" refers to small rivers and mountain torrents; here, the term "second half" means that the specific type of small river is used in the sense of that form.
The general meaning is that it has the nature of a minor generality (*kṣudrasāmānya*).
In this context, the commonality between the two is their capacity to lead toward a further effect. [The phrase] "with its logical justification" means:
The meaning is that the propriety of the arising is established by way of its being qualified by that [other factor].

Although such a justification would not be appropriate for a trivial commonality because it is not perceived as such, nevertheless, the justification for that [commonality] when it is qualified by its transition to another effect should be understood as pertaining to the qualifying element, according to the maxim: "Affirmations and negations apply to things with their qualifiers."
The same applies in subsequent cases as well.

Here, because it is observed that a specific instance of the minor (*kṣudra*), namely the mountain-river (*nagāpagā*), leads to the completion of its effect, there arises the understanding that it is appropriate for the general category of the minor (*kṣudrasāmānya*) to likewise lead to the completion of its effect;
thus it is in all instances.
Having thus spoken words that were as many as necessary for his purpose, Mādhava ceased;
for the great, by their very nature, are speakers of measured speech.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) He states the support of the particular by means of the general through similarity: "as far as the purpose extends" (*yāvadartha*).
This is a description of the cessation of speech by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The meaning is: "of such descriptions" refers to whatever extent of meaning one intends to express. "Mahīyāṃsaḥ" means the great ones.
Here, the excellence [consists] in the cessation of speech regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The great ones are distinguished by their measured speech; this is the commonality.
Cessation from speech is a shared characteristic in the case of measured speech as well, because it too consists in the cessation of much talking.
The very justification for the excellence of abstaining from unwholesome speech is itself the justification for this [measured speech].
“O Earth, be firm!
O Serpent, support her! O King of Tortoises, you must uphold this pair!”
O elephants of the quarters, show your desire to support him; the Noble One draws the bow of Hara to its full extent.
In this instance, the act of stringing the bow of Hara—which serves as the cause—is the corroborative support for the effect, namely the stability of the earth and so forth.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, kha) states, using similarity (*sādharmya*), that the corroboration of an effect by its cause is expressed in the verse beginning with "The earth... (*pṛthvī...*).
The similarity between cause and effect consists precisely in their possession of non-contradictory properties;
likewise, their possession of contradictory properties should be understood as their dissimilarity.
This is the speech of Lakṣmaṇa at the moment the bow was broken.
The meaning is that because the noble Rāma draws his bow—whose ends are like those of Hara’s—tightly, for that reason the earth and other elements become stable and so forth.
[He addresses] this earth;
[the two words] "earth" and "serpent" constitute the second [pair].
In that triad— the triad consisting of the Earth, the Serpent, and the King of Tortoises—
he desired to maintain the intent to uphold [the world].
Otherwise, however, the meaning is that by the very weight that would result from stringing the bow to its full extent, all three would lose their stability.
Regarding this:
it should not be argued that the stability of the earth and so forth cannot be the effect of the drawing of the bowstring, because instability and the like are what constitute its effects;
for it is through the possibility of instability and so forth that the maintenance of specific stability and the like constitutes its effect.

Nor should it be argued that, since the state of having the bowstring drawn (*ātatajyīkaraṇa*) occurs after [the previous moment], how can the stability of the specific quality (*viśeṣa*) and so forth existing prior to it be considered an effect even in that case; for when there is an effect of the knowledge of that [quality], it is metaphorically designated as its effect, just as the *nāndīmukha* rite is designated as being caused by the wedding.

In this context, the common property (*sādharmya*) between these two—the cause and the effect—is the possession of a characteristic that delimits their respective causal and effected states without contradiction.

The justification that it is appropriate for the earth and other such things to become stable due to such a cause is the "instruction on stability" (*sthirībhāvopadeśa*), which has a single purpose. Some also state that its very appropriateness (*aucitya*) constitutes the justification. Since the fourfold set of justifications—beginning with *kārya* (effect)—is of the nature of the figure of speech *hetu* (cause), the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* disregards them and states only the fourfold division of *arthāntaranyāsa*, because a cause is that which brings about an effect.
Furthermore, because it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of an effect,
the author will later explain its distinction from that [effect]:

in such passages as "One should not perform an action impulsively," the act of careful deliberation (*sampadvaraṇa*) is the effect, which supports the cause consisting of acting with reflection, namely, the absence of impulsive performance.
These are examples based on similarity (*sādharmya*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ga):
He states the support of the cause by means of the effect through similarity as follows: "all at once," etc.
One should not perform an action impulsively, without reflection; for lack of discernment and acting without deliberation are the very seat of supreme calamities.
However, when one acts with deliberation, not only are there no misfortunes, but there are even successes—as he says: "For they choose... and so forth.
In this context, greed is justified precisely by the quality of acting with deliberation;
for it is appropriate that one acts with deliberation when the task at hand is the attainment of prosperity. This is the argument.
An example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is as follows:
"Even when propitiated in this manner, a wicked person torments the three worlds;
he is pacified by retaliation, not by kindness."
In this case, the general is supported by the particular.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, gha):
It will be stated that an example of the support of the general by the particular through dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*) is to be inferred.

Therefore, without citing that specific instance, he provides an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) to support the general principle through a particular case, beginning with "In this way" (*ittham*).
In the verse that makes known Tāraka Asura’s role as the tormentor of the three worlds, Tāraka Asura is a specific wicked person characterized by being the tormentor of the three worlds.
The property of being worshipped is a property contradictory to that [tormenting], and it belongs to the wicked person in general, who is the one being made cognizant [of the truth].

Thus, tranquility is the dissimilarity from the state of being an affliction; the justification of a particular wicked person distinguished by the state of being an affliction is itself a form of justification for the state of being an affliction, according to the logical principle that "when there is a qualifier... (viśeṣaṇe hi).
For the pacification of a wicked person occurs only through retaliation;
thus, there is the understanding that for a particular wicked person like Tāraka—who is characterized by hostility toward the world—it is appropriate to cause distress to the universe.
In the verse "one should not act impulsively," the absence of impulsive action is supported by its contrary effect: the fact that such action brings about calamity.
The same applies to the others.
*Vijñapriyā*:
It will be stated that the illustration for "establishing the effect by means of the cause through dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyeṇa*) is to be inferred.

Therefore, without stating that [the reason], one might hastily provide an example of "establishing the cause by means of the effect through dissimilarity" (vaidharmyeṇa); to address this, he says "hastily" (sahasā). This refers to the absence of a hasty presentation of the cause.

The state of being a word for an impossibility (*āpatti-padatva*) is the logical support (*samarthaka*); since it is opposed by the state of perfection (*sampad*), the meaning is that it possesses contradictory properties (*viruddha-dharmavat*).
Here, the contradictory properties are "non-existence" (*abhāvatva*) and "existence" (*bhāvatva*).
For here, the understanding is that for one who acts only after reflection, it is appropriate to refrain from acting impulsively due to the obstruction of success by the [potential] effect;

"and so forth" means that the support of a general qualification by a specific instance, as well as the support of an effect by its cause, which were not illustrated by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmyeṇa), are to be understood in this manner.

In this regard, the establishment of a general principle by means of a specific instance through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is as follows: “Because of the wickedness of its own qualities, a beast of burden is not yoked to the pole;
a gaunt ox, whose shoulders have not yet developed calluses, sleeps soundly.”
Thus [it is said].
The meaning of this is as follows: a beast capable of bearing a load being placed upon it is yoked to the pole for the purpose of carrying that burden.

And that [burden] arises solely from the wickedness and malice of the qualities (guṇas), because their quality of being "pole-bearers" (dhūryatva) causes the suffering of carrying the load; thus, it is their malice.
He says that such suffering does not occur in the absence of [physical] qualities: "asaṃjāta... etc.
A *kiṇa* is a swollen area resulting from the friction of a yoke;
a cow whose hump has not yet developed, being thin and sluggish, sleeps happily.
The meaning is that he is not yoked to the burden.

Here, the general category of "a beast capable of bearing a burden" (*dhūrya-prāṇin*)— which is being yoked to the burden— is established by means of a specific instance of a beast not being yoked, such as a camel or an ox, which possesses the contradictory property of being yoked [to other things], and by means of the contradictory properties of "being at ease in sleep" (contrary to the state of a burden-bearer) and "having a hump" (contrary to the state of a burden-bearer).

Since it is understood that it is appropriate for a draft animal (*dhurya*) accustomed to sleeping comfortably to be yoked to the burden, the justification of the yoking itself constitutes the justification of the draft animal being yoked;
this follows the maxim: "When a qualified [subject] is mentioned, [the qualification is also implied].
An example of the justification of an effect by its cause through dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*) is as follows: "That lord of the Rākṣasas, arrogant in his might, conquered all in battle."
For one who has not tasted such a pungent yet delicious flavor as that of Rāma’s arrow is indeed like that.
Thus,
here Rāvaṇa’s victory— the effect— is supported by the cause, which is the tasting of the bitter flavor of Rāma’s arrows;
for it is understood that his victory would be appropriate only through not tasting them, since it is impossible when they are tasted.
When existence and non-existence constitute the dissimilarity between those two,
and the reason is expressed through the meaning of a sentence or a word, it is called *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of the causal mark).

Vijñapriyā: (vi, ca) He states the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga*: when [the causal relation] is complete through the relationship of action and its agent (*kriyākārakabhāva*), it is a sentence (*vākya*); when it is incomplete, it is a word (*pada*).
This very figure of speech is called *hetvalaṅkāra* (the ornament of cause) and *kāvyahetu* (poetic cause).
An example of its function as the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārthatā*) is as follows:
“O beloved, that blue lotus which was submerged in the water, possessing a luster equal to your eyes, has been hidden by the clouds;”
"The moon imitates the luster of your face;
even those royal swans, whose gait imitates your own, have departed. Yet fate does not permit me even the mere diversion of your likeness."
In this case, the statements of the first three quarters of the verse serve as the reasons for the fourth quarter:
"That which is your eye... (Vijñapriyā, vi, cha).
This is Rāma’s speech addressed to Sītā—who was brought to him through meditation during the rainy season and who had been carried off by Rāvaṇa:
"O beloved! Even that mere diversion which arises from seeing objects resembling you is not permitted to me by fate.
To the objection, "Surely, let the resemblances of your eyes and face be seen in the blue lotus, the moon, and the gait of a swan," he replies:
As for the phrase "that which is your eye":
due to the rainy season, the blue lotus is submerged in water,
and the moon is obscured by clouds.
The meaning is that the royal swans have gone to Lake Mānasa.

Regarding the phrase "three-footed sentences," since each of the three sentences is complete in itself through the relationship of action and its factors (kriyākārakabhāva), the term "reasons" (*hetavaḥ*) here means they possess the sense of reasons (*hetvarthakāḥ*).

The status of being a "thing" (padārthatā) is as in my own verse: "Hara does not bear on his head the Gaṅgā, which is muddied by the mass of dust kicked up by the hooves of your horses, out of fear of its great weight."
In this case, within the second half-verse, the first half-verse functions as a single-word reason:
"vijñapriya tvadvājī" (O you who are dear to the wise, your horse...).
"Shaken off" means he has been shaken out;
"he does not hold" is what is intended;
[this refers to] "a single word."

The meaning is that [the example] ending with *paṅkilām* constitutes a single word because it is not completed due to a lack of connection with a verb (*kriyānanvaya*) and because it forms a compound (*samāsa*). An example of multiple words is as follows, from my own work:
“They behold the river of the waters of your gift, flowing along countless paths.”
O King, she protects her own self, the triple-pathed river, upon the head of the fierce one.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
jha) "They see her as innumerable"— here too, it is imagined that she is concealing herself.

In this context, because the phrases "here they behold," "going upon countless paths," and "the river carrying your water of charity" are incomplete due to the lack of connection with a verb, the statement regarding the going upon countless paths— viewed in relation to the going upon the three paths—
serves as the cause for concealing that vision.

Here, some do not favor the figure of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth) on the grounds that its purpose is already served by the *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) residing in the meaning of the sentence, since the relationship of cause and effect is already established.
That is incorrect; for in this context, the logical reason (*hetu*) is threefold: the indicator (*jñāpaka*), the producer (*niṣpādaka*), and the corroborator (*samarthaka*).
Among these, the indicator is the object of inference (*anumāna*).

The producer of *kāvyaliṅga* is the *samarthaka* (the corroborator), whereas the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) is the *samarthya* (that which is corroborated); thus, because their causal relationship is distinct, *arthāntaranyāsa* is separate from *kāvyaliṅga*.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ña) He states the intended meaning of the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* with the words "In this regard, some...
and "By that which pertains to the sentence-meaning...".

Regarding the examples shown by one capable of performing the task, since the causes therein pertain solely to the meaning of the sentence, the scope of inference (*anumāna*) is that which makes [the cause] known.

However, this was written by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* while disregarding the distinction between the scopes; for in his view, only a question is a "cause" (*hetu*) that makes something known, and it is not the figure of speech "Cause" (*hetvalaṅkāra*), because in that case it is permeated by the figure of speech "Answer" (*uttarālaṅkāra*).
In other cases, however, a cause that is both productive (*janaka*) and informative (*jñāpaka*) belongs strictly to the figure of speech known as *hetu* (Poetic Cause).

For this very reason: "O smearing of ashes, may it be auspicious to you! O rosary of Rudrākṣa beads, may it be well! Alas, we are today being cast by the Lord—pleased by our worship—into the great delusion called 'liberation,' which destroys the world and consists of the bliss of serving you, [a delusion] which serves as a staircase to the abode of the Son of the Mountain and adorns it."

Thus, in this verse, the fact that liberation cuts off the light of happiness is cited as an example of the figure of speech *hetu* (causal), by stating it as the reason for its being a "great delusion" (*mahāmoha*). In this context, since the state of liberation being a great delusion is unreal, the cutting off of the light of happiness cannot possibly be its generative cause; therefore, it can only be its indicative cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*).

Furthermore, an inference (*anumāna*) occurs only when there is a presentation of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) as residing in a single substratum (*ekadharmigata*), and only when the probans is presented specifically as a cause.
In this case, however, by the phrase "cutting off the light of happiness," there is merely an indication of the reason (*hetu*), but not its formal status as a logical reason.

This is because even you, in the verses yet to be cited as examples of inference, will state reasons only in their capacity as actual logical reasons; for an inference is not established merely by saying, "The mountain possesses fire, because of smoke."

Therefore, the mere indicative reason (*jñāpaka-hetu*) is not the domain of the figure of speech *anumāna* (inference); rather, it is only the reason as demonstrated [in poetic form] that constitutes its domain.
Consequently, it has been stated that the inferential nature of inference belongs only to the indicative reason when it is presented in such a manner.
That which brings about the *kāvyaliṅga*—
it should be noted that this [definition] also does not apply in cases such as "the smearing with ashes" (*bhasmoddhūlana*).
In the verses “tvadvājirājī... and “paśyantyasaṃkhyā...,” there is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) because the cause cannot be the producer [of the effect].

For instance, in the passage beginning with “yattvannetra-,” the sentence of the fourth quarter depends upon the sentences contained in the first three quarters as its producers; otherwise, due to its state of expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatā*), it would simply be incoherent.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṭa) Regarding the example of the figure of speech *uktahetu* (stated cause) in the verse beginning "yattvanetrasamānakānti," [the author] states the following because it is impossible for blue lotuses and the like to be the generative causes of the gods' lack of ability [to see], due to their being submerged in water; thus, he explains their status as generative causes through a "painful" (or strained) poetic construction.
For instance, the statement of the fourth quarter, "That which is in your eye," indicates divine power;

otherwise, if the reason beginning with "that which is in your eye" were not provided, the sentence would be inconsistent, as the expectation for a reason would remain unfulfilled due to its presence.

In the phrase "the sentence consisting of three quarters," the meaning is "the meaning of the sentence. By way of being the producer [of that meaning], it is because it possesses a cognition free from expectancy; specifically, by way of producing the divine eye. And thus, by way of producing the qualifying portion in the form of the objective status (*viṣayatā*) of such a cognition, it is said to produce the qualified [object] itself, according to the maxim of the "qualified" (*saviśeṣaṇanyāya*).
This is not well-stated;

for if one accepts that [a figure] produces its object by virtue of producing the status of being the object of the indicative portion, then it would follow that this occurs in both the figure of inference (*anumānālaṅkāra*) and the figure of indication (*jñāpakālaṅkāra*).
Therefore, disregarding such an arduous classification, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* has not accepted *arthāntaranyāsa* as the "corroboration of cause and effect";
that alone is superior.
However, in cases such as "One should not act impulsively..."—
“I tell you the truth: one should never associate with wicked people who delight in harming others.”

Just as in the aforementioned examples, even by mere instruction, because there is no further expectation, the matter is understood by itself; thus, the avoidance of immediate injunction is accomplished along with its supporting reasoning. Therefore, this *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different fact) is distinct from *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) due to the presence of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
— *Vijñapriyā*.

(Vi, ṭha) [Objection: But in this case, even in verses such as "One should not act impulsively" (*sahasā na vidadhīta*), the first half of the verse remains expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) without the meaning of the second half, such as "for they choose" (*vṛṇate hi*).
Therefore, according to the reasoning stated, there too it would be *kāvyaliṅga* alone and not *arthāntaranyāsa*. This is the meaning.

He states that there is no such expectation in that case with the words "sahasā" (suddenly), etc. For in passages such as "they choose [the Lord] being free from expectation even by mere instruction," the sense is already established through the absence of expectation; therefore, the agent performs the act of choosing—which is the object—along with its justification, namely the absence of a sudden injunction.
Is it not the case that a reason becomes valid by the force of expectancy?
In that regard, he provides an illustration for its status as an instruction: "by those devoted to harming others.
In this context, [the phrase] is "not in what is to be enjoined."
Thus, by means of the suffix *kṛtya* and others, even here in the word "vidadhīte," the understanding of an injunction (*vidhi*) arises from the injunctive suffix; this is the meaning.

The distinction is that in passages such as "parāpakāra... and so forth, because there is no mention of a thing to be justified (*samarthanīya*), there is no *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a corroborative instance) at all.
However, this must be noted: in cases such as "sahasā" (suddenly), since the purpose is fulfilled by the nature of the instruction itself, let there be no *hetu* (cause) figure of speech.

But in cases such as "O Earth, be firm," since the instruction is possible only when stability is already established, the drawing of the bowstring necessarily requires a cause; thus, the occurrence of the *hetu* figure is unavoidable there, as in:
"Hara does not bear the Gaṅgā on his head out of fear of its great weight."
For that [road] has indeed become muddy with the dust kicked up by the rows of your horses."

For here, by the employment of the word *hi* (for/since), the nature of the reason is made explicit— just as in the expression "because of its being muddy"— and thus this is not a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*), since a poetic figure consists solely in a striking or charming peculiarity (*vaicitrya*).
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ḍa) Where there is a mention of the cause merely as a cause, there is no figure of speech called *hetu* because of the absence of poetic charm (*vaicitrya*); thus he says: "He places [it]," and so forth.
Regarding this, he says: "The word *hi*," because the word *hi* indicates the state of being a cause.
*Locanā*:

(lo, ai) Here, the reason (*hetu*) is threefold, because by its threefold nature the division of the domains of the figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) is established. To the question "How is it threefold?", he says: the *jñāpaka* (informative reason) is that which makes known—by its very state of being established—that which is not yet indicated and not yet understood.
Where there is a statement of two things possessing the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhaka*),

as for example in "where the arrows fall upon the weak women" (*yatra patantyabalānām*), etc., the falling of the arrows is not the producer of Madana’s running, but rather it is the producer of that which is already established through its expectancy;
likewise in "one should not perform an action impulsively" (*sahasā vidadhīta na kriyām*), etc.

Otherwise, the three quarters beginning with "yattvanetre" would be incoherent, because the state of this lover—his inability to find diversion through the likeness of the heroine—would not be perceived *svataḥ* (inherently).
The meaning is that since it possesses inherent capacity for justification, it remains complete even in the absence of the [final] sentence.

"Gatārtha" (already understood) means that the expressed meaning is apprehended as being free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatā*) by virtue of its distinction from the passage beginning with "yattvanetre."
He confirms what has already been stated with the words "precisely distinct":
by being clearly manifest as the object of expression,
[it is distinct] from *vaicitrya*, which is a non-worldly aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*).

And since this does not cease to be a cause by bringing about a variety of the *kāvyaliṅga*, it is the ornament named *kāvyaliṅga*. Inference (*anumāna*), however, is knowledge through a striking manner (*vicchitti*) because of the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) from the probans (*sādhana*). *Vijñapriyā*: And since this [cause] does not cease to be a cause by bringing about a variety of the *kāvyaliṅga*, it is the ornament named *kāvyaliṅga*. Inference (*anumāna*), however, is knowledge through a striking manner (*vicchitti*) because of the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) from the probans (*sādhana*).
(vi, ḍha) He states the figure of speech *anumāna* (inference): "But *anumāna*...

The meaning is that it is the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) through the means of proof (*sādhana*) by way of a particular mode (*bhaṅgī*). And this mode consists in the form of a superimposition (*āhāryāropa*).

To exclude cases such as "fire-possessing [the mountain] because of smoke," the qualification stated by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*— that the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) must reside in the same locus (*dharmin*)— must indeed be applied here.

Otherwise, in an inference such as "the earth is stable" where the reason consists of the drawing of a bowstring and the stability of the earth, there would result the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasakti*), even though the two loci (the bow and the earth) are distinct.
Locanā:
(lo, o) "By way of *vicchitti*," that is, by means of a striking variety evoked by the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*).

In cases such as "The mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," when there is merely a worldly statement regarding a subject possessing common properties (*sadharmī*), there is an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).

The universal is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*). The probans (*hetu*)—characterized by its presence in the subject (*pakṣasattva*), its presence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*), and its exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛttatva*)—is the means of proof (*sādhana*).

Thus, even according to the usage of words, wherever there is a presentation in the form of the relationship between the probandum and the probans, there exists the figure of speech known as inference (*anumānālaṅkāra*).
In *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic indication), however, the relationship between cause and effect is understood through the mere contemplation of the meaning.
For example:
"We know that in the heart of this lotus-eyed woman, the moon of her beloved's face shines within."
By the spreading nets of light from that [moon], her limbs became pale and her lotus-eyes took on the state of buds.
Here, the aesthetic charm arises by virtue of metaphor (*rūpaka*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṇa) This is a description of a woman separated from her lover, whose eyes are rolling.
"We know" means "we infer. The syntactical connection is with the word "asyāḥ" (of her).
The inference is as follows: she possesses a moon-like face within [her heart], because her lotus-eyes are closed and her body has become pale due to its dependence on that [moon's] luster.
Here, he demonstrates the strikingness [of the figure]: "In this case, it is *rūpaka* (metaphor).
One should also understand that there is *apahnuti* (concealment) regarding the aspect of the paleness of the limbs, in which the face and eyes are metaphorically identified as the moon and lotus.
— *Locanā*.

(Lo, au) By means of the nets of radiance from that moon; for that reason, because it was stated by internalizing the figure of speech (alaṅkāra) of metaphor (rūpaka)— which, by virtue of the metaphor, attributes the nature of a lotus to the eyes—
as for example:
“Wherever the gaze of these women falls, there sharp arrows descend;
therefore, I believe it is Love himself who runs before them with an arrow fixed upon his bow.”
In this case, there is a striking charm (*vicchitti*) arising from the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet.
The distinction between the two is that while in *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) there is a perception of something as being uncertain, here it is perceived as certain.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta) He provides another example by way of a different poetic figure (*vicchitti*), beginning with "where [the arrows] fall.
In the word *śarāḥ* (arrows), one should understand a distinction that indicates they are not the arrows of the God of Love (*smara*).
The word "I think" (*manye*) here means "we infer.
The inference is as follows: "The women are preceded by the God of Love who has fixed his arrows, because the arrows falling in various directions are distinguished by the cast of their own glances.
It should be understood that the arrows consist of flowers.

Their sharpness, however, is the attribute to be superimposed. He states the distinction of this [figure] from a particular type of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) with the words "in *utprekṣā*" (*utprekṣāyām*).
This means: in the case of *hetūtprekṣā* (fancying a cause).

Thus, it should be understood that in the two examples shown above, although the words "jānīmahe" (we know) and "manye" (I think) are expressive of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), there is no *utprekṣā* at all in those two cases [where they are absent]. However, it should also be understood that in the absence of those two words, there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of doubt (*sandeha*) in both instances. — *Locanā*.

(Lo, a) It is not only by resorting to another figure of speech that this strikingness (*vicchitti*) serves as the motivator for this particular figure; thus, he shows another example with the words "Or, for instance" (*yathā vā*).

In these two other examples, the state of being in the heart and the running of Smara—which serve as the causes—are the probanda (*sādhya*), while the budding of the lotus and the falling of the arrows are the probans (*sādhana*), just as in the [inference]: "This mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," and so forth.
Thus:

"Even while still on its own source, that which has fallen from the ears of young women—a blue lotus—is avoided by those who desire purity; for the waters, having cast it out with their waves, leave it upon the shore."

Here, the means of proof (*sādhana*) consists of a general property in the form of avoiding what has fallen, belonging to clear waters, which serves as a specific property in the form of excluding [the waters] from the blue lotus—
just as in the case of "This is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*," and so forth.
And thus, this particular strikingness (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) functions as the instigator of a distinct poetic figure called *vitarka* (deliberation).
The effort expended in defining [the nature of doubt] is based solely on a lack of reflection;
the sense is that it arises from a mere possibility due to being unascertained and not definitively determined.
This is unlike cases such as "this mountain possesses fire," where, because it is ascertained, [the property] like possessing fire is established.
The designation [of the reason] through non-difference from the possessor of the reason is the cause for [the reason's status as] a reason. 10.63.
As in my own verse: “The playfulness of youth”—here, the cause of subjugation (the heroine) is stated as the act of subjugating [the hero];
this figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) is based on the identification (*adhyavasāya*) between playfulness and laughter.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, tha) He states another figure of speech called *hetu*, distinct from *kāvyaliṅga*: "by way of non-difference" (*abhedena*).

The meaning is that the figure named *hetu* consists in the expression of the cause as non-different from the effect, which possesses that cause. He demonstrates this in the verse beginning with "of youth" (*tāruṇyasya*) by saying "subjugation" (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
Regarding the relationship of cause and effect between grace and laughter, he says "grace" (*vilāsa*).

The meaning is that grace and so forth are produced solely by youth and the like; because the heroine is the ultimate cause of this lineage [of qualities], there is a superimposition of non-difference (*abhedādhyāsa*), and it is based upon and embellished by that.
The intention is that beauty (*śobhā*) consists precisely in the presence of these many qualities.
And in this case, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* maintains that it is indeed *lakṣaṇā* (indication) of the pure *sāropā* type, for this is not a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*). —
*Locanā*.
The meaning is that the expression [of the two] as non-different arises from their indication as having a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
The "cause" (*hetu*) is the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) known by that name.
Its introduction follows immediately after inference (*anumāna*), because it relies on a striking deviation (*vicchitti*) between cause and effect.
It has its root in *adhyavasāya* (imaginative determination).
This is because the manifestation of variety is determined as *vilāsa* (sportiveness), and the abundant outburst is determined as *hāsa* (laughter).
Furthermore, if adversity is favorable, or if it is accompanied by favorability, [it constitutes the sentiment].
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) He states another ornament called *anukūla* [favourable]: "That which is favourable" (*anukūlam*).
The meaning is that if there is hostility (*prātikūlyam*) toward what is favourable, it is that which produces or is connected with the attainment of a desired object.
Locanā: (lo, i) *Anukūla* is the name of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*). It means that which follows favorably, or that which brings about favorability.
Since this too is rooted in the diversity of causes, its definition is that of another figure of speech (hetu-alaṅkāra).
The meaning of "of this offender" is as follows:—
“O slender one, when you are angry, having inflicted a wound with your fingernails,
then bind his neck firmly with the nooses of your arms.”
And because this particular variety of *vicchitti* manifests as distinct from all other ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), it is logical that it constitutes a separate ornament.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"You are angry"—this is a statement by a female friend to an indignant woman (*māninī*).
The word *yadi* means "if" or "when.
O slender one (*tanvi*), if you are angry, then having inflicted nail-marks, bind the neck of this lover firmly with your two noose-like arms—this is the meaning.
Here, the inflicting of nail-marks and the binding with arm-nooses are contrary [to the desired effect].
It is connected to the desired pleasure of the hero.
In this case, the favorable object is suggested (vyaṅgya);
however, in some instances, it is also directly expressed (vācya).
"Even though the god of love, who bears the makara on his banner, brings pain to my mind incessantly, he is welcome to me,
provided that he strikes me while aiming at her whose eyes are like those of a madira flower."
In this context, it should be stated that the word *abhimata* (intended) means "desired.
He states the reason for accepting an ornament not mentioned by others: "And of this...
[Verse 10.64]: "For the sake of conveying a specific quality of the subject matter intended to be expressed."
"Paralipsis (*ākṣepa*) is a semblance of negation; it is twofold, according to whether the object is yet to be stated or has already been stated.
[Commentary: *Vijñapriyā* explains the fourfold figure of speech, Paralipsis, with the words "of the thing" (*vastunaḥ*).
The meaning is that *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) is an ornament consisting of a semblance of negation regarding a matter intended to be spoken, characterized by the intention not to actually negate it.
He states the purpose of this semblance of negation: "for the sake of understanding a specific distinction.
First, he describes its two-fold division: "that which is yet to be spoken," and so forth.
The meaning is: an apparent negation of that which is about to be stated, or has already been stated, or is intended to be stated.
The statement of what has been stated or is intended to be stated occurs because it was the object of a prior desire [to speak].
— *Locanā* —
(lo, ī) Now, by means of the specific quality of the object being implied (*gamya*), he describes the remaining figure of speech, *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), with the words "of the thing" (*vastunaḥ*).

This is the meaning: when the negation of a subject intended for expression—which, because it is topical (*prākaraṇika*), is improper—becomes sublated in its literal form and thus leads one to understand its appearance as a mere semblance (*ābhāsa*), that is the figure of speech *ākṣepa*.
And to show that this negation is not fruitless here, he says: "a distinction" (*viśeṣa*).

The meaning is: for the sake of understanding a particularity by way of its being grounded in the general nature [of the subject]. Negation that is coextensive with existence (*sattā*) constitutes the figure of speech *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), which is of two kinds: in some cases having a subject to be stated hereafter, and in others having a subject already mentioned.

In that regard, concerning the subject matter to be described hereafter, there are two varieties: in some cases, there is a negation of everything that has been indicated in general; in others, when one part has been stated, there is a negation of another part.

Furthermore, regarding the subject matter already mentioned, there are two [other] varieties: in some cases, there is a negation of the essential nature of the thing itself; in others, there is a negation of the description of the thing.
Thus, there are four varieties of *ākṣepa* (paralipsis).
In order, they are as follows:
“O friend, I say something for the sake of my companion who is distressed by hundreds of the arrows of Love.”
"Rest here for a moment, my friend; or rather, what can I say to one whose heart is so merciless?"
Here, there is a negation of the separation generally indicated by the friend regarding the subject matter about to be described. *Vijñapriyā*: "O you whose arrows are Love... (*smaraśareti*).
This is a statement by the heroine’s friend, wishing to describe to the hero the state of separation experienced by the heroine.
The address "O friend" (*sakhe*) is used because he is her friend through his friendship with her companion.
The syntactical connection is: "Having rested here for a moment, I shall speak.
The mention of resting first is due to the great amount that remains to be told.
The meaning is: "toward those like you, whose hearts are merciless."
Regarding this:
although the specific details of the state of separation—such as paleness and emaciation—are yet to be described, there is a general indication of it through the mention of her "cruel heart.
Furthermore, by virtue of the semblance of a prohibition (*niṣedhābhāsa*), there arises the understanding of its specific nature as being inevitably fatal.
Locanā:
(lo, u) This is because the phrase "distressed by the arrows of Smara" indicates in general the separation that is about to be described;
for there has been no mention yet of the specific various states of the woman separated from her lover that are to be described.
“O deer-eyed one, in your absence, seeing the fresh jasmine flower now withered—alas!
she is utterly distressed now; oh, what is the use of these futile words?”
In this context, the portion stating "he will die here" has not been mentioned.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, pha) states the semblance of a denial of that portion: "In separation from you... [and so forth].
"Excessively now":

previously, she was one whose life was sustained by the sight of jasmine flowers blooming due to the influence of the season; but now she will die. This is an apparent negation (*niṣedhābhāsa*) of this unstated portion.
The portion beginning with "vīkṣya" (having seen) has already been explained.
Thus, the result [of this passage] is the comprehension of a specific quality of death—the subject of the prohibited speech—namely, its being impossible to describe:
"O young man! I am not a messenger; 'you are dear to me' is not my business."
She dies; this is your transgression—this is the word of the Dharma we speak.”
Here, there is a negation of the fact of being a messenger (*dūtītva*).
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding the aforementioned object of negation, he states the negation of the essential nature of the act of speaking with the word "O boy" (*bālaa*).
“O child, I am not a messenger; ‘stay, you are dear to me’—this is not my business.
She is dying, and this is your infamy; we speak these words of Dharma.”
Thus,
he was addressed as a "child" because of his lack of familiarity with the Dharma and his role as a speaker of the Dharma;
the denial of his own status as a messenger was intended to indicate that the mere act of preaching the Dharma was his objective.

The word "stay" was spoken to indicate that even my consent for the heroine's action does not exist; likewise, the word "you are dear" was spoken to indicate that the duty common to all living beings must be observed, in which case neither one's own affection nor the affection of others is a determining factor—
the sense being that you are not dear to her or to me.

In this case, regarding the subject already mentioned—that "she dies here"—there is a negation of the very fact intended to be stated, namely the speaker's role as a messenger (*dūtītva*), by means of the object itself, but not a negation of the statement of that fact.
Nor should it be asked how the negation of the role of a messenger relates to the subject of death already mentioned;

for it relates to that subject indirectly, insofar as it concerns the role of a messenger which serves to avert death. Here, there is the apprehension of a specific quality—truthfulness—for the purpose of turning away from unrighteousness (*adharma*).
“How can that slender-limbed woman pass the night in separation from you?
What is the use of speaking before one who is so cruelly resolved?”
In this context, there is a prohibition of that which has already been stated as being spoken.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, bha) states the prohibition of speech: "in separation" (*virahe*).
The negation here is of the very statement regarding the incapacity for destroying the night that was previously mentioned.
"Here" (*atrety*) means: "here," in the phrase "of the very statement that was spoken," which signifies "of that which was actually uttered."
In this case, there is the apprehension of a specific excellence consisting of the intensity of the suggested sorrow.
In the first example, the excellence perceived is that death is inevitable;
in the second, it is the impossibility of being described, and so forth.
In the third [case], regarding the state of being a messenger, there is the quality of speaking according to the facts;
in the fourth, there is the intensity of suffering.
And this is not a prohibition of what has been enjoined.
Because the negation here is merely apparent (*abhāsa*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ma): In the four verses mentioned, he demonstrates the realization of the specific forms described—beginning with "here, first."
In the third [verse], "dūtyā" is indeed the correct reading;
thus, the meaning is "being indeed female messengers.
Now, one might object: "Bathing should be performed every day, but never at night."

In this context, just as there is a prohibition against bathing at night despite the injunction for daily bathing, so too is this a case of both injunction and prohibition. And since that does not constitute a poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*), he raises an objection with "But not... and provides the resolution with "In this case..."
The meaning is that a negation of reality is indeed not an ornament, whereas a semblance of negation is certainly an ornament.

Locanā: (lo, ū) Furthermore, because there is an absence of aesthetic charm (*vicitritva*) due to the negation of what has been prescribed, [the author] dispels the confusion regarding its conflation with figures such as "pettiness" (*kṣudratva*), which are identified among the ornaments by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and others— stating, "And this is not so," in reference to the negation of what was prescribed here.
For example:
"By slaying this deer with an arrow, let the progress of the southern wind be halted;
thus should the king of the Śabaras, dwelling in the caves of the sandalwood mountains, be entreated."
"Or rather, let this wretchedness remain as a falsehood; the Kirātas do not desire enmity with the Maruts, for he dispels the exhaustion of the Śavara women during their dalliance."
For here, the negation by the second line of what was stated in the first verse is indeed real (*tāttvika*).
And thus, there is no confusion with a prohibited injunction (*niṣiddhavidhi*), as it is said:
"Where is the lineage originating from the Sun, and where is my intellect of limited scope?"
"Out of delusion, I desire to cross the ocean that is so difficult to traverse by means of a mere raft."
“A dull-witted man, seeking the fame of a poet, will become an object of ridicule,
like a dwarf who, out of greed for fruit reachable only by a tall man, stretches out his arms.”
"Or rather, since the gateway has been opened by former sages in this lineage,
my path lies within it— like a thread passing through a gem already perforated by a diamond."
In this context, when that which was negated by the two preceding verses is affirmed by the third verse, the negation is merely apparent;
another type is considered a semblance of an injunction regarding an undesirable matter. (Viśvavidyā 10.65)
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ya) He states another variety of the figure of speech *ākṣepa* [paralipsis] with the words "of that which is undesired" (*aniṣṭasya*). The meaning is: if there is an apparent injunction (*vidhyābhāsa*) regarding an undesired matter which actually conveys a prohibition, and if—just as previously mentioned—it serves to bring about a specific understanding, then that is another form of the figure *ākṣepa*.
Locanā:

(lo, ṛ) Having thus stated one type of *ākṣepa* based on a semblance of a slight negation, he states the second, which is its opposite—a semblance of an undesired injunction—with the words "of that which is undesired" (*aniṣṭasya*).
This is the meaning.

The negation of what is desired and the impossibility of the attainment of what is undesired result in a conclusion that rests upon a semblance (*ābhāsa*); this is the seed of the poetic figure *dvitīyākṣepa* (the second type of suggestion).
The word "tathā" (likewise) is used as before for the purpose of conveying a specific distinction.
For example:
“Go, if you must go, my beloved;
may your paths be auspicious.
May my birth also occur in that very place where you have gone.”
In this case, because sexual intercourse is undesirable, the injunction takes on a faltering form and results in a prohibition;
furthermore, the specific quality understood is that sexual intercourse must be absolutely avoided.
*Vijñapriyā*:
In the verse, "Go, if you must go, my beloved," death is suggested by the mention of birth.
Regarding the phrase *praskhaladrūpa*: the meaning is "one whose form is becoming disordered."
He shows the specific understanding with the words "and the distinction" (*viśeṣaśca*).
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) This is indicated by the second half [of the verse], beginning with "even for me, that which is absolutely to be avoided," and so forth.
"Let him go, let him go! What is the use of his staying? Release, release me, friend; speak with respect!
We are unable to look upon him with our eyes, for the beauty of his lips is marred by the marks of biting."
This example cited by Rāghavānanda is incorrect;

for, like the examples given here, the idea that "she should never go" as a mere semblance of prohibition on the part of the heroine during such an offense does not even enter the intellect of the ignorant.
[Next: "Vibhāvanā is said to be the production of an effect in the absence of its cause."
Because its causes are either stated or unstated, it is proclaimed to be of two kinds.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
la) He states the ornament of concealment (*vibhāvanālaṅkāra*)— namely, "concealment" (*vibhāvanā*)—
as [the non-mentioning] of a cause or a fallacious cause (*hetvābhāsa*).
The production of an effect must be stated as arising from its specific causes and so forth;
the basis for [the distinction between] "stated" and "unstated" is the production of the effect.
He explains this with the words: "without a cause."
Locanā:

(lo, ḷ) Following this objection, because it serves as the basis for contradiction (*virodha*), the demonstration of the poetic figures rooted in contradiction (*virodhamūlālaṅkāra*) is undertaken next—beginning with *vibhāvanā*.
It is said [in the definition]: "having shown the absence of some cause whatsoever, which is composed by the poet for the sake of producing aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*). This is the meaning.
In this way, the meaning of the sūtras in other such instances is to be interpreted;
for in reality, since an effect cannot arise in the total absence of a cause,
[the sūtra] says "is said."
The meaning is that this *vibhāvanā* (poetic conceit of omission) is both one where the cause is mentioned and one where the cause is not mentioned.
Even when the arising of an effect is described as occurring without its [stated] cause, it is logically proper that it must depend upon some other cause;
and that other cause is either mentioned or unmentioned, thus making two types.
For example:
"The waist of the fair-browed maiden is slender without effort, her eyes tremble slightly with apprehension, and her body captivates the mind even without ornaments— at such an age."
Vijñapriyā:
"Without effort" means that the middle part is moderate.
I suspect that this is due to the very nature of doubt itself, according to the propriety of relative degrees;
here, the cause consisting of age and beauty has been stated.
In the reading "The body of the deer-eyed one shines" (*vapurbhāti mṛgīdṛśaḥ*), it is not so stated.
When the cause exists, the absence of the effect is *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation), and it is likewise twofold.
*Locanā*:
(Lo, e) "The absence of the effect is expressed by words," and so forth, as before.
It is so because it has both stated and unstated causes.
Among these, those with stated causes are as follows:
"Even the wealthy are free from arrogance; even the young are not fickle."
Even though they possess great majesty, they remain ever vigilant.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
śa) He states the figure of speech *viśeṣokti*— namely, "when the cause exists"—
meaning, when it has been stated that [the cause] exists.
The meaning is that the absence of fruit has also been stated. "Even for the wealthy" refers to those kings who are worthy of description.

He clarifies this very point with the word "vinā" (without). And this [term] *vibhāvanā* is etymologically appropriate (*anvarthā*) because it denotes a specific kind of production of an effect through dependence on something else due to the absence of its cause.
Here, the possession of great majesty is stated as the causal factor (*nimitta*).
In this very fourth quarter, in the reading "How many are there upon the earth?", that which was not explicitly stated [is implied];
and the state of having an inconceivable cause is not mentioned separately as a distinct variety, because it is simply the case of having a cause that was not explicitly stated.
For example—
“Alone, that god whose weapon is the flower conquers the three worlds;
though his body was taken away by Śambhu, his power was not taken.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṣa) Another variety of the form of the inconceivable cause (*acintyanimitta*) is mentioned by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
Since that is indeed nothing other than the form of the unmentioned cause (*anuktanimitta*), he states "inconceivable" (*acintya*) so that it need not be mentioned separately.
He demonstrates the aforementioned example of an inconceivable cause with the words "just as he alone," which connects with the phrase "the three worlds.
In this context, even the act of stealing his body serves as an inconceivable cause for the theft of his strength.

And here, the absence of an effect is also established by way of the presence of something contrary to that effect; likewise, in *vibhāvanā* (the description of an effect despite the absence of its cause), the absence of a cause is established by way of the presence of something contrary to that cause.
Thus, in the verse beginning with "He who steals away childhood" (*yaḥ kaumāraharaḥ*), there is *vibhāvanā* because of the depiction of something contrary to the cause of longing.
In the verse beginning with "yaḥ kaumāra-", there is the figure of speech *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation) because the cause [of youth] is connected with yearning, which is contrary to its effect;
thus, there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of *vibhāvanā* (poetic fancy) and *viśeṣokti* here.
A pure example of this, however, must be sought elsewhere.
Vijñapriyā:
"(vi, sa) Of that which is contrary to the cause of longing.
For the cause of longing is indeed the absence of such [loved ones] as a wife and so forth.
The meaning is: of that which is opposed to it, namely the presence of such offspring and so forth;
and of the cause, [it refers to] the effect opposed to it—namely, the absence of longing (*anutkaṇṭhā*) which is the effect of such a cause.

The meaning is "of that which is contrary to it. Regarding the statement "a pure example is to be sought," the two pure examples for *vibhāvanā* (peculiar causation) and *viśeṣokti* (special mention) are, respectively, "emaciated without effort" (*anāyāsakṛśa*) and so forth.
The phrase "even the wealthy are free from madness," and so forth, exists [in the source];
the meaning is that the very nature of those two must be sought in that manner.

For instance, in cases such as "emaciated without exertion" (*anāyāsakṛśam*), although there is the perception of "absence of doubt" (*aśaṅkā*)— which is the opposite of "doubt"— and "not being an ornament" (*abhūṣaṇatva*)— which is the opposite of "being an ornament"— the figure of speech *viśeṣokti* is not perceived.

Indeed, *viśeṣokti* would not occur merely through the perception of an absence of result consisting in the absence of liveliness (*tāralya*), nor through the perception of an absence of result consisting in the absence of charm (*manohāritva*).

Similarly, in cases such as "even though he is wealthy," although wealth—which is not contradictory to poverty—is perceived, there is no perception of *vibhāvanā* (the poetic figure of "causation without a cause").

This is because poverty and the like do not stand in a relationship of being the cause for effects such as the absence of intoxication; for if they did, then even upon perceiving wealth—which is contradictory to poverty—one might perceive the absence of such effects and thus have *vibhāvanā*.
(Locanā)

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "the absence of the effect here" (*kāryābhāva*) has already been clarified in the first chapter itself. The method [of *saṃdeha*] is that "confusion" (*saṅkara*) is a state of uncertainty due to the absence of the fault regarding the principle of the inclusion of one [among many].
The example of the word [is given] by way of the presence of something contrary to the effect (*kāryaviruddhasadbhāvamukhena*) within the figure of *viśeṣokti*.

However, unlike [the figure] "He is one, yet three," where the effect is presented through its opposite, nor like *vibhāvanā*, where the presence of a cause's opposite is presented; a pure example [of this figure] is characterized by the absence of mutual commingling with others, as follows:
"Salutations to that Makarakeṭu (Cupid), whose power is irresistible, who, though burnt like camphor, remains potent in every person."

Here, the absence of power—characterized by the effect of burning—is presented by way of the existence of a contrary power that is opposed to incapacity; thus, the figure *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation) is quite clear.
In this same manner, *vibhāvanā* (causation by the extraordinary) and the others are also [to be understood]. Furthermore:
"The *jāti* (universal) is [combined] with the four beginning with *jāti*; the *guṇa* (quality) with the three beginning with *guṇa*. (VisSd 10.67).

When an action appears as if mutually contradictory with another action or a substance, or when a substance appears as if contradictory with another substance, that is "contradiction" (virodha), which has ten forms.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ha) He states the ten-fold ornament of apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsālaṅkāra*) beginning with "jāti" and so forth.

In the case of genus (*jāti*) and the rest, there is a connection with mutually contradictory [factors] such as genus, quality, action, and substance, according to their respective grammatical genders.
Furthermore, "quality" (guṇa) should be understood as a mere property distinct from genus (jāti) and action (kriyā).

Regarding the phrase "by the three, beginning with quality," the contradiction of that [quality] with genus is not mentioned separately because it is already included in the previous enumeration, being of the same nature as the contradiction between genus and quality.
The same applies to the latter two [syllables] as well;
however, it should be understood that *dravya* (substance) consists of a single manifestation (*ekavyaktika*).
— Locanā:

The meaning is that although [the object] may appear as if contradictory through four factors— genus, quality, action, and substance— in the final analysis there is indeed no contradiction, for otherwise it would entail a defect.
Since contradiction occurs only between a quality and a genus, or between a genus and a quality, there are exactly three types of "contradiction with a quality" (*guṇaviruddha*).
In the same way, there is indeed a unity between that which is contradictory to action; this is the tenfold contradiction of form (*ākṛti-virodha*).
In order, for example:
"In separation from you, the Malaya breeze is a forest fire, and even the rays of the moon are hot."
The summer sun, though devoid of passion, pierces even the lotus petal, which is as delicate as the heart of a woman free from desire.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) Therein, he demonstrates the contradiction with birth by means of four [verses] within a single stanza— beginning with "In separation from you"—
where the phrase "in separation from you" is to be construed with everything, including the Malaya breeze and so forth.
Here, there is a contradiction between the two universals (*jāti*) of "forest-fire-ness" and "Malaya-breeze-ness.
Nor is this a case of metaphor (*rūpaka*),
because what first presents itself to the mind is precisely the contradiction between the two universals that are pervaded by the respective attributes of "burning-ness" and "coolness."
In the phrase "even the moonbeams," there is a contradiction between the genus *moonbeam-ness* and the quality of heat (*uṣṇatva*).
In the phrase "the heart," there is a contradiction between the genus *not-being-a-bird* and the action [of flying], through their difference.
In the phrase "even the lotus petal," there is a contradiction between the genus *lotus-petal-ness* and the substance—the summer sun—by way of identity (*tādātmya*).

In this case as well, because contradiction (*virodha*) itself is what first presents itself due to the fact that it is pervaded by contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmavyāpyatva*), and because the particle *api* indicates contradiction, this is not a metaphor (*rūpaka*).
Furthermore, the sun's being pervaded by heat occurs through identity (*tādātmyena*);
and even though there are twelve suns, there is no contradiction of genus (*jātivirodha*) here.

Because the term *ravi* (the sun) here refers specifically to that which causes the six seasons to proceed— due to the qualifying adjective *nidāghīya* (belonging to the summer)— and because it [the sun] is singular:
“O King, through the performance of numerous household chores involving constant contact with the pestle,
the hands of the wives of the twice-born, though naturally hard, become as tender as lotuses.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, kha) He states the contradiction between qualities regarding excellence—“*santata*,” etc.
O King! Previously, by means of [the practice of] *santata* and so forth, the hands of the wives of the twice-born, which were once hard, have become as delicate as lotuses.
“Because you perform service with female slaves through the gift of prosperity, your hands possess such delicacy.
Herein lies the contradiction between the qualities of hardness and delicacy.
“Of the Unborn who takes birth, of the effortless one who has slain his enemies...”
Who knows your true nature while you are sleeping or while you are awake?
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ga) He states the contradiction between the quality and the action with the words "of the unborn" (*ajasya*).
This is a hymn of praise by the gods directed toward Īśvara.
In the phrase "of the unborn" (*ajasya*), there is a contradiction between the quality of being birthless and the action of grasping at the birth of qualities.
Likewise, there is a contradiction between the qualities of being effortless and being in a state of sleep, and the actions of slaying enemies and staying awake. [As it is said:
"Without the embrace of her beloved, for the fawn-eyed woman..."
The moon, the lord of the night of the Rākā, became filled with the flames of poison.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, gha) He states the contradiction between the quality [of fragrance] and the substance [the body] with the words "by contact with the lap of her beloved.
The meaning is: "without him," that is, for one who is separated from her lover.
The "lord of the night of the dark fortnight" is the full moon;
here, the moon is a substance (*dravya*) because it consists of a single individual instance.
There is a contradiction between that [moon] and the quality (*guṇa*) of being filled with flames of poison, by way of identity (*tādātmya*).
This form of the intoxicating-eyed one, which is a delight to the pair of eyes yet difficult to attain even through the activity of the mind, gladdens my heart and yet torments it.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṅa) He states the contradiction between [the act of] action and [the nature of] action with the words "pair of eyes" (*nayanayugeti*).
*Āsecanaka* means that which dispels heat through sprinkling, or alternatively, that which is sprinkled with nectar (*amṛta*).
Difficult to attain by other women;
here there is a contradiction between the action of passion and so forth [and her state].
Locanā:

(Lo, au) “*Tadāsecanakam*—there is no end to one’s satisfaction from seeing it,” according to the *Amara-kośa*. *Madira* means one who has intoxicated the *cakora* birds. [The verse begins with] “*Tvadvāji*” and so forth.
In the fourth quarter of the verse beginning with "vallabhotsaṅge," if the reading were "madhyandinadinādhipaḥ," there would be a contradiction between two substances (*dravyavirōdha*).
[The author] states the contradiction between action and substance (*kriyā-dravyavirōdha*) in the passage beginning with "tvadvājirajaḥ."
In this case, *hara* (the bearer) is the substance (*dravya*),
and there is a contradiction between it and the action of bearing qualified by the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) through identity (*tādātmya*).
However, in reality, this is not a suitable example, because for one who bears the Ganges, it is precisely the quality (*guṇa*) consisting of the burden of the action of bearing that is contradicted.
However, this example should be understood as having the specific reading: "O Hara, release the Gaṅgā from your head, for she is a heavy burden";
that is, in the reading "madhyandinadinādhipa" (the midday sun).
Because the opposition between the moon and the sun—characterized by their opposing qualities of coldness and heat—is immediately apparent, there is no metaphor (*rūpaka*) here either.
Furthermore, since there is only one sun for all days and so forth, and not multiple ones in various locations, there is no contradiction regarding genus (*jāti*).

In this instance, in the verse beginning with "In separation from you... (*tava viraha-*), because words such as "wind" (*pavana*) denote multiple individual instances, they are terms of genus; thus, there is a mutual contradiction between these terms of genus, quality, action, and substance, represented respectively by the forest fire, heat, the piercing of the heart, and the sun.
It appears at the outset;
because it is caused by separation, there is composure.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, cha) Here, in the first verse, he demonstrates the contradiction with the four [types of universals], beginning with "here, in your separation," and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "of the wind and so forth" (*pavanādīnām*), the moonlight, the bees, and the lotus petals are included.
The meaning is that all of these denote many individual instances (*bahuvyakti*).
"From the outset" means superficially.
He demonstrates that there is no contradiction with their stated genus by saying, "because it has separation as its cause. The resolution is the absence of contradiction.
The meaning is as follows: contradiction consists in the fact that two individuals are contradictory;
the state of being caused by that [contradiction] is merely the superimposition of those two individuals.
It does not mean that there is a real co-location of two contradictory things.
The passage beginning with "evam" and so forth is clear.
In the verse beginning with "of the unborn" (*ajasya*), there is a contradiction between the quality of being unborn and such actions as the taking of birth;
however, this is resolved by the extraordinary nature of the Lord's power.
In the verse beginning with "tvadvāji-," there is an apparent contradiction (virodha) in the statement "even Hara does not bear the Gaṅgā on his head";
however, the resolution is achieved through the bold poetic assertion (kaviprauḍhokti) of the poet in the passage beginning with "tvadvāji-.
The rest is clear.

In *vibhāvanā*, because it is presented through the absence of the cause, the effect itself is perceived as that which is sublated; and in *viśeṣokti*, through the absence of the effect, it is the cause itself [that is so perceived].
But here, there is a distinction in that both [cause and effect] are mutually sublated.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ja) Since both *vibhāvanā* and *viśeṣokti* involve the appearance of a contradiction—namely, the presence of the effect despite the absence of the cause, and the presence of the cause despite the absence of the effect—it would follow that they are cases of "apparent contradiction" (*virodhābhāsa*). To distinguish them from that, he says: "In the case of *vibhāvanā*... [and so forth].
The meaning is: because it is described as occurring simultaneously with the absence of the cause.
Regarding the term "viśeṣokti" (the description of a specific effect), it refers to the mere collection of causes;
for it is precisely that [collection] which is perceived as being sublated at the time when the effect comes into existence.

In the examples of *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation), it is precisely because of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of whatever cause is specified as the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) that such variety arises;
otherwise, if the absence of the effect were merely due to the absence of some other cause, what variety would there be?
Locanā:
Regarding "in the absence of a cause" (*kāraṇābhāve*), the meaning is "powerful" (*balavat*);
the same applies elsewhere.

"Inconsistency" (*asaṅgati*) occurs when cause and effect exist in different locations. *Vijñapriyā* (vi, jha) states: "He describes the figure of speech 'Inconsistency' with the words 'of cause and effect.'"
The meaning is: [this occurs] at the time of arising, because the two are perceived as being necessarily in the same location.
Therefore, this ornament does not apply when a staff and a jar are in different locations at other times, nor when two effects are always in different locations despite their distinct positions.
For example—

"She is young while we are timid of heart; she is a woman while we are faint-hearted; she possesses a pair of full and elevated breasts while we are burdened by weariness; she is able to move despite being encumbered by heavy hips while we are unable to walk; it is truly marvelous that we have become so incompetent through faults that belong to others."
And because this [figure] is a sublater, when there is a contradiction between two things residing in the same locus, it is the figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra* (contradiction).
*Vijñapriyā*: "She is a girl... (*sā bālā*).

This is the speech of one who is weak due to separation, having remembered his beloved whom he wishes to see. "The girl" (*bālā*) refers to one characterized by the softness inherent to childhood; her action is her very speech, which is marked by timidity, and that [timidity] arises from our own weakness caused by separation. In reality, even though she is a girl, it is illogical for her to speak of full breasts.
"She" refers to a woman, because timidity is a characteristic of women;
her inability to move is also due to weakness.
He expresses her capacity to convey the poetic figure of *virodha* (contradiction) with the words "of her."

The figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra* (contradiction) is the general rule (*utsarga*) because it is defined by the necessity of having its elements located in different places (*bhinnadeśatā*), since this is not explicitly stated [in the definition of *ekadeśavivartirūpaka*].

And since this [figure of contradiction] is an exception (*apavāda*) due to its being defined by the necessity of having its elements in different places, the meaning is that "contradiction" (*virodha*) occurs between two things situated in the same place, provided they avoid the scope of this [exception].
— *Locanā*.
Regarding the state of being located in different places, the rule for reliability is that the effect must be in the very same place as the cause; this is the restriction.
The sense is that this applies only to things situated in the same place, and not to those situated in different places, because the rule of exception is stronger than the general rule.
[But] if the qualities or actions of the cause and the effect should be contradictory... (VisSd 10.69).
When there is the failure of what has been undertaken and the occurrence of misfortune,
or when there is a union of two discordant things, that is considered the "uneven" (viṣama) figure.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) He states the fourfold figure of speech *viṣama* (the incongruous): "two qualities or two actions.
If the two qualities or two actions belonging to two things to be accomplished (*hutukāryayoḥ*) should be mutually contradictory—that is, opposed to one another—then these two constitute *viṣama*.
He states the third [point] with the words "of that which has been commenced": "futility" means the absence of the intended result;
rather, it means the arising of misfortune.
He states the fourth type of incongruity (viṣama) with the words "of two dissimilar things" (virūpayoḥ).

The meaning is: that connection which is perceived between two things described as being dissimilar—that is, unfit for mutual relation. And this is to be understood as occurring when two *kka* suffixes are employed.
Locanā: (lo,
i) That application of conjunction between two dissimilar forms, that is, two forms of different kinds,
occurs in sequence as follows:

“Immediately upon receiving the touch of his hand, the blade of his sword— dark as a tamāla tree in every battle— gives birth to a fame as white as the autumnal moon, which serves as an ornament for the three worlds.”

In this context, the production of white fame from the sword-blade, which is the cause, contradicts the established principle that "the qualities of the cause indeed initiate the qualities of the effect.
Regarding this, [the author] states the contradiction between the qualities of the cause and the effect with the words beginning "sadyaḥ" (immediately).

The blade of the sword of that king, dark as a *tamāla* tree, takes the form of a line; having come into contact with the hand of that monarch in battle after battle, it immediately produces fame as white as the autumnal moon—this is a marvel.
The epithet "of the three worlds" (*triloka*) qualifies the fame.
Here, the author states "here" (*atra*) because the qualities of blueness (in the cause, the sword-blade) and whiteness (in the effect, the fame) are reversed.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the qualities] are contrary to the quality [of whiteness].
Regarding the phrase "the production of white fame," the ultimate meaning is that the fame being produced is white.
Now, one might ask: "What is the peculiarity in the case of contradiction? To this he says: "The qualities of the cause...
