The meaning of "of persistence" is "by way of a rule.
Thus, the meaning is that the peculiarity consists in the demonstration of the opposition between two contradictory things.

Although this rule applies only to the relation between an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and its effect, the poet, having observed it there, has applied that same principle elsewhere as well and described it thus:
"O lotus-petal-eyed one, you bestow upon me this intense bliss."
But this separation, brought about by you alone, torments my body all the more.”
Here, from the cause of the woman’s form which produces joy, arises the separation that produces distress.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ḍa) states the contradiction between cause and effect: "intense joy" and so forth.
"Kuvalaya," and so forth, are vocatives.
Regarding "here":
the meaning culminates in the production of the heat-generating separation, which is the arising of the act of heating produced by the separation generated by itself.
And thus, the meanings are that the two actions—bestowing bliss and causing torment—which belong respectively to the woman and the resulting separation (as cause and effect), are contradictory.
This has been described by contemplating the very variety of an action equal to the action produced by this [separation].
“This ocean is a mine of jewels; thus it was served with the hope for wealth.”
"Let alone wealth; even his mouth was filled with briny waters."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi ḍha) He illustrates the two [types of] misfortune—the failure of an undertaking and the arising of calamity—with the words "this... and so forth.
Thinking, "This ocean is a mine of jewels," I served it, having approached it with the hope of obtaining grain.
Let alone wealth being far off, let it be beyond reach;
rather, his face was filled with salt water—this is the meaning.
Here, not only was the desired gain of wealth not attained, [but he suffered this further].
The filling of the mouth with alkaline waters;

"Where is the forest, adorned with tree-bark, and where is royal splendor, worshipped by the great Indra? Alas, the conduct of the Creator, who invariably acts in opposition, is truly difficult to endure."
Here, there is a conjunction of two discordant things, the forest and royal splendor; this is my [view]. *Vijñapriyā*: [This is my view.]
(vi, ṇa) He states the union of two incongruous things with the words "Where is the forest?
This is the speech of Kauśalyā as she grieves for Rāma:
"Where is such a forest, where tree-bark alone serves as ornament, and where is the king," and so forth.
The conjunction of these two things, which are described in two separate locations as being incapable of mutual connection, occurs in a single locus, namely Rāma.
This should be understood similarly in cases such as "Where [is] the lineage of the Sun? and so forth.
Or as it is said:
"The worlds were swallowed by the vast belly of Him who lies upon the ocean at the end of the eon;
yet that same [belly] was drunk up, as it were, by a single glance from the eye of one particular city-woman, trembling with intoxication."
Vijñapriyā:
Even in the absence of the two [previous] views, he says "by the vast" (*vipulena*).
At the time of the dissolution of the eon (*yugakṣaya*), the worlds were swallowed by the vast belly—meaning the interior—of Viṣṇu, who rests upon the ocean.

Furthermore, the meaning is that Viṣṇu, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, was drunk by a certain city-woman—the agent—with a single glance that was "incomplete" (*asakalā*) due to the intoxicating playfulness of her eyes, being "partial" (*ekadeśarūpā*) in its form.
Here, the sense is that for one who possesses a belly capable of drinking the entire world, it is a contradiction for him to be drinkable by the side-glance of a single woman.

However, according to the view of the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, this is not an example of the fourth type of the *viṣama* (incongruity) ornament; for in his view, since the contradiction is perceived here even without the two [required] negatives, and because it has not been stated by anyone [else as such], it does not qualify as that specific variety.
Therefore, this verse was shown by him as an example of the second type of *viṣama* (incongruity), characterized by the contradiction between the action of cause and effect.
For the belly is a part and thus the cause, while Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the possessor of the belly, is the whole and thus the effect.
For those two, the acts of being drunk by the world and being drunk by the side-glances of women are contradictory.
Locanā:
(lo, ī) "Tad" means that.

By way of illustration (*upalakṣaṇatayā*) of these types of *viṣama* ornament mentioned in the Sūtra, the meaning is that other varieties should also be cited according to the principle of the lack of correspondence between two related things.

In that regard, he provides an illustration by way of a mere direction: "By the extensive," meaning by that which is not limited and does not fall short; "equally" means in accordance with the fitness of the object worthy of praise.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) He states the poetic figure named *sama*—namely, "the equal" (*sama*).
The meaning is that the poetic figure called *sama* is that praise which arises from the suitability (*aucitya*) or correspondence between two things that are mutually appropriate.
Locanā:
(lo, u) Herein lies the disparity between the part and the whole;
in some cases, [this occurs] between two things of the same class—

“Even when consumed by a single Asura and swallowed by the gods until it was exhausted, this poison did not become harmless; for even after being drunk by the gods until its destruction, the ocean of poison rises up again, fresh and new.”
In this case, even though there is a connection with contrast (vyatireka), there is a commingling of two figures,
but it is not the absence of the figure of disparity (viṣama).
For example:
"The moonlight has reached the moon; the daughter of Jahnu has descended into the ocean, her worthy match.
Thus, delighted by the union of equal virtues, the citizens there raised a single voice, harsh to the ears of rival kings.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) "The moon," and so forth.
This is a popular saying of the citizens when Indumatī chose [Aja] for herself.
"Those citizens who possess affection through the union of aesthetic flavor (rasa) and excellence (guṇa)—thus they explained the first statement of one person;
that is to say, they elucidated its meaning by means of other words having that same sense.
"The moon," and so forth, is the statement of another person.
Aja [is born] as the moon and the ocean;
Indumatī [is born] as the moonlight and the daughter of Jahnu;
thus there is the attainment of that which was already established separately.
The moonlight, however, is not established as separate from the moon;
therefore, the qualification "freed from clouds" is used to bring about that separate establishment.
The meaning is that once it has been separated from the cloud, its attainment occurs upon the cloud's departure.
Locanā: (lo,
ū) The definition of the *samā* [type] is that which is the opposite of the *viṣama* [type],
regarding two objects intended to be shown.
The daughter of Jahnu is Gaṅgā;
if even her [flow], which is contrary to that [earth], results in desired fruit, then so it is with the work of one who is opposed to that [worldly nature].
As it is said:
"He bows down for the sake of advancement, he gives up his life for the sake of livelihood,
and he suffers misery for the sake of pleasure— who is more foolish than a servant?"
Vijñapriyā: (vi, dha) "She bows down. For bowing (*praṇāma*) is the state of being bent low; it is the opposite of elevation.
"He gives up his life-breaths"— the word "in battle" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Although the relinquishing of the life-breaths is not the cause of life itself, nevertheless, in this context, the word *vimuñcati* refers to the act of relinquishing the life-breaths.
She suffers and seeks suffering,
because she is engaged in activities that produce suffering. —
Locanā:

(Lo, ṛ) The performance of acts such as prostration—which are contrary to what is required for the attainment of the desired result, such as the elevation [of status] mentioned in the preceding examples—is the fruit of the seed of the *vicitra* (the "marvelous") ornament.
When there is an excess of either the substratum (*āśraya*) or the superstratum (*āśrayin*), it is called *adhika* (the "excessive").
— *Locanā*:

(Lo, ṛ) The meaning is that the ornament called *adhika* (excess) is of two kinds: [1] where there is an excess [of one thing], and [2] where there is a greatness of both the locus (*āśraya*) and the located (*āśrayin*).
As for what has been stated by some—that *adhika* is said to be when there is an excess of one thing even though it is actually small—that is not correct. [Example:
"The sky is supported here somewhere; the vast netherworld (*pātāla*) is here somewhere; and right here, too, lies the continuous stream of waters from the base of the mountains."
Oh, how vast and expansive is this sky! How much of it remains, since even its very name—"empty," which implies that its filling is still far off—has not yet vanished?
Because [the definition] is over-narrow (*avyāpti*) in such cases;
for here, there is no "thinness" (*tanutva*) of the sky.

Furthermore, because this figure of speech has a substratum that is distinct from the relationship of locus and located (*āśrayāśrayi*), it functions as an exception (*apavāda*) that sublates the figure of "the Uneven" (*viṣama*).
As an example of excellence in terms of the substratum (*āśrayādhikya*): "What more can we say of the greatness of this ocean, wherein Hari lies quite unknown, having cast the worlds into its belly?"
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, na) He states the ornament named *adhika*—namely, "āśraya" etc. The meaning is that *ādhikya* is a description by way of excess.
"What is more? means:
Hari, having cast the worlds into his belly, sleeps there quite unknown;
because he sleeps within a mere portion of the ocean, the meaning is that he sleeps entirely unknown to those who behold the ocean.
The meaning is: "What more can we say regarding the greatness of this ocean?

Here, even though Hari has placed the worlds within his belly, he sleeps with only a small portion [of his body] resting upon him; thus, the superiority of the ocean, which serves as his support, is described.
An example of the superiority of that which is supported (*āśrita*) is as follows:

“The joys arising from the arrival of the ascetic did not find room within the body of the enemy of Kaiṭabha, in which the worlds rested in full expansion when he withdrew his self at the end of the age.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pa) He states the description of the excellence of that which is dependent [on another]—namely, "yugānte" and so forth.
This is a description of the intensity of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s joy upon Nārada’s arrival.

The earth— the occurrence of the arrival of the ascetic Nārada— did not find room, meaning it found no space to remain, within that body of Viṣṇu, the enemy of Kaiṭabha, in which the worlds dwelt with full expansion and without constraint at the time of the end of the age, when he had withdrawn all living beings and drawn them into his own belly.
Even though there is a distinction between their bodies, their oneness should be understood through the superimposition of oneness based on their being the body of Viṣṇu.
Here, the joy of those who have taken refuge [in them] is excessive.
They are mutually the cause of a single action for one another. (Viṣṇu-sahasranāma-stotra 10.72)
“She is radiant with you, and you too are radiant with her;
the night is radiant with the moon, and the night sky is radiant with the moon.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pha) He states the ornament called *anyonya* (mutuality)—namely, "anyonyam" (mutually).
"One action" (*ekā kriyā*) means an action of a single kind.
The meaning is that there is a mutual action between the two. By the words "by you" and "that," even in the latter half [of the verse], the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration) is employed.

When something to be produced is without a substratum, is both one and manifold in its range, and pertains either to that which is incapable or to that which is otherwise; [then it is a case of *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*]. (ViSd 10.73)
The accomplishment of an effect through destiny is, therefore, a threefold particularity (*viśeṣa*).
Vijñapriyā:
[The author] states the threefold figure of speech called *viśeṣālaṅkāra* with the words "that which is to be placed" (*yadādheyaṃ*), etc.
The word "yād" (that which) is connected to all three [verses].
"Anādhāram" means existing without a support (*ādhāra*), that is, described as being without a substratum.
In the phrase "anekagocaram" (having many objects), the word "ekadā" (at one time) is to be supplied.
However, since the figure of speech *paryāya* (exchange) will be discussed later regarding sequential occurrence, the meaning here is:
when an agent performing some [intended] action, by chance, accomplishes another task that was impossible for him to achieve. An example of this in sequence is as follows:
“How indeed could those poets not be worthy of veneration, whose words— possessing a multitude of no small virtues— delight the worlds even for an entire kalpa after they have ascended to heaven?”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, bha) "Even to heaven" means:
how could those poets not be worthy of veneration here, whose words—though they have ascended to heaven—are filled with many a multitude of virtues and delight the worlds? This is the meaning.

In this case, although the poets— who serve as the substratum through their relationship with the agency of composition— do not exist [in the literal sense], there is the persistence of the words (*giraḥ*) which are supported by them:
"In the forest, in the region of a river, and even in the caves of mountains,
your enemies see you alone before them, resembling the God of Death."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ma) "In the forest" means that enemies who have fled from the forest and other such places see you alone, appearing like the Destroyer (Antaka), right there in those very locations.
In this case, there is no intention to express a sequence in the perception [of these roles]:
“My wife, my counselor, my intimate friend, and my dear pupil in the practice of the arts—
tell me, what has not been taken from me by Death, who was indifferent to compassion, in taking you away?”
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ya) "The housewife" refers to this speech of Aja as he mourns for the deceased Indumatī.
Tell me, what has not been taken from me by Death, who is cruel and devoid of compassion, in seizing you?
To the question "What was taken?", he says: "The wife," and so forth.
The connection is: "O beloved pupil in the art of amorous play (*kāmakalā*), in private."
In this case, the accomplishment of a task—namely, the abduction of the wife and others of the slayer of Tāraka (Rudra)—is described as having occurred through destiny.
However, *vyāghāta* (contradiction) is that by which any object is made otherwise than it was originally fashioned.
If another person employs that very same means but in a different way, as for example:
“The mind-born god was burnt by her glance,” and so forth.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ra) He describes the figure of speech *vyāghāta* (contradiction): "In *vyāghāta*...

The meaning is this: when one person has performed a certain action upon an object by means of a particular method, if another person performs that same action in a contrary manner by means of that very same method, then that contrary performance is *vyāghāta*.
For example: "Those women who, with their very eyes, restore to life the God of Love whom [Śiva] had burnt with his eye..."
"Those victorious, beautiful-eyed women of Virūpākṣa praise you."
This is the illustration.
The meaning is that they "sustain life by the glance of Hara," specifically by that glance which takes the form of side-long looks (*kaṭākṣa*);
for a woman’s side-long look kindles passion.
Victory is achieved not only through action,
but also through form; thus he says, "of Virūpākṣa," referring to the deformity of the eye of the one to be conquered.
The sense is that even in that case, there is "victory" (jaya) because the very quality of being charming in the eyes of the conquerors constitutes their defeat.

Here, by the same means of vision that causes burning, women effect the opposite of burning—namely, life itself—through that very same visual means. And if a task is performed easily in a manner contrary [to its expected result], it is called *viṣamokti* (the incongruous). (VisSd 10.75)
It is simply "contradiction" (*vyāghāta*). *Vijñapriyā* (vi, la) states another type of the figure of contradiction: "and by ease," etc.

The word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin another type of contradiction (*vyāghāta*). The meaning is: if an effect contrary to one stated by another is produced or demonstrated by that other person as being characterized by ease (*saukarya*) in relation to the cause stated by the former. By means of the word "ca," he carries over the term "contradiction"—that is, it is simply "contradiction."
"Stay right here, my beloved; I shall return quickly in just a few days.
You are delicate and unable to endure hardship;
your delicacy, O fortunate one, is my reason [for staying]."
For you, being delicate, could not endure the excessive and incomparable exhaustion caused by separation.
In this passage, the hero states that the heroine’s delicacy is the cause for her inability to accompany him;
however, the heroine, on the contrary, presents it as a reason why accompanying him would be even easier than before.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, va) "Right here" refers to the first half of the verse, which is the hero's speech to his wife who wishes to go along with him as he desires to travel to a foreign land:
"You stay right here; do not go with me."
"I shall come quickly in a few days; I will arrive.
[The suffix] *tṛn* is used here in the sense of the future (*bhaviṣyat*).
This is because you are gentle.
And the meaning is not that she is unable to endure the exertion of traveling;
this is the statement of the wife in the latter half [of the verse]: "O fortunate one!
The very reason for my gentleness is my intention to go together with you—that is, to accompany you in death."
Since she is delicate, she has not endured—and will not endure—the unequal distress of separation;
here too, the suffix *tṛn* is used.
In this context, the phrase "here" indicates that the heroine is being made to understand the opposite of the task stated by the hero.
"By way of being the cause for going together" means that the cause for remaining is [established] by way of being the cause for going together. "With ease" means...
The meaning is that while it is easy for gentleness (*mṛdutva*)— which has been described as the cause for staying together— to accompany [the other], staying together is difficult for gentleness,
because through its state of staying, it produces an inability to endure separation.
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) Here, however, it is the justification of a possible cause for the accomplishment of something by means of its producing that which is contrary to it.
In this very example, "thou [art] here," the softness of the heroine's accompanying the hero is not perceived as the effect; rather, it is the fulfillment of her accompanying him.

In the case of the *viṣama* ornament, however, as in the example "This is a mine of jewels" (*ayaṃ ratnākaraḥ*), the meaning is that there is a non-occurrence of the intended effect, namely the acquisition of wealth, and instead, the occurrence of misfortune.
Having thus determined the figures of speech based on contradiction (*virodha*), the variegated figures of speech are now defined through a serial arrangement (*śṛṅkhalābandha*).
When each preceding element serves as the cause for each succeeding one, that is the "garland of causes" (*kāraṇamālā*).
Locanā:
"(Lo, e) param" means "the supreme";
it refers to the poetic ornament known as *kāraṇamālā* (the chain of causes).
As it is said:
"From association with those of refined intellect, learning arises; from learning comes discipline;
from discipline comes the affection of the world; and what cannot be achieved through the affection of the world?"
—That, moreover, is the *mālādīpaka* (garland-illumination).
The connection of the subjects with a single property [is such that] each subsequent one [is superior] to the preceding;
*Locanā*:
"(lo, ai)" means that each subsequent one brings about further excellence.
For example:
"When you had entered into battle, arrows were drawn upon the bow;
by those arrows the enemy's head was struck; by that [head] the earth was gained; by the earth you [were honored]; and by you, fame."
In this context, the act of inspiring fear is the *dharma*.
Vijñapriyā states,
"one after another," referring to the *kāraṇamālā* ornament.
This is clear with its illustration.
He states the *mālādīpaka* (garland-lamp) ornament—namely, "that garland" (*tanmālā*).
This too is clear with its illustration.
He states the *ekāvalī* ornament: "pūrvaṃ pūrvam" (the former, the former).

The meaning is: if, in each preceding instance, whatever is a qualifier is established as a qualifier for each subsequent [term], or is excluded, or is indicated as the counter-positive of the absence of that qualifier.
The meaning is that each preceding qualifier becomes a qualifier for each succeeding [term], whether it be the succeeding term itself or its absence.
Thus, each subsequent [term] stands as the qualified (viśeṣya) with respect to each preceding [qualifier]. (VisSd 10.77)
If it is either established or excluded, then that single string (ekāvalī) would be of two kinds.
*Vijñapriyā*: (vi, ṣa)
The examples in successive order are as follows:
"A lake with blossomed lotuses; a lotus frequented by bees."
Where the bees, accompanied by song, produced music that evoked the memory of love.
“That is no water which does not contain beautiful lotuses, and that is no lotus upon which a bee does not alight.”
There was no six-legged bee that did not hum sweetly, and there was no humming that did not captivate the mind.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, sa) "The lake has blossomed.
Here, regarding the king of lakes, the qualities such as the blossomed lotuses and so forth are successive qualifiers of those parts of it, namely the lotuses and so forth.
But regarding the exclusion (*apoha*), he says: "That is not water.
The term *yatrasucārupaṅkajam* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound [meaning "that in which there are beautiful lotuses"].
The same applies to the phrase beginning with *alīna* and so forth.
Here, qualities such as being "exceedingly beautiful lotuses" (*sucārupaṅkajatva*) are mentioned as the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) to the clouds that serve as qualifiers of the water.
*Locanā*: (Lo, o) "The lotus is from the lake..."
The bees belong to the lotus;
the songs of the bees are employed as a qualification [for the water].
In the passage beginning with "not that water," the beautiful lotus is presented as a negation of the water.
The same applies elsewhere.
In some cases, even the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is seen to be established as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) in successive stages and subsequently excluded (*apohita*),
as for example:
“There are pure ponds, lotuses bloom within the ponds;
bees alight upon the lotuses, and they produce music as they settle on the bees.”
The same applies to the process of exclusion (*apohana*). *Vijñapriyā* explains:

"In these two cases, the exclusion of the status of being the qualified (*viśeṣyatā*) in each subsequent qualifier with respect to each preceding qualifier has been shown"; thus he says: "in some cases, even the qualified [is excluded]."
"Reservoirs come into being"—
here too, it should be understood that this occurs "in autumn.
"He makes [them]."
The act of singing is the agent;
the meaning is that it performs a determination (vyavasāya) of its state within the lotuses by way of being well-connected.

Here, in the context of purity and so forth, the ponds and other objects, which serve as the qualificands (viśeṣya), function as qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa) through their distinction from the blooming lotuses and so forth.
The same applies even in the case of exclusion (*apohana*).
For example: “Those ponds do not burst open in which there are currently no lotuses;
nor are there lotuses elsewhere than where the fish have not fallen.”
This should be understood from the passage beginning with "... and so forth:
"The excellence of an object in successive stages is called its essence (sāra). (ViśSd 10.78)
Locanā: (lo, au) *Sāra* is the name of an ornament (*alaṃkāra*).
For example—
“In a kingdom, the essence is the earth; in the earth, the city; in the city, the palace;
in the palace, the bedchamber; in the bedchamber, the couch; and on the couch, the beautiful woman—the very essence of the god of love.”
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ka) He states the ornament of the essence (*sārālaṅkāra*)— namely, "the ever-increasing" and "the essence in sovereignty."

In the case of the neuter noun *sāra*, there is both the *jahat* (abandoning) and *ajahat* (non-abandoning) [of gender]; therefore, here it is *ajahat-liṅga*. However, in the phrase "Have you worshipped the maiden who is the essence (*sāra*) of the three worlds?", it is *jahat-liṅga*.
Regarding the term *varāṅganānaṅga*: the meaning is that she is a beautiful woman (*varāṅganā*) who is the very essence (*sarvasva*) of the bodiless god of love (*anaṅga*).

Now, in such instances as "in this kingdom" (*nanv atra rājye*), if the locative case is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*), then since excellence would not be perceived in relation to the king and so forth, the excellence [of the kingdom] would be rendered purposeless.

Furthermore, because there is no relationship of general and particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-bhāva*) between the kingdom and the earth, or between the palace floor and the couch, or between the excellent woman and the bed, the act of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) would be untenable;
for in cases such as "among men, the Kṣatriya is brave," selection occurs only when a relationship of general and particular exists.

It is said: [The locative case is used] because of a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) from among those things, by supplying the word "among them" (*teṣu*) as follows: "Of whatever things there are in the kingdom, among them the earth is the essence;

of whatever things there are on the earth, among them the city is the essence," and so forth. Thus, in the word *teṣu*, the locative case expresses selection (*nirdhāraṇa-saptamī*), while in the word *rājye*, it is the locative case expressing the sphere of reference (*viṣaya-saptamī*).

In phrases such as "on the earth" (*vasudhāyām*), the locative case denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). As for "enumeration according to order" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*): it is the sequential assignment of items that have been mentioned in order. *Vijñapriyā*: [This refers to the rule: "When there is an equal *Laghusiddhāntakaumudī*: "'According to order' (*yathāsaṃkhyam*): when there is an equal number of terms in both the subject and the predicate, their mutual connection is understood by way of their of their respective sequence. *Sārasvatavyākaraṇa*: "'According to order' (*yathāsaṃkhyam*): when there is an equal number of terms in both the subject and the predicate, their mutual connection is
(vi, kha) He states the figure of speech known as *yathāsaṃkhya* (enumeration):

"yathāsaṃkhyam" means that after the initial mention [of items], there follows a subsequent mention (*uddeśa*) of those associated with them according to that same sequence—the sequence of first, second, and so forth, as they were originally indicated.
— *Locanā*.
(lo, a) Now, the figures of speech based on the logic of sentences are being discussed.
The figure named *yathāsaṃkhya* (enumeration according to order):
*anūddeśa* means a subsequent mention (*nirdeśa*) following after a prior enumeration (*uddeśa*).
The actions mentioned, such as opening [the eyes] and so forth, are connected respectively with the *vañjula* tree and the others, as follows:
"Open [your eyes]; pluck [the flowers] with your nails; it blows—cover it with the hem of your linen garment; they are entering the pleasure-grove—frighten them with the tinkling of your bracelets."
"O fortunate one, such are the secret conversations among her friends with one another during your absence, amidst the *vañjula* trees, the southern breezes, and the cuckoos."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ga) "Unmīlantī" etc. This is a statement by a certain woman who is recounting to her lover the conventional expressions used by his friends during the time of separation from the heroine.

O fortunate one! During her separation from you, her friends have established secret conventions among themselves regarding the three types of plants, such as the *vañjula* and others; this is the meaning of their mutual discourse.
To the question of what kind of discourse they are, he says:
"unmīlanti" (they bloom), and so forth.
The meaning is "they are blossoming.
This is the first statement of one friend, referring to the blossoming caused by the *vañjula* flowers mentioned previously;
and the other friend's initial reply begins with the words "with [her] nails," and so forth.
"She carries" (*vahati*)—this second statement is a designation by the friend regarding the act of carrying performed by the southern wind mentioned in the second [line].
"With the hem of her garment," etc., is the second reply from the other friend.
"Play," etc., is the third reply from the other friend.
Thus, after those [factors] have been stated in the sequence beginning with the first, there follows their enumeration in that same sequence as they are associated [with one another]:
"In some cases, one [factor] occurs in many; in others, many occur in one, according to the sequence. (Viṣṇusmṛti-sāra 10.79)
If it exists or is produced, then it is accepted as a synonym (*paryāya*).
Vijñapriyā:
He states the figure of speech "Synonym" (*paryāyālaṅkāra*) with the words "in some cases, one... and so forth.

In some cases, a single [cause] may exist in many [effects], or it may be produced through a sequence according to the order of causes; likewise, if many [causes] proceed toward a single [effect], or if that which proceeds toward a single [effect] occurs or is produced in sequence, then it is intended as a "succession" (*paryāya*). This is the meaning. For example, in sequence:

“Having rested for a moment upon her eyelashes, the first drops of water struck her lower lip; crushed by their descent onto the fullness of her breasts, they then fell upon the folds of her belly and reached her navel in succession.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṅa) Regarding that, he speaks of one [entity] existing in many places with the word "sthitāḥ" (situated).
This is a description of the sequence of the falling water from fresh clouds upon the limbs of Pārvatī as she performs ascetic penance.
The first drops of water reached her navel in succession;
he describes that sequence as "they remained" (*sthitāḥ*).
Due to the density of the eyelashes, they remained there for a moment, and then they struck the support [of the cheek].
Because the lower lip is tender, it is struck even by drops of water;
this refers to the swelling of the breasts (*payodhara*).
Since the suffix *kṛt* expresses a state (*bhāva*), the breasts are described as being swollen.

Because of their hardness, [the semen] falls there; from there it is crushed, and then it slips into the folds because of their high and low positions. Because of the depth of the navel, it does not go elsewhere from there.
Herein lies the self-arisen abode.
Locanā:
(lo, ā) "Staying for a moment," and so forth—first, a single drop of water occurred sequentially upon many [parts] such as the eyelashes;
likewise, there were various kinds of playful women, wolves, and others in the city of the enemy.
“Where graceful women, languid from the weight of their hips, stroll about,
there, in your enemy’s city, jackals, crows, and female jackals run to and fro.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ca) He says "they roam" (*vicaranti*) to express the state of many [beings] existing together in one place;
the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that this occurs where your enemy's city is located.
In this regard, the playful woman has made her dwelling in the enemy city of the heart of a wolf and others.

Her hand— once stained with red lac from her breasts and reddened by the ball, its fingers scarred by the plucking of *kuśa* sprouts— is now devoted to the rosary of prayer beads, having been turned away from the flow of passion.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) He states that one [act] is being performed by another in many places with the words "visṛṣṭā" etc.
This is a description of Pārvatī’s commencement of her ascetic penance.
By her, the hand was made devoted to the rosary;
that is to say, it was occupied with it and rendered distinguished by [the presence of] *kuśā* sprouts and so forth.
Thus, there are two predicates here.
And what is the meaning to be understood? It is that [the lover] has turned away from the lower lip;

for he has desisted from the lower lip—which was previously a place for the giving of tribute (kara) due to the outpouring of passion, and because of the absence of playing with a ball—precisely for the sake of bestowing his own passion. Furthermore, the qualification beginning with "on the limb of the breast" is merely a description of its essential nature.
Or rather, it is for the purpose of indicating that "now no cosmetic ointment is applied to the breast";
in this case, the application of those two [ointments] is being performed.
— Locanā:
In the verse beginning with *visṛṣṭa*, one hand [is placed] on the lower lip and so forth:
"The bright necklace was placed by the wives of your enemies upon those two."
Large teardrops are deposited upon their two breasts.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ja) He states that many things are being produced in one place with the words "yayor" (of which two).
Here, it refers to the many pearl necklaces and teardrops [being produced] together in one place, namely on the breast, by the wives of the enemies.
Locanā:
(lo, ī) In examples such as "yayoh" and so forth, necklaces and teardrops have been placed upon the breasts.
Among these, in some cases the substratum is of a composite nature, and in others it is of a non-composite nature.
In some cases, even the substratum [is included].
Locanā:
(lo, u) "Having a composite form" means having a combined nature.
The opposite of that is being solitary (*ekākībhūta*). For example,
in the phrase "they remained for a moment," the drops of water occurred sequentially upon a support such as the eyelashes in a non-congregated form.
In the phrase "they roam about" (*vicaranti*), the wolves and other creatures, who constitute the contents [of the city], appeared in their collective form within the enemy's city in succession;
so it is with the rest.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, jha) Since both the state of being combined (*saṃhata*) and the state of being uncombined (*asaṃhata*) are possible for the substratum and the superstratum (*ādhārādheya*) among these, he shows this with the intention that their difference or non-difference is not intended to be expressed: "among these" (*eṣu*).
"Combined form" (*saṃhatarūpa*) means a form consisting of many conjoined elements; "uncombined form" (*asaṃhatarūpa*) means a form where each individual element is not conjoined.
He states that in some cases the superstratum also possesses this twofold nature: "in some cases, even the superstratum" (*kvacid ādheyam api*).
Here, he demonstrates that the substratum (*ādhāra*) is not a composite (*asaṃhata*), as in the phrase "as they remain for a moment.
In this case, however, the fact that the objects supported (*ādheya*)—the drops of water—are composite in nature is not a point of distinction.

For those who define this ornament (*alaṅkāra*) as being constituted by multiplicity, it is precisely the states of being composite or non-composite that serve as the distinguishing factor; yet here, the drops are constituted as a single entity across multiple substrata.
The collectivity of the bases (*ādhāra*) is, for example: "In the self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*), the maiden choosing her husband cast her eye successively upon the assembled kings.
The non-collectivity of the objects supported (*ādheya*), however, is as follows:
"When the princess choosing her husband rejected each preceding suitor one after another..."
Then, at that moment, the king became especially agitated regarding her.
This is what should be understood here.
It shows the collective nature of multiple substrata existing within a single locus by means of the phrase "they roam about.
Since the plural number in "wolves and so forth" indicates their gathering together as a group, the sequence [of the actions] is relative to the movements of the playful women.
The same applies elsewhere.
In the verse beginning with "yayorāropati," the teardrops also possess a form composed of many aggregated units.

Furthermore, the distinction here from the figure of speech *viśeṣālaṅkāra* (peculiar excellence) lies in the fact that [the action] occurs sequentially across multiple locations rather than in a single location.
Because there is no exchange in the case of *parivṛtti*.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ña) One might ask: what is the distinction between this and the figure of speech *viśeṣa*, which was defined as "sometimes one [thing] in many" and "one having many objects"? To this, he says: "And here... [etc.].
The meaning is that there is a distinction between the two [types of *parivṛtti*] based on their functioning either successively or simultaneously.
He states the difference from the *parivṛtti* ornament (*alaṅkāra*) which will be discussed later by saying "and because of the absence of exchange" (*vinimayābhāvāt*).
Exchange, consisting of the mutual taking up of each other's attributes, exists only in [the case of] *parivṛtti*.
But here, it is only a single [thing] residing in multiple substrata that is intended, not a grasping by way of a universal property (*sāmānya*) belonging to such substrata; this is the meaning.
Exchange (*parivṛtti*) is a barter (*vinimaya*) that occurs with equals, inferiors, or superiors. (VisSd 10.80)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) He states the ornament of exchange (*parivṛtti*): "Exchange" means a mutual transfer between two things that are either equal or unequal.
The exchange of the deficient and the excessive is twofold: giving less and taking more, or giving more and taking less.
The examples follow in order:
"Having given a sidelong glance, the deer-eyed one seized my heart."
But by me, having given my heart, the fever of love has been taken up.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭha) Regarding that, he provides one example of exchange (*vinimaya*), wherein more is given than received and less is taken: "Having given a sidelong glance...
This is clear.
In this verse, [the first half] is with equal [syllables], while the second half is with fewer;
and as for that aged Jaṭāyu, who has now gone to heaven, what indeed is there to be grieved for now?
By whom, through the sacrifice of a worn-out body, fame as radiant as the rays of the moon was purchased.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍa) Having mentioned giving less while taking more, he says "tasya ca" (and of him).
This is the speech of Rāma.
For one who is advanced in years and extremely aged, there is nothing at all to be grieved for. One simply grieves; there is truly nothing worthy of grief.
By means of which [wealth], through the expenditure of this worn-out, decayed body, fame as bright as moonbeams—white like the rays of the moon—has been purchased.
Here, by the giving away of the worn-out body, there is the purchase of radiant fame;
thus, there is a superiority [of the latter] over the former.
In this context,
through an excess [of cognition], whether from a question or even without a question,
if there occurs an exclusion of other such things based on a stated object, that [exclusion] is then either verbal or objective.
Enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*):
Vijñapriyā (vi, ḍha) states that there are four kinds of the figure of speech enumeration: "whether from a question or without a question," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: when, due to the speaker's intention or the absence thereof, whatever object has been mentioned as the substantive (viśeṣya) of a particular attribute to be questioned, and from that which was stated, there is understood— either verbally or by implication— the exclusion (vyavaccheda) of other similar objects to be mentioned from association with that attribute, then it is the figure of speech called *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification), characterized by such exclusion.
The examples in order are as follows:

“What is the most enduring ornament here? Fame, not jewels. What is the duty to be performed? Noble conduct and virtuous deeds, not vice. What is the unimpeded eye? Intellect, not the physical organ. Who other than you knows how to distinguish between the real and the unreal?”
In this context, that which is to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*) is the literal meaning (*śābda*), such as "jewels" and so forth.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṇa):
Here, they say that the exclusion based on the literal meaning is stated by way of a question: "What is the ornament?"
In this world, the question is: "What is the most firmly established ornament?
The answer is: "Fame," not "jewels."

By virtue of its worthiness of adoption, there is an exclusion (vyavaccheda) of the connection [of fame] with any other similar being who serves as a qualifying attribute for that which is to be questioned.
This should be understood in the same way in all cases.
The question is: "What is the thing to be done?"—referring to that which was practiced (ācarita) by the noble ones (āryas), such as Vasiṣṭha and others.
"Good deed" is the answer.
Since the fault consisting of his sexual intercourse with a *caṇḍālī* was to be performed at that time, the exclusion of what is similar to a good deed is not a fault; this is the literal meaning.
Likewise, in the subsequent [verse], "What is the unimpeded eye?"...
*Dhiṣaṇā* means intellect (*buddhi*), not the eye.
Regarding the reading *jānātīti tvadaparaḥ*, this is a statement of praise by the questioner—who is satisfied with the answer—addressed to the person who provided the reply.
Regarding the reading *tadaparaḥ*, the meaning is "one whose supreme faculty is *dhiṣaṇā* (intellect)."

Regarding the phrase "that which is to be excluded" (*vyavacchedya*) here: it means "exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*). This is because in the Sūtra, it is the exclusion itself that is expressed by the words, and not that which is to be excluded.
The same applies in the subsequent verses:
"What merit is to be constantly honored? What is the true scripture that is to be served? Who is the Lord Viṣṇu who is to be meditated upon? And what is the supreme state to be desired?"
In this context, the purpose of exclusion is for the sake of [avoiding] evil and so forth.
These two [terms] are preceded by a question.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ta) He demonstrates that the meaning [of the word] consists in the exclusion of others (*anyavyapoha*)—namely, "what is to be propitiated" (*kimārādhyam*).

Although being "propitiated" (*ārādhyatva*) means being the object of propitiation (*ārādhanāviṣayatva*), and propitiation is an action that causes the pleasure of a deity, nevertheless, in this context, "being propitiated" means being the object of a person's activity (*puruṣapravṛttiviṣayatva*).
By this, the sense is: "merit is to be propitiated, that is, to be acquired"; thus, the phrase "nothing else" in the subsequent [verse] serves as an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).
The traditional teaching of the virtuous is association with the good;
the supreme state is liberation.
As for the case where it is not preceded by a question:

“The devotion of the great is seen to be generally directed toward existence itself rather than worldly prosperity; their passion is for the scriptures rather than the arrows of youth and desire; and their concern is for fame rather than the physical body.”
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, tha) Regarding the fact that the exclusion [of other meanings] is verbal even in the absence of a prior question, he says: "Devotion arises"—this refers to the weapon of Kāma in the form of a young woman.
The connection of the words is as follows: in all instances beginning with "devotion," this is generally observed among the great ones.
“Strength is for the sake of allaying the fear of the afflicted; extensive learning is for the approval of the wise.
For that Lord, not only his wealth, but even his possession of virtues serves the purposes of others.”
And regarding its being rooted in *śleṣa* (paronomasia), a specific variety of its charm is as follows:
“While that king, who had conquered the world, was protecting the earth, there was a mixing of colors in paintings and a breaking of the string in bows,” and so forth.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, da) He demonstrates that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) has meaning when preceded by non-peace: "Power" (*bala*).
Power is prowess; for the destruction of the fear of the afflicted, that is, of those who are tormented, and for their approval, which means for their joy.
Learning is knowledge;

therefore, it is not only the king's wealth and riches that serve the purpose of others, but his possession of qualities such as strength is likewise a producer of the purpose of others, which consists in the destruction of the poverty of those who seek help.
In the case of "clarified butter is longevity" (*āyur ghṛtam*), which produces the intended purpose, the word for the purpose is used figuratively through superimposition (*sāropa-lakṣaṇika*).
Here, there is no cognition of exclusion (*vyapoha*) regarding its own primary meaning.
[This applies to] "in paintings," and so forth.

The punning connection (*śleṣa*) of the qualities of these two colors—neither among the Brahmins and so forth, nor among the subjects—produces the cognition of exclusion (*vyapoha*). [Objection: If the inference of a question arises from its answer, then how can there be an answer when the question itself is repeatedly impossible? (VisSd 10.82)
Vijñapriyā: (vi, dha) He states the two types of *uttara* ornament— namely, *uttara*—
as "unnaya" (*unnayana*), which is suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
Regarding the word "yaccha" (grant):
the term "asakṛt" (repeatedly) is to be construed with both [parts of the compound].

The meaning is that even though there have been repeated questions, the answer is one that is impossible—because it is of a different character—and thus not immediately perceived despite being given repeatedly.
Locanā:
(lo, ū) "Uttara" refers to the ornament known as *uttara*.
By the word "asakṛt" (repeatedly), it is indicated that there is no aesthetic charm (*cārutva*) in providing a reply—whether impossible or otherwise—only once, following a question.
As in my own verse: "My mother-in-law is unable to endure being left alone, and my husband has gone far away;
I am a young woman all by myself—how could you possibly live here?"
Vijñapriyā: "To behold" (vīkṣitum)—
this is a statement spoken by the messenger herself.
The demonstration of the mother-in-law’s inability to see in the literal sense is intended to show the impossibility of her even going to the place where you cook and eat.
Here, since there is no explicit negation, the figure of speech *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) should also be understood.
By this, the traveler’s request for lodging is implied.
“What is uneven? The path of women. What is to be gained? A person who appreciates virtue.
What is happiness? A good wife. What is difficult to abandon? A wicked person.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pa) He states the second reply—“uneven” (*viṣama*)—as follows: “What is the uneven course of fate? That people are appreciative of virtue (*guṇagrāhī*).”
What is happiness?
A virtuous wife.
What is difficult to grasp? The world of the wicked.

"Thus it is concluded: the meaning is that because the discrepancies such as the adverse course of fate and so forth are not immediately perceived through their distinctness from the object [of perception], the cognitive process comes to rest right there.
— *Locanā*
(Lo, ṛ) What is it? “What is an adverse turn of fate? A person who appreciates virtue. What is happiness? A good wife. What is difficult to grasp? A wicked person.”
In this case, because there is no intention to exclude others (*anyavyapoha*), it is a distinction [from] *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification).
Nor is this inference (*anumāna*),
for that [inference] is accepted only when there is the presentation of both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).
Nor is this *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication),
because the latter [the answer] does not function as a cause for the former [the question].
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, pha) "Because it does not produce the question"—
this statement regarding the absence of *kāvyaliṅga* in the case of an indicative cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*) should be recalled from the previous discussion on *arthāntaranyāsa*.
However, since the capacity of a question to indicate [an answer] is sublated by the figure of speech *uttara*, there is no room for *kāvyaliṅga* in that instance.

Locanā: (lo, ṝ) The meaning is that there is no intention to exclude others; rather, it is because the mere manifestation of the irregularity of the connection with previous births, such as by the course of fate, has been fully grasped.
Thus, because it is easier to distinguish this variety of the *uttarālaṅkāra* from other figures of speech, he distinguishes it later with the words "and not" (*na ca*).
The apprehension of another meaning by means of the *daṇḍāpūpika* logic (the "stick-and-cake" principle) is accepted as *arthāpatti* (presumption).
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ba) He states the figure of speech *arthāpatti* (presumption): "by the maxim of the staff and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*). This is a specific logical principle (*nyāyaviśeṣa*), which he will demonstrate himself.
By that principle, the implication (*vyañjanā*) is the arrival of another, unstated meaning from what has been said. This is the meaning.
And that principle should be understood as obtainable through verbal *śleṣa* (paronomasia);

otherwise, it would undesirably apply even to cases such as *samāsokti* and *aprastutapraśaṃsā*. Since by the statement "the stick was eaten by the mouse," the eating of the cake (*apūpa*) associated with it follows by implication, another matter arises through a fixed common logic; this is the principle known as *daṇḍāpūpikā*.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, bha) He demonstrates that principle with the words "by a mouse.
Here, "staff" refers to the stick used for pulling out the dung from its respective spot.
*Apūpaḥ* means flour-cake (*piṣṭaka*).
The eating of that stick occurs because of the smell of that flour-cake.

Likewise, the eating of the flour-cake associated with it is necessary; therefore, by the statement "the stick was eaten by the mouse," it follows by implication that this was said by someone—this is the remainder [of the sense].
Regarding the phrase "thus, that which is restricted and similar":

the meaning is that when something is restricted, because it follows the same logical principle (*nyāya*), another object—a different referent from what was previously stated—is brought forth and perceived.
He demonstrates the two-fold nature of that which is obtainable through such a principle by saying "in some cases."
Locanā:
By means of the suffix *kan*, [the word] *daṇḍāpūpikā* is formed, like the maxim of the staff and the cake; such a principle is also called *daṇḍāpūpikā*.
By whatever method there may be, the arrival of another thing through implication— that is to say, its logical necessity— is "establishment" (*siddhi*).
He demonstrates this very point with the words "by the mouse," which implies [the presence of the cat] by way of implication.
For instance, just as one might ask how a mouse that has eaten a stick accompanied by a cake could have abandoned the cake, so too should it be understood here.
Therefore, the meaning is that this is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) where there is an implication of another matter through a similar logic.
And herein there are two varieties: in some cases, the non-contextual matter follows from the contextual matter, and in other cases, the contextual matter follows from the non-contextual matter.
The examples in order are as follows:
“This necklace rolls upon the circle of the breasts of the fawn-eyed women; such is the condition even of pearls—what then can we say of us, the servants of Love?”
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ma) Therein, he demonstrates that the non-contextual meaning [is] accessible through that same logic by means of the phrase "this is the method" (*hāra*) and "it rolls" (*luṭhati*).
The meaning is that she remains with a specific gait characterized by the turning of her limbs under the influence of contempt for the circle of breasts.
This state consists of standing in a manner of contempt,
as if thinking, "Who are we?"

The meaning is that because it must be understood as "this is the condition of the servants of Smara" and "of us, who are the servants of Smara," there is an excessive rolling about on the ground. Here,
since the description of beauty dependent upon ornaments has been introduced, the pearls are the contextual subjects (*prākaraṇikyaḥ*).
In this context, by the phrase "who are we?", that principle is obtained.
Locanā:
(lo, e) *muktāḥ* refers to pearls, and also to those who have attained *niḥśreyasa* (the supreme good).

Thus, by the rolling of the jeweled bracelets upon the breasts of the liberated women—meaning, by the same logic, even for the servants of Love—he lamented with a voice choked with tears, having abandoned even his innate fortitude;
"Even iron, when excessively heated, attains softness; what need be said of embodied beings?"
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ya) He states the attainment of the relevant meaning from the irrelevant by saying "vilalāpa" (he lamented).
That King Aja [lamented] his innate, natural...

In this context, "here" (atra) refers to that which is not part of the subject matter; from that non-contextual [element], the acquisition of the meaning of the contextual [element] occurs. Furthermore, through words such as "what kind of story" (kaiva kathā), the application of that same principle is obtained.

And here, when the same logical principle (*samānanyāya*) is rooted in *śleṣa* (punning), there is a specific variety of charm, as seen in the example cited: “This necklace... and so forth. This is not inference (*anumāna*), because the same logical principle lacks the nature of a [logical] relation (*sambandha*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding the phrase "in being rooted in paronomasia" (*śleṣamūlatve*):

in the verse beginning with "This necklace" (*hāro 'yam*), the word *muktā* is paronomastic, as it applies both to the meaning of "a pearl" and to the form of "unfastened" (*mukta*) in the sense of "abandoned" by the God of Love (*smara*).
Furthermore, the word *luṭhati* ("rolls") is paronomastic, as it applies both to the meaning of "remaining with contempt" and to the act of "embracing."
In the verse beginning with *vilalāpa*, the word *tapta* (heated) is *śliṣṭa* (homonymous), applying both to contact with fire and to the pain of separation;
likewise, the word *mārdava* (softness) is *śliṣṭa*, applying both to physical delicacy and to timidity.
Thus, by means of the phrase "this necklace" (*hāro 'yam*) and so forth, the entire verse beginning with *vilalāpa* is included.

"Not this," [he says], because in the case of "This is a necklace," there would follow the consequence that the rolling of the lover clinging to the breasts is inferred from the rolling of the necklace clinging to the breasts; and in cases such as "she lamented," softness would likewise be inferable from the heat.
This is due to the application of the same logical principle (*samānanyāya*).

The meaning is "by the logic of the stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikānyāya*). This is because there is an absence of the nature of a relationship, specifically an absence of the nature of a relationship in the form of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Although there is indeed a pervasion between the state of clinging to the breasts and rolling about, and between extreme heat and softness, [the relationship in question lacks that specific form].

The intention is that it is not an inference because the logical reason (*nyāya*) presents itself first [in consciousness] and because there is no statement of the relationship between the probandum and the probans (*sādhyahetubhāva*).
*Locanā*:
(lo, ai) "Connection" (*sambandha*) means inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
This is not a scriptural presumption (*śāstrīyārthāpatti*).
For in that case, the meaning is that Devadatta is fat and does not eat during the day; thus, there is an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between fatness and eating.
"Alternative" (*vikalpa*) refers to the contradiction between two [propositions] of equal strength, which is characterized by cleverness.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, la) He states the ornament of conceptualization (*vikalpālaṅkāra*)—namely, "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*).
"Equality in both alternatives" (*koṭidvaye samānatvam*) means having equal strength (*tulyabalatā*).
Cleverness (*cāturi*) consists in being composed of a different figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*).

For this very reason, in the phrase "in the act of creation," although there is an option between the Moon and Madana as the Creator (*prajāpati*), it is not the figure of speech *vikalpa* (option), because it is not composed of a different figure of speech.
As, for example:
“Let either the heads or the bows be bent; let either the commands or the bowstrings be made into ear-ornaments.

Here, there is a contradiction because the bending of the heads and the bows serves as an indication of peace and war respectively, and since it is impossible to perform both peace and war at the same time; furthermore, this contradiction results in the adoption of one side or the other.
And here, the equality of strength between the two—the bow and the bending of the head—is to be understood as being conceived through their mutual rivalry;
and the cleverness (*cāturya*) here lies in its containing a simile (*aupamya*).
The same applies to the phrase, "Let them be made ear-ornaments."
Vijñapriyā:
The passage beginning with "namayantu" is not a verse;
rather, it is merely a statement of inquiry by the victorious king toward the kings who were to be conquered.
The meaning is: let the kings either bow their heads for the sake of prostration, or let them bend their bows for the sake of battle.
And likewise, let my command be "filled to the ear"—that is, let it be heard by filling the ear—or let the *maurva* [bowstring] be drawn to the edge of the ear for the sake of battle.
To make the contradiction clear here, he says: "here, of the bows... (atra dhanuṣām).

Having thus demonstrated the contradiction because peace and war are characterized by [mutual exclusion] and because they indicate that [exclusion], he shows here the possibility of an option based on desire (*icchāvikalpa*) with the words "And that" (*sa ca*).
This is because the fulfillment of desire is sufficient through the adoption of one side;
for an option based on desire is only possible when [the alternatives] are of equal strength.
And "equality of strength" here means [strength] from both; "from two" means from the presence of both.
Furthermore, because both [the self and others] act for their own benefit, the two possess equal strength;
he demonstrates this possession of skill by saying "and skill.
*Aupamya* means comparison (*upamā*).
This is an *upamā* (simile) based on the similarity between the head and the bow in their act of bending, and between the command and the bowstring in their act of being made into ear-ornaments.
This is an illustration; it should be understood that equal fitness [for comparison] arises through the connection of both [terms] with a single action. — *Locanā*.
When two things of equal strength are enjoined toward a single effect, there is a conflict because it is impossible to bring both to completion at once; however,
since that conflict results in their resorting to the same level [of operation], it is in fact no conflict at all.
Thus:
"May the eyes or the body of Hari bring about the pacification of your distress.
Here, there is beauty supported by *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Locanā:
[The word] *śleṣa* [is used] in the sense of "may they both perform," because here the dual and singular forms are identical in shape;
and because here both the eye (*netra*) and the body (*varṣman*) are equally capable of alleviating suffering.
“Let the unconquered wealth be given to a god or to a brahmin.
[The commentary] Vijñapriyā explains the exclusion of one endowed with cleverness (*cāturya*) by the word “let it be given.”

We consider that the occurrence of contradiction here is rooted solely in a lack of careful attention—since there is no contradiction because the giving of wealth to both gods and Brahmins is possible at one and the same time;
or else, the contradiction was shown by taking into account the restrictive rule "either to the gods or to the Brahmins," or by intending the gift to refer to a single individual instance.
Thus, due to a lack of ingenuity in this regard, this is not a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).

This is a case of "conjunction" (samuccaya): when there is one means capable of accomplishing an effect, if another [means] were also to perform that [action], it would be according to the maxim of the "pigeons in a barnyard. (Viśuddhimārga 10.84)
"Two qualities, or two actions, or a quality and an action may exist simultaneously.
Vijñapriyā (vi, ṣa) states: "This is the fourfold figure of speech called *samuccaya* (accumulation)."
The phrase "the pigeons' simultaneous landing on the threshing floor where grain is being pounded" means that it occurs by way of a particular maxim (nyāya).
He states another threefold division with the words "guṇa-ādi":
the meaning is that if two qualities, or two actions, or both a quality and an action were described simultaneously.
Locanā:
"The word 'samuccaya' (collection/union) [is explained by] the third quarter; it serves to distinguish it from meditative absorption (*samādhi*)."
And this is very clear in the commentary itself:
"its maker" means the accomplisher of that effect.
As it is said by me:
“O, you steady breeze!
Alas, your birth is from the sandalwood mountain, your courtesy toward the world is unsurpassed, and your acquaintance is with the waters of the Godāvarī.
Yet, if even you burn every limb of mine like a raging forest fire, what will the forest-dwelling cuckoo—who is himself dark-natured—say of this?”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, sa) "O, you who possess fortitude! This is an address to one who is slow-witted, characterized by the possession of steadfastness in the form of desisting from what ought not to be done.
"O sandalwood! [is the next address].
The address as "fragrant" is because of the connection with sandalwood, which is produced by the great multitude;
"courtesy" (dākṣiṇya) refers to the fact that only that which arises from the southern direction possesses a discernment that is extraordinary in the world.
Regarding "familiarity":
just as coolness is associated with water, greatness is said to arise from association with the Puṇyanadī river.

If you, being such as this, burn every limb of mine like a forest fire during our separation, then [the one who suffers] is more insane than I, foul-natured, black-complexioned, and crooked by nature.
And being a forest-dweller, unacquainted with worldly conventions, what could the cuckoo say?
The meaning is that he would burn [the listener] all the more.
—Locanā:
(Lo, ā) A steadfast one by lineage and method, and through his erudition; a mountain among kings, capable of bearing the earth—a certain great man.
His courtesy is the southern quarter, and his innate straightforwardness is the south.
"Malinātman" means dark-natured and crooked-minded;
"santaḥ" refers to those who are excellent due to their causes, such as fortitude and so forth.
Here, although there is a single cause for burning—namely, the nature of being born from sandalwood trees—there is the employment of other causes, such as courtesy and the like.

In this case, because all the causes (*hetu*) are beautiful, there is "good conjunction" (*sadyoga*). In this very same fourth quarter, because of the conjunction of "intoxication" (*matta*) and other such unattractive [causes], there is "bad conjunction" (*asadyoga*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ha) Regarding this: the reading is "adāhakatve" (in the state of not being combustible);
the reading "dāhakatve" (in the state of being combustible) is merely an error.
The fact that sandalwood, patience, and so forth are non-causes of burning has already been explained in the commentary on the verse itself.
Regarding the phrase "in the fourth quarter":
it means that intoxication and the like are causes with respect to burning.
Existence and non-existence refer to what is to be accepted and what is not to be accepted.
The application of existence and non-existence is as follows:
"The moon is grey with daylight; the beloved woman has lost her youth; the lake is devoid of lotuses; and a face, though well-formed, is without words."
A wealthy man devoted solely to riches, a virtuous person who is constantly in poverty, and a wicked man who has gained access to the king's palace—these seven are like thorns in my heart.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) "The moon," etc. The meaning is that these seven—the bed and so forth, characterized by their greyishness—are like seven thorns in the mind.
Because it causes pain like a thorn through the perception of impropriety,
he demonstrates that impropriety regarding them with the word "the moon" (śaśī):
for it is improper that he, whose form is radiant, should be grey with the day.

Thus, for a woman whose youth has faded, it is improper that she possess passion; or for a passionate woman, it is improper that her youth have faded. Likewise, it is improper for a lotus pond to be devoid of lotuses; and for a person of handsome appearance who is a fool, it is improper that he be devoid of letters—that is, of learning.
Whether it be a master’s devotion to wealth, or the mastery of one devoted to wealth;
whether it be the perpetual poverty of a virtuous person, or the virtue of one who is perpetually poor.
The meaning is that either the wickedness of one who has entered the king’s courtyard, or the presence in the king’s courtyard of a wicked person, is improper.
Here, there is a combination of the good and the bad based on the existence or non-existence of those who are pitiable and those who are authoritative.

In that context, there is the quality (*sattva*) of one who is pitiable due to a defect dependent on fate, and the absence of quality (*asattva*) of one who is pitiable due to a defect within one's own power.
In this regard, there is the paleness of the moon;
and in the case of a passionate woman, there is the state of having lost her youth, whether considered as a subject to be controlled or as the loss of youth itself.
The lake being devoid of lotuses,
a handsome form being the ignorance of one who cannot read,
and a virtuous person being in distress— these are beautiful precisely because they are pitiable due to their faults.

Some say that here the presence or absence of excellence belongs solely to the attributes (vidheya): in the case where the state of being subject to passion resides in her whose youth has faded, there is either the lord’s devotion to wealth residing in him who is devoted to wealth, or the wickedness residing in the one who has entered the king’s courtyard, where the attribute of being subject [to passion] resides; or, because the attribute is deplorable due to its inherent fault, it lacks excellence. Thus, they maintain that the quality of being good or bad belongs only to the attributes—namely, the excellence of the moon and so forth, and the lack of excellence of the wicked man; this is called the "conjunction of the good and the bad" (sadasadyoga).
Others, however, say: "The conjunction of the good and the bad consists in the moon and so forth being inherently beautiful, while the graying and so forth are unattractive.

For here, since the graying and such are entirely inherent in the moon and other objects, it is specifically this particular strikingness (*vicchitti*) that produces the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).
Furthermore, in the verse "Seven arrows are in my heart," there is a synthesis of all seven as being arrows.

However, the phrase "the villain has gone to the king's palace" incurs the fault of a break in sequence (*kramabheda*) because, throughout the context, the sequence begins with the excellence of the subject (*viśeṣya*) alone.
Furthermore, here all the causes descend together in unison, like pigeons in a barn (*khalekapotavat*).

The distinction from the figure of speech *samādhi* (compensation), however, is that while in *samādhi* another cause falls in by chance (*kākatālīyanyāyena*) even when all the means for a single effect are already present, in this case they enter simultaneously.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, kha) Since even in the previously cited verse only the things to be enjoined (*vidheya*) possess that nature, the author—considering that there might be a difference of opinion—demonstrates the aforementioned connection with existence and non-existence by saying, "In this regard, some...
According to this view, existence and non-existence belong only to the subjects (*uddeśya*), which are the qualificands (*viśeṣya*).
He states another opinion: "But others," etc.
In this view, there is a connection between the subject and the predicate, or between the substantive and its attribute, whether they exist or not.

According to their view, that very state [of connection] constitutes a specific charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*), which produces aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*); he demonstrates this with the words "For here," etc.
The meaning is that, according to their view, the strikingness (*camatkāra*) arises from whether the subject (*uddeśya*) exists or does not exist.
For them, the mere existence or non-existence of those [qualities] constitutes the ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
On the contrary, in the first case, such a specification results in a violation of the proper sequence (*kramabhaṅga*).
(vi, kha) It demonstrates that very point with the words "in all cases" (*sarvatra*).
This means: in every sentence where there is a relationship between a subject (*uddeśya*) and a predicate (*vidheya*), such as "the moon is grey" (*śaśī dhūsaraḥ*).
And this is the fault.

It should be understood that when the wickedness (*khalatva*) residing in the king’s courtyard is the predicate (*vidheya*), the subject (*uddeśya*)—the state of being wicked—is indeed excellent; thus, this is not a fault.

Furthermore, he states the distinction between this [figure] and the ornament *samādhi* (which consists in the arrival of another cause by chance when an effect could be easily accomplished by a single cause): "And here, in the case of *khale*... [and so forth].

"Of one alone" means that when a single [cause] is sufficient as a complete causal factor (*sādhaka*) with respect to an effect, the operation of incomplete causes does not constitute sufficiency. *Locanā*.
In the second alternative, he shows the happy rebirth (*sugati*).
He clarifies the third quarter of the verse concerning the subject (*viśeṣya*), such as the moon, the beloved, and so forth, with the words "and here" (*iha ca*).
Regarding the phrase "by way of the *kākatālīya* maxim": [this refers to a fortuitous coincidence].
“O young woman, your eyes are reddened and your beloved’s face is darkened;
your face is cast down, my friend, yet within it the fire of love blazes.”
In this context, in the first sense there is simultaneity of two qualities, and in the second, simultaneity of two actions.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ga) He states the *samuccaya* (conjunction), which consists in the simultaneity of two qualities or two actions, with the words "and when red" (*aruṇe ca*).
Here, the two *ca*s indicate simultaneity.
Since those two [conjunctions] indicate the simultaneity of whichever [elements] follow them, he says: "here, in the first [case]."
An example of simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is as follows:
"O Lord of Kings, your eye has suddenly become turbid toward your enemies, yet it possesses a beauty like that of a white lotus; and [at the same time], [your enemy's] life has fallen."
Upon their bodies, the glances of calamities became clearly manifest.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
gha) And "defiled" refers to harmful adversaries.
"O Lord of the Earth" (*mahīpatīndra*) is the form of address.

Here, in the first half-verse, there is a succession of qualities (*guṇottara*), whereas in the second half-verse, there is a succession of actions (*kriyottara*); thus, there is a simultaneity between these two.
Regarding the word *dhunoti*:

the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* states that this [suffix -ti] is seen even when there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇya*), as in the case of "the place of battle" (*raṇasthala*) which functions as a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*).
For example: "You, with sword in hand, are upon the field of battle;
and the gods, uttering cries of 'Excellent!', are in the abode of the gods."
In this instance, there is a difference of locus (*adhikaraṇa*) consisting of the battlefield and the celestial abode. However,
in such cases as "He brandishes his sword and spreads his fame," this [figure] is seen even when there is a single locus.
Nor is there *dīpaka* (illumination) here;

for these types of *samuccaya* (conjunction), involving the simultaneity of qualities and actions, are invariably rooted in *atiśayokti* (poetic exaggeration) consisting of a reversal of the temporal sequence between cause and effect, whereas *dīpaka* lacks such a basis in *atiśayokti*.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,

ṅa) Regarding the example "dhunoti cāsi," having raised the objection that there might be the fault of *dīpaka*— whereby a single agent (*kartṛkāraka*) connected to multiple actions would illuminate multiple actions— it is refuted with the words "na cātra" ("but not here").

The meaning is that these types of conjunction (*samuccaya*), which consist in the simultaneity of qualities (*guṇa*) or actions (*kriyā*), are based on *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) characterized by the reversal of that temporal restriction which consists in the sequence of cause and effect.
This is because, in all the examples shown, although there exists a causal relationship between two qualities or two actions, their simultaneity is asserted.
He states "of the *dīpaka*" [in the verse] because such a state does not exist in the case of *dīpaka*.
This is an elliptical indication; it should be understood that the non-intentional mention of simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) therein is also a differentiator.
Thus, the intended meaning is that the qualification "provided both of those are absent" must be supplied. The resolution [to this problem] is as follows:
when a task is easily accomplished, [the completion may occur] due to destiny or the arrival of another factor. (Viṣṇusmṛti 10.85)
For example:
"To dispel her pride, this thundering of clouds has arisen by good fortune as an aid for me as I am about to fall at her feet."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ca) He states the ornament of concentration (*samādhyalaṅkāra*)—namely, "concentration" (*samādhi*).
The meaning is that when a task is easily accomplished by a single cause alone, another object in the form of a cause happens to appear by chance.
"mānamasyā iti" means that since the thundering of clouds acts as an excitant for the shattering of pride, that too has arrived by chance as another cause for the breaking of her pride.
[The verse continues: "If one who is unable to retaliate against an enemy resorts to a counter-measure..."
The disparagement of that very person is what actually establishes his excellence.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) He states the ornament of the adversary (*pratyanīkālaṅkāra*): "The adversary" (*pratyanīkam*).
If someone, being unable to retaliate—that is, to counteract—an enemy, instead insults another who is related to that enemy, such an act serves to establish the very superiority of that same enemy.
The meaning is that it results in excellence.
Locanā:
(Lo, ī) Having thus shown the figures of speech based on the logic of sentences, [the author proceeds].
He shows that [the argument] relies on worldly convention by saying "an adversary" (*pratyanīka*).
This refers to a multi-pronged army, and here it serves as an illustration for anything related to one's own class (*svasāmānya*) in general.

Because it is described as an object belonging to the enemy that serves as a substitute due to being subject to attack by him, it is the ornament named *pratyanīka* (counter-array). "Belonging to him" means belonging to the enemy;
"of that very one" means of the enemy alone.
As in my own verse: "This lion, resembling her jar-like breasts, crushes her elephant-temple-like [shoulders], as if thinking, 'She has surpassed my waist with her slender waist.'"
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ja) "In the middle" means that the meditation on the lion in the first half [of the verse] is for the purpose of shattering the jar of the enemy.
In this context, because of the victory over her own center by the middle [line], the heroine is the enemy of the lion; therefore, the two frontal globes of the elephant are like her breasts.
— *Locanā*:
(Lo, u) Here, the connection with the heroine [is established] through the two elephant-ivory globes (*ibhakumbha*).

Her own connection is her connection with the jar-like breasts (*kucakumbha*), which arises from a relationship of similarity; and this [connection] can also occur when one performs a desired action for a favorable person, as in the verse beginning:
"Though distressed by separation, she constantly falls [into his arms], imitating your very breath," and so forth.
The conceptualization of a well-known object of comparison as the object of comparison itself, or the statement of its fruitlessness, is called *pratīpa* (the inverse). (VisSd 10.87)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, jha) He states that *pratīpa* (the inverse ornament) is of two kinds—namely, "of the well-known" (*prasiddhasya*).
The meaning is that *pratīpa* is twofold: either the conception of the well-known standard of comparison (*upamāna*) as the object of comparison (*upameya*), or the statement of its fruitlessness.
For example, in sequence:
"That blue lotus which was submerged in the water possesses a luster equal to your eye," and so forth.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ña) As for the passage beginning with "But that which is not this," etc.:
the correlate (*pratiyogin*) of its similarity is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

And here, by the statement "possessing a luster equal to your eye," the luster of your eye is designated as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) through its being the counter-correlate to the luster of the blue lotus; thus, there is the conceptualization of the luster of the blue lotus—which is well-known as the standard of comparison—as the object of comparison (*upameya*).
