[As it is said: "If that face were so, the story of the moon would be silenced; oh, if that splendor were so, gold would be surpassed!"* *Note: This verse is a famous example of *pratīpa* (the inverse comparison), where the expected standard of comparison is instead made the object of comparison.*

If that eye of yours is surpassed by blue water-lilies, what then is nectar if it is your smile? Fie on Cupid’s bow if they are your eyebrows! But why say more? The truth is, the Creator’s process of creation has turned away from repeating things already made.
In this instance, because the moon and other objects convey their splendor solely through the face and so forth, they are rendered fruitless.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṭa): He provides an example of the fruitlessness of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—namely, "If that face were... and so on.
It should be understood that if the mouth and other [organs] exist, the sealing (mudritatva) of the hare-marked moon and so forth results in futility.
"Hā" means "I grieve";
it means that defeat has been incurred.
Regarding the phrase "tacced":
it means "if that smile of hers" [should occur].
Who is the inferior one?
Having spoken thus, he concludes with the words "what more need be said?
The process of creation by the Creator— the sequence of emanation— is "averse to repetitive things," meaning it is averse to that which is redundant,
namely the conceptualization of another similar object.
In this context, the meaning is "one who is averse due to seeing the fault in the form of fruitlessness. It should be understood that the word *vimukha* itself has such a sense.
And having spoken of the absolute excellence of an exceedingly excellent thing...
Even when the status of the standard of comparison is merely imagined, some have declared it to be *pratīpa* (the inverse).
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṭha) Even when there is an assumption of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) as being the standard of comparison itself in certain cases, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* defines this ornament as follows: "Having stated... even to the utmost" (*uktvā cātyantam iti*).

The meaning is: even after stating the extreme excellence of an object that is already most excellent, [the figure occurs] when it is nevertheless designated as having been conceived as a standard of comparison.
Furthermore, that description should be understood as culminating in a censure [of the subject] by virtue of the context of its juxtaposition;
otherwise, since the comparison would be perceived merely as a comparison in its own right, the quality of being "contrary" (pratīpa) would be impossible.
Moreover, there would be an over-extension [of the definition] to a comparison such as, "The face is exceedingly beautiful, like the moon."
As it is said:
"O Hālāhala, my dear father, I alone am the teacher of the most terrible things."
Do not be arrogant;
for are there not indeed words such as yours from wicked people in this world?
Vijñapriyā: (vi, ḍa) "It is I myself," [she says]. O Hālāhala!
"O dear one,
do not be so arrogant as to think, 'I alone am the foremost teacher of the most cruel [arts].'"
The meaning is: "Do not act with such pride.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Indeed" (*nanu*).
"Indeed, O sir, in this world there exist many words of the wicked that are like yours, that is, equal to you"—this is the meaning.

The word "bhūyaḥ" (furthermore/more) is an adverbial qualifier for the act of speaking (*sāntakriyā*). Through its abundance, one should understand the abundance of the words themselves. Here, by the first quarter-verse, the excellence of the preeminence is stated.
But if that [similarity] is not stated, this is not an ornament;
for example: "A Brāhmaṇa speaks like Brahmā," and so forth.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ḍha) Here, by the phrase "those which are seen as if they were you," there is an indication of *halāhala* poison specifically as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Furthermore, due to its co-occurrence with the negation of the mirror, it results in a censure of that [poison].
Here, he connects what was stated as being "extremely liberated" by means of the first quarter-verse.

He states the purpose of that qualification—namely, that its gravity is expressed in comparison to other very terrible [sins]—by saying: "if that were not mentioned," [it would follow that] this is not an *alaṅkāra* (poetic figure).
But the meaning is that these are merely similes.
He demonstrates this with the words "just as Brahmā":
the meaning is that just as Brahmā speaks the Veda, so do the Brāhmaṇas.

Although the statement that "Brahmā alone is the supreme speaker of the Veda" constitutes an expression of the Brāhmaṇa’s absolute excellence— and thus, despite being a comparison, this is not [the figure of] *Upamā*— nevertheless,

for the sake of establishing a contrary effect (*pratīpa*), it was stated previously that because of the specific manner of co-utterance, the description results in the censure of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*); therefore, it should be understood that this [figure] is excluded by that very [definition].
*Mīlita* (the concealed) is the hiding of an object by something possessing similar characteristics.
In this [figure], an object with identical characteristics is sometimes adventitious.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṇa) He states the figure of speech *mīlita*:
"It is called *mīlita*.
*Guptiḥ* means concealment.
By "having identical characteristics" is meant having identical marks;
that which is adventitious belongs to the [subject], while that which is innate is its function.
For example, in sequence:
"The mark of musk upon the chest of Hari, located on the breast of Lakṣmī,
was not noticed by Bhāratī because it was eclipsed by her splendor, which resembled a blue lotus."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ta) "On Lakṣmī’s chest" means that on the surface of Hari’s chest, the mark of musk from Lakṣmī’s breasts was not perceived by Bhāratī.
The meaning is that it was swallowed—that is, covered—by the very luster of Hari out of fear of the blue lotus.
In this regard, the Blessed One’s dark splendor is innate; [as it is said:
"In her, the rays of him who always has ruby earrings have rendered all things crimson."
Even the faces of amorous women, though flushed with anger, did not cause apprehension among the youths.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) She says "always" by means of the characteristic of a visitor:

in that city, even the faces of amorous women, though flushed with anger, are always rendered crimson by the rays of earrings set with red gems and stones; thus, they cause young men to suspect that [the women] are angry.
The meaning is that they do not produce [the effect].
In this context, the redness of the ruby earring is adventitious (*āgantuka*).
"Commonality" (*sāmānya*) is the identification of the subject with something else through qualities that are similar. (VisSd 10.89)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) "The universal" means: if it is described as the identity with what is other, or the non-apprehension of the difference from what is other. This is the meaning.

However, in the case of the [cognition of] a form (*rūpaka*) and the [cognition of] illusion (*bhrāntimad*), there is a distinction from that [other type], because it is either induced (*āhāryā*) precisely through the non-apprehension of difference (*abhedāgraha*).
For this very reason, he will explain in the commentary on the example: "non-apprehension of difference.
For instance—
“With their braided hair adorned with jasmine and their bodies anointed with beautiful sandalwood paste,
the women going to meet their lovers move happily and unnoticed in the moonlight.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, dha) "Mallikā" means that which is not distinguished [from the moonlight], its difference from the moonlight being unperceived.
In *mīlita*, the inferior quality is concealed by a superior quality;
here, however, because both possess equal qualities, there is a failure to perceive their distinction.
In *tadguṇa*, due to the abandonment of one's own quality, there is the assumption of a much more excellent quality.
For example:
"He spoke, making the bees that were falling upon the periphery of his lotus-like face white by means of the rays from his sharp teeth."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, na) He states the ornament of "accepting their virtues" (*tadguṇa*): "the acceptance of their virtues" (*tadguṇagraha*) is the taking up of an exceedingly excellent quality.

"He spoke" means that he spoke while imparting whiteness to the bees hovering around the lotus— which was a pretext for the face of Balabhadra, serving as a mask for his countenance— by means of the rays of his teeth, which were like emerging rays of light.
In this case, the meaning is that the bees abandon their own quality by attaining whiteness.

The distinction is that in *mīlita* (the "merged"), there is the concealment of the primary object by another object, whereas here, what is perceived is being overwhelmed by the quality of another object.
Vijñapriyā:
He states the distinction of this [ornament] from the *mīlita* ornament: "In the case of *mīlita*," and "of the subject matter (*prakṛta-vastu*)."
The concealment or non-apprehension of the qualities and essential nature of the subject under discussion means its non-perception.
"Overpowering" (ākrāntatā) means making [the subject] one's own locus.
However, when the cause is present, the failure to imitate that form is *atadguṇa* (non-possession of its qualities).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pha) He states the ornament *atadguṇa* [the "non-possession of its quality"] with the words "tadrūpa" etc. *Ananuhāraḥ* means non-apprehension.
In the sense of a cause for grasping;
as for example:
"Alas! Even though my heart is filled with intense passion..."
O you who are white with virtue, how is it that even while seated here, you do not feel passion?
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ba) "Alas, it is dense!
This is the outpouring of a heroine who is in love with a hero who does not reciprocate her affection.
"Guṇagaura" means "white by virtue of his qualities," or it is an address using a compound meaning "one whose quality is white."
The grammatical connection is "even though seated in the heart.
In the phrase *rāgapadarajyasi-pade*, the words *rāga* (passion) and *padarajas* (dust of the feet) are linked through their shared quality of redness (*rakti*) and affection (*anurāga*).
Here, the state of being seated in the heart—which possesses passion—is the cause of the redness.
Or as it is said:
"The water of the Gaṅgā is white, the water of the Yamunā has the luster of collyrium; for you, O royal swan, who plunge into both, that same whiteness of yours neither increases nor decreases."

In the former case, although the redness of the hero—who is denoted by the term *guṇagaura* (white with virtues)—is as if attained through contact with a heart intensely colored [by passion], it is not fully realized.

In the latter case, even though there is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), despite the contact between the swan (*haṃsa*) under discussion and the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, the swan does not assume their nature.
Furthermore, this differs from *viśeṣokti* (causation of non-appearance) because it relies on a specific aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) consisting in the non-apprehension of qualities.
And because there is no production of a different color from the uneven [arrangement],
in both of the cited verses, *Vijñapriyā* states "as before" (*pūrvavat*) to indicate that these qualities are not perceived and to show the distinction between the two examples.

"With a heart overflowing" means that because it is filled with passion (*rāga*), the heart has attained an excess of quality; yet the state of being "red" (*rakta*)—meaning the hero's [passionate state]—has not reached completion.

Having thus demonstrated here, by means of the subject matter, the failure to perceive the qualities of the hero's actual heart, the author shows in the following verse the absence of the intended result, which consists in perceiving the qualities of the non-subject (*aprakṛta*) instead of the subject (*prakṛta*). This is indicated by the phrase "in the next [verse]."

Although the royal swan (*rājahaṃsa*) is also not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*), the author says "in the case of *aprastutapraśaṃsā*" while showing that its status as the subject is relative by virtue of being the one addressed.
Regarding the phrase "and here," he states the distinction of this [figure] from *viśeṣokti*, which consists in the absence of a result despite the presence of a cause.

The meaning is that in *viśeṣokti* there is simply the absence of a result in general, whereas here the distinction lies in a specific mode consisting in the absence of the particular result that is the recognition of merit.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that even in the figure of speech *viṣama* (the Unequal), there is a non-apprehension of the qualities of the cause by the effect due to the influence of a quality in the effect that is contrary to the cause?
Thus, since the relation of cause and effect exists in both examples shown, such a state of 'not possessing those qualities' would be no different from the figure *viṣama*.
To this, he says: "By means of another color," etc.

In the figure of speech *viṣama* (the incongruous), the distinction lies in the production of another quality that is contrary to the cause; this is the meaning. However, when a subtle matter, having been perceived through appearance or gesture, is indicated by some fortunate person, that is called *sūkṣma* (the subtle). (VisSd 10.91)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ma) He states the subtle ornament (*sūkṣmālaṅkāra*): "perceived" (*saṃlakṣita*).
The meaning is that it is indicated by way of a turn of phrase (*bhaṅgyā*), that is, by means of a specific mode.
"Appearance" (ākāra) means configuration;
"intimation" (iṅgita) means action—this is the meaning.
"Subtle" means not perceptible by those of dull intellect.

In this regard, by way of *ākāra* (gestural expression), as follows: "Seeing the saffron on her neck discolored by a continuous stream of sweat-drops trickling from her face, a certain slender friend, revealing the woman's masculinity, smiled and drew the outline of a sword upon her hand."
In this case, the amorous role-reversal (*puruṣāyita*) of one woman, indicated by another through a mark of saffron, is signaled by the drawing of a sword-blade—the mark of a man—upon her hand.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ya): "Flowing from the mouth."

A certain female companion, seeing the saffron on the neck of another heroine divided into two parts by streams of sweat flowing from her face, smiled and drew the outline of a sword upon that heroine’s hand, thereby suggesting her masculinity— that is, her acting the part of the man during sexual union.
Regarding the phrase "here [it is] observed":
this refers to the observation of perspiration moving toward the back during the pleasure that has arisen.
By gesture, for example:
Having perceived that the lover’s mind was fixed on the time of their secret rendezvous, the clever woman closed her play-lotus with a glance from her smiling eyes that conveyed her intention.

In this instance, the lover’s intention regarding the time for the rendezvous, indicated by the movement of his eyebrows and other gestures, is revealed by the closing of the lotus at the time of nightfall.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"Regarding the phrase 'the time for the rendezvous'..."

Having perceived that the rogue—the companion and suitor—was intent upon the time for the rendezvous in his desire to test her, the clever heroine closed her play-lotus with a smile and an intention conveyed through her eyes; such is the meaning.

"The intention regarding the time" refers to the inquiry about the time, while the "twinkling of the brow," though not explicitly stated, is a gesture obtained through the force of contextual fitness.
*Vyājokti* (the art of concealment) is the hiding of a matter that has become manifest despite efforts to disguise it.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, la) He states the figure of speech *vyājokti* [the artifice of concealment] with the words "by artifice" (*vyāja*).
"Of that which has burst forth" means of that which has become manifest; "by artifice" means by means of a pretext.
As it is said:

"May Śiva protect you—he who, his entire ritual engagement thrown into disorder by the bristling of horripilation and other signs as he was embraced by the hand of the Daughter of the Mountain while she was being presented by the Lord of Mountains; and who, upon seeing the circle of Mothers in the inner apartments of the mountain, smiled and exclaimed, ‘Ah! the coldness of the hands of the Snowy Mountain!’"
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
va) "O Lord of Mountains"—
may Śiva protect you!
Of what sort?

One who was disordered— that is, thrown into confusion— by the horripilation, trembling, and perspiration arising from the touch of the hand of Girijā as it was being offered and released by the Lord of Mountains through an embrace.

Distressed by the interruption of his engagement in the entirety of the wedding rites, he exclaimed, "Ah! How wonderful is the coolness of the hands of the Mountain-dweller (Himavat)! and was gazed upon with smiles by the ladies within the mountain palace—the circle of Mothers such as Gaurī and her attendants—along with their own retinues.
This is not the first type of apahnuti (concealment), because the object that performs the concealment is not explicitly mentioned;
moreover, the distinction from the second type of apahnuti was demonstrated during the discussion of that [second type].
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, śa) He states the distinction of this from the previously mentioned denial (*apahnuti*) with the words "this is not...
and "of those who practice denial."
The meaning is that it is a case of "denying the subject matter at hand" (prakṛtāpahnavakārī), because the non-contextual object— the thing being established— is not explicitly stated.
This is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa).

It should be understood that even the negative particle (*nañ*) and other such words whose function is negation (*apahnava*) do not denote [the object being negated], because the cause of the negation— such as whiteness— is denoted, whereas [qualities] like horripilation are not at all negated. This refers to the second type of *apahnuti*.

The meaning is that this is a second type of *apahnava* (concealment), based on the definition stated as: "When, having somehow indicated some secret matter, one conceals it through a pun (*śleṣa*) or otherwise, that too is *apahnava*," and based on the example "At the time of the clouds...
It was demonstrated in the discussion of that [first type].
The meaning is that this was shown by writing "it is *vyājokti* (artful speech) because the matter to be concealed was mentioned first by the concealer";
however, in this case, the matter to be concealed—such as the bristling of hair (*romāñca*) and so forth—was not mentioned first by Śiva.
*Svabhāvokti* (description of nature) is the description of the form of one's own action when the meaning is difficult to grasp. (VisSd 10.92)

Regarding the two difficult [types], where the meaning is known only by the learned poet (*kavi*), such as the actions and nature of children and the like who are themselves the sole locus of that [meaning]:
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṣa) states the figure of speech *Svabhāvokti*: "Svabhāvokti... [and so forth].
The phrase "durūhārtha" does not mean "of an extremely difficult meaning";
rather, the grammatical connection is "the action regarding the meaning is difficult.
And since the "meaning" refers to [actions such as] killing children and so forth, he explains it exactly in this way: "of the two difficult [actions]."
The grammatical connection is with the words "durūhayoḥ" (of two difficult-to-grasp) and "svayoḥ" (of their own).
He explains the meaning of the word "durūha" as "kavimātra" (accessible only to poets);
the sense is "of those whose objects of knowledge are different from that of poets."
He explains the term *arthapada* as referring to children and so forth: "of the object" (*arthasya*). A *ḍimbha* is an infant;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of those whose knowledge is merely unrefined.
This refers to two [beings] who share the same support and are fixed solely upon that [support].
As it is said by me:
“Striking with his tail and repeatedly tearing up the surface of the earth with his forefeet, then suddenly cowering within himself and leaping swiftly into the sky with great prowess;”
With a roar of hissing *huṃ* sounds, driving away all creatures in every direction, this jackal has entered the forest, possessed by rage and with eyes red and swollen.
Vijñapriyā: With his tail—
[this refers to] this tiger, whose eyes are reddish, swollen, and wide-open, who has entered into a powerful opposing force, that is, a multitude of adversaries.
What kind [of being] was it? Striking the surface of the earth repeatedly with its tail, burning and scratching it with its forefeet;
then immediately after, contracting its body and curling its limbs, leaping swiftly into the sky with great strides;
thus terrible with its crackling, quivering hiss, driving away living creatures in every direction.
Likewise, one who is possessed by anger has eyes wide open and reddened;
here, there is a description of the form and actions beginning with "reddened" (*aruṇa*).
[This applies to] a marvelous object, whether it be past or future.
That which appears as if it were directly perceived is declared to be the ultimate reality.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ha) He states the *bhāvika* ornament with the words "of the marvelous" (*adbhutasya*).
The meaning is "or rather, thus."

The meaning is this: it refers to that which is described as the appearance of a marvelous object—whether past or future—as if it were being perceived, or as if it were being seen by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For example:
"Victorious is the sage, the lord of yogis, the great-souled one born from a water-jar."
By which those two divine fish and tortoises were seen within a single mouthful of water."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) Regarding the word "sage" (*muni*):

while drinking from a single cup of water that was actually the ocean, he beheld by the power of yoga the fish and tortoise—the lords of those beings—descending [into the water] in both the past and the future.
It is for this very purpose that the term "Lord of Yogins" (yogīndra) is employed.
Or as it is said:
"I see collyrium here in your eyes."
I behold your form, which shall soon be adorned with a full array of ornaments.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
kha) "It was" means that even in the absence of actual collyrium during youth, it was as if there were collyrium because of its inherent beauty.
Because the beauty of one who will possess ornaments is seen even without them, it is called "possessing future ornaments.
Nor is this a poetic quality (*guṇa*) known as *prasāda* (transparency),
because when past and future things appear as if present, that quality is not the cause [of such an appearance].
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ga) But surely, even though the past and the future are unfit for direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they appear as if being directly perceived because they are objects of rapid cognition.
And thus, since such an object is the content [of cognition], that object, even when made known by a word, is indeed vivid (*viśada*).

And thus, regarding the "clarity of meaning" (*arthavaimalya*) which is called *prasāda* by others as a poetic quality (*guṇa*), [the author] suspects that this very thing is simply the ornament named *bhāvika*, since there is no distinct variety of it that differs from that; he then resolves this with the words "nor is this...
and "of the past and the future...

The meaning is: when those two (the past and the future) are to be grasped as appearing before the eyes (*pratyakṣāyamāṇatve*), that appearance is without cause, because it manifests as being causeless.
And thus it has been stated that the very variety consisting of the manifestation of causelessness and distinctness is the *bhāvika* ornament;
nor is it the *adbhuta* (marvelous) sentiment, because this [ornament] serves as the cause for wonder.

Vijñapriyā: (vi, gha) [Objection: Surely, the pursuit of a cause when there is no cause is nothing but astonishment; thus, this must be the sentiment of the marvelous (*adbhuta-rasa*) itself. He raises this doubt with the words: "And it is not the marvelous."
He explains: "It is understood as wonder.
This ornament consists precisely in the state of things yet to come or already past appearing as if they were being perceived directly, characterized by the knowledge of their causelessness;
for it is precisely that which serves as the cause for the sense of wonder.
The meaning is that it is not so, because its nature is wonder (*vismaya*).
Likewise, the intention is that there is no rasa of the marvellous (*adbhuta*) here, but rather the figure of speech is *bhāvika*.
Nor is the figure of speech hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
Because there is an absence of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*),
it is not a case of error (*bhrānti*);
for past and future things are manifested precisely as past and future.
Vijñapriyā:

[In the commentary on verse 6, ṅa: She raises the objection that this might be a type of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) distinct from the four kinds of *atiśayokti* mentioned, because it conveys an excellence of the heroine's form—stating "And not *atiśaya*..."—and then provides the resolution—stating "By means of *adhyavasāya* (identification/superimposition)."
The sense is this: all varieties of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) are constituted by *adhyavasāya* (identification).

Since that [identification] is absent here, it is improper to postulate another variety of it based merely on the cognition of its specific excellence (*rūpātiśaya*). He raises the suspicion that it might be a case of *bhrāntimat* (illusion) because it makes known a past or future form as being present—[to which he replies] "nor is it an illusion," and so forth.
He explains: "It is real" (*bhūta*).

The delusion here consists precisely in the error of identifying the subject at hand with something else; it is not that unreal or future objects are the subject at hand, such that there would be a delusion regarding their being past or future.
Rather, the meaning is that having taken past and future objects as the subject, their true nature is revealed in relation to those very objects.
This is because, in this case, only the two attributes of the eyes— their form and their nature as belonging to a heroine who possesses a particular beauty— are described.
Nor is this *svabhāvokti* (description of nature), for its essential character consists precisely in the accurate description of the subtle nature of a worldly object as it truly is.
However, this object possesses a particular strikingness (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) whose nature appears as if directly perceived (*pratyakṣāyamāṇa*).

Furthermore, if this strikingness can occur even when there is a description of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvokti*) of an object in some instances, then there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of both [figures of speech].
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ca) He raises the objection regarding *svabhāvokti* (description of nature) with the words "And not... (*na ca*). He provides the resolution with the words "Of that... (*tasyāḥ*).

A worldly object is such as a child or a tiger; the nature belonging to it consists of subtle properties (*sūkṣmadharma*). This nature takes the form of properties that exist only in that [object] and are not known by poets or ordinary people. Regarding that [nature], as it has been described there...
The meaning is "its own nature.

Regarding this, he says "nūtanatā" (novelty) and explains it with "asya tu" (but of this). The meaning is that, in comparison to that [previous case], there is here a distinct mode of presentation (*vilakṣaṇabhaṅgi*).
"But surely it was said: 'This boy is seen with speech whose syllables are not yet distinct;
and his smile, beautiful with the sprouts of emerging teeth, is already seen as something yet to be.'"

Having considered what figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) could apply here to an action such as that of a mere child, which is yet to come or has already passed, he provides the resolution with the words "If, however" (*yadi punar*).
*Saṃkara* (commixture) consists in the coexistence [of figures] in one place through their independence.
"Though he possesses no parasol here, he is seen on all sides as if surrounded by white parasols; alas!"
Though he possesses no yak-tail fan, he is always fanned by one; who can this extraordinary being be?
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, cha) Where neither past nor future entities appear as perceptible, but rather only that very entity itself is described as appearing perceptible, this is not this ornament (*alaṅkāra*); having stated this, he demonstrates it with the example: "Even though without a parasol," and so forth.
"Even though this king is without a parasol, he appears as if surrounded on all sides by white parasols in every direction;
he appears as if being fanned by a fan for the sake of luxury"— this is to be connected with what precedes—
because his limbs are cool."
In this case, since there is a description of that which is already appearing as if perceived, this is not an *alaṅkāra* (poetic figure),
because the very essence of this [figure] consists in the state of appearing as if perceived by virtue of the description itself.
However, where there is a state of appearing as if perceived even when describing that which is not appearing as if perceived, it is appropriate for this to be an *alaṅkāra*.
As in the cited example beginning with "āsīdañjanam" and so forth. *Vijñapriyā*: Regarding this [point]:
The meaning of "only for that which appears as if it were present" (pratyakṣāyamāṇasyaiva) is [the exclusion] of that which has already occurred and that which is currently being fanned by a breeze.
By the use of the particle *eva*, there is an exclusion of past and future things; the meaning is not that past and future objects themselves possess the quality of appearing as if they were present.
Having thus clarified the absence of such a state [of appearance] in this verse, he demonstrates it [with the words]: "by virtue of description" (varṇanāvaśena).
In this context, because it is the very nature [of the teaching],
that is, because it is the nature of the meaning of this verse; indeed,
the meaning is that past and future objects appear as if they were being perceived directly.
However, in the case of the figure *bhāvika*, there is also a further distinction due to the combination of past and future states; thus he says: "But where...
The meaning is that it culminates in the state of being as if directly perceived (*pratyakṣāyamāṇatva*).

But in the case of the phrase "even though without an umbrella," the superimposition (*āropa*) of being an umbrella and so forth due to a particular brilliance is indeed merely inference (*anumāna*); such is the distinction between them.
Thus, it should be understood that in this case, there is indeed the figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra* (contradiction).
The *udātta* (the exalted) is said to be the description of a pre-eminence surpassing the world;
or else, it occurs when the conduct of great beings serves as an accessory (*aṅga*) to the subject at hand. (VisSd 10.94)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, jha) He states that the ornament *udātta* is of two kinds—beginning with "In the world... (*loke*) and "Or else" (*yadvā*).
The meaning is: when the conduct of great beings (*mahat*) serves as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the subject at hand and enhances it.
The examples follow in order:
“In which [city], the moonstones of whose pavements surpassed the circles of clouds...”
“Through the falling of moonlight, the pleasure grove increases its growth with the waters flowing from the wounded [trees].”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ña) "Rendered inferior" means that in her city, the circle of clouds— that is, the mass of rain-clouds— was rendered inferior by those [palaces] through the falling of moonlight.
The pleasure grove accepts—that is, attains—growth through the waters of the moonstones (*candrakāntamaṇi*) that form the floors;
the meaning is that it flourishes by being watered.
The phrase beginning with "cast down" (*adhaḥkṛta*) is an epithet of the floor.

In some places, the reading is *maṇḍalāyām*. It should be understood that the "construction of the city" (*puryā adhaḥkaraṇam*) refers specifically to the construction of the paved floors (*kuṭṭimaiḥ*) below.
Therefore, this is a description of the king’s extraordinary prosperity, who possesses such paved floors.
“Being praised by the first Creator, whose lotus-throne is split from his navel,
that Puruṣa, having withdrawn these worlds through his yogic sleep appropriate for the end of the age, shall recline upon him.”
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ṭa) "Grown from the navel" means one who is sleepless due to yoga appropriate for the end of the eon.
At the end of the age, that Puruṣa Viṣṇu, whose yogic sleep is habitual, having withdrawn the worlds, reclines upon this ocean;
what kind of person is he? He is being praised by the Creator—the primordial Brahmā—just as he was at the beginning.
By what kind of Creator? By one seated upon a lotus grown from his navel—that is, situated upon an exceedingly radiant lotus located at his navel.
Here, there is the non-contraction of the seat of the sun of the eyes;
the sense is that due to the destruction of the world, even in the absence of the [physical] sun, the lotus of the eye-sun blossoms.
Here, the ocean is the subject of description (*prakṛta*), and its excellence consists in such an act of Brahmā being praised—namely, his deed in the form of Viṣṇu’s reclining upon it.
When rasa, bhāva, their semblances (tadābhāsa), and the subsidence of bhāva attain the status of being subordinate, then they become poetic ornaments (alaṅkāra). (VisSd 10.95)
"Rasavat, Preyas, Ūrjasvin, and Samāhita," in this order.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṭha): Now he states the figures of speech beginning with rasa, starting with "rasa and bhāva."
When rasa is subordinate, it is *rasavat*;
when bhāva is subordinate, it is *preyas*;
and when two ābhāsas are subordinate, it is *ojasvin*.
When it serves as an auxiliary to the appeasement of an emotion (*bhāva*), the sequence is "composed" (*samāhita*).
Its two semblances (*tad-ābhāsa*) are the semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*) and the semblance of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*).
Among these, the figure of speech *rasavat* arises from the connection with rasa, as for example:
“‘This is that [act] of drawing up the tongue’—and so forth.
Here, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*).
The same applies elsewhere as well.”
It is called *preyas* because it is exceedingly dear.
As in my own verse:
“Her eyes, with pupils wide and languidly half-closed, and her creeper-like arms slightly loosened from the embrace of my neck...”
Constantly recollecting her, whose cheeks are covered with droplets of perspiration, he finds no inner peace.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍa) He states the meaning of the word *preyaḥ*, which is derived from the word *priya* by adding the suffix *iyasun* in the sense of excellence:
"because of being exceedingly dear."
In this context, he illustrates the *preya* ornament when a state (*bhāva*) serves as a constituent of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) with the verse beginning "āmīlita" (eyes closed).
This is the speech of a lover in separation who, remembering the state following the climax of passion (*ratyuttarāvasthā*) of his beloved, reflects upon it:
"As I remain there, constantly and incessantly recollecting that beloved state of passion, my inner mind finds no peace."
She was one whose eyes had their pupils turned back due to languor, as if closing from the cessation of passion;
she was one whose creeper-like arms were slightly slackened in the embrace of my neck;
and she was one whose moon-like cheeks were covered with drops of perspiration.

In this context, the erotic sentiment of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra*) is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the emotion (*bhāva*) called remembrance (*smaraṇa*), and that [remembrance] is a subordinate element to the erotic sentiment of separation (*vipralambha*).
*Vijñapriyā*:

Regarding the phrase "herein" (*atrei*): although there is no *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) because remembrance (*smaraṇa*) is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) here, this was stated with the intention that even a subordinate expressed meaning can constitute an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
In reality, however, the word "remembrance" (*smaraṇa*) here refers to the anxiety (*cintā*) suggested by remembrance.
For it is untenable to state that remembrance is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of trust when it is merely denoted (*vācya*);

rather, it is only when it is suggested (*vyaṅgya*)—just as in the case of a subordinate element of another—that its status as an ornament (*alaṃkāratva*) is accepted by all theorists of poetics, beginning with the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
Thus, the meaning is that the erotic sentiment of union (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*) is a subordinate element of the thought [of trust].
Because the state of the time of enjoyment has been contemplated,
in this respect there is indeed the *rasavad* ornament. "And that" (saca) means:
The meaning is that this transitory emotion (vyabhicāribhāva) called "thought" (cintā) is a subordinate element (aṅga) of "love-in-separation" (vipralambha),
because separation is intensified by thought.
Here, the poetic figure (alaṃkāra) is *praryya* (the figure of suggestion).
*Ūrjas* means strength; when there is an engagement in what is improper, that [strength] is present here, hence it is *ūrjasvin*.
For example—*Vijñapriyā*:
(Vi, ṇa) Explaining the meaning of the term *ūrjasvin* and providing an illustration of it, he says: "*Ūrjaḥ* means strength.
He states that this [strength] exists even when there is no engagement in impropriety by saying: "*Anaucitye*...

By this, although such [strength] is absent when one engages with another's wife without force, the common etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of this technical term (*saṃjñā-śabda*) has been shown.

Here, he provides an example of forceful seizure (*balātkāra*) itself: "In the entire forest, having abandoned their own wives, the Pulindas take delight in the throngs of the women of your enemies. ("vane 'khila-kalā-saktāḥ parihṛtya nija-striyaḥ / tvad-vairi-vanitā-vṛnde pulindāḥ kurvate ratim" //)
Here, the semblance of the erotic (*śṛṅgārābhāsa*) serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the emotion (*rasa*) of love directed toward the king;
the same applies to the semblance of an emotional state (*bhāvābhāsa*).
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ta) In the forest, among the multitude of women belonging to your enemies, the Pulindas abandon their own wives and take pleasure [with them]. He states the reason for abandoning their own wives with the word "akhila" (all):
the meaning is that because these women possess knowledge of all the arts of love (*kāmakalā*), they are attached to them.
Regarding the word *atra* (here):

it means because of the excellence of the king through the humiliation of his enemies' wives, and because of the excellence of the state of being [the object] (*viṣayabhāva*) resulting from that very [humiliation]. Likewise, even in the case of the appearance of an emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*), as for example: "O Great King, what can we say of your majesty, which is difficult for others to attain?"
For your enemies praise you with their hands folded in supplication.

Thus, here, the manifestation of the emotion of love (rati-bhāva) directed toward the enemy through the praise of that enemy serves as a subordinate element (aṅga) to the emotion of love directed toward the king.
This is "Resolution" (samāhita), which is a form of avoidance.
For example:
“The pride of your enemies, manifested in the constant brandishing of their swords, in frowns, threats, and roars, was seen; yet upon seeing you, it vanished somewhere in an instant.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) "Parihāra" means the abandonment or relinquishing of a state that has just arisen, which culminates in its destruction.
"Avirala" means uninterrupted.
Arrogance (*mada*) is pride; its cause is their being seen in close proximity and so forth.
The meaning is that upon seeing you—when there is a vision of you—that arrogance vanished somewhere in an instant and was no longer perceived.
Here, the subsiding of the emotion called arrogance is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the emotion of love (*rati*) directed toward the king.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, da) Regarding the phrase "of that which is called pride" (*madākhyasya*): although, by the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) of the term "having reached its pacification," there is an absolute absence of pride, and thus [an absence] of its pacification;

Nevertheless, this was stated with the intention that even for a suggested sense (*lakṣyārtha*) that has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*), it may still function as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) within the category of "subordinate suggestion" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*).

In reality, however, the status of being the *rasavat* ornament belongs exclusively to that where the suggestion is not subordinate (*aparāṅgabhūtavyaṅgya*), as agreed upon by all theorists of poetics beginning with the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*; it does not belong to a subordinate suggested sense.
Thus, in this very verse, the poet’s intense emotion and its subsequent destruction due to the loss of his beloved are what is suggested.
This very same [figure] is to be understood here as the ornament of *samāhita* (the unified).
When there is a presentation of a state (*bhāva*), a transition (*saṃdhi*), or a mixture (*miśratva*), they are designated by those respective names. (VisSd 10.96)
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, dha) But since the emergence of emotion (*bhāvodaya*) and so forth are subordinate, they are merely figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) according to their own names; thus he says: "In the emergence of emotion" (*bhāvasya codaye*).
"In mixture" (*miśratve*) means in the state of emotional confusion (*bhāvaśabalatva*).

Because of the mixing—characterized by the simultaneous existence—of preceding states with succeeding states that are more powerful, there arise the poetic figures (*alaṅkāras*) named Bhāvodaya (the emergence of a state), Bhāvasandhi (the conjunction of states), and Bhāvaśabalatā (the commingling of states). The examples follow in order: “The enemies, together with their friends, have begun to drink wine;”
Having heard your name from somewhere, they have fallen into a miserable state.
In this instance, the arising of fear is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the emotion (*bhāva*) of love directed toward the king.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, na):
Therein, he provides an example of the arising of another subordinate element with the verse beginning "madhupāna... (at the drinking of wine).
Regarding this:

among the *kṣaṇas* first identified within the middle of the verse, the "arising" (*udaya*)—which refers to the excellence of the state of being the object of the king—is an auxiliary element (*aṅga*). [As in:
"Eager for the touch of the limbs of her lover from another birth..."
May Pārvatī, who is modest in the presence of her friend, protect us always.
Here, the *saṃdhi* (fusion) of longing and bashfulness is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the emotion (*bhāva*) of love directed toward the deity.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, pa) He illustrates the fusion of subordinate elements (*aparāṅgabhāvasaṃdhi*) with the verse beginning "janmāntarīṇa."
Regarding this: here, the status of longing (*autsukya*) and bashfulness (*lajjā*) as poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) has been illustrated.
"She was unable to endure her own asceticism, which flared up at that moment; yet she was a connoisseur of the confidential conversations of the Mountain’s Daughter."
Or may the Destroyer of Smara, simultaneously assailed by the removal of the disguise of the deceitful boy and by the absence of both haste and slackness, grant you joy.
Thus, in the example provided by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, there is the figure of speech *sandhi* (juxtaposition) between the two suggested emotions of agitation (*āvega*) and joy (*harṣa*).
“O you fickle one, move away! Who is this girl? What are you doing? Give me your hand! Alas, alas! This is a transgression; where are you going?”
"Thus, O Lord of the Earth,
the daughter of one who dwells in the forest and is your enemy speaks while gathering certain fruits and sprouts."

In this instance, the intermingling (*śabalatā*) of doubt, envy, fortitude, memory, fatigue, dejection, awakening, and eagerness serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the dominant emotion (*bhāva*) of love directed toward the king.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, pha):
He illustrates the state of being a subordinate element through intermingling (*aparāṅgabhāva-śabalatvam*) with the verse beginning "paśyet kaścit... (May someone see...).
O Lord of the Earth!
A certain woman, having drawn forth desire through some purpose while gathering fruits and tender shoots for the sake of devouring her enemy—who has retreated to the forest—speaks thus.
To the question "In what manner does she speak?", he says: "She might see," and so forth.
In this context, in the phrase "paśyody," the doubt is suggested (*vyaṅgya*);
in "cala capala re," there is steadfastness (*dhṛti*);
and in "kumārī," from the recollection of her being a maiden, there is the recollection of her duty (*kāryatva*).
"Whence this haste? is the consolation.
"A hand to hold" refers to the awakening that consists of the firm conviction: "This [body] is indeed not my own. "Where are you? means "Where are you going?"
In this case, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is the eagerness to turn back from that recollection.
Here, between the two—the dejection and the contradiction—there is no relationship of the sublated and the sublator.
In other cases, however, there is a variegation (*śabalatā*) due to the greater strength of each subsequent element in its capacity to sublate each preceding one.
[The *bhāva*] is a limb (*aṅga*) of the state of passion for the king's domain; because the king is the subject under discussion, it is thus [the case] only for his enemies' daughters.

Here, some say: "Ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) are indeed those that assist *rasa* and so forth by means of the forms of the expressed (*vācya*) and the expressive (*vācaka*); however, since *rasa* and so forth are only assisted by the expressed and the expressive, it is not proper for them to possess the status of being ornaments."

Others, however, maintain: "In this context, the designation of 'ornament' (*alaṅkāra*) based merely on the assistance rendered to rasa and so forth must be accepted as figurative (*bhākta*), in accordance with long-standing tradition. [This refers to the view that] it consists of the expressed (*vācya*) and the expressive (*vācaka*). *Vijñapriyā*: (vi, ba) "In the form of the expressed and the expressive."
The nature of the expressed and the expresser consists of the meaning and the word-form; their adornment is that which makes them beautiful, such as simile, alliteration, and so forth.
"By means of that" means by way of that [primary element].
"But rasa and so forth" means rasa and so forth that have not become subordinate members (aṅga).
He states the view of others who accept that even subordinate elements such as rasa and so forth can function as ornaments (alaṅkāra): "But others...
There is no fixed rule that [an element becomes an ornament] by way of enhancing the beauty of the expressed meaning (vācya) or the expressive word (vācaka);
rather, the sole determinant of such status is its capacity to assist the primary rasa.

However, by virtue of their being designated as "meaning-ornament" (*artha-alaṃkāra*) and "word-ornament" (*śabda-alaṃkāra*), the term "ornament" (*alaṃkāra*) is directly denotative (*śakta*) only with respect to those two [types of figures] due to conventional usage.
But in other subordinate elements such as *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) and so forth, the term "ornament" is figurative (*bhākta*); that is to say, it is metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*).

And others [say]: “The status of being an *alaṅkāra* (ornament) arises merely through the assistance provided by rasa and so forth; however, in primary cases such as *rūpaka* (metaphor), it is based on the superimposition of the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and so forth, according to the maxim of ‘the breast of a goat’ (*ajagala-stana-nyāya*).
— *Vijñapriyā*.

Regarding those who maintain that the term "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) applies even to subordinate elements such as *rasa* and so forth by virtue of its primary power alone and not figuratively, the author states their view with the words "And others...

By the phrase "merely by way of assisting *rasa* and the like," it is asserted that subordinate elements such as *rasa*—just like similes (*upamā*) and other figures—are ornaments primarily and in their own right, rather than being the referents of the term "ornament" in a figurative sense.
Thus, the meaning is that the term "ornament" is powerful (denotative) in both cases.

Now, one might ask: "If everything is indeed denotable by the term 'ornament' (alaṅkāra), why is the conventional usage of 'ornament' restricted only to metaphor (rūpaka) and the like? To this he replies: "In metaphor and the like. The meaning is that the superimposition of the denoted [meaning] and so forth—the perception of denotability—is as purposeless as a newborn infant's sucking at its mother's breast. However, the learned authorities maintain: "The designation 'ornament' applies to those [elements such as rasa] which, being subordinate members assisted by their own manifesting denoted meanings and denoters, benefit the principal element (the *aṅgin*)—such as *rasa*—by way of embellishing the denoted and the denoter."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ma) "But those who are proficient [say]..."—
even according to this view, both are indeed denotable by the term *alaṃkāra* (ornament).
However, in the former view, the state of being a medium for the assistance of rasa and so forth must be required there;

whereas in this view, as in the case of simile (*upamā*) and the like, even rasa and other elements that serve as subordinate members (*aṅga*) are designated by the term "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) precisely because they assist rasa through the medium of assisting both word and meaning. Thus he says: "by means of their own manifestors," and so on.

The meaning is as follows: the expressed (vācya) and the expressive (vācaka), which are the suggestors (*vyañjaka*) of the rasa and other elements that constitute their own subordinate parts (*aṅga*),—by assisting those subordinate rasas and so forth through the mediation of the embellishment of the expressed and the expressive, and thereby indirectly benefiting the principal element (*aṅgin*), namely the rasa—they obtain the designation of "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*). The assistance rendered by the words and meanings to the subordinate rasas and so forth occurs solely through the power of suggestion (*vyañjanā*); conversely, the assistance rendered by them [the subordinate rasas] to the words and meanings occurs by virtue of being distinguished by that which is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). Thus, a mutual assistance is demonstrated.

However, they maintain that in *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation), only the metaphorical behavior (*vyavahāra*) of the heroine and so forth constitutes the ornament (*alaṅkāra*), and not the aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), because the latter lacks the aforementioned method [of suggestion].
For this very reason, the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* stated:

"In the case of *samāsokti*, the conduct of the hero and heroine which is suggested possesses the status of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) independently of its assistance to rasa and the like. This is what he expresses with the words "in *samāsokti*. (Vijñapriyā, vi, ya)
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should be understood that such a nature exists even in *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
"For this very reason" means: precisely because even rasa and the like, when functioning as subordinate elements (*aṅga*), are denotable by the term "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*).
“Where rasa and the like are subordinate to another sentence-meaning as the primary element,
in that poem, my view is that rasa and the like constitute an ornament.”
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ra) "In the primary" means that in a poem where the primary element is the dominant factor (*aṅgin*), elsewhere—namely, in forms such as rasa and so forth—the rasas and so on are subordinate members (*aṅga*). This is the meaning.
The singular number is used because it relies on the unity of being subordinate parts (*aṅga*).
The meaning is that my view is that in this poetry, *rasa* and the like constitute the "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*), which is denoted by the term *alaṅkāra*.

Furthermore, if the status of being an ornament were based merely on providing assistance to *rasa* and the like, then the same would undesirably follow for the expressive words (*vācaka*) and so forth as well.

And thus, that which has been stated by some—"When rasa and the like are the primary element (aṅgin), there is the alaṅkāra called Rasavat and so forth; but when they are subordinate (aṅga), there is the second alaṅkāra, Udātta"—that too is refuted.
Vijñapriyā:

(Vi, la) [Objection: Surely, ornaments such as bracelets and earrings are so called only because they enhance the beauty of the body; therefore, by the logic already stated, let things like the subordinate sentiment (*aṅgarasa*) or metaphors (*upamā*) be considered ornaments. However, since *samāsokti* lacks the quality of enhancing the subordinate sentiment and so forth, it cannot be an ornament. To this, he replies with the words "yadi" (if).

In some cases, [the figure] constitutes an ornament by its own inherent charm (*vaicitrya*) even when it serves to enhance the principal figure (*aṅgin*) in a *samāsokti*; its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), however, is not the enhancement of the principal figure.
The meaning is that if it were defined in such a way, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

However, some maintain that the quality of being a *rasavat* ornament belongs only to the *aṅgirasa* [type], whereas for a rasa and so forth that has become a subordinate element (*aṅga*), they assert it is simply the second type of *udātta* ornament, as stated in the verse: "That which is suggested, being a subordinate part of the subject matter, shall be the conduct of great men.
Thus, he says that because our demonstrated example is not covered by that [definition], those [opponents] are refuted, in accordance with the consensus of the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*.

In the phrase "the girl whose pupils were half-closed, languid, and rolling," the emotion (bhāva) called remembrance (smaraṇa) is stated as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the erotic-in-separation (*vipralambha*); however, because it does not constitute the life-story of any great personage, the definition of the figure *udātta* (the noble) does not apply there.
This would be the case even if these very figures were mutually mixed.
Then there are the separate figures of speech (alaṅkāra), as well as combination (saṃsṛṣṭi) and commixture (saṅkara).
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, va) Now, he states that when multiple ornaments exist in a single word through their blending, there arises a distinct ornament called *saṃsṛṣṭi* in some cases, and in others, one called *saṅkara*: "If these very [ornaments]...
meaning that even though they are distinct ornaments...

Therefore, it should be understood that there is no exclusion of the fundamental figures of speech; likewise, even when a conflation (*saṅkara*) is possible— such as when it is stated that a *samāsokti* contains various figures within it due to its being pregnant with a simile (*aupamya*), or when it is stated elsewhere that a figure gains greater beauty when it is evoked by another figure— the status of that figure as *samāsokti* or the like is not contradicted.

Just as even among worldly ornaments, when they are mixed together, they possess a distinct beauty and thus constitute separate ornaments, so too, when the aforementioned poetic ornaments are mixed with one another, there are two distinct ornaments called *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction) and *saṃkara* (commixture).
Among these—
"The coexistence of these [three] without mutual dependence is called *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction).
Of these— namely, word-ornaments (*śabdālaṅkāra*), meaning-ornaments (*arthālaṅkāra*), and [the figures of speech]— for example:"
“May the Lord protect us from the lower realms— he whose eyes are like smiling blue lotuses, the swan that destroys the darkness of saṃsāra, the slayer of Kaṃsa.”

Here, there is the figure of speech *yamaka* (rhyme) in "pāyāt apāyāt," and *anuprāsa* (alliteration) in "saṃsāra" and so forth; thus, there is a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of two verbal figures of speech.
In the second quarter-verse, there is a simile (*upamā*).
And since there is a metaphor (*rūpaka*) in the second half [of the verse], there is a commingling (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of two semantic ornaments (*arthālaṅkāra*).
Thus, because both are present, there is a commingling of a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*) and a semantic ornament (*arthālaṅkāra*).
— *Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, śa) Therein, he states the definition of *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling): "of these, without mutual dependence.
The meaning of "May the God protect," and so forth, is clear.
*Haṃsa* refers to the Sun.
Here, he first demonstrates the coexistence (saṃsṛṣṭi) of two verbal figures: "In this [verse], 'pāyāt'...
and "In 'saṃsāra-' etc., there is alliteration (anuprāsa).
This means that in the phrase "dhvāntavidhvaṃsahaṃsa," there is alliteration.
Right here, he speaks of the commingling (saṃsṛṣṭi) of two figures of sense (arthālaṅkāra) as well—namely, "in the second quarter" and "in the second half.
In the first half, there is a simile (upamā) of a smiling blue lotus;
in the second half... [the same].
The meaning is that this is a "successive metaphor" (paramparitarūpaka): the slayer of Kaṃsa is the form of the sun, and the world, which accomplishes that [slaying], is the form of darkness.
And thus he says, "of both," indicating that there are two types of "conjunction" (saṃsṛṣṭi).

And "conjunction" (*saṃsṛṣṭi*). Because the word "and" (*ca*) is present, the syntactical connection is "and thus. He states that there is a mutual conjunction of even those two types of conjunction with the words "and in this way."

Furthermore, there are three types of *saṅkara* (commixture): when figures of speech stand in the relation of principal and subordinate; when they reside in a single substratum; and when they are characterized by doubt. (VisSd 10.98)
Vijñapriyā:

(VI, 6) He states that confusion (*saṅkara*) is also threefold—namely, "in the relationship of primary and subordinate" (*aṅgāṅgitve*), meaning such [confusion] occurs when figures of speech stand in a relationship of primary and subordinate;
he states another kind—"likewise" (*tadvat*), meaning when figures of speech reside in a single locus or within a single sentence.
He states another variety: "and when there is doubt" (*saṃdigdhatve ca*).
This means when there is a doubt regarding two figures of speech, resulting in two alternative possibilities (*koṭidvaya*).
An example of the relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is as follows:
Vijñapriyā:

Regarding the phrase "the relationship of part and whole (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is as follows": although the relationship of part and whole is threefold—namely, the relationship of produced and producer (*janyajanakabhāva*), the relationship of the qualified and the qualifier (*prakṛṣyaprakarṣakabhāva*), and the relationship of the indicated and the indicator (*jñāpyajñāpakabhāva*)—nevertheless, he provides an illustration specifically of the form of the relationship between the indicated and the indicator.

“The Mandākinī long encircled the base of his feet, as if to quickly soothe the pain of churning the ocean that was wrapped in the sloughing skins of the lord of serpents whose coils were loosened by the force of her being drawn forth.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ha) "With its speed drawn forth"—this is a description of Mount Mandara.
At the very base of that Mount Mandara, in the form of its lower part, the Mandākinī river moved at the edge of the foot's root; the meaning is that she performed service-like activity.
Regarding the question "for what purpose?", he reflects: "as if for the sake of allaying the pain caused by churning in the ocean.
The meaning is: "for the sake of the swift and immediate cessation of the pain produced by the churning of my husband, the ocean"—that is, as if for that very purpose.
It is a prayer of the form: "The pain of churning previously generated by that very [churning] shall quickly perish once the churning has ceased."
Now, one might ask: "Did the Mandākinī not already exist at the foot of Mount Mandara even before the churning?
By what kind of activity does she now serve him? To this, he says: "With her speed drawn forth" (*ākṛṣṭavega*).

Because of the suffix *ktavat* (indicating a past passive participle), it means: from the body of Vāsuki, the lord of serpents, who had become the rope, as it was slipping away due to the force of being pulled.
The meaning is: by way of wrapping a cloth of that form—a "nirmoka" or leather jacket (carma-kañcuka) from the body—in the manner of unwrapping it.
This is not a wrapping with a leather jacket;
rather, the meaning is that Mandākinī herself has completely encircled the base of his feet like a footstool.
Here, by the concealment of the snake-skin (*nirmokapaṭṭa*), there is the superimposition (*āropa*) of the Mandākinī; thus, this is *apahnuti* (concealment).

And since that [concealment]—by means of the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*)—gives rise to a pun (*śleṣa*) in which "the wrapping around the base of the serpent" is [identified with] "the wrapping around the base of the foot," it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that [pun].
Furthermore, the pun—that "the wrapping around the base of the serpent" is indeed "the wrapping around the base of the foot"—is an auxiliary to the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
Furthermore, the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) "as if for the sake of allaying the pain of churning" is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*);
and since that poetic fancy leads one to perceive the behavior of a hero and a heroine between the ocean and the Mandākinī, it is a subordinate element of the implied metaphor (*samāsokti*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ka) Therein, he first demonstrates *apahnuti* (concealment) with the words "nirmoka...
and "sā ca...".
That [is] *apahnuti*; by the actual state of things—that is, by the essential nature of the object that is the Ganges.
In reality, however, the meaning is that because its nature is to envelop,
it brings about *śleṣa*;
that is, it makes *śleṣa* known.
The meaning is that, in the absence of the superimposition (*āropa*) of the Gaṅgā upon the snake's slough, there would be no perception of the connection (*śleṣa*) intended for the feet.

And he states that this *śleṣa* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*)—namely, "and the *śleṣa*"—by demonstrating the hyperbole: "the act of encircling the base of the foot is itself service. This is a hyperbole consisting of the attribution of non-difference where there is actually difference.

But it is not a metaphor (*rūpaka*), because the act of service—the substratum of the metaphor—is not explicitly stated; rather, service is understood solely through the connection with the word *pāda* (foot) in the sense of "service" (*caraṇa*).
The meaning is that the pun (*śleṣa*) is the indicator of that [metaphor].
He states, "the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) also," because it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the expressed poetic fancy (*vācyotprekṣā*).

This, however, is an *aṅga* of excellence (*prakarṣaka*), because the mere act of wrapping cannot serve to alleviate the pain of churning without the knowledge of how to serve; thus, there is an excellence of that [wrapping] through such a supposition (*utprekṣā*).
It is not, however, an *aṅga* of indication (*jñāpaka*), since that [supposition] is understood from the word "as if" (*iva*) itself.

Nor is the knowledge of service a productive factor (*janaka*) of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), because it does not produce that which consists of a doubt with an intense alternative (*utkaṭakoṭi-saṃśaya*).
He states that "the knowledge of the poetic fancy" is also a supporting factor (*jñāpaka-aṅga*) for the *samāsokti* (speech of compendium), saying: "And the poetic fancy...

For, without the poetic fancy consisting in the purpose of allaying the agitation of churning, the knowledge of the behavior of the hero and heroine in the ocean and the Gaṅgā would be impossible, as they are insentient.
Or as it is said:
"The twilight is full of passion, and the day is its forerunner;
oh! how strange is the course of fate, that even so, there is no union."
In this instance, [the figure] *samāsokti* is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of *viśeṣokti*.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, kha):

Having explained the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) among multiple figures of speech, he states that the same applies between two figures, beginning with "or as... (*yathā vā*).
This is a description of the evening twilight (*sāyaṃsandhyā*). Following the day, the twilight is possessed of color— that is, it is red— and the day is its precursor, existing before it.
Oh, what a marvel! Strange and extraordinary is the course of destiny, since even so there has been no meeting;
for a meeting in the form of a single convergence is only seen when two things situated one before and one behind come together at once.
However, there is never a meeting of the day and the twilight,
because at the time of twilight, the day does not exist;
here, therefore, there is a *samāsokti* (poetic suggestion by ellipsis).
Here, there is *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) consisting in the cognition of the story of a hero and a heroine who, like [the two in] Rāgava, are deprived of union by fate.

The meaning is that although the cause of union—existing in the form of a prior and subsequent state—is present, there is an *viśeṣokti* (statement of distinction) consisting in the absence of the result, which is the union itself; thus it serves as a "reason for making known" (*jñāpaka-hetu*).
This is because the cognition of the absence of union between the hero and heroine is impossible without the cognition of the [hero's] story.
An illustration of the *janaka-rūpa-aṅga* (the constituent cause) has not been shown;
it is as follows: "Those Pulinda hunters do not take away the necklace from the wives of our enemies in the forest;
for they mistake that [necklace], red with the luster of their bimba-like lips, for a garland of *guñjā* berries."
“In this case, because the beauty of the lips, which resemble the *bimba* fruit, is captured by the necklace, there is the figure of speech *tadguṇa* (the quality of another).

And because that [figure] generates the illusion of it being a necklace of *guñjā* berries, there is the figure *bhrāntimān* (illusion); thus, *bhrāntimān* is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) that heightens the excellence of *tadguṇa*.
An example of the blending (*saṅkara*) of doubt (*sandeha*) is as follows:”
“This lunar orb shines in the sky, piercing the continuous darkness and bringing delight to the eyes of beautiful women.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ga) He states the doubt and confusion regarding many ornaments with the words "this appears":
"this lunar orb appears in the sky."
What kind [of face] is it? It pierces the dense, pervasive darkness and the blinding gloom of ignorance, while bestowing intense joy upon the eyes.

In this regard, is there a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) based on the identification of the face with the moon, or is it a metaphor (*rūpaka*) consisting in the superimposition of moonhood upon the face pointed out by the word "this"?
Alternatively, is this *tulyayogitā* (parallelism), because the two subjects—the face and the lunar orb—are connected by a single common attribute;

or rather, is it *dīpaka* (illumination), since the moon is not the subject under discussion; or perhaps it is *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation), because the unstated subject, the face, is understood through the similarity of its qualifiers?

Alternatively, since the face, which is the subject at hand, is understood through the description of the moon, which is not the subject at hand, there is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise); or, since the time that inflames the god of love is described by way of the description of the moon, which is its own effect, there is *paryāyokta* (periphrasis). Thus, due to the doubt regarding these many figures of speech, there is a *saṃdehasaṅkara* (blend based on doubt).
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, gha) Here, he demonstrates that these [figures] fall within the scope of doubt—“here” being the point. The meaning is that this lunar orb in the sky appears, by implication, upon the face of the heroine.
Thus, because the locus of the superimposition—the face—is not explicitly mentioned, it is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole);
however, he states that if the face were mentioned by its own word, it would be *rūpaka* (metaphor), using the words “but” (*uta*) and so forth.
He demonstrates *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing) with the word "or" (*athavā*).
Thus, the meaning is that this face being described and the lunar orb in the sky both shine.
[This applies] to both of them, which are the subjects under discussion (*prakṛta*).
Even when describing the shining of both [the moon and the face], the meaning is that there is a sequential occurrence.

However, since the face alone was introduced as the subject at hand, while the moon is mentioned specifically as its point of comparison, the moon is not the subject at hand; therefore, the meaning is that this is *dīpaka* (illumination), which consists of the connection of a single attribute to both the subject at hand and that which is not.
He demonstrates *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) with the words "But what... (*kiṃtu*).
Since the description of the moon alone was the subject at hand, he says "or else" (*yadvā*) to indicate that this is an instance of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
He explains it as "being the effect" (*kāryabhūtā*),
because the rising of the moon is the effect of the time of twilight.

Or, for example, in the case of "I see the moon-face," there arises a doubt: is this a simile (*upamā*) where the face is like the moon, or is it a metaphor (*rūpaka*) where the face is actually the moon?
Such doubt ceases, however, when either a supporting factor (*sādhaka*) or a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) is present.
For example,
in the expression "he kisses the moon-like face," the act of kissing is favorable to the face and thus supports the simile (upamā),
whereas it is unfavorable to the [actual] moon and thus subverts the metaphor (rūpaka).

In the expression “the moon-face shines,” the property called *prakāśa* (shining), which establishes the metaphor (*rūpaka*), is possible because it is figuratively attributed (*upacarita*) to the face; thus, it does not sublate the simile (*upamā*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi ṅa) He shows the doubt regarding two ornaments with the words "or as follows" (*yathā vā*).
The phrase "kissing the moon of the face" means that it is directly connected to a face that is similar to the moon and favorable to the face;
however, it does not refer to a moon consisting of the face itself, because kissing for the purpose of sexual enjoyment is impossible in the case of [an actual] moon.
Conversely, it would be unfavorable to the [actual] moon.
Because kissing, which resides in the mouth, is perceived as non-different from the mouth itself, it is impossible for it to exist in the moon [reflected] therein; thus,
it is called "the manifestation" (*prakāśa*),
meaning it is known by the name of its substratum (*tibhi*).

The meaning is that since that property (dharma) exists directly in the moon alone, it serves as a proof for the metaphor (rūpaka) because it is directly connected to the moon, which is perceived as the substantive (viśeṣya).
However, it does not subvert the simile (upamā); therefore, he says: "because [the property] is applied figuratively to the face.
This means that even when the face is similar to the moon, the superimposition (āropa) of the moon's properties is possible.
“O King-Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī embraces you intensely.

Here, the embrace by a woman is not appropriate for a hero (nāyaka) in a state of similarity; thus, because the embrace by Lakṣmī is impossible in the case of the king, it subverts the simile (upamā), whereas it is possible in the case of Nārāyaṇa, so it constitutes a metaphor (rūpaka).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ca) He states the proof for [the word] *rūpaka*: "He is a king-Nārāyaṇa.
Here, Lakṣmī is the wife of Nārāyaṇa, but not his prosperity (*sampat*).
Therefore, he says: "the woman" (*yoṣita*).

And because of its occurrence in relation to Nārāyaṇa, it is a metaphor (*rūpaka*). In a metaphor, since Nārāyaṇa alone is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), the connection with the embrace occurs in that very [subject].
Thus:
"The lotus-face of the deer-eyed one shines with its flickering eyes.
Here, because the presence of eyes on the face is possible, it serves as a means for establishing the simile (upamā).
The impossibility [of the object] in the case of a lotus constitutes a sublation of the metaphor (*rūpaka*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, cha) states that this is a proof for the simile (*upamā*), saying: "the lotus-face" (*vadanāmbuja*).

He explains that [the compound] "cañcalalocanam" (with tremulous eyes) is a proof for the simile (*upamā*) because, through the analysis (*vigraha*) "that in which the eye is tremulous," the possession of tremulous eyes is possible only in the face, which is comparable to a lotus—stating "herein.

Likewise, in cases such as "the beautiful lotus-face" (*sundaraṃ vadanāmbujam*), when a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is employed, a compound of comparison (*upamitasamāsa*) is not possible according to the rule "that which is compared with tigers and the like [forms a compound] when the common attribute is not expressed"; thus, this [expression of the common attribute] is a sublater (*bādhaka*) of the simile.
And thus, in this case, it is simply a *rūpaka* compound by virtue of its inclusion in the group beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*.

Regarding the word "thus" (*evam*), the *Vijñapriyā* explains: even according to this grammatical rule, where the *upamā* compound is prohibited, [the author] says "thus" because there is still a sense of comparison.

In examples such as "the beautiful lotus-face," the construction of a compound based on simile (*upamāsamāsa*) is not possible when a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is explicitly employed; thus, the connection here is that this serves as an obstacle to the simile. That attribute is "beauty" (*sundaratva*), and he shows the grammatical rule of Pāṇini which establishes its status as an obstacle to the simile: "upamitam... (Pāṇini 2.1.56).
By this rule of Pāṇini, the compound of comparison (upamā-samāsa) such as *puruṣavyāghra* ("man-tiger") occurs only when the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is not explicitly employed.
Thus, because of this teaching, that compound is prohibited precisely when the common property is employed.

From the statement "here indeed" (*atra hi*), it follows that in the usage *sundaraṃ vadanāmbujam* ("the beautiful lotus-face"), since it would constitute a compound of comparison, [the rule] does not apply; therefore, the meaning is that the cognition of the comparison arises only when the common property in the form of "beauty" (*sundaratva*) is not employed.

Now, [one might object]: "In cases such as 'The man is a *mayūra-vyaṃsaka* (a swindler like a peacock),' because the quality of being a swindler (*vyaṃsakatva*) and so forth exists in the referent, the rule for *mayūra-vyaṃsaka* compounds applies only where the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is mentioned first; however, it does not apply when the standard of comparison is mentioned last. This is the meaning.
An example of simultaneous entry into a single substratum (*ekāśrayānupraveśa*) is as follows, from my own work:

“If she were to look at me even for a moment with but a sidelong glance, then a dense bliss would flash forth, obscuring all other objects of sense; what then would the commencement of an embrace be like for that lotus-eyed one, when her silken garment is torn away by her jar-like breasts rising with horripilation?”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, jha) He describes the commingling (*saṅkara*) of ornaments consisting of figures residing in a single substratum with the words "with a sidelong glance" (*kaṭākṣeṇa*).
And that single substratum is, in some cases, a single sentence and in others, a single word.

Nor should it be said that when two words reside in a single sentence there is necessarily *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction), because this is not the case when they stand in a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).
Nor should it be said that in such a case there is a confusion (*saṅkara*) of the categories of *aṅgāṅgibhāva*.
Even then, because there is no departure from entering into a single substratum;

"with a sidelong glance" means that if that heroine were to look at me for even a moment— that is, for a very brief duration— then a dense bliss, in which all other objects are concealed, would manifest.
Then, what kind of embrace could there possibly be for that lotus-eyed woman?
The meaning is: "I have already achieved my purpose through her very glance; therefore, I shall not neglect the embrace.
Or rather: "What kind of embrace could there possibly be that exceeds the casting of a sidelong glance?"
The meaning is that it will indeed be indescribable.
Of what nature is the commencement of the embrace?
It is such that the garment is pierced through and slipped away by her two jar-like breasts, which are covered in horripilation and are therefore rising upward.

Here, in the phrase "even with a sidelong glance for even a moment," there is a convergence (*anupraveśa*) of alliteration (*che kānuprāsa*)—taking the letter *kṣa* from the word "nirīkṣeta"—and of rhythmic alliteration (*vṛttyanuprāsa*) within a single locus. Thus, in this very instance, there is a convergence of alliteration and the figure of speech based on implication (*arthāpatti*). Vijñapriyā: In this passage, regarding the phrase "even with a sidelong glance for even a moment" (*kaṭākṣeṇāpīṣatkṣaṇamapi*), there is a convergence of chekānuprāsa (alliteration of distinct consonants) and vṛttyanuprāsa (rhythmic alliteration), both taking the letter *kṣa* from the word "nirīkṣeta" as their common locus. In this same way, there is a convergence here between alliteration and the poetic figure of arthāpatti (presumption).
