(vi, ña) Here, he demonstrates the existence of two kinds of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) based on a single locus in the form of a sentence: "In this [verse]," *chekānuprāsa* occurs when there is a similarity in the intrinsic nature (*svarūpataḥ*) of multiple consonants, because that is what is defined as *chekānuprāsa*; however, since a sequence of conjunct consonants is impossible, the meaning is that *chekānuprāsa* occurs once for each such individual *kṣa*-sound.
He states that when such [sounds] possess multiple phonemic forms through association with other *kṣa*-sounds, it is *vṛttyanuprāsa*, as in the phrase "nirīkṣeta" and so forth.
Since it has already been stated that alliteration (*vṛttyanuprāsa*) does not occur when multiple [sounds] appear more than once,

"entry into a single substratum" means entry into a single sentence. Thus, because the alliteration of *che* (the *chekānuprāsa*) composed of two instances of the letter *kṣa* generates alliteration through its association with another instance of the letter *kṣa*, there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) in the relationship of subordinate and principal.

Since this [type of combination] also exists here, he provides an unambiguous example by resorting to a single compound word—namely, *āpātatastatraiva*. He demonstrates the co-inherence (*ekāśrayānupraveśa*) of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the poetic figure of presumption (*arthāpatti*) in that very same instance with the words "and thus, right here. The meaning is as follows:

because even a mere glance from her side causes such intense trembling, the embrace of her breasts is established by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*); thus, there is the poetic figure of presumption (*arthāpatti*), consisting in the resulting indescribable bliss.
Or, for example, in the verse beginning "The destroyer of the darkness of saṃsāra," there is a combination of metaphor (*rūpaka*) and alliteration (*anuprāsa*).

Or, for example, in the phrase "They became the cause of *kurabaka* and *aravaka* flowers," there is a combination of two types of rhyme (*yamaka*), namely: *rabakā ravakā* as one instance, and *bakāravakāra* as another.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṭa) In the compound within a single word, [the author] speaks of the commingling (*saṅkara*) through mutual entry into a single substratum (*ekāśrayānupraveśa*), which is devoid of the commingling of the relationship between part and whole (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*); as in the phrase "or as," namely, "of the metaphor (*rūpaka*) and the alliteration (*anuprāsa*)."
From the verse beginning with "kurubakā" [and] "kaṃsaniṣūdane sūryatāropaṇāt":
here, there are two instances of *yamaka* (rhyme) contained within a single sentence.
Nor should it be argued that there is a confusion of the "supported" and the "supporting" here because the subsequent *yamaka* is carried out by means of the preceding *yamaka*;
for the subsequent *yamaka*, extending up to the letter *ra* in the word *kāraṇatām*, is itself carried out by the preceding *yamaka*.
The same applies to the phrase: “*kalakalolakaloladṛśe*.”
In this case as well, there are two *yamakas*: "lakalo lakalo kalola kalola.
Or, for example:
"On days when the new moon has risen and the travelers have departed..."
The peacock flocks are dancing to songs that have crept forth in secret.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṭha) She demonstrates the entry of both simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*) into a single substratum with the verse beginning "abhinava": "On those days which were fond of fresh clouds, like an audience of travelers..."
A great expanse where flocks of peacocks perform songs and dances with outstretched tails.

"Thus [is] the refined [Sanskrit]. Where the song is extended, such a dancing of flocks of peacocks—meaning that which is endowed with the characteristics of dance—is greatly honored and shines on those days; this is the sense. The verbal root *maha* means 'to honor'."

He states the specific qualification of the day suitable for dancing with the word "abhinava" (fresh/new): "in those [days] where the fresh clouds themselves are *rasika*—that is, full of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—for the sake of witnessing the dance;
and likewise, in those [days] where travelers are like members of an audience (*sāmājika*), as if they were the primary members of a gathering eager to behold the dance and so forth."

In this context, it should be noted that there is a suggested metaphor (rūpaka) of the days as the very existence of the dance, serving as the locus for both the aesthetic connoisseurs (*rasika-sāmājika*) and those who witness the performance and are like the leaders of society.

Here, in the phrase "among the traveler-connoisseurs" (*pahiasāmāiesu*), the metaphor of "traveler-connoisseurs" (*pathika-sāmājika*) enters into the simile (*upamā*) of "the traveler's darkness" (*pathika-śyāmāyita*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍa) Here, he demonstrates the entry of simile and metaphor into a single substratum—by the word "here.
The meaning is that the phrase "wherein [the sky] has become dark like a traveler" constitutes a simile.
In the phrase "among the travelers and the spectators," he demonstrates the suggested metaphor (*vyaṅgyarūpaka*) on these very days:
"those in whom there are travelers who are spectators. The meaning is: those [days] in whom the spectators themselves are the travelers.
"Entered"—this means it takes the form of the existence of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).

This work, the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, composed by the illustrious Viśvanātha Kavirāja, son of the great poet-moon Śrī Candraśekhara—let the wise, having examined it, easily understand the entirety of the principles of literary aesthetics (*sāhityatattva*). (VisSd 10.99)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍha) "O Śrīcandra"—
here, "O dull-witted one" is the form of address.
In some places, the reading is "kāvye. O wise ones,

having examined this *Sāhityadarpaṇa* composed by Śrī Candrāloka and others, know— meaning understand— the entire essence of literary aesthetics (*sāhityatattva*) with ease, that is, in a manner characterized by great facility.
Locanā: (lo, ū) "Śrīcandraśekhara"—
in this [name], the word *candra* has the sense of "excellent" (*śreṣṭha*) in the compound *mahākavicandra*.
The king of poets named Viśvanātha, whose praise the wise proclaim as follows:

“O Earth, why do you tremble? Or rather, bear the burden! For by Drobinda—who has taken the incarnation of sporting in the temple of Nanda—Śrī Viśvanātha, the virtuous author renowned as the ‘King of the Kings of Poets,’ has now caused the heads of the Lord of Serpents to shake upon hearing his words.”
The connection [of the verse] is: "having observed the work named Sāhityadarpaṇa composed by him.
May this composition, which delights the minds of poets, become celebrated in the world for as long as Śrī, whose face resembles the bright moon, adorns the body of Nārāyaṇa. VisSd_10.100 //
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṇa) "As long as" means:
as long as Śrī, whose face resembles the bright moon, adorns the body of Nārāyaṇa.
The meaning is: "May this composition remain celebrated in the world, gladdening the minds of poets for as long as [the sun and moon endure].
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) Now, at the conclusion of the book, he offers an auspicious benediction according to his own desire, beginning with the word "yāvat" (as long as).

May this elaborate exposition of the words of the *Sāhityadarpaṇaviveka*— which has attained the grace of the lotus-feet of my father, the wise one who performed infinite deeds— delight and perfectly please [you] until the moon and the sun, as it is worshipped by the assembly of the learned.

Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa* composed by the sovereign of rhetoricians, the Great Chamberlain (*Mahāpātra*), the Minister of Peace and War (*Sāndhivigrahika*), the illustrious Viśvanātha Kavirāja.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"Thus," and so forth.

The entirety of speech is the playful heroine (nāyikā), and the serpent (bhujaṅga) is her lover because he pursues her. Thus ends the explanation of the tenth chapter in the commentary on the *Sāhityadarpaṇa* composed by Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra. By virtue of its well-knit Sanskrit composition, this commentary is easy to ascend; it is skilled in distinguishing the various waves that are difficult to cross due to their irregularity.
To cross the great ocean of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, this commentary exists as a boat—O wise ones, do not fear! (1)
It is no wonder that objects are reflected in a mirror;
it is truly marvelous that my own commentary has become a mirror in which they are reflected. // 2 //
O wise ones, let this commentary, which brings delight through careful attention, not be disregarded; for the flavors of astringent betel are indeed savored gradually.
